skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: Excludes terms specific to MARINE CONSTRUCTION SITE.
A dock or basin, often inland, used for mooring yachts and other small pleasure craft.
A large park for keeping deer. In medieval times the prime purpose was for hunting.
A wooden stake fence, often associated with deer hunting.
A weekend retreat for Royal parties and others, when hunting in the Royal forests, or as a viewing station for the chase.

An earthwork feature used by hunters to trap deer comprising a steep ditch into which the deer are chased with an enclosure to hold them at one end, known from the Isle of Rum and a debateable example in Cumbria.
A building used for the shelter and protection of deer, especially in winter.
A small area of managed woodland, created to provide cover for deer and other game.
A pond or pool with arms covered with nets into which wild birds, are lured and then caught. Monument type includes water feeder channels.
Structure used for viewing deer hunt.
A building, site or structure associated with the hunting of animals.
Bank to let deer cross ditches, fences or roads, into, but not out of, a deer park.

Sites, buildings, structures, features and areas of land associated with cultivation, the rearing of livestock, gathering, hunting & fishing. Includes farm based processing of foodstuffs & storage of agricultural produce.
A building used as a social venue by people interested in, and involved with, the sport of hunting.
Position often screened by earth, stone or wood from which game is shot.
An establishment or building where the breeding and training of birds of prey takes place.
A house or range of buildings in which dogs are kept, eg. hunting hounds.
A building for housing deer overnight.
An area of land, heavily though not totally covered with trees, set aside for the royal hunt by Norman and Plantagenet kings.
An enclosure used for corralling deer.
A small area of managed woodland, created to provide cover for foxes.
A building used to shelter deer hunters.
A place where pheasants are reared and kept.
A building or room used for small scale manufacture. Use more specific term where possible.
A workshop forming part of a domestic dwelling.
A farm or group of buildings where Silkworms are bred. The Silkworm when changing into a pupa spins a cocoon made of silken filaments, these are then unwound and used to manufacture silk thread.
A farm building erected in the 18th and 19th century which were architect-designed rather than built in the local vernacular style.
A farm on the estate of a manor.
A farm on which liquid sewage was regularly used for irrigation as a means of sewage disposal.
The homestead of a farm consisting of a farmhouse and working farm buildings, with yards, other working areas and usually a garden to the house.
A rustic building of picturesque design, often associated with a model farm, country house or estate. Although ornamental in design they are intended to be functional.
A building or group of buildings used for the raising of mink, a semi-aquatic mammal which is farmed for its fur.
A farm where stallions and mares are kept for breeding.
Areas of land used primarily for agriculture. See also GARDENS, PARKS AND URBAN SPACES.
A tract of land, often including a farmhouse and ancillary buildings, used for the purpose of cultivation and the rearing of livestock, etc. Use more specific type where known.

A structure, based on drawing number (3329/41), intended to be the headquarters for the coordination of an airfield's defences. Constructed above ground this design was found to be vulnerable and was superceded by the (11008/41).
A concrete structure designed to be the headquarters for the coordination of an airfield's defences. Constructed partially underground it was only intended to be occupied during an attack.
A bridge carrying a tramway.
A bridge, often over a canal or road, allowing access between two parcels of land.
A bridge with two or more decks allowing it to carry various modes of transport at the same time.
A bridge which takes a towing path over a branch canal, basin, etc.
A bridge that incorporates one or two spans that tilt at the abutments, to move up and out of the way of shipping. The most famous example of which is Tower Bridge, London.
A bridge whose deck is directly supported from pylons by straight cables without vertical suspenders.
A bridge whose deck is hung from above by large cables, chains or pinned iron or steel bars hanging from towers.
A curved structural span which is supported at the sides or ends. May vary in shape from the horizontal flat arch through semicircular and semielliptical forms.
A type of bridge which was designed for temporary use and then capable of being moved to another site. Use for temporary bridges which have remained in situ since erection.
A bridge on which dwellings or commercial premises have been built.
A bridge whose upkeep and repair was financed by the exaction of a toll.
A bridge, carrying a footpath or road, usually across marshy or waterlogged ground.
A bridge manufactured from prefabricated sections.
A bridge which is fortified at one or both ends.
A bridge that crosses over a railway.
A bridge carrying a road over land or water.
A type of concrete bridge, developed in the 20th century, that consists of reinforced concrete deck slabs that sit on the supporting bridge piers and/or abutments.
A bridge in which the load is carried by a single beam, or beams, spanning the space between two supports.
A bridge over a canal.
A bridge used for carrying liquids, usually water, although sometimes oil, in a pipeline over a river. Mid 19th century onwards.
A structure of wood, stone, iron, brick or concrete, etc, with one or more intervals under it to span a river or other space. Use specific type where known.
A bridge made up of many relatively small members joined together in a series of interconnecting triangles.
A bridge whose trusses or girders form parapets on either side of the deck.
A bridge built to enhance or compliment the surrounding landscape. Mainly found on estates or in parkland and usually 18th and 19th century.
A bridge carrying a railway track across a river, valley, road etc.
A high-humped, narrow, cobbled bridge used by trains of packhorses, often located in upland areas where the bulk of goods were carried by horses.
A type of bridge which has machinery and movable elements, eg. to allow vessels to pass.
A bridge which takes the towpath across the canal.
A type of bridge which completely encloses the traffic using it.
A bridge supported by large beams or girders, originally of wood or iron, now usually of steel or reinforced concrete.
A bridge crossing under railway property.
A narrow bridge for people and animals to cross on foot.

Sites, buildings, structures & features related to the conveyance of goods &/or passengers. Includes man-made routeways, mechanical structures & some vehicle types where it is deemed necessary to record such as monuments.

A tall building, either round, square or polygonal in plan, used for a variety of purposes, including defence, as a landmark, for the hanging of bells, industrial functions, etc. Use more specific type where known.
A watchtower used to guard prisons, camps or other facilities.
A law court exercising summary criminal jurisdiction, preliminary hearings and some civil jurisdiction. Formally established by name following legislation of 1949.
A place, hall or chamber in which justice is administered.
Buildings, engineering constructions and machinery, used for the purpose of supplying a town, etc, with water distributed through pipes.
Site and structures associated with the supply of clean water.
A building or range of buildings used for the cleaning, crushing and loading of freshly mined coal.
Includes terms for components of site. See also terms in MINING INDUSTRY SITE grouping.
An existing factory that was converted for use as aircraft works in the run up to or during the Second World War.
A factory or works which has been temporarily turned over to the manufacture of goods for the war effort.
A way between different places, used by horses, travellers on foot and vehicles.
A road or track specifically used by drovers or herders to drive their animals to market.
A place where (young) holiday-makers and hikers can be put up cheaply for the night.
A building, usually containing several dormitories, used as a cheap, short term residence. Use more specific term if known.
The residence and sometimes workplace of industrial workers.
The dwelling of a blacksmith, nailer, sword cutler, etc, often adjacent to, or containing, a BLACKSMITHS WORKSHOP.
A site or building associated with active or passive defence of the landing ground and buildings of an airfield.

Sites, buildings, structures & features used in the defence of the civilian population. Includes civil defence sites, weapons stores, training sites, military signals & active defence structures such as anti-aircraft sites.
Obstacles placed in open spaces and alongside roads designed to prevent the successful landing of enemy airborne forces.

A sunken, circular, concrete pillbox used on airfields. They remained flush with the surface to permit the free movement of aircraft but, if attack threatened, could be raised hydraulically or by a counterbalance, and manned to give covering fire.
A pillbox built to a design drawn up by the Air Ministry. Usually found on or near airfields.
A trench in the form of a flattened 'W' with a flat concrete roof covered in turf, supported on concrete pillars. The name derives from the resemblance to a child's drawing of a seagull in flight.
A flatbed lorry with a concrete defensive position fitted on the back enabling the "pillbox" to be driven to where it was most needed in the event of an airborne force landing on the airfield.
A building in which animals are housed. For non agricultural use see ANIMAL HOUSE and narrow terms in RECREATIONAL class.
A building in which cattle are housed overnight, normally tethered in stalls.
A fortified structure used to protect civilians and military personnel from enemy bombing.
A portable indoor air raid shelter in the form of a steel topped table, often with wire meshing around the sides.
Establishments authorized to sell or allow the consumption of alcoholic liquors on their premises.
Garden area next to public house used for the comsumption of alcoholic beverages.
A public house licensed for the sale of wine and other alcoholic drinks.
The public house was a 19th century development, distinctive from the earlier BEER HOUSE by its decorative treatment and fittings.
Permanently moored historic maritime craft preserved and converted into a museum and open to the public.
A building, group of buildings or space within a building, where objects of value such as works of art, antiquities, scientific specimens, or other artefacts are housed and displayed.
A brick tower, based on drawing number (9290/42), usually added to an existing building. Used for the drying of parachutes.
Buildings, structures and sites directly associated with the operation of military airfields. See also AIR TRANSPORT SITE in the TRANSPORT Class.
A purpose-built building with a brick tower constructed on one end, based on drawing number (9294/42). Used for the drying of parachutes.
A purpose-built building with a steel framed tower, based on drawing number (11595/42). Used for the drying of parachutes.
A purpose-built building with a tower used for the drying of parachutes.
A hut consisting of a frame of reinforced concrete posts into which panels could be slotted. Designed by the British Concrete Federation (BCF) during WWII.

A hut consisting of a frame of reinforced concrete posts into which concrete panels were slotted. Designed by the British Concrete Federation during WWII to be resistant to bomb blasts & used for military accommodation, child nurseries and clinics etc.
Areas of indeterminate function.
A length of straight, curved or angled earthwork or cropmark of uncertain date or function.
A linear groove worn into the surface of a road or thoroughfare by the continuous passage of wheeled vehicles. Usually expected to occur in pairs.

Sites, buildings, structures & features categorized by their form rather than their function, where this has been deemed to be useful for retrieval purposes. Careful consideration will be given to the inclusion of new terms within this class.
Use only for natural features mistakenly assumed to be archaeological or natural features with archaeological significance.
A complex of buildings used for the processing of metals. Use more specific type where known.
A place for sharpening metal objects like tools and weapons.

skos:Concept.skos:altLabel: Very Heavy Bomber Station Control Tower (294/45)
skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: A control tower designed for use on Very Heavy Bomber Station Airfields. Designed to Air Ministry drawing number 294/45 they were the first to be have a Visual Control Room
A building, originally used as a shelter for the duty pilot or officer on watch on an airfield, and later used to direct air traffic. Use more specific type where known.
The first standardized design for a building for the duty pilot. It took the form of a small bungalow with a bay window on the front elevation.

skos:Concept.skos:prefLabel: Royal Naval Air Station Control Tower
skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: A control tower constructed on RNAS stations by the Royal Marine Engineers. Built to a common ground floor plan they could be built with one, two or three storeys above this depending on the requirements of the station.
A high building at an airport from which air traffic is controlled by radio.

A central tower with a single-storey wing either side. The tower contained the watch office on the ground floor, observation room on the second with each wing containing an office for the Chief Flying Instructor or the officer commanding and their aides.
The residence of a priest.
A residence for all clergy having the sole or subordinate charge of a living.
Buildings used as non-permanent homes.
A communal room or building attached to flats.
A form of Neolithic burial monument comprising a large circular stone or earthen mound, with a low and narrow entrance passage leading to a wider and higher stone built chamber.
Site types normally or frequently associated with burials which in some instances may have had solely religious or ritual functions.
A Neolithic burial monument comprising a stone-built chamber within a mound of earth or stone. Use more specific type where known.
A megalithic tomb of Neolithic date comprising a chamber bounded by large upright orthostats, often only three or four in number, which support a large capstone.

A form of Neolithic burial monument primarily found in Cornwall and the Scilly Isles. It comprises a round cairn, usually with a retaining wall or kerb, and an entrance leading directly into a chamber.
A Neolithic burial monument comprising a stone-built chamber within a mound of stones. Use more precise term where known.
A Neolithic burial monument comprising a stone-built chamber within an earthen mound. Use more precise term where known.
A tract of land with trees, sometimes acting as a boundary or barrier, usually smaller and less wild than a forest.
An area of cultivated, managed woodland producing wood which is used for a variety of purposes.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the farming of fish.
A free-standing building with enough space to hang and dry nets.
A shed in which delicate plants are reared from seedlings for planting out later.
A building in a garden or park designed to provide a shady retreat from the heat of the sun.
A tower built on a prominent part of an estate to provide panoramic views of the surrounding countryside.
A rustic building of picturesque design, often associated with a model farm, country house or estate. Although ornamental in design they are intended to be functional.
A garden house situated to provide a commanding view.
A single-storey structure, usually situated against the exterior of a walled garden's south facing wall, used for storage and often accomodation.
A building or room containing a collection of preserved plants (usually pressed and dried specimens).

A structure, often found in 18th century landscape gardens, that demonstrates eccentricity or excess rather than practical purpose. They can take many forms - ruins, sham castles, towers, hermits' cells or grottoes.
A small ornamental building in a garden, usually one-storeyed and consisting of one room. Use a more specific term where known.
A covered arcade, often attached to a building, open on one or more sides.
A building made chiefly of glass, used to grow plants and fruit in. Use more specific type where possible.
A structure, partly underground, for the preservation of ice for use during warmer weather.
A structure in a garden used to house gardening implements, etc.
A turret, tower or look out occupying a prominent position to provide a view, either a separate building, or part of a villa.
Ornamental garden building constructed within the branches of trees.
A garden building on an estate used by fishing parties.
A tall, polygonal structure with ornamental roofs at each storey which is associated with Buddhist temples; the style was adapted for secular eyecatchers and pavilions in the 18th century in England.
A chalet designed in the Swiss style, eg. Kenwood, London.
An isolated building, circular in plan, generally consisting of one apartment with a domed roof, eg. Mausoleum at Castle Howard, Yorkshire.
A building, in a garden, park or open space, either housing a fountain or the machinery which powers one.
A picturesque garden building decorated with tree roots, often serving as a HERMITAGE or ARBOUR.
An often ornate building housing the source of an ornamental cascade, eg. Chatsworth House.
An ornamental building, usually decorated with or displaying shells.
A large tent which can be used as accommodation for parties and exhibitions.
A rustic garden building made of wood with moss pressed between the wall slats. The mosses could be of different types, forming a mossery.
Includes some structures that are not strictly buildings. Use a more specific term where possible.
A dwelling, located at the entrance, or gates, to an estate or park, etc.
A hall, apartment or large room, designed or used primarily for festive or state functions.
A decorative building in the form of a dairy, used for recreation.
An area of a garden with a semi-circular backdrop formed by an ornamental, architectural structure or a natural feature grown to the required shape eg. a hedge

Planned &/or landscaped areas designed for aesthetic or recreational purposes. Includes all sites, buildings, structures & features normally associated with parks & urban spaces including street furniture.
A garden building, usually in the Gothic or classical style. The term can be applied to many types of garden building with an interior space in which to stand or sit. Use specific type where known.
A rustic building of picturesque design.
A roofed, lightweight structure, usually attached to a house, provdiing access from and to the garden.
A house or shelter for the storage and/or launching of boats.
An observation tower is a structure used to provide panoramic views of the surrounding area. They are often used as attractions at seaside resorts e.g. Blackpool Tower.
Sites, buildings, structures, features & areas of land associated with sport, leisure & entertainment. Includes sports grounds, hunting forests, cinemas, theatres etc.
A purpose-built firing platform on which an anti-aircraft battery could be emplaced.
Sites, buildings and structures for the control and mounting of anti aircraft artillery. Also, structures for passive or indirect defence against enemy aircraft.
A building offering accommodation to people who are visiting a town or locality renowned for its mineral springs.

Sites, buildings, structures & features associated with health (for example, treatment of the sick) &/or social welfare (for example, alleviation of poverty), including all charitable foundations & all forms of state defined social welfare.
Buildings and structures associated with good health and recreation.
A light, ornamental building or structure built to incorporate, or in association with, a mineral spring.
A building used by visitors at a health resort.
A spa building to which water was pumped from springs or wells; usually also serving a social function as an ASSEMBLY ROOM, eg. as at Bath.
A building housing a Finnish-style steam bath.
A pond storing water to supply a HAMMER POND.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the production and use of water power.
Buildings, structures and sites for regulating the flow of water.
The horizontal beam on a lock gate.
A building housing electrical or electronic equipment used for communicating over long distances. Use specific type where known.
An office or central station of a local telephone system where the various lines are brought to a central switchboard and communication between subscribers is achieved.
A telephone exchange housing one end of an underwater cable and used to send messages overseas.
A boundary marker for the payment of tax or duty.
A cast-iron or stone boundary post, obelisk or plate found on roads, railways, canals etc around London marking the boundary within which a duty was payable on coal.
skos:Concept.skos:altLabel: City Of London Coal Duties Boundary Marker

skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: A site on which rigs, towers and other associated structures and buildings used for the testing of helicopters and helicopter parts are located.
A purpose built apparatus for the testing of helicopters.
A structure which protects an area of ground from the weather.
A structure providing protection from the elements to passengers waiting to board a ferry service at a dock, riverside, harbour or quay.
A simple, lean-to structure, such as those built by the dock companies to provide shelter for dock workers waiting for work.
An open sided building known to have been used for sheltering cattle.
A water-filled hole used for the disposal of aggregate originally used as ballast in ships.
A pond with underwater arches where the poles for masts were stored to prevent them from drying and splitting.
A place where boats are built and stored.

Sites, building, structures & features associated with the construction, maintenance & supply of maritime craft. Includes associated ancillary structures such as navigation aids, dockyards, wharves, etc; does not include vessels.
A stone-faced enclosure, with entrance closed by a floatable caisson or by gates, which can be pumped dry for inspection, maintenance, or repair of the hull or underwater fittings of a ship or ships.
A site where wrought iron or steel chains were manufactured.
A structure comprising two upright spars, joined at the top to form a triangle, with a hoisting tackle suspended from the apex. Used to lift cargo or other weights.
Specialized engineering workshop particularly for the production of marine engines or other large components of ships.
A factory where seaplanes are manufactured.
A craft or repair workshop in a boat yard, harbour or naval dockyard.
A dockyard crane permanently mounted on a lighter.
Place where ships and boats are dismantled.
An old ship hull used as a base for lifting tackle.
A large, watertight enclosure in which the water is maintained at the high-tide level so that vessels remain constantly afloat in them.
A pair of SHEER LEGS mounted on shore or on a SHEER HULK, used as a crane to hoist a mast and lower it into place on a ship.
An enclosure in which ships are built and repaired, and all sorts of ships' stores are brought together.
A site containing slipways and associated buildings used specifically for the repair of ships and larger ocean-going craft.
A workshop for combining flax or hemp as a preparatory stage of rope making.
A dock with gates which open for access for some hours before and after high water.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the construction and repair of ships and boats.
A place where boats or ships are built or repaired.
Floatable vessel used as a floodgate in docks.
A type of bridge which has machinery and movable elements, eg. to allow vessels to pass.
A movable bridge lifted at one end by chains or ropes either to stop traffic passing over it or to let traffic pass under it.
Buildings and structures associated with canal transport.
A building or room, where business and/or administrative activities to do with the canals was conducted.
A gate which allows water to pass into a dock, etc, at flood tide, and by which it is retained during the ebb tide.
Buildings, structures and sites for regulating the flow of water.
A searchlight battery, which points out to sea, used to locate enemy shipping
A site in which one or more searchlights were positioned to locate enemy aircraft or surface vessels for the benefit of batteries and night fighter aircraft.
A building or complex, housing powered machinery and employing a large workforce for manufacturing purposes. Use specific monument type where known.
A factory where furniture is manufactured.
A building housing a flight simulator designed to air ministry drawing number 1762/39.
A building containing a flight siumlator used to provide safe training for pilots.
A building used by an organization or society instituted to promote the study of mathematics through lectures, research, etc.
A building in which a society or organization is instituted to promote science, art, literature, education, etc. Use more specific type where known.
A line or track consisting of iron or steel rails, on which passenger carriages or goods wagons are moved, usually by a locomotive engine.
A small-scale railway, often for the transportation of children at a place of recreation.
A grave or sepulchre including a monument. Use specific type where known.
A horizontal stone placed across a grave.
A burial site for an animal, usually commemorated by a gravestone or other structure.
A tomb or memorial, resembling an altar, often with a recumbent effigy on top.
A tomb designed in the form of a cist or stone box placed over a burial. Its outward form often reproduces the features of the classical sarcophagus or medieval effigy base.
A type of tomb in the form of a slab raised on freestanding legs.
A tomb with a raised canopy over it.
An umbrella-shaped pavilion, Indian in origin, constructed over a funerary site. Can also refer to a funerary monument or cenotaph constructed in this style.
A building containing a number of areas for bathing, some of which are naturally heated by thermal springs.
A building containing the colliery showers. Also often containing first aid and mine rescue facilities.
A building, usually open to the public, containing a number of areas for bathing. In the case of such a complex containing baths for swimming, also index with INDOOR or OUTDOOR SWIMMING POOL.
A hot steam bath introduced from the East, in which heavy perspiration is followed by soaping, washing, massage and cooling.
Baths containing water impregnated with mineral substances in which patients bathe for medicinal purposes.
Originally partially covered baths shaped somewhat like a slipper, now usually a number of single baths of the modern domestic style installed for hire at public baths.
A building where people could bathe in salt water. Salt water was believed to have medicinal properties.
Sites, building, structures & features associated with the supply & drainage of water & the disposal of sewage and waste water. Includes bodies of water, waterways & associated ancillary structures.
A building used to store military equipment and ammunition.
A building used for the storage of artillery pieces.
A factory manufacturing sports equipment.
A factory or works used for the forging and sharpening of a variety of tools including scythes, spades, etc.
Building or buildings used for the production of Gas Masks. Consider double-indexing with the term WAR PRODUCTION FACTORY if appropriate.
Three storey house with a topshop; machinery powered by shafting through the upper floor.
A works used for the production of parchment from animal skin.
A factory, or group of buildings, containing apparatus used to extract specific properties, e.g flavour or scent, from natural ingredients.
A factory, mill or warehouse constructed with the minimum amount of combustible materials.
An industrial complex involved in the production of chemicals.
A factory used to manufacture fibreglass.
A factory built as a pattern for improved design.
A place in which turpentine is produced.
A building or site used for the production of frameworks of beds.
A building where pins are manufactured.
A building or site used for the manufacture of swords.
A place where tobacco is made into cigarettes, cigars, etc.
A building or buildings used for the manufacture of metal boxes or cases.
A factory where brushes are manufactured. Use for all types of brush.
A factory making flame retardant materials.
A factory where security safes are manufactured.
Factory for making Chenille a yarn produced by placing short lengths of yarn (the pile) between two core yarns (the core) these are then heated to set the pile in place.
Factory for the production of safety fuses used in the ignition of gunpowder for blasting.
A site where all the processes for the production of glass and objects made from glass are carried out.
A purpose-built factory for more than one occupier (eg. for several different workshops).
A factory manufactoring caravans.
A factory where general hardware, fittings, items of ironmongery are produced.
The cleaning and sorting of horse hair mainly for use in the upholstery trade.
A modern small factory or workshop, often in the form of a prefabricated shed.
A factory for the manufacture of vehicles
A site where canvas, coarse, unbleached cloth, made from hemp or flax, was manufactured.
A site used for the production of dyes from natural ingredients.
A factory where nails are manufactured.
A factory that manufactures toys.
A factory or complex containing machinery for the manufacture of printed materials.
A factory for the manufacture of leather goods, such as shoes, saddles, etc. Use TANNERY for the manufacture of leather.
A building or complex producing umbrellas, parasols and canes.
An engineering works that produces machinery specially for use in textile making.
A building or complex, housing powered machinery and employing a large workforce for manufacturing purposes. Use specific monument type where known.
A factory in which is ink is prepared from pigments and additives.
A site where the manufacture of glass bottles takes place.
A building or buildings where electronic components or devices are designed, developed, manufactured and assembled.
A factory manufacturing timepieces, including clocks and watches.
A factory used for the production of acetate.
A building where tallow is produced, ie. solid animal fat that has been separated by heating, usually for making candles.
An engineering works that produces tufting machinery especially for use in the manufacturing of carpets.
A factory used to make packaging equipment.
A type of factory building, often single-storey, designed so that windows incorporated into the vertical faces of its saw-tooth roof can allow the maximum amount of natural light into its interior.
A factory in which varnish is manufactured.
A building or site for the industrial manufacture of locks.
A works site making and/or maintaining drive belts for industrial power.
A building manufacturing bandages.
Factory producing asbestos sheeting and or asbestos fibre.
A factory where musical instruments are manufactured.
A complex of buildings used for the manufacture of pottery.
A building or buildings used for the production of paints, varnishes, colours and distemper.
A building or buildings used for the manufacture of all types of wax.
A large factory or series of workshops for the manufacture of clothing.
A factory where china products are manufactured.
A building or buildings used for the manufacture of shoe and leather polish, etc.
A factory where furniture is manufactured.
A works where cotton waste is stored or processed.
A building or site used for the manufacture of small arms and artillery pieces, etc.
Factory or workshop making bits, spurs and other small metal objects associated with horse harness.
A small works used for the production of agricultural tools such as hay rakes.
A factory for processing rubber or manufacturing rubber goods, such as tyres.
A factory or site for the manufacture of food stuffs from raw ingredients.
A factory where linoleum is manufactured.
A factory or building where furniture is upholstered.
Any building designed or adapted to accommodate trades and manufacturing activity. Use more specific site where known.
A factory or plant for the manufacture of ice using mechanized refrigeration techniques.
A factory for the production of plastics by chemical processes.
A site where small electrical goods such as radios, lamps and heaters are manufactured.
A factory where matresses are made.
A building or buildings used for the manufacture of candles.
A factory where ribbons are manufactured.
A factory which produces artificial imitations of mineral water, such as soda water.
A factory where glue is produced.
A building or buildings used for the production of whistles.
A building or buildings used for the production of pens.
A building or site used for the manufacture of weapons, ammunition and military supplies. Use more specific type where known.
A factory making laminate flooring.
A factory that manufactures watches.
A building or buildings used for the manufacture of crucibles.
A factory used to make packaging.
A factory manufacturing insulation material for electrical cables.
A factory used for the industrial manufacture of firelighters.
A site where cement is manufactured for the building industry.
A building where matches are manufactured.
A factory or works which has been temporarily turned over to the manufacture of goods for the war effort.
A commercial building, or buildings, used for the production of soft drinks.
A factory manufacturing fireplaces.
A site containing a forge for the manufacture of cutlery.

A factory used for the production of artificial limbs. They were often located within the precincts of a hospital, to enable fittings to take place and help the amputee to get used to wearing the limb.
A building or buildings where soap is manufactured.
A place where paper, frequently printed in ornamental designs, used for covering the interior walls of buildings, is manufactured.
A site where wrought iron or steel chains were manufactured.
A factory for the production of missiles
A factory where floorcloths are manufactured.
Sites, buildings, structures & features relating to the provision of knowledge and skills.
A group of colleges and associated buildings belonging to a university.
The gate of a sluice which can be opened or shut to let out or retain the water.
A barrier of concrete or earth, etc, built across a river to create a reservoir of water for domestic and/or industrial usage.
A manmade barrier built across a river in order to increase the depth of water.
A raised floor along the side of a line at a railway station, for convenience in entering and alighting from a train.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with railway transport.
A bookbinding workshop.
Buildings and sites associated with the printing and publishing industry.
Series of wire mesh screens used for grading lumps of coal according to size.
A building where matches are manufactured.
A complex of buildings where barytes is processed for industrial use.
Buildings and sites associated with the production of materials made from minerals.
Houses specifically of nuns/canonesses or religious women.
An abbey of Franciscan nuns also known as Minoresses or Poor Clares.
A structure, usually or concrete or sandbags, in which a machine gun was emplaced.
A gun emplacement which conforms to Department of Fortification and Works drawing number 55414.
A gun emplacement associated with a coastal battery.
A defensive structure or site where an anti-tank gun is emplaced.
A gun emplacement which conforms to Department of Fortification and Works drawing number 55415.
A gun emplacement which conforms to Department of Fortification and Works drawing number 55422.
A fortified site in which a gun, mortar or cannon is positioned.
A gun emplacment which conforms to Department of Fortification and Works drawing number 55503
Gun emplacement for static or mobile light anti aircraft artillery.
A plinth or pedestal, usually of concrete, to which an anti aircraft or coastal battery gun was fitted. Holdfasts are often the only evidence for a weapon which survive.
A usually permanent defensive work. Use specific type where known.
A pit or emplacement surrounding a concrete pedestal, or 'thimble', which was used to mount a spigot mortar. Deployed by the Home Guard during WWII as an anti invasion measure.
A gun emplacement which conforms to Department of Fortification and Works drawing number 55483.
A gun emplacement which conforms to Department of Fortification and Works drawing number 55491.
A factory used for processing raw materials. Use more specific mill type where known. See also TEXTILE MILL, for more narrow terms.
A water-powered forge or wire mill which manufactured metal wire combs for use in the textile industry.
A factory where metal wire is manufactured.
A communal residence of secular priests and/or other clerics sometimes with the condition of learning and education attached.
A building used for the education of, and as a residence for, chantry priests.
A communal residence of secular vicars whose duties included the education of choristers attached to cathedrals and collegiate churches.

Sites, buildings, structures & features related to the practice of rituals & religious beliefs, including funerary rites. Includes ancillary buildings, structures & features of uncertain use, which are thought to be ï¿½ritualï¿½ (eg. hill figures).
An area of land, usually enclosed, set aside for the breeding of hares.
Site of small scale industrial production often involving hand work and craft skills.
A place where ceramic tiles are manufactured.

A building of basic construction, usually smaller in size than a house and constructed from a variety of materials such as mud, turf, branches, wood, brick, concrete or metal. Use more specific type where known.
A round hut, similar to a CHARCOAL BURNERS HUT, associated with forest industry. The bark was later used in the tanning process.
A furnace or oven for burning, baking or drying. Use specific type where known.
A large, "bottle-shaped", oven of brick construction used in the baking or firing of pottery.
A building or part of a building used for the storage of goods or merchandise. Use more specific type where known.
A building where sugar is stored.

The rarest of the recognized types of round barrow, consisting of a flat, wide circular mound, which may be surrounded by a ditch. They occur widely across southern England with a marked concentration in East and West Sussex.
A round barrow featuring a low, wide mound surrounded by a ditch which may be accompanied by an external bank.
A Neolithic burial monument comprising a stone-built chamber within a circular or sub-circular earthen mound. See RELIGIOUS, RITUAL AND FUNERARY Class List for context.
A round barrow featuring a small mound separated from a ditch of much greater diameter by a wide berm. The ditch may be accompanied by an external (or occasionally internal) bank.
A round barrow featuring a mound surrounded by a ditch, with no intervening berm. The ditch may be accompanied by an external bank.
Artificial mound of earth, turf and/or stone, normally constructed to contain or conceal burials. Use specific type where known.

Hemispherical mound surrounded by a ditch (or occasionally two or more concentric ditches), often accompanied by an external (or occasionally internal) bank. Mound and ditch may sometimes be separated by a berm. Use specific type where known.
A form of round barrow intermediate between the Bell Barrow and the Disc Barrow. Only use where it is not possible to determine specific type.
A round barrow in which the mound and ditch are separated from each other by a berm. The ditch may be accompanied by an external (or occasionally internal) bank.
A university or college building set apart for residence or instruction of students. They can be located either on or off campus.
A place where students live, sometimes on a college campus.
Buildings and structures associated with the process of brewing and malting.
A brewery building where malt is mixed with hot water to form wort.
A device used to trap or kill animals considered to be pests, eg. rats.
An artificial navigable waterway used for the transportation of goods. Nowadays also used for recreational purposes.
A canal that can accommodate ocean-going ships, usually built across an isthmus or to give access to a river port e.g. Manchester ship canal
An establishment in which people, usually children, are taught.
19th century school administered by a school board.
A factory where collars, for shirts and other garments, are manufactured.
A large factory or series of workshops for the manufacture of clothing.
Obstacles like concrete cubes, cylinders or pimples erected in the defence of Britain.
A road block formed by placing curved rails, "hairpins", in sockets in the road surface.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the preserving of food.
A building or subterranean structure used for the storage of meat.
A workshop or factory where brass articles are made by casting molten material into a mould.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the smelting of metals.
A brass manufacturing complex incorporating battery mill furnaces, hammers, etc.
Includes bleaching, dressing, dyeing and printing.
A site used for the production of dyes from natural ingredients.
A site used for the production of dyes from controlled chemical reactions. In use from the mid 19th century onwards.
A lock, often containing a fish ladder, which allows fish to swim upstream bypassing a weir or other obstacle.
An area where fish are naturally present, eg. part of a river.
A mound used to elevate buildings associated with a fishery e.g. smoke houses, above the level of a flood plain.
A device for catching fish, may be a portable or permanent structure, often a fence or row stakes made in a river, harbour, etc
A holding tank/pen on a river or seashore for raising and preserving fish and/or for catching them easily.
A series of steps designed to enable fish to ascend a fall of water or a dam.
A site containing plant and machinery for the manufacture of steel.
Production of steel by reheating wrought iron in charcoal filled containers.
Pasture to which animals were driven for grazing, with associated temporary huts for domestic or agricultural use.
Any factory used for the manufacture of textiles.
A factory where lace is manufactured.
A site where copper or copper based alloys are produced by smelting copper ore.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the manufacture of products from metals.
A stone, situated alongside a road, providing directions to travellers.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with road transport.
The residence of a cloth cutter.
A purpose-built area of hard material of indeterminate use.
Sites, buildings, structures, features & areas of land, both natural & man-made, which cannot be assigned to a particular class (for example, railings).
A building or site used for the storage of goods or equipment.
A building or site used as a storage and distribution centre.
An area of ground, set apart for the burial of the dead.

A high status, walled, Roman burial ground containing cremations and/or inhumations in mausolea, tombs, barrows, coffins or cists. Dating from the late 1st to the 4th Century AD. DO NOT USE for cemeteries of later dates which are walled.
A building used for the finishing, drying and storage of lace.
A structure inclined towards the water on which a ship may be built or lowered into the water.
A plot of earth used for the raising of flowers and shrubs.
A bed raised above the level of the surrounding walks. A common feature of medieval and Renaissance gardens.
A hall used for the promotion and selling of horticultural produce and practice.
A hall used for housing public displays.
A hall used for the promotion and selling of agricultural produce and practice.
A meeting hall, or sale room in a town, for manufacturers and traders.
A large room with fixed seating, designed for lectures.
A place where sails are manufactured.
A small concentration of dwellings.
A suburb of a town, especially Roman or Medieval, situtated or extending beyond its formal limits, usually demarked by defences.
A trough or gutter for conveying liquids such as water or molten metal. It can be cut in the surface or formed of wood or other materials.
A channel used for or formed by the conveyance of water. Can be natural, eg. a river or artificial eg. an aqueduct. Use more specific type where known.
A building, often located in a park, where players can change and store equipment and from where spectators can watch the game.
A building, usually at a sports ground, with facilities for players and spectators.
A mill where long-staple hair, often from llamas, is made into yarn.
Any factory used for the manufacture of textiles.
Muslim funeral mosque.
A Muslim temple or place of worship.
A garden designed in the style of the elaborate gardens of the Renaissance, eg. formal, geometrical layouts of lawn and paths, stone steps, balustrades and statuary and fountains.
An enclosed piece of ground devoted to the cultivation of flowers, fruit or vegetables and/or recreational purposes. Use more specific type where known.
A bridge, usually resting on raised arches, carrying a road across low-lying land or water.
A bridge, usually resting on raised arches, carrying a railway across low-lying land or water.
A bridge, usually resting on a series of arches, carrying roadways or railways over low-lying areas.
A workshop in which saggars - fire clay boxes to protect ware from direct action of flame and gases during firing - were manufactured.

Buildings, sites and structures associated with the production of pottery. Use only for sites where there is evidence of pottery manufacture but no specific monument, otherwise use more specific term.
A site where household rubbish and other waste products can be disposed of. May take the form of a pit, rubbish tip, landfill site or incineration plant.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the disposal of domestic and industrial waste.
A chemical works engaged in the production of Ammonium Perchlorate, a product used in the explosives industry.
An industrial complex involved in the production of chemicals.

A structure comprising of two walls of stone or wood with nets or fish traps attached. Located in coastal waters, on shelving coastlines or in river estuaries they form large enclosures with a V or L shaped plan. The narrow point on the seaward side.
A fence or row of stakes, often with nets attached forming an enclosure within a river or harbour and used for catching, or holding, fish.
Earthworks and buildings added around a bastion to enhance protection of the bastion.
A flanking tower, or projection from the main walls of a defensive work from which a garrison can defend the ground in front or on the flank.
A place used to hide something or someone.
A structure which can be an area within a building, a separate building within a complex or a detached architectural component of a building
An area used for the breeding and rearing of rabbits.
A large body of water surrounded by land.
An artificial lake, often made by damming a stream. A common feature of landscape parks.
An unidentified feature on the seabed recorded by fishermen as an obstruction to trawling.
Buildings or sites used in the preparation, treatment and working of raw animal hide into leather products such as gloves or saddles, etc.
A manufacturing complex where the hides of animals are turned into leather, consisting of buildings for fleecing and drying, as well as treatment pits.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the control, accommodation, service and testing of aircraft.
A site, including an airfield and customs house, where air passengers embark and disembark.
A landing and taking off area for civil aircraft, usually with surfaced runways and aircraft maintenance and passenger facilities.
A bishop's court for ecclesiastical causes and offences, formerly having wider jurisdiction in matters of moral discipline.
A grave lined with slabs of stone or slate and covered by a large slab of stone. Commonly found on the Isle of Man.
A place of burial. Use more specific type where known.
A jettied house where the upper storey only overhangs the end elevation of the building.
A house where the upper storeys rest on projecting floor joists and so create the effect of an overhang.
A site where small electrical goods such as radios, lamps and heaters are manufactured.
A place where an anti-corrosion coating of zinc is added to iron and steel products to prevent them from rusting.
A site where metal is worked. Use specific type where known.
A terrace or row of dwellings, with a NAIL SHOP attached to each house.
A workshop with a forge for the melting and working of white metal, ie. low-melting alloys. Also used for a smith specializing in decorative or finely finished wrought iron work.
A workshop used for the manufacture of items of jewellery and/or timepieces from precious metals and precious or semi-precious stones.
Place where a smith works iron. May be for small scale local use or within a larger industrial complex.
A place where metal knives and edge cutting tools were manufactured.
A place where padlocks and rim locks for doors are made from iron and brass.
A place where watches and timepieces are manufactured and mended.
A workshop used by a craftsman who works in base or precious metals.
A large wooden structure built alongside the water's edge where ships may lie for unloading.
A large wooden structure built alongside the edge of a canal where narrow boats may lie for the loading and unloading of goods.
House owned by the church, often used for meetings.
A place where people meet for entertainment, discussion or assembly. Use more specific type where known.
A meeting hall of the verderers, who were the officers appointed to maintain the King's forests.
A hall built as part of a complex and used for the recreation of the workers or inhabitants. Usually associated with model estates, factories, flats etc.

A building used by the society, fraternity or order organized under this name with initiatory rites, mystic signs of recognition and various degrees of dignity or honour, for social or benevolent purposes.
A place where members of the British Legion meet.
A hall built for the use of people living within a parish boundary.
A hall in a village used for meetings and other functions.
A place where a yearly or half-yearly court of record is held by lords of certain manors.
A hall used by the members of a trade union for meetings and social functions.
Traditionally, the hall of a crafts, trade, or merchants' guild. Nowadays, often used to describe a TOWN HALL.
A meeting hall of the Temperance Society.
A large building used for the transaction of the public business of a town, the holding of courts of justice, entertainments and other activities.
A hall in which public assemblies and meetings can be held.
A county judicial building where the Quarter Session and the Assizes for the County were held.
A meeting hall, sometimes equivalent to a GUILDHALL, but also associated with some early mining industries.
A meeting place for freemasons.
A purpose-built hall (usually 19th century) which was available for public hire and could be used for a variety of activities, eg. lectures, meetings, balls and concerts.
A hall associated with a church, used for holding functions, meetings and for conducting parish business.
A building, often close to a churchyard, used for the entertainment of poor people on their wedding day.
The meeting hall of a secular or ethical society.
A large, metal or wooden structure, used for raising, lowering and moving heavy objects. Use more specific type where known.
A crane, located in an engineering workshop or similar establishment, which can be moved on rails and thus used anywhere within the workshop.
A crane suspended from running rails in the roof of an engineering workshop or similar establishment.
A building housing an electric powered mine ventilation fan.
A building housing a fan used for the ventilation of mines
Buildings, sites and structures associated with sporting activities.
Range used by the Navy with reinforced observation huts which housed quadrant equipment to record accuracy and damage.
An earthwork or structure on a rifle range used to mark a set distance from the rifle butts (usually at 50 or 100 yard intervals).
A shelter on a firing range from which the wepaons testing can be viewed in safety.
A piece of ground, or a building, on which artillery may be fired at targets.
An area of ground used for the testing of, and practicing with, weapons against fixed and moveable targets.
A piece of ground over which small arms or large artillery may be fired at targets. For rocket and missile firing use ROCKET TEST FACILITY.
A type of large steel framed aircraft hangar introduced by the Royal Air Force in its Expansion Period with a number of designs between 1934 and 1939, to accomodate heavy bombers.
A structure used for the housing and servicing of aircraft.
A railway yard with associated buildings used for the maintenance and storage of locomotive engines and rolling stock.
A building or structure of unknown function found on a farm. Use more specific type where known.
A separate compartment for livestock in which they are free to move about.
A shelter for the parson during the burial service.

A late 17th - early 18th century house with a central chimney and fireplaces and a central door on the front; this door opened closely against the fireplaces, leaving a small lobby for access to the rooms.
The rural residence of a country gentleman.
A house having four rooms of equal height on each of two floors; in larger houses there are often two parallel and equal roofs.
Traditionally the chief residence of a land owner. Now used specifically to describe the residence of the Lord Mayor of London.
A house which bears signs of fortification. These often include crenellated battlements and narrow slit-like windows.
A free-standing house, not joined to another on either side.
A cottage for workers on a country house estate.
A house constructed with a basic timber framework; between the members are panels which can be infilled with timber, wattle and daub, plaster, brick or other materials.
Mud walled building found on the Solway Plain.
The residence of a verger, typically a layperson who assists in the ordering of religious services within the Anglican church.
Circular structure, normally indicated by one or more rings of post holes and/or a circular gulley, and usually interpreted as being of domestic function.

A stone building with external access to the domestic accommodation via a permanent stair. The ground floor is normally used as a byre in rural contexts, but in an urban setting it may be intended for one of a number of other non domestic uses.
Residences of religious people and members of the clergy.
A cottage erected over a short period of time, by people who had no legal right to the land. Squatters were often tolerated by the landlord as they provided cheap labour.
Cottage provided for guests to a country house.
A house in which a passage runs across the building, usually adjacent to a hall, between front and back entrance doors.
The residence of a prison governor.
The residence of a telegraph keeper, associated with a telegraph station.
Originally, a house of higher social status in a town or port, often with a storage cellar.
A building for human habitation, especially a dwelling place. Use more specific type where known.

A term for a type of house, with varying definitions according to period. Roman villas were high-status and usually associated with a rural estate, whereas Georgian and later period villas were often semi-detached, town houses.
The residences of people involved in transport work.
The residence of a person employed in the textile industry.
A building providing lodgings for police constables.
The residence of a well keeper.
The place where a house stood or had once stood, often adjoining a garth or croft.
The residence and sometimes workplace of industrial workers.
A house occupied by an employee of a waterworks. Usually found in association with a pumping station or waterworks.

Standard dwelling of the non-ruling classes of Japan until the mid twentieth century. Minkas are timber-framed houses with mud-plastered panels and thatched roofs. The design varies from region to region. Minkas served as home as well as workplace.
A forester's cottage.
A laithe with an attached house.
A boat roofed over and fitted up as a home for living in permanently or temporarily.
The residence of health workers. Includes single dwellings of doctors, nurses etc. but not multiple dwellings eg.NURSES HOSTEL
The main dwelling-house of a farm, it can be either detached from or attached to the working buildings.
A gentry house in a town or city, either detached or in a terrace.
A purpose-built dwelling for the manager of a factory, works, textile mill, etc, often found within the complex itself.
A house, the inhabitant of which keeps an official register e.g. a registrar's house near a cemetery would keep an official record of deaths and burials.
The residences of people associated with the sea.
A small house, usually on the estate of a country house, forming part of a widow's dower and intended as her residence.
A purpose-built residence for an artist, containing a studio.

A building or buildings ranged around a courtyard on at least three sides. They occur in the Iron Age, as well as being an influential plan type of house from the 15th century onwards. Index with appropriate period.
Residence of a leading land-holding family within the district.
A rustic building of picturesque design.
A Swiss-styled house, usually with steeply pitched and projecting roof.
A house with a pitched or gabled roof with a double slope and gables on two or more sides.
Used where an existing building is designated as the residence of an official.
A house joined to another to form one building.
A dwelling house forming part of a Chartist Land Colony.
A large house dating from the 16th century onwards, built as a symbol of the wealth and status of the owner but not intended to be defensible unlike the castles and manor houses it replaced.
A house in which a member of the Royal Court lives.
The residence of a keeper of a royal park etc.
Use where the intervening arcade is closed but timber-framed.
The residence of an engineer.
A one-storey house.
A building that housed humans and cattle under one roof, with a shared entrance providing access to the cattle housing (usually downslope) and the dwelling area.
A terrace house sharing a common wall with its neighbours.
The principal house of a manor or village.

Accommodation given rent-free along with or as part of a corrody, which is a provision of an annual allowance of food and money by a religious house to an individual, usually in return for service or by purchase. Term used until mid 16th century AD.
The residence of a marsh keeper.
A storehouse in 16th and 17th century houses.
A house in a line of houses attached to and adjoining one another and planned and built as one unit.
The dwelling place of a farm worker.
The residence of a person entrusted with the management of a great house or castle.
The residence of a teacher, often on the site of a school.
A house built using experimental building techniques and materials.
A house provided for the treasurer of a cathedral, palace or similar.
Places of residence.
A house consisting of a public hall with private living accommodation attached. Built from the medieval period onwards.
A purpose-built dwelling for the supervisor of a factory, mine or other industrial complex.

A type of prefabricated house erected, to 11 approved designs, as part of the Temporary Housing Programme, between 1944 and 1948. This scheme was devised to relieve the post-war housing shortage at a time when conventional materials were unavailable.
A house built by a local authority.
A pillbox constructed for use in training exercises forming part of a simulated defensive position
Buildings, structures and sites for the training of military personnel.
A finishing process for cloth involving the pounding of the cloth with heavy weights.
A building used by an association of persons for social and recreational purposes or for the promotion of some common object.
A building owned by a constituency political party which provides a meeting place for local political activities and also provides entertainment facilities for its members and guests.
A building used to smoke fish or meat.
The dwelling of a blacksmith, nailer, sword cutler, etc, often adjacent to, or containing, a BLACKSMITHS WORKSHOP.
A hall in a village used for meetings and other functions.
A place where people meet for entertainment, discussion or assembly. Use more specific type where known.
An abbey or priory of Augustinian canonesses.
A dispersed farmstead where the farm buildings and farmhouse are loosely grouped together within the boundary of the farmstead.
A farmstead where the buildings and yards are loosely arranged, with no focal yard. Use more specific type where known.
A depot for the storage of various minerals.
A laundry built in conjunction with a PUBLIC BATHS.
A building where clothes are washed.
A cemetery comprising inhumations or cremations interred in stone cists.
A burial ground for Nonconformists. Use more specific term where known.
A burial ground for victims of cholera.
A burial ground for military personnel.
A burial ground for followers of the Eastern Orthodox church.

An area used for the deposition of human remains where the principal funeral rite is the burial of the corpse complete. Generally indicated by the discovery of articulated human skeletal remains, occasionally with evidence of coffins and/or grave goods.
A burial ground for Roman Catholics.
A burial ground for followers of the Islamic faith.
A burial ground for followers of the Jewish faith.
A burial site for animals.
A burial ground for victims of the plague.
A place of burial for members of the French Protestant Church.
The space enclosed between the gates and side-walls of a lock.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with water transport.
Similar in design to the FROMSON HANGAR but designed to drawing number 3752/43 and used for storing aircraft with small wingspans.
A small arched hangar built by the Canadian company Fromson of Byfleet to drawing number 3971/43. Used only as storage sheds on RNASs.
An aircraft hangar designed to be moved from site to site as necessary.
A place where furs are made into finished products.
A glasshouse used to grow and display tender decorative plants. May be either an extension to a house or freestanding.
A greenhouse for the growing of figs.
A glasshouse used for the cultivation of tropical plants.
A glass-house or hot-house constructed for the cultivation of a grapevine.
A building with a regulated moderate temperature for the cultivation of plants.

A forcing house used for various types of fruit which first appeared in the 19th century. Lean-to houses were used for wall-grown fruit and free-standing houses for fruit grown in pots or for trees planted in the ground.
A building used for an agricultural and/or subsistence purpose. Use more specific type where known.
A greenhouse used for growing palms and/or tropical plants.
A garden building or greenhouse, containing pools in which Water Lilies are grown.
A building made chiefly of glass, used to grow plants and fruit in. Use more specific type where possible.
A 19th century glasshouse built specifically for the fostering of camellias.
A glasshouse used for growing pineapples.
A glasshouse for the cultivation of ferns.
A gallery or building in a garden, usually south facing, used for the growing of oranges and other fruit.
A protected building or site used for the safe storage of chemical weapons
An establishment for the storage of food for use during wartime or similar states of emergency.

Sites, buildings, structures etc associated with the civil administration of settlements & enforcement of the laws of the land. Includes local & central government, settlements granted by the crown or ruling administration does not manorial settlements.
A building housing material used to explain the significance of a site or landscape to the public e. g. an archaeological site or nature reserve.
Buildings and structures associated with educational and artistic recreational activities.

A building that houses material that can be used to facilitate the study of a site, landscape or an historical event/period. Such centres are often found in close proximity to the sites and/or landscapes that they seek to encourage the study of.
A building in which works of art are displayed, permanently or temporarily.
A building or room in which images of outside objects are projected on to a screen from a long-focus lens using natural light.
A building incorporating a model representation of the planetary system projected onto the ceiling.
A pavilion used for exhibitions, e.g. the exhibition pavilions at the Great Empire Exhibition, Wembley, 1925.
A hall used for housing public displays.
A building, room or suite of rooms where books, or other materials, are classified by subject and stored for use by the library's members.
A building in which a view is projected onto a wall by means of a lens.
A building, usually circular, or containing circular rooms, for the exhibition of panorama paintings.
A building housing a variety of facilities, such as theatres, galleries, concert halls, etc.
A place where photographs are displayed for sale.
A building, group of buildings or space within a building, where objects of value such as works of art, antiquities, scientific specimens, or other artefacts are housed and displayed.
Area of a garden for the cultivation of ferns.
For commercial or non commercial use. See narrow terms in each class.
A public house where no alcohol is sold.
A vault used for the storage of cider.
A building, or part of a building, for the milling and pressing of cider apples to produce cider (or pears for perry) and for storing the drink in barrels.
A HORSE GIN used for domestic cider manufacture, especially on farms.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the large-scale production, processing and preserving of food and drink.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the production of wine and cider.
A press used to extract the juice from apples, which was then used to make cider.
A press in which the juice is extracted from grapes in the manufacture of wine.
An establishment where wine is produced.

Device for extracting juice from apples, usually crab apples, for use in cooking and medicine. Consists of a stone base carved with channels in the upper surface which was used with an upper weight, often secured with a wooden beam wedged into position.
A factory concerned with the commercial manufacture of cider, as opposed to domestic production.
Sites, buildings, structures & features related to the sale, exchange &/or storage of goods or services. Includes commercially operated catering establishments & lodging premises.
Civil building in Cornwall and Devon for assay and sale of tin ingots.
Factory making slippers.
A factory where boots and shoes are manufactured.
A site where iron is smelted or iron goods made.
A drainage structure that extends across and beneath roadways, canals or embankments.
A factory, mill or warehouse constructed with the minimum amount of combustible materials.
Block of flats incorporating broad, street-width balconies to give access to dwellings and connect to other blocks.
A rectangular multi-storey block of flats, greater in width than height.
A tall, multi storeyed building either used as business premises or, more usually, as residential accomodation.
An outfall from a canal, river or reservoir.
A dam constructed on the reaches of a canal or river designed to retain the water and to regulate its flow.
A stone or boulder which lies lengthways on the ground and may be used as a table, altar etc. Use only for isolated stones.
A building used for the daily administration of the Royal Navy.
A building used as the command centre of a military operation.
A large-scale site where medicinal drugs are maufactured.
A factory used for the industrial manufacture of chlorophyll for medical purposes.
The masonry beneath a lock gate, sometimes projecting several feet from the gate.

Land which has been temporarily taken over for use by the military or civilian authorities. During wartime land was requisitioned for various purposes, such as for argriculture or for military training/events etc.
A mine used for the extraction of the mineral Witherite. When secondary mineral, use with term for product, eg. LEAD MINE.
Sites where minerals are extracted from the ground.
A fortified house of two or three storeys, the lower floor being used to house animals and the upper for domestic use.
A nursery for infants, where they are taken care of while their mothers are at work.
A room or a building set aside for infants and young children.
A hospital department concerned with the reconstruction or repair of parts of the human body using transferred tissue, either in the treatment of injury or for cosmetic reasons.
A separate functional unit of a hospital not necessarily on the same site.
A plantation of shrubs.
An ornamental grove, thicket or shrubbery pierced by walks.
Block, often made of concrete, to secure smaller maritime craft. Many were made during the Second Wold War to secure craft which were to be used in the D-Day landings.
A large, level structure, usually of stone or timber, built alongside water to allow warships to moor for the loading and unloading of guns.
A large wooden structure built alongside the water's edge where ships may lie for unloading.
A large wooden structure built alongside the edge of a canal where narrow boats may lie for the loading and unloading of goods.
A large wooden structure built alongside the edge of a river where boats may lie for the loading and unloading of goods and passengers.
A Jewish graveyard headstone.
A stone, slate, iron or wooden structure used to mark the site of a grave. Use only where evidence of the form is uncertain otherwise use more specific type.
A stone placed over or at the head or foot of a grave, or at the entrance of a tomb.
A building housing a flight simulator designed to air ministry drawing number 4188/42.
A building or room where railway tickets may be bought and administrative duties associated with a railway are conducted.
A place in which gunpowder and other explosives are stored in large quantities.
A building in which a supply of arms, ammunition and provisions for an army is stored.
A bridge decorated with shells forming an ornamental feature.
A factory, where preserves such as jam and marmalade, are manufactured.
A square, concrete pillbox-like structure with 36in thick walls and a single large embrasure used to emplace a Vickers Medium Machine Gun. The entrance was protected by an external blast wall.
An abbey or priory of the Trinitarian brethren also named Maturins.
A residence of the Bonhommes brethren, who followed the Augustinian rule.
An abbey or priory of Premonstratensian canons.
A place of worship and residence for followers of Buddha.
An abbey or priory of Savigniac monks. Order merged with Cistercians c1147.
An abbey or priory of Cistercian monks.
An abbey or priory of Carthusian monks.
An abbey or priory of Gilbertine monks.
An abbey or priory of Grandmontine monks.
An abbey or priory of Augustinian canons.
A place of residence and worship for Anglican monks.
An abbey or priory for monks of the Benedictine order.
Use only for a monastic house of unknown status, religious order and uncertain authenticity.
An abbey or priory belonging to the Tironian order.
Houses specifically of monks, canons or religious men but not friars.
An abbey or priory of Cluniac monks.
An institute provided by a regiment for the improvement of the soldiers and to reduce excessive drinking.
A factory where nails are manufactured.
A manufacturing complex incorporating furnaces, calciner and condenser flues. Use SMELTERY for more modern type of plant.
A town for citizens of Roman or Latin status with a constitution governed by charter, which if possessing only Latin rights could be promoted to the status of a colonia.
An assemblage of public and private buildings, larger than a village and having more complete and independent local government.
A site used for the manufacture of lasts, shoemaker's models of the foot for shaping and repairing footwear. Lasts can be from a variety of materials, such as wood or iron.
A factory where boots and shoes are manufactured.

An establishment used for the manufacture of reeds and healds, which are components of a textile loom with related functions, in that they move and control the threads, and similar wire-based construction.

Includes all stages of production process of textiles, eg. wool, cotton, linen, etc, and textile products. Use only for sites where there is evidence of textile manufacture but no specific monument type, otherwise use more specific term.

A large octagonal pillbox, with a projecting entrance, equipped with loopholes for eight light machine guns and a light anti-aircraft mounting sited in a central well which was accessed from inside the pillbox. Designed by DFW branch 3.
An anti aircraft battery usually mounting smaller, faster weapons such as Bofors guns or a single anti-aircraft machine gun, intended to engage fast low flying aircraft.
A kiln in which lime is made by calcining limestone or in some areas chalk.

A kiln in which lime is made by calcining limestone. This type of kiln usually consists of a circular bowl surrounded by pennanular banks with a funnel exit on the lower side. They normally survive as an earthwork. Superseded by Flare Kilns.
A workshop with equipment for the making and repair of ships' rigging.
A craft or repair workshop in a boat yard, harbour or naval dockyard.
A house or building where goods are made or prepared and displayed for sale and sold. Use more specific type where known.
An establishment where people get their hair dressed and cut.
Sites, buildings and structures for the defence of the coastline from sea and air invasion.
An observation post for a naval officer in charge of a marine minefield.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the extraction of metal ores.
A ravine formed by using water to reveal or exploit a vein.
A site used for the separation of oil into its constituent parts by heating in an enclosed vessel(s).
Buildings and plant used for the refining of oil or the production of chemicals using oil.
A row of houses whose facade in plan follows the concave arc of a circle or ellipse, eg. The Royal Crescent, Bath.

A multipurpose hut constructed from stone and turf, covering a square or polygonal plan. It has drystone walls and a slightly corbelled roof, usually topped with slabs. Can be either free-standing or embedded in a Cornish hedge. Particular to Cornwall.
A tunnel used to test scale model propellers and hulls to consider the impact of caviation on wake, propulsion, vibration and noise.
Sites associated with the manufacture and engineering of vehicles.
A mechanical structure, consisting of a roller or beam on supports, round which a rope or chain is wound, and used for various purposes, eg. raising a bucket from a well, etc.
Buildings and structures associated with lifting and winding at the site of a mine.
A place where architectural ornaments such as stone vases and urns are manufactured.
A booth, shed or stall erected at the side of a road, canal, bridge or gate where a toll must be paid.

An earthwork feature used by hunters to trap deer comprising a steep ditch into which the deer are chased with an enclosure to hold them at one end, known from the Isle of Rum and a debateable example in Cumbria.
A building, site or structure associated with the hunting of animals.
A building or workshop where fine furniture, often veneered, is made.
A workshop used by a joiner; a craftsman working with wood and producing more ornate work than that of a carpenter.
Workshop for producing crates, particularly for the packing of pottery.
A workshop where wooden brushes are manufactured on a small scale.
A workshop in which products are made using wood and timber.
A place where products are manufactured from wood.
A large building used for the accommodation of paying travellers and guests.
A large, luxuriously appointed hotel.
A type of warehouse, usually one-storeyed.

This is a pit used in the glass industry for the production of cylinder glass. The only surviving examle in England is at the Hartley Wood Glasworks, Sunderland. It is a feature of 19th century and later glassworks
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the production of glass.
A pit over which a corpse has been cremated on a pyre into which the remains and debris, and sometime grave goods, collapse and are buried. Generally confined to the Roman period.
A place where dead bodies are buried together. Often unconsecrated ground.
A fortress and dwelling, usually medieval in origin, and often consisting of a keep, curtain wall and towers etc.
A castle without a motte.
A temporary settlement or encampment erected by construction workers (eg for reservoir construction).

An upright, or originally upright, stone featuring a hole which is often large enough in diameter for a person to pass through, eg. Men an Tol, Cornwall. Do not use for perforated portable stone artefacts.
Buildings and structures associated with a private aviation club undertaken as a leisure pursuit. Usually situated on or near an airfield.
A building or complex used for the temporary detention of people with no legal right to be in the UK who have refused to leave voluntarily.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the enactment and enforcement of public law.
A factory used for the production of thick, flat glass used for shop window panes, etc. Plate glass is produced by rolling and casting rather than traditional blowing.
A building where violins are manufactured and the art of violin making is taught.

The earliest side-opening standard type of aircraft hangar designed in 1913 and used in WWI. Originally constructed from wooden trusses and struts, some examples have steel frames. It comprised a single or coupled shed with rear workshops.
