The earliest side-opening standard type of aircraft hangar designed in 1913 and used in WWI. Originally constructed from wooden trusses and struts, one example has steel frames. It comprised a single or coupled shed with rear workshops.
skos:Concept.skos:altLabel: Royal Flying Corps Side Opening Aircraft Hangar

skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: A factory or complex containing machinery for the manufacture of printed materials.
A factory complex consisting of PRINTING SHOPS, COLOUR HOUSES, DYE HOUSES, etc, in which patterns are printed onto calico.
A mill which contains machinery for separating grain from the chaff.
A wing in a workhouse to accommodate vagrants overnight.
A specialist unit within a hospital complex. It may be a separate building or sometimes linked by a corridor or covered walkway to a main building.
An interment of human or animal remains. Use specific type where known. If component use with wider site type. Use FUNERARY SITE for optimum retrieval in searches.
Deliberate interment of a complete, or substantially complete, animal. Use the object type thesaurus term ANIMAL REMAINS where skeleton is fragmentary.
A site or structure associated with the activities of the Royal Observer Corps. The Corps was reformed on 1 January 1947 and disbanded in 1991.
A command centre used to co-ordinate information received from Royal Observer Corps observation and monitoring posts.
A path or road for pedestrians, laid or beaten in with stones or other materials.
A pavement walkway for pedestrian use, often raised above the level of a road or path.
A concrete, concave wall 200 feet in length used as an acoustic listening device to detect approaching enemy aircraft.

An early warning structure built during and after WWI along the south and east coasts of England. Sound detecting acoustic dishes and walls could detect the sound of approaching enemy aircraft at a distance of 8 to 15 miles.
Sites and structures associated with the cutting and processing of peat.
A site where peat (vegetable matter decomposed in water and partly carbonised), used for fuel, is cut.
A structure used to dry peat on.
Includes sites associated with extraction.
A covered walk, walled on one side and usually arcaded on the other, surrounding or partly surrounding an open area in a monastery or similar complex of Christian buildings.
An establishment for the testing of eyesight, making up of optical prescriptions and the sale of spectacles.
A room specifically used for the display of furniture and other related materials
A room used for the display of merchandise for sale.
A factory or group of buildings used for the production of plated goods. Plating is the process whereby one metal object is coated with a thin layer of another metal.
A complex of buildings used for the processing of metals. Use more specific type where known.
A floor area, covered in sand, onto which hot metal from a furnace is cast.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the metal industry.
A concrete, circular concave dish 20 feet in diameter used as an acoustic listening device to detect approaching enemy aircraft.
The residence of an admiral of a port.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the production and use of steam power.
A building housing a turbine.
A 19th century Tudor revival garden.
Sites for the manufacture of substances or items by controlled chemical reactions.
Includes processing and manufacturing of all forms of wood.
A temporary settlement or encampment erected by construction workers (eg for reservoir construction).
A site where aircraft are stored, dismantled and processed for the recovery of serviceable parts.
A site where artefacts are manufactured from jet.
A building where the administrative functions of a Trade Union are carried on.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the production and use of paper.
A building used to aid in the drying of goods, for example, by means of flowing air.
A hopper for the storage of ash.
A shed, often found at a quarry, in which rough stone is shaped or dressed.
A large tank where particles suspended in water, or other liquids, are allowed to sink to the bottom forming a sediment.
Apparatus used for applying a mechanical force, or to perform a particular function. Use more specific type where known.
An ancillary building in a factory or other industrial complex where manufactured goods are packaged.
A building or site used for the manufacture, assembly and testing of weapons, explosives and associated military hardware.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the engineering industry.
An open area used for drying products manufactured using an industrial process.

An area of land owned by a developer, whether a private entrepreneur or a public authority, and divided into plots for leasing or sale to manufacturing or commercial concerns which may share some common services.
Surface workings including shallow shafts, lode workings, open-pit methods and quarrying including some mines of stone, clays, compounds, etc. See also MINERAL EXTRACTION SITE.
The place where metallic ores were crushed and washed to remove waste, forming a concentrate which could be used in a smelter.
Buildings and structures associated with the mining industry.
Buildings and sites associated with the manufacture of clothing.
A tall pole topped with a bell used to summon the workforce to their place of work.
Buildings used in the production of animal food.
A group of buildings or rooms equipped with apparatus for scientific experiments or other research, testing and investigations.
A building, structure or site used for the storage of charcoal.
An inclined ramp of earth, stone or brick used to deliver fuel to the firing hole of a kiln. Mediaeval and later.
An area or defined space believed to have been used for trades and/or manufacturing activity. Only use when evidence for more specific site type is lacking.
A site where rough stone is processed, shaped, worked or formed into finished products.
A large, usually metal, container used for the storage of liquid fuels.
The residence and sometimes workplace of industrial workers.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the construction and repair of ships and boats.
A temporary settlement or shanty-town erected by railway construction workers or "navvys".
18th-19th century stone-lined pit which held the balance bob for a pump-rod or flat-rod system. It includes examples where the surviving feature is a pillar for the bearing, rather than the pit.
A depot for the storage of various minerals.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the generation and transmission of power.
A stone-lined pit in which seaweed was burnt. The calcined ashes were used in the manufacture of soap and glass, amongst other things.
A chamber in which minerals, metals, etc, are subjected to the continuous action of intense heat. Use specific type where known.
A building housing a winching mechanism.
Machinery for lifting pieces of stone or loaded trucks out of a quarry.
A single storey building designed so that windows incorporated into the saw tooth roof catch the available light.
Buildings or sites used in the production of items derived from the parts of animals not used for consumption.
One of a pair of large circular stones used for grinding corn in a mill.
Sites, buildings, structures & features related to the extraction, processing & manufacture of finished goods. Includes structures associated with the supply, storage &/or transmission of power.
An area of shallow linear cuts made by the removal of turf for fuel or building material.
A large disc of stone revolving on an axis, used for grinding, sharpening and polishing.
A site for the storage, preparation and launching of missiles.
A missile base armed with the Thor Intermediate Range Ballistic Missile. Thor Missiles were deployed in Britain under joint British/US control between 1959 and 1964.
An unlit, highly visible and distinctive feature on the coast that can be used by mariners for navigation during daylight only.
A conspicuous object, such as a beacon, used by mariners to aid navigation at sea.
A piece of sculpture usually representing the head, shoulders and breast of a person.
A representation in the round of a living being, allegorical personage, eminent person or animal, etc, sculptured, moulded or cast in marble, metal, plaster, etc.
A sculptured group comprising a chariot drawn by four horses.
A decorative or ornamental structure purposefully situated in a garden. Such as sculptures, sundials, bird baths, gnomes etc.
A figurative or abstract design in the round or in relief, made by chiselling stone, carving wood, modelling clay, casting metal, or similar processes.
A community of Protestant followers of Hussite doctrines, first founded by Moravian emigrants in Saxony, Germany.
A planned village or settlement, usually developed by a philanthropic industrialist , to house workers. Most include facilities for the education and betterment of the workers and their families.
A natural flow or current of water issuing from a source.
A channel used for or formed by the conveyance of water. Can be natural, eg. a river or artificial eg. an aqueduct. Use more specific type where known.
A graduated post or pole adjacent to an area at risk of flooding to indicate the depth of water during a flood.
A post, made of wood, metal or other material, erected to mark a particular spot in the landscape. Can be used for various reasons such as measurement, calibration etc.
A school where specialist skills, relating to a particular subject, are taught. Use specific type where known.
A place where the creative arts are taught to students.
A factory where seaplanes are manufactured.
A factory where aircraft are assembled.
A structure of wood, stone, iron, brick or concrete, etc, with one or more intervals under it to span a river or other space. Use specific type where known.
A bridge carrying a road over land or water.
A place where money is coined under public authority.
An indoor or outdoor market where butter was sold.
A structure, often movable, used as a platform for the display of a traders goods in a market.
A market consisting of stalls erected in the street and selling a variety of goods.
A market for the sale of cheeses.
A market where cattle, pigs, sheep and poultry are bought and sold.
An indoor or outdoor market where hay and straw is sold.
A market where fish is sold.
A market building, pre-19th century, incorporating other function rooms, eg. theatres, courtrooms, schoolrooms.
An open market where cloth and other textiles can be traded.
A place where meat is displayed for sale.
An outdoor or indoor place where flowers were sold.
An indoor or outdoor market where leather and untreated animal hides are sold.
An area, often consisting of widened streets or a town square, where booths and stalls may be erected for public sales.
An indoor or outdoor market where fruit and vegetables are sold.
A purpose built covered market hall, usually 19th century, although earlier examples do exist, eg. that at Abingdon, Oxfordshire c.1680.
A market appointed for the sale of wool.
A place where processed wood is sold.
An indoor market used for the sale of antique goods.
An open space or covered building in which cattle, goods, etc, are displayed for sale.
A market where goods are bought and sold in bulk, rather than by retail.
A street market.
A place where manganese ore is extracted. Use with other ores extracted and MINE where relevant.
Sites and structures used for the transportation of goods and people under roads and rivers, or through hills, etc.
An underground foot tunnel primarily constructed to allow for the passage of pedestrians beneath an over ground obstacle.
A town founded as an act of government by charter to house Roman or Latin citizens, usually retired legionaires who had been granted land within a territorium.
A town for citizens of Roman or Latin status with a constitution governed by charter, which if possessing only Latin rights could be promoted to the status of a colonia.
An assemblage of public and private buildings, larger than a village and having more complete and independent local government.
A planned administrative capital for local government which provided amenities for the Roman and peregrine (non-Roman) inhabitants of the town.
A civilian settlement outside a Roman fort.
A building, usually part of a hospital complex, in which contaminated clothes, bedding and utensils are disinfected.
A building, site or structure associated with various racing sports.
A racing track, often within a permanent stadium, for racing dogs, usually greyhounds and whippets.
A small building used as a shelter by a shepherd.
Field or area of ground where washed new cloth is stretched out to dry.
A building or site where phosphorous-based fertilizers are produced by controlled chemical reactions.
A building or site used for the production of both chemical and organic fertilizer.
A hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of sailors and/or their families. For Royal Naval seamen use ROYAL NAVAL HOSPITAL.
An establishment providing medical or surgical treatment for the ill or wounded. Use narrower term where possible.
Regular courtyard farmsteads where the buildings are arranged as two ranges at right angles to each other.

Regular courtyard farmsteads where the buildings are arranged as an E-shaped plan around two cattle yards. Cattle housing and stabling typically extend as three ranges from the longer main range which includes a barn or mixing house.
Regular courtyard farmsteads where the buildings are arranged as an H-shaped plan, commonly with cattle housing to two or more cattle yards.
Regular courtyard farmsteads where the buildings are arranged around three sides of a yard which is open to one side.

A farmstead with multiple yards which are grouped together and regularly arranged (other than the defined E, F, H, T or Z plans). The yards may relate to one or more buildings or ranges which may be of either loose courtyard or regular courtyard form.
Regular courtyard farmsteads where the buildings are arranged around all four sides of the yard.

Regular courtyard farmsteads where the buildings are arranged as two linked ranges to create an L-shape. They can comprise a barn and an attached shelter shed to a cattle yard or an interlinked cattle housing and fodder range.
A farmstead where the working buildings are arranged around a yard.

Regular courtyard farmsteads where the buildings are arranged as an F-shaped plan around two cattle yards. Cattle housing and stabling typically extend as three ranges from the longer main range which includes a barn or mixing house.
Regular courtyard farmsteads where the working buildings are carefully planned as linked ranges and are focused around one or more working yards. They often result from a single phase of building.
An uncommon form of a regular courtyard farmstead where the buildings are arranged in a Z-shaped form.
The major tower of a fortification, often acting as its last defence.
A Norman keep, in the form of a circular or polygonal enclosure surrounded by a wall.
A workshop used for the production of pottery moulds.
A mound kerbed with wooden stakes or boulders.
A mound in excess of 150 metres in diameter, of Late Neolithic date and presumed ritual function, eg. Silbury Hill.
A natural or man-made earth mound on which a gallows was erected.
An artificial mound of earth indicating either the former site of a windmill or built as the base of a post windmill.
A natural or artificial elevation of earth or stones, such as the earth heaped upon a grave. Use more specific type where known.

A mound of fire-cracked stones, normally accompanied by a trough or pit which may have been lined with wood, stone or clay. Assumed to be locations where heated stones were used to boil water primarily for cooking purposes.
A pillow-shaped, flat topped rectangular mound often surrounded by a shallow ditch used to farm rabbits.
A long, narrow mound of earth or stone and of uncertain date and function. Use more appropriate term where possible.
An artificial hill constructed in Tudor gardens, especially, to provide a good view.
An earthwork used as a boundary marker.
An earthen mound, usually within an ornamental garden, on which a tree was planted.
An area of ground indicating the site of a horse or man-powered winding mechanism.
The residence of a person employed in the textile industry.
A building for human habitation, especially a dwelling place. Use more specific type where known.
A wooden or metal structure covering a shipbuilding slip way.
A post mill in which the drive is taken down to the base of the mill by putting an upright shaft in the hollowed post.
A tower-like structure of wood or brick with a wooden cap and sails which are driven around by the wind producing power to work the internal machinery. Use with product type where known.
A type of windmill, mainly timber-framed, whose body, containing machinery and carrying the sail, rotates about an upright post.
A concept dating in England from the second half of the 18th century, when hardy North American plants were relatively easy to obtain.
A crude shelter for persons engaged in the production of pure carbon by the controlled burning of wood and other organic materials.
A crane for lowering loaded coal waggons onto a ship.
A place where stained glass is manufactured, traditionally for church windows.

Component part of a mungo and shoddy mill, where non-wool fibres from shredded material are destroyed by either soaking rags in an acid solution or rotating them in drums in a hot acidic gas followed by heat. The result is an all-wool product.
A mill in which poor quality woollen cloth was made from fibres produced by grinding light woollen rags.
A processed used to increase the thickness of the natural oxide layer on the surface of metal parts. The part being treated forms the anode of an electrolytic cell.
Sites and structures associated with the storage of water and waste water. Use only where the exact form or function is unknown otherwise use more specific term.
The structure at the top of a draw well.
A building or site used for the manufacture of weapons, ammunition and military supplies. Use more specific type where known.
A factory where explosives and the components of munitions of all types are brought together for assembly.
A terrace of houses built on a slope giving the roofline a stepped appearance.
Buildings designed for the accommodation of large numbers of people, rather than single families, etc.
A terrace with windows and doors on one side only, often built facing inwards onto a burgage plot, or sometimes on a steep slope, with no apertures on the uphill side.

A distinctive form of terrace found in the northeast consisting of a long, two storey terrace indistinguishable from a conventional house externally, save that each unit has two front doors, one leading to a separate dwelling or dwellings upstairs.
A continuous row of WEALDEN HOUSES.
A terrace of BACK TO EARTH HOUSES.
A row of houses attached to and adjoining one another and planned and built as one unit.
A terrace consisting of a double row of houses sharing a common back wall, characteristic of industrial cities in the North of England.
An armoured fighting vehicle. Often survive as commemorative monuments, targets and coastal wrecks.

Armoured military vehicle with its own firepower, which operates on tracks for troop mobility over rough terrain. Some may be adapted, or purpose-built, to be amphibious, and may then be double-indexed as AMPHIBIOUS VEHICLE.
A building, originally used as a shelter for the duty pilot or officer on watch on an airfield, incorporating an operations room.
Watch Office with operations room designed to Air Ministry drawing number (7345/41

A steel aircraft hangar evolved from the German "Lamellendach", a segmental roof design of the 1920s using a diamond shaped web of pressed steel producing a hangar with a shallow curving profile. Used for both military and civil purposes.
A factory used for the industrial manufacture of firelighters.
An industrial complex involved in the production of chemicals.
A factory where linoleum is manufactured.
A crane mounted on a large metal gantry, used for the lifting of large-scale building materials, etc.
A large tank used for soaking alumina-bearing shale in water and chemicals, the initial stage in the alum-making process.
A group of buildings or works where the evaporation and crystallization of sodium aluminium sulphate solution is performed.
A channel which carried processed alum as liquid from the alum quarry/works to the alum house
A building used for the crystallization process in alum making.

A section of the water channel on a canal or river shut off above and below by lock gates provided with sluices to let the water out and in, and thus raise or lower boats from one level to another. Use more specific type where known.
A lock at the point where two waterways join together.
A burial vault built to contain the remains of members of a single family, household or dynasty.

A built structure, generally below ground, designed for the interment of several burials over a period of time. Usually constructed with a door or sealed entrance to allow reopening for further burials.
A monastery governed by a prior or prioress. Use with narrow terms of DOUBLE HOUSE, FRIARY, MONASTERY or NUNNERY.
A priory dependent on a foreign mother house. Use with narrow terms of DOUBLE HOUSE, MONASTERY or NUNNERY.
A residence used during short visits by an official and attendants of the Knights Hospitallers for administrative purposes on their estates.
A subsidiary form of preceptory provided with a chapel. Use specific type where known.
A building where timber was allowed to dry and harden, to render it fit for use as a working material.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the processing of timber.
A building, or part of a building, used to house doves and pigeons, usually placed at a height above the ground, with openings and provision inside for roosting and breeding.
Pit for soaking animal hides as part of the tanning process.
Baths containing water impregnated with mineral substances in which patients bathe for medicinal purposes.
A building, usually open to the public, containing a number of areas for bathing. In the case of such a complex containing baths for swimming, also index with INDOOR or OUTDOOR SWIMMING POOL.
A distillery for the manufacture of perfumes from herbs.
Sites used for the production of drugs and other medical products.
A works where bleach is manufactured.
Timber or stone built structure, traces of which are found within some long and round barrows, in which human remains were interred prior to mound construction.

Regular courtyard farmsteads where the buildings are arranged as an F-shaped plan around two cattle yards. Cattle housing and stabling typically extend as three ranges from the longer main range which includes a barn or mixing house.
Regular courtyard farmsteads where the working buildings are carefully planned as linked ranges and are focused around one or more working yards. They often result from a single phase of building.
A workshop for the manufacture of clothing, eg. tailor's workshop.
A place where knitted fabrics and legware garments were manufactured.
A place where shoes and boots are mended.
The dwelling and workshop of a framework knitter.
A place where hats are made and sold.
A place where processed cloth is cut for use as garments or soft furnishings, etc.
A workshop for testing guns, incorporating louvred sheds to serve as firing ranges.
Buildings and structures associated with signal communication.

A signalling structure used on WWII airfields, comprising a concrete square base with a kerbed border into which concrete signal symbols could be placed to advise pilots in the air of current airfield state e.g. directions of landing and airfield circuit.
A building occupied by a club or commonly used for club activities.
A building housing an electric powered ventilation fan for use in deep mine shafts
A wall used in the game of handball.
A building in which a sport is played. Use more specific type where known.

A building or tower used to communicate information to shipping or other stations using signals such as flags, fires or lights. Roman signal stations took the form of a stone tower surrounded by a ditched enclosure and were used to warn of Saxon raids.
A signal station incorporating equipment for visually conveying coded communications.
Buildings and structures used for sending and receiving signals.
Large concrete letters representing the ground-to-air airfield code. It has been used to show pilots in WWII the name of the airfield they were above e.g. DW for Dunkeswell.
Buildings and structures associated with the acquisition of electronic signals for the purpose of intelligence gathering.
A building or site used for naval communications.
A building or site incorporating equipment used for detecting the presence of enemy aircraft or ships. Radar Stations can also be used to aid aircraft navigation in dark or poor conditions.
A structure which allows aircraft fitted with radar equipment to 'home' in on an airfield in the dark or in poor visibility, and land safely. Radar beacons can also be used as navigation aids.
A carving, often a bust or full-length figure, originally found above a ship's cutwater. Use as an external feature only.
A building or site used for the manufacture of pins.
A building or complex where corks and stoppers are made for use in bottling.
A building or complex where cork is treated and processed to be used in various products.

Heavy anti aircraft battery used from June 1944-May 1945 to combat the V-bomb threat. They are distinct from normal HAA batteries, being laid out in a V-shape, and early on were mainly for mobile 3.7-inch guns.
WW2 LAA battery consisting of two or four 40m guns or Bofors guns. Associated structures included tented accommodation, ammunition shelters, a 100 gallon water tank, latrines, wash-house and kitchen.
Gun emplacement for static or mobile light anti aircraft artillery.

Unspecified Second World War anti-aircraft battery. There were three types of battery. The U2P and U20P had different arrangements of DFW55373 projector sites for the 20-barrelled 3" projectors. The U9P mounted 12-barrelled projectors.
An anti aircraft battery usually mounting weapons with a larger calibre ammunition such as the QF 3.75 inch (94mm) gun.
A command post used to direct the guns of an anti aircraft battery.
A site containing one or more artillery pieces and/or rocket launchers for firing at enemy aircraft.
40mm gun emplacement created between 24th-26th June 1944 as part of the fourth deployment of Diver LAA guns to the Kentish Gun Belt. Each site had an extant searchlight battery.
Factory for making Chenille a yarn produced by placing short lengths of yarn (the pile) between two core yarns (the core) these are then heated to set the pile in place.

A signalling structure used on WWII airfields, comprising a concrete square base with a kerbed border into which concrete signal symbols could be placed to advise pilots in the air of current airfield state e.g. directions of landing and airfield circuit.
A place of worship for members of Protestant sects dissenting from the established Church.
A place of worship for followers of Emmanuel Swedenborg who believed he was the medium through which the New Jerusalem would be founded on earth. The church was formed in 1787.
A mechanical device consisting of a system of signal lights operating in sequence, placed at road intersections and pedestrian crossings to regulate traffic.
Structures erected on or near a public highway.

skos:Concept.skos:prefLabel: New Connexion Of General Baptists Chapel
skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: A place of worship for members of the New Connexion of General Baptists,an orthodox Baptist church which broke away from the General Baptists in 1770 when the latter became influenced by Unitarianism.

A place of worship for General Baptists, a movement established by John Smyth in 1603 and which grew out of the original Baptist church. They believed in free will and are often referred to simply as Baptists.
A place of worship for Baptists. The first Baptist church was formed by Thomas Helws in 1611 and gave rise to the General Baptist Movement.
Stop-line against invading tanks in form of a ditch during the defence of Britain.
A natural ditch the depth and/or width of which has been increased so as to prevent the progress of a tank or armoured vehicle.
A building housing transformers to convert AC electricity supply to DC supply for use by tramcars.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with tramway transport.

An often squat building with thick, loopholed walls and a flat roof, designed to accommodate a variety of weapons, usually strategically positioned to cover a vulnerable point in a defensive system. Many were built to standardized designs.
A pillbox which has been modified from a standard Directorate of Fortifications and Works design. Double index with specific type where known.
A large, decorative garden ornament resembling a vase.

A large octagonal pillbox, with a projecting entrance, equipped with loopholes for eight light machine guns and a light anti-aircraft mounting sited in a central well which was accessed from inside the pillbox. Designed by DFW branch 3.
An anti aircraft battery usually mounting smaller, faster weapons such as Bofors guns or a single anti-aircraft machine gun, intended to engage fast low flying aircraft.
A site where lime (calcium carbonate) is made.
Usually a complex of buildings for the processing of raw materials. Use specific type where known.
A building or large scale site for the manufacture and/or storage of weapons, ammunition and equipment.
Used for the laying out and marking of the smaller parts of a ship prior to construction.
A level space in a garden occupied by ornamental flower beds.
A parterre consisting of an area of turf often with a pattern cut into it.
A building, on an airfield or military base, used for the maintenance and storage of motor vehicles.
A road used primarily, but not exclusively, for the rapid transport of military vehicles, equipment and personnel.
A site, usually including hardstandings and associated buildings, used for the storage of military vehicles.
Sites and structures for the transport of military personnel, vehicles and armaments.
A canal built as a military obstacle, but also used for the transport of military stores, equipment and personnel.
A landing and taking-off area for military aircraft. Often includes ancilliary structures and buildings for the maintenance and storage of aircraft, etc.
An administrative building used to organize and co-ordinate the activities of members of the armed forces.
A building used for a variety of administrative purposes, usually at a military base.
A factory where tweed, a twilled woollen fabric with an unfinished surface, is manufactured.

Area in a deer park where a single deer was chased by dogs over a set distance, with bets made on the outcome. It usually includes a stand (for viewing) and can also include three distance markers, a finishing post and a ditch behind the last post.
A large park for keeping deer. In medieval times the prime purpose was for hunting.
An outfall from a canal, river or reservoir.
A dam constructed on the reaches of a canal or river designed to retain the water and to regulate its flow.
The residence of a lightkeeper.
The residences of people involved in transport work.
A chapel built on, or at the end of, a causeway.
A small private chapel in a church or house, either attached or in a separate building.
A church built within the bounds of a parish for the attendance of those who cannot reach the parish church conveniently.
A chapel where Roman Catholics worship.
A place of worship within the grounds of a cemetery.
A place of worship for military personnel.
A chapel for a prison, either attached or in a separate building.
A freestanding building, or a room or recess serving as a place of Christian worship in a church or other building. Use more specific type where known.
A chapel attached to or founded by a college.
A chapel attached to, or inside, a church, endowed for the celebration of Masses for the soul of the founder.

A place a worship situated at the end of, or built onto, the structure of a bridge. Often associated with bridge maintenance through the collection of donations, they may be endowed as a chantry for the celebration of Masses for the soul of the founder.
A chapel where the followers of the Anglican tradition worship.
A place of worship at the site of a mortuary.
A chapel situated within the demesnes of a manor. Can be a separate building or an integral part of a manor house.
A chapel in a church for penitents.
A place of worship for members of a guild.
skos:Concept.skos:altLabel: Guild Of The Holy Cross Chapel

skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: A chapel dedicated to our Blessed Lady, often placed to the east of the High Altar, sometimes in other positions.
A chapel within a parish church or other religious building for use by the lord of the manor and his family
A place where appropriate acts, rites and ceremonies are performed to honour or revere a supernatural being, power or holy entity. Use specific type where known.
A chapel for the use of travellers and pilgrims.
A chapel adjacent to, associated with or containing a well.
A chapel for a private residence.
A chapel within a parish church containing an altar and one or more tombs.
A hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of military personnel and/or their families.
A shaft designed to allow for the adequate circulation of air through a transport tunnel, for example.
A tall, hollow pipe, usually cast-iron, resembling a lamp-post. Used to ventilate sewer systems.
A lake, often artifical, in a park or open space, used for the recreational rowing and sailing of boats.
A large body of water surrounded by land.
A sign, often mounted on a post next to a roadside, giving directions or other instructions.
A place of meeting and worship for Open Brethren, a non exclusive fundamentalist puritan sect which was created when the Brethren split in 1847.
A place of meeting and worship for Exclusive Brethren, an exclusive fundamentalist puritan sect which was created when the Brethren split in 1847.
A building used for services by a nonconformist protestant sect, especially by Quakers and Presbyterians.
A place of meeting and worship for Brethren, a fundamentalist puritan sect founded in Ireland in the late 1820s and established in England in Plymouth in the 1830s.
A type of drying house, usually circular with a conical roof.
A reinforced concrete block designed to obstruct the progress of a tank or armoured vehicle. Use more specific type where known.
Cubes of solid concrete, usually with sides of 3 feet 6 inches or 5 feet which when placed in rows were intended to form a substantial barrier to enemy armoured divisions in the event of invasion.
A defensive gun battery positioned to face out to sea to fire on enemy ships and amphibious craft.
A command post used to direct the guns of a coastal battery.

A small, circular Late Neolithic/Early Bronze Age enclosure which bears a morphological resemblance to henges, but may belong to another category of circular earthwork-defined monuments, or is enclosed by something other than a bank and ditch.
A late Neolithic/Early Bronze Age earthwork enclosure distinguished from a henge primarily by its larger size, irregular shape, and greater complexity of internal features.

Circular or sub-circular enclosure defined by a bank and (usually internal) ditch, with one or two (rarely more) entrances. Of ceremonial/ritual function, they contain a variety of internal features including timber or stone circles.
A channel for conveying vegetables.
A group of buildings where consumer goods, such as small machines and electrical components, are manufactured.
A factory manufacturing bearings, including ball bearings for use in precision equipment.
Use for blocks in Emergency Medical Scheme hospitals (WWII).
A monument consisting of parallel lines of banks, ditches, stones, timber posts or trees which appears to mark out an approach to another monument or monuments. Use specific type where known.
A monument consisting of parallel lines of standing stones, which appears to mark out an approach to another monument or monuments.
Sites and structures associated with the disposal of waste water and waterborne refuse.
A hole dug in the ground to act as a, usually temporary, communal toilet facility.
A small room or building containing a lavatory and, in more recent times, washing facilities.
A site used for the manufacture of lasts, shoemaker's models of the foot for shaping and repairing footwear. Lasts can be from a variety of materials, such as wood or iron.
A house with an aisle on one side only.
A barn in which a central space is separated from a side aisle by posts and braces.
A building with an aisle on one side only.
A building with an aisle along one or both sides. Usually a row of posts separates the main space from the aisle.

A flour mill which uses one or more pairs of horizontal millstones to grind wheat into flour which millers call a ï¿½sudden deathï¿½ process; within not more than 90 seconds complete wheat grain becomes wholemeal flour.
A factory where flour was produced for use in food products.

A circular pillbox, usually consisting of a concrete pipe with a timber and corrugated iron roof, surrounded and covered by earth and sandbags. Built to a design by Norcon Ltd, a company dealing in concrete pipes.
A refuse heap.
A refuse heap of discarded shells.
A specialist hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of eye disorders and diseases.
A hospital providing medical, surgical or psychiatric testing and treatment for patients with specific illnesses or injuries.
For the production of clay tobacco pipes.
A circular, metal or wooden cover, covering a hole in the pavement where domestic coal deliveries were dropped into a store below.
A plant used for the manufacture of tubes and tubing, from wrought iron or steel.
A free-standing structure, in the form of a cross (+), symbolizing the structure on which Jesus Christ was crucified and sacred to the Christian faith. Use specific type where known.
One of 12 roadside crosses erected by Edward I in memory of his wife, Eleanor of Castile, the most famous being Charing Cross in London.
A place of worship for Jewish people.
A post box mounted in, or on, a wall.
A box in which letters are posted or deposited for dispatch.
A weekend retreat for Royal parties and others, when hunting in the Royal forests, or as a viewing station for the chase.
A dwelling for the keeper of a canal wharf.
A body of water, building or structure found in a park or garden used as a water supply or ornament. Use more specific type where known.
A fall of water. Use for artificial waterfalls if naturalistic in form, otherwise use CASCADE.
The limit line of a county.
A site or building used for the manufacture of goods made from pewter, an alloy of tin and lead.
A double lock placed between tidal water and a canal, etc..
A house or shelter used by drovers, herders or shepherds during the seasonal moving of livestock from the highlands to the lowlands. Use more specific type where known.
A small building used as a shelter by a shepherd.
A house or hut for a nightwatchman; including parish watch houses in churchyards and private watch houses, eg. in dockyards, factories, etc.
A building where animals are deliberately fattened before being killed for their meat.
A temporary fieldwork, usually a few feet in height, constructed for defence against enemy forces.
A usually temporary earthwork or fortification, the latter constructed by military forces operating in the field. Use more specific type where known.
A large, rectangular pillbox based on the FW3/28 with the addition of a small infantry chamber to one side of the main gun chamber.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the manufacture of timber products.
A building where matches are manufactured.
A flat, and usually level area of mown and cultivated grass, attached to a house.
A lawn planted with camomile plants which when walked upon release a fragrant smell.
Structures used for the lifting or hoisting of goods, machinery, vehicles, people and livestock.
A hoisting mechanism powered by electricity.
A stationary hoisting machine consisting of a rotating drum around which a cable, rope or chain is attached.
A mill used for the processing of tin ore by crazing, stamping or smelting.
Mill for fine grinding of tin ore between millstones.
Building or structure housing a form of ore crushing device associated with tin mines.
A site where products containing sugar or honey, such as cakes, sweets, crystallized fruits or jam, were manufactured.
An RAF Base, used specifically for the storage and maintenance of barrage balloons.
A site or building used for the storage and maintenance of both land and sea vehicles and from which terrestrial or maritime operations could be carried out.

A site, usually with docks and control buildings, used for the storage, maintenance and deployment of military vessels or the administration of the Royal Navy. May also include accommodation buildings for personnel.
A military base for the training of SOE operatives in the skills and techniques required to survive in enemy-occupied territory.
Coastal base for the docking, launch and maintenance of submarines.
A military base used for training service personnel.

A site, usually with an airfield, hangars and control buildings, used for the storage and deployment of military aircraft or the administration of the Royal Air Force. May also include accommodation buildings for personnel.
A building or group of buildings, often surrounded by a system of fortifications, used as a residential and training site by members of an armed force.

Sites used for the accommodation, welfare and recreation of servicemen, especially those serving in the Royal Air Force. Use only for sites associated with military installations. For non-military sites use DOMESTIC class and its narrower terms.
A site and associated buildings used by the military for various purposes. Use only where exact function is unknown otherwise use more specific term.
A site where a body of troops is temporarily or permanently lodged, with or without entrenchments and fortifications.
Buildings and structures associated with the performance of musical, oratory and dance events.
A club or cafe where popular music is played for dancing.
An educational establishment for the training of police cadets.
An educational institution for the training of teachers.
A college where the applied sciences and the mechanical arts are taught.
A training college for chefs and other catering students.
A college where specialist skills, relating to a particular subject, are taught. Use specific type where known.
An educational establishment where the art of garden cultivation is taught.
An establishment where the theory and practice of medicine is taught.
A training college for the instruction of military trainees in the theory and practice of warfare.
An establishment, often forming part of a university, for higher or tertiary education.
An educational establishment where agricultural theory and practice is taught.
An establishment dedicated to the study of theology and religious training.
A college where subjects relating to trade and commerce are taught.
An establishment dedicated to the study of God and religion.
A shore establishment for the teaching of maritime theory and practical skills.
A fighter satellite station watch office built to Air Ministry design drawing number 3156/41.
A small single storey structure with just one room containing a pyrotechnic cupboard and built of rendered brick with a flat reinforced concrete roof
A hollow, concave formation or place, which has sometimes been dug out.
A small, usually inexpensive, restaurant with a limited menu of light meals served at counters or tables.
For commercial or non commercial use. See narrow terms in each class.
A small house or a portion of a house used as a self-contained apartment.
A building used for fabricating balloon and airship envelopes.
A factory where aircraft are assembled.
A structure used to test the aerodynamics of aircraft or vehicles.
Construction works for the production of rigid or dirigible airships.
Sites used for the manufacture of aircraft.
A factory for the manufacture of rocket motors, both for civil and military use.
A site specializing in the manufacture of parts for the Aerospace industry.
A factory where aircraft engines are assembled.
A site used for the functional testing of aircraft and their components.
A mill used for the preparation of raw fleece etc, for spinning by a coarse form of carding.
A large, circular hollow, often with a platform and seating built into the sides, used for preaching.
A bridge built to enhance or compliment the surrounding landscape. Mainly found on estates or in parkland and usually 18th and 19th century.
A bridge decorated with shells forming an ornamental feature.
A large, undergound watercourse.
A gate which allows water to pass into a dock, etc, at flood tide, and by which it is retained during the ebb tide.
A large store for textiles.
A large building used for the storage of finished cloth.
A mill used to process logwood, the inner red wood of a South American tree used widely in dyeing. Imported in the form of logs and cut and ground into dye by a mechanical process.
A mill used to process raw timber.
A large tank used for training divers.
An undefined structure used in the training of people in a certain skill.
An open area of water, usually artificial and enclosed by dock gates or locks, lined with wharves, warehouses and berths to enable vessels to load and unload.
A site where ores are smelted. Use more specific site type where known.
A factory producing metallic aluminium by an electrolysis process.
Defensive fortifications such as ramparts, ditches and stone walls, built to defend a town or city.
A fortified wall surrounding a town or city.
An unsocketed earthenware or porous concrete pipe laid end to end unjointed so as to drain the ground.
An artificial channel for draining water or carrying it off.
A long, narrow ditch designed to carry water away from a waterlogged area.
A horizontal tunnel dug specifically for draining, for example, a mine.
A drainage structure that extends across and beneath roadways, canals or embankments.
A large drainage channel used for improving the land.
A windmill with a stationary timber body which contains the grinding machinery, and which supports a rotating cap in which the sails rotate.
A structure used for the housing and servicing of aircraft.
An aircraft hangar designed to house seaplanes.
A side-opening steel framed shed. A smaller version of the SEAPLANE SHED (TYPE F) they were built from 1916 on RNAS seaplane bases
A steel framed seaplane hangar designed for Royal Navy Air Stations by the admiralty in 1917-1918.
A military side-opening aircraft hangar originally designed for seaplanes and used RNAS bases from 1916. Steel framed with asbestos or corrugated iron cladding.
A mill used for the manufacture of walking sticks.
A farmstead where mostly detached buildings have developed around three sides of an open cattle yard.
A farmstead where mostly detached buildings have developed around one or more sides of an open cattle yard.
A factory used to make packaging.

A gate, made of wood, used as a livestock barrier by continuing a fence line across a river or stream. The gate usually consists of a series of droppers, that can float up and down depending on water levels, attached to a length of cable or wooden pole.
A heavy grating, often made of wood or iron, usually lowered vertically as a defensive barrier at the entrance to a gatehouse or barbican.

A pit in a road or trackway covered with a grid, usually of metal poles (but can be of wood or stone) with sufficient space between the poles to prevent animals from crossing, without restricting access for vehicles and people.
A construction of wood or metal used to enclose an area of land, a building, etc.
An obstruction, usually manmade, which is used to restrict or prevent access to a settlement, building or area of land. Use more specific type where known.
A movable stucture which enables or prevents entrance to be gained. Usually situated in a wall or similar barrier and supported by gate posts.
A bank, often faced with stone, with a hedge planted on top.
An enclosing structure composed of bricks, stones or similar materials, laid in courses. Use specific type where known.
Usually a row of bushes or small trees planted closely together to form a boundary between pieces of land or at the sides of a road.
A fence or barrier made of metal or wooden rails.

Purpose-built structure, other than a bollard, to prevent vehicle or pedestrian access to a road or site, for example concrete blocks to obstruct vehicles accessing beaches on the north-east coast for illegal sea-coaling.
A building used for the daily administration of that branch of the RAF dealing with training pilots.
A water pond in which lilies are grown.
A pond with underwater arches where the poles for masts were stored to prevent them from drying and splitting.
A pond used for the rearing, breeding, sorting and storing of fish.
Pond, created specifically for providing power to water-powered forges, blast furnaces, helve or other hammers.
A pond or pool with arms covered with nets into which wild birds, are lured and then caught. Monument type includes water feeder channels.
A pond with protection for nesting ducks and other wild fowl
A small pond, usually circular and serving as a feature at the centre of a walled garden, used for the purpose of filling watering cans.
A pond used as a water supply for the operation of a furnace or blast furnace.
Pond for storing cut lengths of timber to prevent them becoming seasoned.
A small artificial pond of water often found in parks and gardens, for decorative purposes.
A pond used for dissipating heat by evaporation from steam engine condensate. Mid 19th century to mid 20th century.
A pond used for the punishment, by ducking in water, of offenders.
An ornamental garden feature, sometimes with an associated bath house.
A shallow pond, often artificial, fed by the condensation of water from the air, occuring on high land which has no other adequate water supply.
The area of water retained above a mill dam for driving a mill.
A pond storing water to supply a HAMMER POND.
A pond located at or near a swannery.
A shallow pond, often located near an ICEHOUSE, built to provide ice during the winter.
A body of still water often artificially formed for a specific purpose. Use specifc type where known.
A structure with a roof to provide shelter from the weather for occupants or contents. Use specific type where known.
Prefabricated small building that is designed and built to be movable rather than permanently located.
A site used for the production of sodium bicarbonate, soda ash or caustic soda.
A stone used to instruct a coachman to take an extra trace horse to assist on roads of a steep gradient.
A factory where carpets are manufactured.
A factory where carpets are manufactured.
A factory where floorcloths are manufactured.
Includes any textile floor covering.
A building where carpets and other floor furnishings were woven.
A factory where linoleum is manufactured.
Originally a large tract of wooded country, owned by the Monarchy, for the purpose of hunting. The royal parks of London, eg. Greenwich, are all open to the public and have been for centuries.
An enclosed piece of land, generally large in area, used for hunting, the cultivation of trees, for grazing sheep and cattle or visual enjoyment. Use more specific type where known.
The residence of the head or president of a chapter, or community of religious persons.
Sites, buildings or stuctures associated with the entire process of salt production.
A coastal site producing salt by solar evaporation of seawater in a series of PONDS, followed by boiling of the concentrated brine in a PANHOUSE
A mill used for the manufacture of twilled dress material of worsted with or without a mixture of cotton or silk.
A furnace in which the flame is turned back over the substance to be heated.
A reverberatory furnace used for forging wrought iron from pig iron using coal as fuel.
An enclosed furnace used for the continuous casting of plate glass.
A defensive position, often constructed from sandbags, designed to protect a group of infantry.
A room where a class of pupils is taught.
A room in a school devoted to the formal instruction of pupils.

A tunnel built alongside a canal tunnel to enable a horse to be unhitched and led through the hillside to meet the barge when it emerged from the tunnel. Mainly built prior to the development of the towpath tunnel.
A manor house, which was granted a royal licence to crenellate.
A house which bears signs of fortification. These often include crenellated battlements and narrow slit-like windows.
A pit where grain is stored.
A pit dug in the ground used to store meat, grain and other foodstuffs. A common feature of Iron Age farms.
A building associated with funerary rites and burials.
A type of carriage house, usually in a churchyard, for storing a hearse.
A roughly hemispherical mound constructed primarily of stones, normally containing or covering one or more human burials. The mound may be surrounded and partly retained by a low stone kerb.
A Neolithic burial monument comprising an approximately circular stony mound which contains a stone-built chamber, with or without additional lateral chambers.
Distinctive clerestory-roofed building, used for the drying and storage of military parachutes.

A brick-built building with four windows on the north-facing wall with a pitched roof and with a dormer roof light on both sides, intended for drying, storing and packing parachutes.The 2355/25 was the first design for a purpose-built parachute store.

One in a chain of stations with semaphore shutters and telescopes which could relay messages according to a planned code. Used from the 1790s by the British Admiralty to speed up communications from London to the ports of Deal, Portsmouth and Plymouth.
A bridge over a canal.
A place where dockyard craftsmen both design and build ships.
A self-contained establishment (out-patients) where pregnant women receive check-ups, counselling and medical treatment.
An institution, sometimes attached to a hospital, where patients may receive treatment or health checks.
Living quarters for animals, birds, etc, as pets or for observation, entertainment, etc.
A pool of water, and ancillary buildings, designed to accommodate penguins.
A cable, usually erected between posts, used to prevent the landing or hostile aircraft.
Obstacles placed in open spaces and alongside roads designed to prevent the successful landing of enemy airborne forces.
A purpose built quay for supplying ships with fuel.
A place where vessels can land passengers and goods.
An area of a port, dock or harbour where a container vessel docks to take on or unload its containers.
A place where a ship lies at a wharf. Use specific type where known.
A structure or building, often within a secluded area of a garden, where people could go for quiet reflection.
A lattice work bower or shady retreat covered with climbing plants.
An extended arbour, eg. the beech arbour at Hampton Court, Middlesex.
A building where military officers are accommodated.

A prefabricated structure of lightweight timber wall sections bolted together. Externally the walls were clad with plasterboard covered with felt. Designed for use as officers accomodation during WWII.
A factory used for the industrial manufacture of chlorophyll for medical purposes.
A large-scale site where medicinal drugs are maufactured.
A dwelling for the keeper of a canal wharf.
The residences of people associated with the sea.
An area of privately owned land attached to, and incorporating, a country house and associated buildings.
A public institution for the care and protection of children without parents.
A residential establishment for the care and accommodation of children and young people.
A large building used for the accommodation of paying travellers and guests.
A large, luxuriously appointed hotel.
School built by the local Education Authority to provide residental schooling at the seaside for children from urban communities.
A kiln in which stone is burnt as it falls through a heated and slightly inclined steel tube.

Sites, buildings, structures and features used for permanent, seasonal or temporary accommodation/habitation & related ancillary buildings. Includes commercial, military and religious sites used for residential purposes as well as industrial workplaces.
A camp kitchen, usually associated with the military.
A sculptured group comprising a chariot drawn by four horses.
A figurative or abstract design in the round or in relief, made by chiselling stone, carving wood, modelling clay, casting metal, or similar processes.
A representation in the round of a living being, allegorical personage, eminent person or animal, etc, sculptured, moulded or cast in marble, metal, plaster, etc.
A piece of sculpture usually representing the head, shoulders and breast of a person.

A decorative design or illustration, often an anthropomorphic or geometrical image, carved into a stone surface, such as a cave wall or free-standing stone. Usually, though not always, of Prehistoric date.

A stone, either in situ or part of a monument, bearing one or more small, roughly hemispherical depressions surrounded by a concentric arrangement of annular or pennanular grooves. More complex designs may also occur.
A site from which troops could be embarked onto transport vessels prior to the D-Day landings can also apply to muster/departure points from which troops embarked for their journey to the Front.
Beaches used for the departure of troops and equipment for the D-day landings.
Submerged obstacles to stop the landing of Seaplanes
Sites, buildings and structures associated with the prevention of an invasion by a hostile force.
A site where tar is manufactured or combined with other substances to produce bitumen, for example.
A hearth constructed specifically for the manufacture of pitch.
A defensive construction situated in the sea, designed to protect the land from seabourne attack. The term applies mainly to those monuments built from around 1860 onwards.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the defence of the coastline from foreign invasion.

A bridge consisting of a lattice girder spanning the distance between the tops of two towers. Designed to transport vehicles across the gap in a container suspended at road level by ropes under a travelling crane on the girder.
A tall, usually steel, structure used to receive and transmit radio telegraphy signals.
A site, including buildings and structures, from which communication signals are transmitted.
A tall, usually steel, structure used to receive and transmit radio signals in order to determine the height, distance and number of aircraft approaching.
A structure, building or site housing equipment for transmitting radio or television signals.
Structures associated with telecommunications.
A garden that has been specifically created to be accessible to both disabled and non-disabled visitors. They may contain scented and edible plants and features designed to make sound etc.
A room or group of rooms usually below the ground level and usually under a building, often used for storing fuel, provisions or wines.
A building in which purified charcoal was produced by distillation of wood in sealed cast-iron retorts heated in fire-boxes. Tarry by-products were sometimes recovered by condensation flues.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the production of charcoal.
A works using sealed retorts to produce charcoal. Wood distillates may be produced as byproducts of this process. They may be found at separate works or comprise part of a gunpowder works.
A sign, situated near a road or bridge, indicating a toll.
A factory in which is ink is prepared from pigments and additives.
Buildings and sites used for the production of inorganic and organic dyes, pigments and paints.
A sugar factory.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the processing of foodstuffs.
A canopy or building to cover the platforms in a railway station.
A place where an anti-corrosion coating of zinc is added to iron and steel products to prevent them from rusting.
A workshop used by a craftsman who works in base or precious metals.
A spoil heap consisting mainly of slag, pieces of refuse material separated from a metal during the smelting process.
An establishment where offenders are confined. Use more specific type where known.
An establishment where offenders who have committed the most serious crimes, e.g. serial killers, are confined.
A priory of Premonstratensian canonesses.
A building which has been fortified, often as a temporary measure rather than as part of the original design

A 19th century establishment for the provision of work for the unemployed poor of a parish; later an institution administered by Guardians of the Poor, in which paupers are lodged and the able-bodied set to work.
An outlying farm or estate belonging to the Benedictine order.

An outlying farm or estate, usually belonging to a religious order or feudal lord. Specifically related to core buildings and structures associated with monastic land holding. Use specific term where known.
A pump used for moving brine (salt water).
A machine used to raise and move water and other liquids, compress gases, etc. Use more specific type where known.
A waterworks pumping station.
A building used to pump sewage from the sewers to the filter beds of a sewage works.
A building in which the lay sisters resided. Lay sisters were not nuns and as such weren't bound by any vows. They could leave the convent and even marry if they wished.
Living and working quarters for the cellarer who was in charge of provisions and the running of the cellar.
A room in a monastery used by monks or nuns as a day room.
Accommodation in a monastery for new monks.
A residence for a member of a religious community eg. Abbot, Prior, Manciple etc. For multiple occupancy use more specific term eg. DORMITORY.
A house with an aisle on one side only.
Use where the intervening arcade is closed but timber-framed.
A house with no row of posts between the central space and the aisles.
A small enclosure for cattle, sheep, swine, poultry, etc. Use more specific type where known.
A pen to separate the boar from the other pigs.
A residential home for older people or people with physical and/or mental disabilities who need care provided by registered nurses.
A privately-funded home for the care of the elderly.
A dry ditch or sunken fence which divided the formal garden from the landscaped park without interrupting the view.
An aircraft, either whole or in part. Aircraft often survive as commemorative monuments, gate guardians or crash sites.
A school where young children, usually under the age of seven, are taught.
A kind of primary school kept by elderly women.
A school attended by children between the ages of seven and eleven.
A school for pre-Infant school children, usually 3-5 years old.
A school where no fees were charged.
A school which combines the functions of both Infant and Junior Schools, teaching children up to the age of eleven. Use specific type where known.
A school in which elementary subjects are taught to young children.
A military dining room where members of the armed forces eat and take recreation.
A building providing dining facilities and recreation for commissioned officers.
A building providing accommodation, dining and recreational facilities for commissioned naval officers.
An area for the testing of rockets and guided missiles. Includes all structures associated with both the firing and testing of rockets and missiles.
A building, site or structure associated with the demonstration and testing of weapons and military equipment.
A rural cross erected to show the way.
A farmstead where the buildings and yards are loosely arranged, with no focal yard. Use more specific type where known.
A dispersed farmstead where buildings are arranged around scattered yards which can be loose or regular in their form.
The residence of a teacher, often on the site of a school.
A hotel adjacent to a railway terminus. Railway hotels were often owned by a railway company.

A crane consisting of a lattice girder carried on a lattice tower forming a T-shaped structure. A hoist is carried along the girder by a 'crab', enabling the crane to perform a variety of tasks eg loading/unloading of ships.
A hall built for the use of people living within a parish boundary.
A building housing machinery for crushing chalk for whiting. Whiting was used in toothpaste, paint, tablets, putty and other products.
A type of pottery oven in which the air passes from the base of the kiln out through the top.
A structure, composed of oven and hovel, used for the firing of pottery ware.
A low-temperature oven for the firing of metallic-based colour onto pottery after glazing.
A type of pottery kiln in which air rises up inside the oven to be forced back down and out through the base of the oven.
A furnace or oven for burning, baking or drying. Use specific type where known.
A large, "bottle-shaped", oven of brick construction used in the baking or firing of pottery.
A structure in which pottery tiles were baked.
A pump used to transfer petrol from a storage tank into cars, lorries and other road vehicles.
An umbrella-shaped pavilion, Indian in origin, constructed over a funerary site. Can also refer to a funerary monument or cenotaph constructed in this style.
A sepulchral monument erected to commemorate a person or persons buried elsewhere.
Any factory or site using machine tools in a manufacturing or processing capacity.
A building or works in which carriages were built. Use RAILWAY CARRIAGE WORKS for sites making railway carriages.

An open area of water, usually artificial and enclosed by dock gates or locks, lined with wharves and warehouses, where barges, narrow boats and other canal vessels can load and unload goods and supplies.

A commercial building, or buildings, used for the production of beer and other alcoholic drinks. Size may range from a single room such as a microbrewery in a public house to a complex of buildings including production line machinery for bottling.
A site where vinegar is manufactured from soured beer, wine or cider.
A pit where calcium oxide (Quicklime) has been hydrated to produce calcium hydroxide, known as slaked lime.
A hole or cavity in the ground, either natural or the result of excavation. Use more specific type where known.
A wash room. Use with wider site type where known.

A settlement with evidence for several hut circles but clearly lacking an obvious boundary. Where it is not certain whether a boundary existed or not, use HUT CIRCLE SETTLEMENT. Characteristic of the later prehistoric period.

A settlement consisting of several hut circles, either grouped together or dispersed. Characteristic of the later prehistoric period. Use specific forms where supported by the available evidence. For isolated hut circles use HUT CIRCLE.

An establishment originally providing terminals to allow the public to access the internet, usually for a fee. They originally provided snacks and drinks to customers although now this is not always the case.
A cheap eating and drinking establishment usually serving snacks and non-alcoholic drinks.
A garden which consists of rocks and rock-loving plants that require little water.
A complex, comprising a workshop and a storage yard, used by a stonemason.
A mill for the removal by mechanical means of the dried wood and seeds of the flax and cotton plants after retting. The resulting 'tow' is then spun into linen and cotton respectively.
Buildings, sites or structures used for the manufacture of linen and/or flax.
The outlet or mouth of a sewer where it dispenses into the sea, lake, etc.
A large drain or conduit for carrying away wastes.

A cathedral in which the chapter was composed of canons who lived in their own houses and were not governed by a monastic rule. Nine such cathedrals existed in England between the 11th and 16th centuries.
The principal church of a diocese in which the cathedra or bishop's throne is to be found.
The principal Anglican church in a diocese in which the cathedra or bishop's throne is to be found.
The principal Roman Catholic church in a diocese in which the cathedra or bishop's throne is to be found.
The principal Eastern Orthodox church in an area.
Smelting furnace into which compressed hot air is driven.
A furnace where metal is manufactured from ore.
A building in which hoops (for masts) were heated.
A naval dockyard building used for the manufacture of flags.
A place where dockyard craftsmen both design and build ships.
Building housing machinery used in the production of wooden pulley blocks for the rigging of sailing ships.
A craft or repair workshop in a boat yard, harbour or naval dockyard.
A building where masts are made and stored.
A workshop with equipment for the making and repair of ships' rigging.
A light, mostly wooden errected structure serving as workshop for the building, storage, repair and maintenance of boats.
A wooden or metal structure covering a shipbuilding slip way.
A place where sails are manufactured.
A building for the storage, repair and maintenance of chains for lighthouses, lightships and lightbouys.
Used for the laying out and marking of the smaller parts of a ship prior to construction.
An alloy of tin, antimony and copper used as a replacement for pewter.
A depot for the transfer of town refuse to river barges before transportation to the REFUSE DEPOT.
A place where domestic refuse is collected for disposal.
A kiln used for extracting salt through the evaporation of salt water.
A dome shaped building, housing training apparatus, including a projector, for training ground gunners in the art of airfield defence. (WWII).
A factory where preserved food is canned.
A mill where mustard is produced.
A factory built for the production of breakfast cereals.
A site where products containing sugar or honey, such as cakes, sweets, crystallized fruits or jam, were manufactured.
A factory or site for the manufacture of food stuffs from raw ingredients.
A factory where cheese is produced and processed.
A factory where fish are processed into food products.
A factory where biscuits are manufactured.
A group of buildings containing machinery for the production in bulk of butter or related dairy products.
A factory, where preserves such as jam and marmalade, are manufactured.
A factory where chocolate products are produced.

A high status building of the medieval period, consisting of a hall and attached room at first floor level with rooms below possibly for storage or living accommodation for a lower status family. The first floor was accessed by an external staircase.
A hangar used for the storage of barrage balloons.
A building appropriated by a school for the purpose of teaching pupils.
The residence of a lightkeeper.
An aircraft hangar designed to Air Ministry specification (drawing number 6910/43). Similar in design to the ROBINS AIRCRAFT HANGAR but larger.
A lake, often artifical, in a park or open space, used for the recreational rowing and sailing of boats.
A place of worship for members of the Seventh Day Adventists Church. This was formed in 1843 by followers believing in the imminent second coming of Christ.
A building used for public Christian worship. Use more specific type where known.
A place of worship for followers of the teachings of Martin Luther.
A nonconformist church for the followers of Edward Irving.
A place of worship for members of the French Protestant church of the 16th and 17th centuries.
A place of worship for members of Protestant sects dissenting from the established Church.
A place of worship for Christian Scientists, a sect founded in the mid-19th century in America who believe that God is the only reality and can bring healing to humanity.
A place of worship for the believers of spiritualism: The belief that the spirits of the dead can somehow manifest themselves and speak with the living.
A place where goods and merchandise are temporarily stored before being transported to or from somewhere by road.
The residence of a drover.
An industrial building, plant or site where crude substances, such as sugar, metal, oil etc., are purified or refined.
A works where crude oil is distilled into its fractions or cuts.
A large area, usually open-air, used for permanent, seasonal or regular shows, events or exhibitions.
An open sided building known to have been used for sheltering cattle.
Buildings and structures associated with the manufacture of rope.
A building associated with rope manufacture, especially in naval dockyards.
An iron cover for a manhole
A place of worship for the followers of Buddha.
Use for places of worship. For later landscape features use, eg. GARDEN TEMPLE.
A marker of some form used to indicate the limit of an area or a piece of land.
Linear earthwork boundary denoting furlongs
The limit line of an area pertaining to a medieval manor.
A fence that indicates the limit of an area or a piece of land.
The limit line of a field.
The limit line of a parish.
A ditch that indicates the limit of an area or a piece of land.
The limit line of a medieval local administrative unit of a hundred.
An earthen bank that indicates the limit of an area or a piece of land.
The limit to an area as defined on a map or by a marker of some form, eg. BOUNDARY WALL. Use specific type where known.
The limit line of a township.
Any wall enclosing a building or complex of buildings, eg. prisons, dockyards, factories, etc.
A system of long, continuous banks and/or ditches dividing land into well defined areas. Possibly used for controlling livestock
The limit line of a county.
A building constructed from prefabricated sections. Use more specific type where known.
A classroom constructed from prefabricated sections.
Specialized engineering workshop particularly for the production of marine engines or other large components of ships.
Large covered spaces where the steel plate used for ship construction was cut and marked out, prior to being craned onto the hull, etc.
A shelter in a public park.
A military side-opening aircraft hangar originally designed for seaplanes and used RNAS bases from 1916. Steel framed with asbestos or corrugated iron cladding.
An aircraft hangar designed to house seaplanes.
The residence of a station master.
A group or complex of fields which appear to form a coherent whole. Use more specific type where known.
A field system with one prevailing axis of orientation, in which most field boundaries are either aligned with this axis or run at right angles to it.
A building with facilities for playing snooker.
A house with a pitched roof with a double slope and gables on the front and rear elevations of the building.
A house with a pitched roof with a double slope and gables on the side elevations of the building.
A house with a pitched or gabled roof with a double slope and gables on two or more sides.
The subsoil traces of prehistoric cultivation, presumed to have been caused by the use of an ard to till the soil.
Manmade marks or earthworks which provide evidence for agricultural cultivation.
The subsoil traces of cultivation, presumed to have been caused by the use of a plough to till the soil.
A glasshouse for the cultivation of ferns.
A missile base armed with the Bristol Bloodhound surface-to-air missile. Bloodhounds were deployed to defend the launch sites of Thor Intermediate Range Ballistic Missiles.
An artificial steep-sided earthen mound on, or in, which is set the principal tower of a castle.
A meeting hall of the Temperance Society.
The official residence of the chief officer of the municipal corporation of a city or borough in England.
Establishments responsible for the research into and the design, development and manufacture of nuclear warheads.
Mixed house of nuns and religious men.
A priory of Gilbertine double order of nuns and canons.
A factory for the manufacture of military tanks.
A factory for the manufacture of vehicles
A factory used for the manufacture of scythes.
A factory or works used for the forging and sharpening of a variety of tools including scythes, spades, etc.
A school founded by the British and Foreign Society to provide non-denominational education. Usually built and supported by voluntary contributions.
A school built and/or supported by voluntary contributions.
A school established by the National Society which was founded in 1811 to promote the education of the poor.
A workshop where baskets were manufactured.
A sheltered port for ships.
A floatable concrete vessel, numbers of which made up the main breakwater of the Mulberry Harbours used to secure beachheads during the allied invasion of Europe in June 1944.
A harbour constructed from floating pontoons or caissons connected end to end.
A watch office with additional rooms given over to the meteorological section, including a forecast room and met store.

Based on the previous all-timber design 2423/39 and the temporary brick and timber design 518/40, the 8936/40 was built with pre-cast concrete slabs replacing the timber floors and staircases with only the balcony and watch office roof in timber.
A building used as headquarters by the Territorial Army, the volunteer reserve of the British army.
A high-humped, narrow, cobbled bridge used by trains of packhorses, often located in upland areas where the bulk of goods were carried by horses.
A building used to store coal.
A fuel store for the storage of dried peat.
A place where material used for burning is stored.
A signal station incorporating equipment for visually conveying coded communications.
An engine powered by high pressure water, originally used in mine drainage.
A machine, powered by steam, gas, electricity or other energy source, which produces energy of movement. Use for stationary industrial engines rather than transport use.
A large drain or conduit for carrying away wastes.
The outlet or mouth of a sewer where it dispenses into the sea, lake, etc.
Manmade constructions used to prevent water flooding the surrounding area. Often taking the form of a bank or wall but may be more elaborate e.g. the Thames Barrier.
A channel dug, or built up, to carry away surplus water from a river or waterway to prevent it bursting its banks and flooding.

A group of four houses in quadruplex form within a single block, of approximately square plan and set in a spacious garden. Such houses were usually provided for supervisory or skilled workers within a textile factory.
A stable found at a coaching inn where horses are housed.
A stable located at a railway station or goods yard. Horses were necessary both for freight and passengers to continue their journey beyond the railway.
A stable, on two or more levels.
A stable used for riding horses or those used to pull coaches, gigs, etc.
