A stable where horses are kept at livery, or are let out for hire.
A stable associated with a horse-drawn tramway system.
A building in which horses are accommodated.
A building combining a pigsty at ground level with a poultry house in a loft over.

A term for a type of house, with varying definitions according to period. Roman villas were high-status and usually associated with a rural estate, whereas Georgian and later period villas were often semi-detached, town houses.
Areas of land that have been designated as national property where habitation and commercial activities are restricted to preserve their outstanding landscapes.
A pier where passsengers can embark and disembark and goods can be transferred to and from vessels.
A form of floating, moveable pier designed for use in open water.
A structure of iron or wood, open below, running out into the sea and used as a promenade and landing stage.

An airfield building housing a turret gunnery trainer used to teach air gunners how to report the correct position of enemy aircraft by practising shooting against projected moving images of enemy aircraft displayed on a target screen (WWII).

A section of the water channel on a canal or river shut off above and below by lock gates provided with sluices to let the water out and in, and thus raise or lower boats from one level to another. Use more specific type where known.
A lock where the gates rise vertically. Rarely found on canals but common on navgable rivers in the Fens, particularly the river Nene.
A complex of buildings used for the processing of metals. Use more specific type where known.
A site used for the extraction of metallic zinc by a variety of processes.

Accommodation given rent-free along with or as part of a corrody, which is a provision of an annual allowance of food and money by a religious house to an individual, usually in return for service or by purchase. Term used until mid 16th century AD.
A mine for the extraction of iron ore.
A working tunnel or gallery in a mine used for the extraction of ironstone.
A site where iron ore is extracted.
A large pit formed by, and for, the extraction of iron ore.
A place where people were put to death. Use narrower monument type where known.
A natural or man-made earth mound on which a gallows was erected.
An aircraft hangar built to Air Ministry design. Mainly constructed on aircraft factory aerodromes.

A permanent military RAF aircraft hangar type, designed in 1924. It features a steel frame (with longitudinal ridge and valley trusses for the roof) reinforced concrete and brick infilling for the walls. Typically 122 foot span by 249 foot in length.
An aircraft hangar built to Air Ministry design number 454/43. Mainly constructed on aircraft factory aerodromes

A building as part of a workhouse, prison or hospital, often including porter's lodge, baths, clothes store, washrooms, casual cells, rooms etc, for receiving inmates/patients. Use term from Components thesaurus if it is part of a building complex.
A building, structure or landscape created to commemorate a person or event.
A structure, building or site commemorating soldiers and civilians killed in war.
A freestanding structure commemorating nations, actions, soldiers and/or civilians that served or died as a result of conflict.
An attached plaque, inscription, mural or display commemorating nations, actions, soldiers and/or civilians that served or died as a result of conflict.
An excavation from which stone for building and other functions, is obtained by cutting, blasting, etc.
A site used for the small scale extraction and working of surface boulders.
A building in a quarry consisting of a series of loading bays in which stone is loaded onto wagons.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the extraction of stone. Includes preparation processes.
A residential home for children with physical or learning disabilities, sensory impairment and/or mental health issues but who do not necessarily need medical attention.

Accommodation used as an alternative to the workhouse following several Poor Law Acts. Modelled on continental examples and first erected at the end of the 1860s, it is based on the idea of a "village" of small houses accommodating a small group.
A residential home for children with physical and/or learning disabilities, sensory impairment and/or mental health issues who need medical intervention and/or care provided by registered nurses.
A public institution for the care and protection of children without parents.
A residential establishment for the care and accommodation of children and young people.
A service building to a country house, farm, etc, used for baking. If commercial premises use BAKERY.
A bakehouse built in association with a group of dwellings who shared the baking facilities. Often found in model settlements.
An unsocketed earthenware or porous concrete pipe laid end to end unjointed so as to drain the ground.
A drainage structure that extends across and beneath roadways, canals or embankments.
A horizontal tunnel dug specifically for draining, for example, a mine.
An artificial channel for draining water or carrying it off.
A large drainage channel used for improving the land.
A long, narrow ditch designed to carry water away from a waterlogged area.
A prepared area of grass on which the game of rugby is played.
A building, site or structure associated with the playing of ball sports.
A building used for the storage of picked fruit.
Terms included here are for small scale agricultural production. See also FOOD AND DRINK INDUSTRY SITE grouping in INDUSTRIAL class.
A factory where china products are manufactured.
a wooden, metal or stone post used to tether a horse, or other animals.
A building offering accommodation to people who are visiting a town or locality renowned for its mineral springs.
Engineering works specializing in the production and maintenance of non-passenger carrying railway rolling stock.
A piece of ice or a floor, often within a building, used for skating.
An inn, with an integral courtyard, for the lodging and entertainment of travellers. Often with open galleried wings overlooking the courtyard.
A public house for the lodging and entertainment of travellers, etc.
Use for distinct structure on a large scale.
A building used to pump sewage from the sewers to the filter beds of a sewage works.
A waterworks pumping station.
A pumping station used as part of a clean water supply system.
An optical instrument for making distant objects appear nearer and larger, often found on the promenade or pleasure pier at a seaside resort or at a site of scenic beauty.
Accommodation, often in private houses or lodgings, provided for military personnel.
Accommodation in hired rooms or a lodging house.
A type of clothier's house, consisting of TOPSHOP and dwelling, used for hand-weaving of textiles.

A confusing and baffling network of winding and intercommunicating paths, often bordered by high hedges or walls. Some early examples are believed to have had ritual uses. Use more specific type where known.
A maze used for the act of penitence.
A target range used for rifle and small arms practice and recreational purposes.
A mound or structure on which an archery, musketry or artillery target is erected. Use specific type where known.
A bridge manufactured from prefabricated sections.
A type of temporary bridge designed by Sir Donald C.Bailey during the Second World War.
A crane or hoist within a building found mainly in the North of England. Can also refer to a projecting crane located above a loading slot.
A mechanical lift or elevator, used to lift goods, etc.
An aircraft maintenance workshop deriving from the use of weather proofing varnish to aircraft canvas called "dope" in order to keep the canvas taut and airtight. From 1912 onwards.
A building found at the site of a mine. Use specific type where known.
A building containing the colliery showers. Also often containing first aid and mine rescue facilities.
A workshop in which carded wool was passed through heated combs to straighten and separate the long and short fibres prior to spinning. Associated with the worsted branch of the textile industry.
A building used to dry teazle heads in. Teazles were used to raise the nap on cloth in teazle shops.
Large wooden hammer beams pounding cloth in a fulling solution.
A factory where worsted, a well-twisted woollen yarn made from long staple wool and used in the manufacture of suits and other garments, was produced.
A mill used for the manufacture of twilled dress material of worsted with or without a mixture of cotton or silk.
A mill for beating and cleaning cloth, using soap or fullers earth.
Recovery and removal of grease (lanolin) from raw wool.
A structure used for drying yarn in open fields.
A mill where long-staple hair, often from llamas, is made into yarn.
A factory used for the manufacture of serge, a heavy woollen cloth.
A factory where short wool was spun into woollen yarn to produce cloth.
A mill for the manufacture of low grade cloth made from ground-up heavy woollen rags.
A factory where tweed, a twilled woollen fabric with an unfinished surface, is manufactured.
A textile mill where felt is produced.
A building in which the fibres of new woollen cloth were raised by brushing with teazle heads.
A house for drying wool after fulling and dying.
Includes worsted and other wool-related textiles.
A building used to dry wool in.
A barn used for the storage and drying of wool.
1st World War end-opening aeroplane hangar.
A dwelling for the keeper of a canal wharf.
An ornate public house that developed in the 1830s after the passing of a law to encourage the drinking of beer in alehouses licensed for the sale of beer only.
The public house was a 19th century development, distinctive from the earlier BEER HOUSE by its decorative treatment and fittings.
Establishments authorized to sell or allow the consumption of alcoholic liquors on their premises.

An establishment where alcoholic and non alcoholic drinks are served, food may also be served. May be a an individual room within a larger multi purpose building such as a sports pavilion or a theatre.
A licenced establishment where wine and other alcoholic drinks are sold for drinking on the premises.
A building licensed for the sale of beer.
Similar in design to the FROMSON HANGAR but designed to drawing number 3752/43 and used for storing aircraft with small wingspans.
A small arched hangar built by the Canadian company Fromson of Byfleet to drawing number 3971/43. Used only as storage sheds on RNASs.
The residence of a dock worker.
A pillbox built to a design drawn up by the chief engineer of South-Eastern Command.
A device used to remove pollutants from gas or smoke produced during industrial processes such as burning high-sulphur fuels.
A large discharge pipe with a valve for drawing water from a water main. Used to help extinguish fires.
An ancillary building to a synagogue, used as a place of worship at the feast of the tabernacle.
A house for storing or drying saddles.
A factory where knitted fabrics are manufacterd using knitting machines.
A factory where hats are manufactured.
A factory where gloves are manufactured.
A factory where shirts are manufactured.
A factory where collars, for shirts and other garments, are manufactured.
A factory or site where wooden clogs are manufactured.
A factory where boots and shoes are manufactured.
A factory or works housing machinery used to produce stockings and socks, using mechanized knitting processes.
A large factory or series of workshops for the manufacture of clothing.
A factory used for the production of red lead used in glass manufacture, or white lead used as the pigment in white paint.
Workshop for the construction and maintenance of boilers within an industrial complex.
An ancilliary building or structure associated with a military base. Use only where exact function is unknown otherwise use more specific term.
A hut, usually built as part of a complex on a military base or airfield and used for the recreation of military personnel.
A building used for the daily administration of the Royal Air Force.
An approximately circular or oval setting of spaced, usually freestanding, upright stones. More than one circle may be present, arranged concentrically.

A stone circle featuring four upright stones standing at the corners of an irregular quadrilateral. The monument may feature more than 4 stones, overall, but the corner stones are often the most prominent.
A building or site used for the manufacture of swords.
A place of worship for members of the Serbian Orthodox Church, the national church of Serbia.
A place of worship for followers of the Eastern Orthodox churches. This family of churches separated from the Western church in the 11th century and recognizes the Patriarch of Constantinople.
A place of worship for members of the Romanian Orthodox Church, the national church of Romania.
A place of worship for members of the Greek Orthodox Church, the national church of Greece.
A place of worship for followers of the Orthodox Catholic Church. Use only where the specific denomination is unknown.
A place of worship for members of the Russian Orthodox Church, the national church of Russia.

A structure consisting of different cells equipped with instrument posts which supported finders. These provided range and bearing of the projected position of the target to guns emplaced in a nearby battery. Errected along the coast in the late 1870s.
A site used for the production of sodium bicarbonate, soda ash or caustic soda.
An establishment where wagering and the placing of bets takes place.
A workshop or factory where brass articles are made by casting molten material into a mould.
A brass manufacturing complex incorporating battery mill furnaces, hammers, etc.
A landing circle marked out in white used as the airfield symbol.
A group of buildings where consumer goods, such as small machines and electrical components, are manufactured.
A site where iron or steel bolts, and often their accompanying nuts, are manufactured. Sometimes referred to as NUT AND BOLT WORKS.
Room, usually part of another building, for storing and preparing roots and other animal feed.
A building used to prepare and store dry food such as hay and straw for the feeding of cattle.
Buildings and structures associated with the production, processing and storage of coal gas.
An industrial complex concerned with the manufacture of gas for domestic use from coal and oil.
Buildings, sites and structures used by mariners for purposes of navigation.
A building specifically built to house life saving apparatus used when conditions prevented the lifeboat from deploying.
A building designed to house a lifeboat, usually with a stone ramp to launch the boat into the sea.
A building on a river or canal in which the water levels are controlled.
A picture or pattern produced by cementing together small pieces of stone or glass of various colours. May be in the form of a floor.

A device, monogram or symbol usually carved on stone or woodwork near a buildingï¿½s entrance points, particularly doorways, windows and fireplaces, to protect inhabitants and visitors from witches and evil spirits.
An area of the floor, wall or ceiling of a building, which has been painted, carved, sculpted or decorated.
A painting executed directly onto a wall.
Casual scribbles or pictographs on ancient walls, stones or other surfaces. In more recent times applied to humourous, satiric or obscene writings or drawings executed anonymously in public places.
A picture or pattern produced by either by cementing together small pieces of stone or glass of various colours or by painting directly onto a wall.
A carved figure or design.
A device, monogram or symbol incised in stonework by a mason as a means of identifying his work. Particularly common in Romanesque and Gothic buildings.
The residence of a vicar, parson or rector.
A residence for all clergy having the sole or subordinate charge of a living.
A large pit formed by, and for, the extraction of iron ore.
A mine for the extraction of iron ore.
A site where iron ore is extracted.
A working tunnel or gallery in a mine used for the extraction of ironstone.
A hospital department, open 24 hours a day, for the immediate reception and treatment of emergency cases.
A factory used for the manufacture and assembly of lorries.
A shop where meat is sold. Often includes large cold stores for the refrigeration and storage of carcasses and a butchery where the carcass is cut up prior to sale.
An outlying farm or estate belonging to the Gilbertine order.
A place where products are manufactured from wood.
A residence of two or three monks of the Augustinian order dependent on a foreign mother house.
A residence of two or three monks dependent on a foreign mother house sent to exploit a distant estate. Alien houses were officially suppressed in 1414.
A path for pedestrians only.
A way made for pedestrians, especially one merely made by walking (often not specially constructed).
A pillbox in which the roof is detached from the walls and supported by a central pillar, thus leaving an embrasure allowing a 360 degree field of fire.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the construction and maintenance of railways and rolling stock.
A building used specifically for testing the boilers of railway engines, both hydraulically and with live steam.
Garden associated with a crematorium where the ashes of the deceased are scattered or buried.
A garden associated with a crematorium where the ashes of deceased infants are scattered or buried.
Houses specifically for men and of chiefly mendicant religious orders. The status of priory is represented in several friaries. Use with PRIORY if required.
A house of friars, originally hermits from Mount Carmel. Also known as ' white friars'.
Covered area for making large engineered constructions such as sections of ships or bridges.
A building, or room within a brewery, where beer or cider undergoes fermentation in vats or tuns.
A bridge crossing under railway property.
A dwelling house forming part of a Chartist Land Colony.
A building used to accommodate ducks.
A building, usually one-storeyed, for dyeing cloth.
A stable where horses are kept at livery, or are let out for hire.
A stable associated with a horse-drawn tramway system.
A stable located at a railway station or goods yard. Horses were necessary both for freight and passengers to continue their journey beyond the railway.
A stable, on two or more levels.
A building in which horses are accommodated.
A stable found at a coaching inn where horses are housed.
A stable used for riding horses or those used to pull coaches, gigs, etc.
A purpose-built model village for the workers on a country house estate.
A type of factory building, often single-storey, designed so that windows incorporated into the vertical faces of its saw-tooth roof can allow the maximum amount of natural light into its interior.

A circular bank in which trees have been planted for ornamental purposes or to create an enclosure. May exist purely as a bank which has been formed over the stumps of the trees which had been planted to form the enclosure.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the processing of non ferrous metal ores.
A stone-lined pit or tank, sometimes circular, for concentrating ores by sedimentation.
A monastic enclave dependent on a mother house.

A residence of two or three monks of the Savigniac order dependent on a foreign mother house. The order was originally founded by monks in Savigny, Normandy, in 1105 and first established in Britain in 1123 at Tulket, Preston.
A house with a range at the end of it, at right angles to the main range.
A house consisting of a public hall with private living accommodation attached. Built from the medieval period onwards.
A building used for the collection and storage of electricity using large lead-acid batteries (accumulators).
A device for converting one voltage of alternating current to another voltage.

Usually dating from the early 20th century these cabinets, sited alongside public highways, were used for the distribution of electricity for street lighting control and later for domestic use. In Wolverhampton these boxes also serviced the tram system.
A tall, metal structure erected as a support for electric power cables.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the production of electricity.
Wooden or ferro-concrete tower for cooling waste, hot water from a power station. The water cascades from the top of the tower to a pond in the bottom.
A building or set of buildings and structures where power, especially electrical or mechanical, is generated. Use more specific type where known.
Building housing switch gear to control electricity supply either to the National Grid, industrial or domestic premises.
A building housing transformers to convert AC electricity supply for domestic use.
A building or structure where electricity is generated.
Building containing transformers to reduce the high voltage of the National Grid to the lower voltage of domestic supply.
A sculpted cross, or a cross incised into stone or trees, to mark a parish boundary.
A wind-powered pump for land drainage.
A private school offering term time accommodation for pupils being taught there.
Usually a cotton spinning factory, although some mills have weaving sheds attached, in which case the end product is completed cloth, not yarn only.
Textile mill producing calico, ie. coarse, unbleached cotton cloth.
A tower or turret in which bells are hung.
A tower containing a curfew bell. The bell was rung in the evening, as a signal that fires were to be extinguished.
A port, dock or harbour where ferries, hovercraft, ocean liners and cargo vessels can load and unload. May include road and/or rail terminals for transportation to the port.

An area of a port, dock or harbour, often including buildings for passport control and customs, where passengers and vehicles using hovercraft services can embark/disembark and where supplies can be taken on board.
A mill where long-staple hair, often from llamas, is made into yarn.
A naval dockyard building used for the manufacture of flags.
A residential district planned as a unit.
A housing estate comprised of housing stock owned and let by a local authority.
A prominent structure situated on land specifically as a guide to navigation for travellers or as an aid/warning to sailors out at sea.
A hospital which has been built either wholly, or partially, underground in order to protect it from attacks by enemy aircraft.

A tower or structure, with a powerful light or lights at the top, usually erected at an important or dangerous point on or near the sea-coast for the warning and guidance of mariners, but can also be erected inland for the guidance of travellers.
A lighted pillar or LIGHTHOUSE, eg. Dunston Pillar, Lincs., erected in 1751 to guide travellers over the heath.
An ornate public house that developed in the 1830s after the passing of a law to encourage the drinking of beer in alehouses licensed for the sale of beer only.
A factory where china products are manufactured.
A building in which pottery ware is made by shaping plastic clay on a spinning turntable, known as a potter's wheel or throwing wheel.
A house devoted to the shelter of the poor and endowed by a benefactor for this use.
skos:Concept.skos:altLabel: Asylum For Aged And Decayed Freemasons

skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: A defensive bank and ditch, circular or oval in plan, surrounding one or more buildings.
A building or site where phosphorous-based fertilizers are produced by controlled chemical reactions.
A building or site producing nitrogen-rich fertilizer.
A chemical works engaged in the production of Ammonium Nitrate, used as a fertilizer or for use in the explosives industry.
A building or site used for the production of both chemical and organic fertilizer.
Buildings, structures or sites used for the production of chemicals used in agriculture, such as fertilizers and weed killers.
A site used by the Air Raid Precautions network. Use more specific term.
A brick built railway signal box, usually with a reinforced correct roof, designed to minimize the effects of blast damage from aerial bombardment and thus protect the signalling equipment.
The main administrative building and headquarters of a regiment
A building used for the daily administration of an army.
An impression made in soft ground by a passing animal or human. The soft ground may have subsequently hardened.
A permanently occupied position or building designed primarily for defence.
A fort with a star trace plan, designed to increase the angles of fire.
A building or site used in the production of enamelled goods.
A small eating and drinking establishment or refreshment bar at a railway station for the use of passengers.
A small eating and drinking establishment or refreshment bar.
Large open hearth furnace often located inside a brick cone for use in steelmaking.
A large dish-like structure designed to observe the invisible outerspace phenomena detected by radio waves, eg. Jodrell Bank.
Mill for grinding bark usually for use in the tanning industry. Use with power type(s), eg. WATERMILL where known.
A mill used to process raw timber.
A commercial premises offering advice on destinations and other travel arrangements, and where travellers may purchase flights,make hotel reservations or book package holidays and tours.
A form of inhumation in which the skeleton is interred, usually on its side, with hip and knee joints bent through an angle of more than 90 degrees.
An interment of unburnt, articulated human remains. Use specific type where known.
1st World War end-opening aeroplane hangar.
An earthen bank indicating the limit of a wood or coppice
A place where ceramic tiles are manufactured.
A mill whose machinery is driven by water.
A water mill where the waterwheel directly drives a vertical shaft with grindstones on.
A plate, usually of wood or metal, set up on a road, canal or railway to mark the miles from or to a place.
A bridge which takes a towing path over a branch canal, basin, etc.

Soil marks and other features of natural origin, including periglacial frost wedging, solifluction deposits, abandoned water courses, etc, recorded to avoid future confusion with features of human origin.
The open space surrounded by a cloister.
Upright stones engraved on the edges with a Celtic script consisting of lines or notches.
Obstacles, including scaffolding and anti tank blocks designed to impede an enemy's attempts to land forces onto open beaches.
Obstacles such as scaffolding, barbed wire and concrete blocks or cylinders placed on a beach to impede the progress of enemy soldiers, vehicles or watercraft landing from the sea.
A single-span aircraft hangar designed by Boulton & Paul of London and Norwich (drawing number 4178/44). Mainly used on aircraft factory sites and at Armament Training Schools.
An optical instrument for making distant objects appear nearer and larger, usually found at an observatory, through which astronomical or meteorological phenomena may be observed.
A telescope which is mounted so as to allow the observation of only those objects in the sky which are passing over a local meridian, an event known as transit.
A textile factory where the process of doubling, the twisting together of two spun yarns, takes place.
A building used to dry wool in.
A finishing process for cloth involving the pounding of the cloth with heavy weights.
A type of calcining kiln used in arsenic manufacture.

A calciner commonly used between 1870 and circa 1900 for extracting arsenic from mined ores and featuring a slightly inclined rotating iron tube with a firebox at the bottom and an ore feed at the top.
Any factory or site using machine tools in a manufacturing or processing capacity.
Engineering works dedicated solely to the manufacture and repair of boilers.

A purpose-built facility providing an area for wheeled sports, such as skateboarding, skating and BMX cycling, equipped with ramps and other structures and obstacles for the performance of tricks and manoeuvres.
Fixed or hardened installation for machine guns. Temporary soft installations are possible as well.
A mill used for the preparation of raw fleece etc, for spinning by a coarse form of carding.
A public house offering lodgings to the passengers, and stabling for the horses of stage coaches.
An artificial paved bank or solid landing place built parallel to, or projecting out from, the shoreline to serve in the loading and unloading of vessels.
A structure, composed of oven and hovel, used for the firing of pottery ware.
A low-temperature oven for the firing of metallic-based colour onto pottery after glazing.
A radar station with sets operating on a wavelength of 1.5m. Chain Home Low Stations were intended for use in locating low-flying aircraft but was also capable of detecting high-flying aircraft.

Part of the WWII air defence radar system, whereby in 1939 a chain of radar stations were established along the south and east coast of Britain. The equipment was based upon apparatus developed for ionospheric research.
A textile mill where felt is produced.

A bridge consisting of a lattice girder spanning the distance between the tops of two towers. Designed to transport vehicles across the gap in a container suspended at road level by ropes under a travelling crane on the girder.
A factory, works or structure used for the manufacture and purification of gas.
A type of late 19th century tenement block for tenants of a higher social status - usually reflected in the more ornate facades.
A purpose-built tenement. Use specific monument type where possible.
A council-owned block of flats.
A college associated with, or forming part of, a university.
A dam which can be raised or lowered to regulate the flow of water.
A dam and sluice combination, associated with an aqueduct, for the extraction of water from a river to feed a reservoir or water treatment plant.
A works used for the production of parchment from animal skin.
A site where iron oxide and iron sulphates, used as brown pigments, are excavated.
An establishment where patients can rest and recover after an operation or illness.

skos:Concept.skos:prefLabel: Hospital For People With Learning Difficulties
skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: A hospital where people with learning difficulties receive medical treatment.
A hospital providing medical, surgical or psychiatric testing and treatment for patients with specific illnesses or injuries.

Nowadays a hospital where patients suffering from psychiatric disorders receive medical care and treatment. Traditionally they were often places where psychiatric patients were kept confined away from society receiving minimal medical care or attention.
A storage facility used for the accommodation and dispersal of vehicles. Often used by the military and emergency services.
A site, usually including hardstandings and associated buildings, where ambulances can be parked and stored.
Platform or structure used for viewing performances.
A type of coal preparation plant for the sizing, sorting and washing of coal.
An educational establishment primarily for children aged 16-18 years old but can provide education for more mature students.
A tower-like structure of wood or brick with a wooden cap and sails which are driven around by the wind producing power to work the internal machinery. Use with product type where known.
A type of windmill, mainly timber-framed, whose body, containing machinery and carrying the sail, rotates about an upright post.
A post mill in which the drive is taken down to the base of the mill by putting an upright shaft in the hollowed post.
Any church which bears signs of fortification. Churches on the Welsh and Scottish borders were often fortified, only allowing access to the tower from a single opening in the nave.
A building in which wrought iron or steel chains were manufactured.
An area, with fixed defences, designed to act as a focal point for a defending force.
A house which has been altered to increase its defensive characteristics.
A building which has been altered to increase its defensive characteristics. Use more specific term where known.
A large pillbox-like structure, often L-shaped or angular, with numerous loopholes used as a defensive position.
An area, often consisting of widened streets or a town square, where booths and stalls may be erected for public sales.

Areas within the urban environment with their surfaces open to the sky, that have been consciously acquired or publicly regulated to serve urban shaping function, in addition others may provide recreational opportunities.
A factory which produces artificial imitations of mineral water, such as soda water.
The residence of a miller, often attached to a mill.

Use to identify a feature, previously thought to be a monument but now disproved, or to avoid erroneous identification as a monument in future. Where a feature is regarded as an antiquity, but is unclassified, use SITE.
A system of lights, controlled fires or dummy constructions, used to simulate a dockyard and thus confuse enemy aircraft into bombing these counterfeit targets.
A system of lights, controlled fires or dummy constructions, used to simulate an airfield and thus confuse enemy aircraft into bombing these counterfeit targets.
A system of lights, controlled fires or dummy constructions, used to simulate a railway yard or sidings and thus confuse enemy aircraft into bombing these counterfeit targets.
A site comprising a system of lights, controlled fires or dummy constructions, used during WWII to provide a counterfeit target for enemy aircraft. Use more specific type where known.
A site equipped for active defensive action against an airborne enemy assault.
Partly subterranean operations rooms for the lighting arrays of the various types of bombing decoys in use during the Second World War.
A decoy site designed to simulate permitted lighting, such as locomotives, furnaces and tramwire flashes, to lure attacking night bombers away from legitimate targets.
A decoy fire positioned close to a legitimate target which would be lit in the event of an incendiary attack in the hope that subsequent bombs would be drawn to the area of the decoy.
A decoy site designed to simulate a burning urban area during a bombing raid in order to lure enemy bombers away from legitimate targets.
A system of lights, controlled fires or dummy constructions, used to simulate a domestic site such as a city and thus confuse enemy aircraft into bombing counterfeit targets.
An object supported by a crosspiece on a post, used by knights as a target in tilting.
A factory used for the industrial manufacture of chlorophyll for medical purposes.
A large-scale site where medicinal drugs are maufactured.
An old ship hull used as a base for lifting tackle.
A building forming part of a colliery ventilation system exhausting stale air from shafts and headings.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the drainage and/or ventilation of mines.
A hall used for housing public displays.
A hall used for the promotion and selling of horticultural produce and practice.
Art applied in pigment to rock wether in the form of a free-standing stone or the walls of a cave.
Refers to art, whether carving or painting, applied to free -standing stones or cave walls.

A large type of military repair hangar mainly used on WWII bomber bases, constructed using steel stanchions and clad in corrugated iron. B 1 hangars were part of a series of prefabricated buildings intended to supplement existing hangars on bases.
Aircraft hangars designed by T. Bedford Consulting Engineers to meet the requirement to repair damaged heavy bombers in situ on their airfields.
The offices of a Government Department responsible for the administration of the country.
A building which houses the administrative functions of a local authority.
A building from which the administration of a county is carried out by the County Council. It is also, historically, the site where the county quarter sessions and assizes were held.
An excavation made in the earth for the purpose of digging out metallic ores, coal, salt, or precious stones etc. Use specific type where known.
A place where coal is mined.
A kiln with a pyramid roof and capped vent in which barley is dried. Found on the site of a malt house.
A house with an open hall whose main span is separated by an arcade from the side aisles.
A building used to accommodate elephants at a zoo or wildlife park.
A small building used as a shelter by a shepherd.
A large tract of land covered with trees and interspersed with open areas of land. Traditionally forests were owned by the monarchy and had their own laws.
An area of land, heavily though not totally covered with trees, set aside for the royal hunt by Norman and Plantagenet kings.
Power station using domestic refuse as its principal fuel.

A type of warehouse found in naval victualling yards, used for the storage of rum, a ration of which was given on a daily basis to members of the Royal Navy, up until the 1980s, when this practice ceased.
A wealden house with only one end being jettied.
A house where the upper storeys rest on projecting floor joists and so create the effect of an overhang.
A medieval house with central open hall and two storey bays, jettied at first floor level, on either side.
A wooden stake fence, often associated with deer hunting.
A multi-purpose, two-storey barn, built on a hillside with entrances at both levels to a first floor threshing barn and ground floor animal housing.
A threshing barn which also houses farm animals and is somethimes used to stotre grain, house carts and other functions.
Open sided barn for the storage of wood produced by the periodic cutting of small trees.
A barn in which a central space is separated from side aisles by posts and braces.
A barn with steam powered threshing.
An isolated barn, cow house or shelter shed with a hayloft. Typically found in areas where farmsteads and fields were sited at a long distance from each other.
A building for the storage and processing of grain crops and for housing straw, farm equipment and occasionally livestock and their fodder. Use more specific type where known.
A barn usually containing a single, central threshing floor.
A large barn used to store the tithe (a tenth part of the annual produce of agriculture etc.) which was paid by the tenants of ecclesiastical lands.
A barn belonging to, or associated with, a grange.
A barn which is constructed with a timber framework; between the members are panels which are infilled with timber, wattle and daub, plaster, brickwork, stone or other materials.
A special type of barn, lacking a threshing floor, usually with open walls, intended for the dry and well ventilated storage of hay only.
A barn used to store hops.

A site used primarily for domestic purposes on at least a semi-permanent or seasonal basis, and which has been surrounded by a bank and ditch, palisade, or some other form of enclosure. Use more specific type(s) where appropriate.

A small, defended settlement dating to the Early Iron Age, located on spurs, promontories or hilltops. The defences are marked by single or double trenches which originally held substantial palisades.
A substantial area of ground surrounded by slight univallate earthwork often interpreted as stock enclosures or as sites where agricultural produce was stored.
An interment of a human body that displays unusual burial practice such as positioning of the body, decapitation, dismemberment or over-secure burial.
A Neolithic burial monument comprising a stone-built chamber within a circular or sub-circular earthen mound. See RELIGIOUS, RITUAL AND FUNERARY Class List for context.
A 'through' BACK TO BACK HOUSE - an interlocking L-shaped plan gave each house two street frontages, thus providing better lighting/ventilation.
A house in a line of houses attached to and adjoining one another and planned and built as one unit.
A house in a terrace consisting of a double row of houses sharing a common back wall, characteristic of industrial cities in the North of England.

A very long, narrow, roofed building, often two-storeyed, used for the manufacture of rope. Often attached to warehousing, an engine house or offices. Can be included within the complex of a textile mill.
An alloy of tin, antimony and copper used as a replacement for pewter.
An area of prepared ground on which a sport is played. Use more specific type where known.
An area of ground used for children to play on, often attached to a school.
A public ground with facilities for games and other activities.
A training ground and fighting arena for knightly sports.
A field or piece of ground used for the playing of games and other activities.
A recreation ground with usually permanent structure. It usually contains rides such as ghost trains, helter skelter and roller coasters.
A sports pitch usually with a synthetic surface (ie. not grass).
A garden or park, with ancilliary buildings, in which wild animals are kept and reared for public exhibition.

A garden or park, with ancilliary buildings, in which young and domesticated animals are kept for public exhibition, especially for children. Children are given the opportunity to come into close contact and handle animals.
Specialized engineering workshop particularly for the production of marine engines or other large components of ships.
A building or site used for the production of anchors.
A stone used to cover a grave.
A slab of stone, either standing or recumbent, inscribed with a cross. Usually found in association with burials.
A small brick structure attached to a house for keeping fish prior to cooking.
An area of hardstanding, surrounded on three sides by a protective wall or bank, used for parking aircraft, in a state of readiness, usually around the perimeter of an airfield.
A turf-covered mound in a curvilinear E-shape, and hard-standing to take an aircraft. There were usually an access point to an air raid shelter at the rear. In use during WW2
A shop which dispenses medicinal drugs and other health-related items. Can include an area for the preparation and manufacture of medicines and other drugs.
A factory used for the industrial manufacture of firelighters.
Building housing a form of early steam engine using steam at atmospheric pressure. Chiefly employed in mine pumping.
Engine driving a continuous wire rope for the haulage of tubs in a mine and at the heapstead.
A building housing a gas engine, used as a power source for driving other machinery.
A building housing an engine. Use specific type where known.
A building housing a turbine.
A round or polygonal building containing a HORSE ENGINE. Commonly found on farms next to the threshing barn, where it is used to power the machinery.
An engine house used to pump water to the top of an ACCUMULATOR TOWER.
Steam engine, usually, driving a centrifugal fan to provide an air blast for a blast furnace.
A building housing a steam engine.
A building housing the engines used to power equipment used by a searchlight, anti-aircraft or coastal battery.
An engine house which used air pressure to power trains on the experimental atmospheric railways of the 1840s.

A site used primarily for domestic purposes on at least a semi-permanent or seasonal basis, and which has been surrounded by a bank and ditch, palisade, or some other form of enclosure. Use more specific type(s) where appropriate.
A settlement showing evidence for one or more hut circles, enclosed by a distinct boundary ditch, wall, earth rampart or similar barrier. Characteristic of the later prehistoric period.
A workshop used for the manufacture of items of jewellery and/or timepieces from precious metals and precious or semi-precious stones.
A place where silverware is manufactured.
A place where gold is worked into articles or products.
A textile factory where the process of doubling, the twisting together of two spun yarns, takes place.
A factory where fish are processed into food products.
An automata or water device which surprises the unwary onlooker with water. A feature of 16th and 17th century gardens.

An artificial aperture from which water springs. The water supply usually came from a lake or reservoir higher up in order to ensure the necessary flow and pressure. More recently fountains have been powered by pumps.
A factory where ribbons are manufactured.

A type of temporary military aircraft hangar introduced in 1940; of steel welded and bolted construction typically clad in galvanized corrugated iron sheets. The T2 became the standard temporary hangar for the RAF in World War Two.
A temporary, steel-framed transportable hangar developed by Teesside Bridge and Engineering Company to replace the obsolete Bellman hangars.
A garden building on an estate used by fishing parties.
The residence and small-scale workshop of a hosier.

A tower or structure, with a powerful light or lights at the top, usually erected at an important or dangerous point on or near the sea-coast for the warning and guidance of mariners, but can also be erected inland for the guidance of travellers.
A lighted pillar or LIGHTHOUSE, eg. Dunston Pillar, Lincs., erected in 1751 to guide travellers over the heath.
A mill used for the manufacture of narrow strips of woven fabric used in the closing or fixing of garments, or for binding the edges of fabric goods.
A mill or works where needles were manufactured.
Traditionally the premises of a chandler, a maker and seller of candles. Now, a shop for the retail of groceries and other provisions.
A type of calcining kiln used in arsenic manufacture.

A calciner commonly used between 1870 and circa 1900 for extracting arsenic from mined ores and featuring a slightly inclined rotating iron tube with a firebox at the bottom and an ore feed at the top.
A mill, including a forge and powered hammers where hot metal is shaped by hammering and rolling.
A trough or gutter for conveying liquids such as water or molten metal. It can be cut in the surface or formed of wood or other materials.
A mill which contains machinery for separating grain from the chaff.
A bank formed at the end of a field by soil which, loosened by the plough, gradually moves down slope through a combination of gravity and erosion.
A terraced field usually found on hillsides. Comprising a flat strip of land, called the tread, and a steep, scarped lynchet or edge, called the riser.
An early form of railway for the transportation of freight by wagons on rails on a road.
A track consisting of flanged strips used in early colliery railways.
A track inlaid into a surface, on which tram cars run for the conveyance of passengers and/or goods or raw materials.
A track inlaid into the road surface of a street or road, on which tram cars run for the conveyance of passengers.
A building used for the storage of equipment.
Sites and buildings used for the storage or equipment, ordnance or vehicles. Use more specific term.

A site used for the safe storage of the art held in the national collections. During the Second World War many paintings, sculptures and works of art were moved to modified mines for safe keeping to protect them against bomb damage.

A type of tower mill, either with turbine-type sails able to take wind from any direction, or with sails working with shrouds to direct wind from one direction. The sails directly drove millstones set beneath them.
A defensive battery positioned facing out to sea enabling the guns to be brought to bear on enemy shipping and amphibious craft.
A command post used to direct the guns of a coastal battery.
A defensive gun battery positioned to face out to sea to fire on enemy ships and amphibious craft.
A grave which has been formed by cutting into the bedrock of a site.

A small, defended settlement dating to the Early Iron Age, located on spurs, promontories or hilltops. The defences are marked by single or double trenches which originally held substantial palisades.
A substantial area of ground surrounded by slight univallate earthwork often interpreted as stock enclosures or as sites where agricultural produce was stored.

An airfield building housing a turret gunnery trainer used to teach air gunners how to report the correct position of enemy aircraft by practising shooting against projected moving images of enemy aircraft displayed on a target screen (WWII).
A factory where jute (plant fibres), was used to make products such as hessian, sacking, cordage and backing materials for carpet and linoleum.
An outwork joined to the mainwork by two parallel wings.
A building for housing deer overnight.
A workshop or factory where bronze articles are made by casting molten metal into moulds.
A parcel of land.
A building or site where bodies are burnt, and the ashes collected for burial or dispersal.
Place for the cremation of animals.
Oven for roasting coal to drive off chemical constituents and reduce it to almost pure carbon, ie. coke.
The residence and office of an ambassador.
A site where clay is mined from the ground.
A constructed space beneath the surface of the ground.
A construction of unknown function, either extant or implied by archaeological evidence. If known, use more specific type.

A mill used for the production of mortar; a combination of sand, lime and water, used to make the joints between courses of bricks in buildings. In more recent times cement has replaced lime to create a quicker drying mortar.
A cluster of closely spaced barrows and related monuments (eg. ring ditches). Use with specific barrow-types where known.
A woollen mill in which the cloth was passed over rollers covered in short spikes to raise the nap in one direction only.
A factory where short wool was spun into woollen yarn to produce cloth.
A brass manufacturing complex incorporating battery mill furnaces, hammers, etc.
A workshop or factory where brass articles are made by casting molten material into a mould.
The residence of a lightkeeper.
A building on a railway system housing levers used to regulate trains on the tracks using signals and to change the points to enable a train to transfer from one track to another.
A calciner used in arsenic production from the 1820s to the 1950s featuring a distinctive, slowly rotating hearth.
Canal docks where the freeboard of a boat was marked. By placing increasing ton weights at 4 points around the boat, its displacement could be marked for toll purposes.
An artificial area of open water, situated on a canal, enclosed by masonry and fitted with dock gates in which ships can be repaired, loaded/unloaded or berthed.
An artificial area of open water, enclosed by masonry and fitted with dock gates in which ships can be repaired, loaded/unloaded or berthed.
A building, or part of a building for the boiling and preparation of animal feed, usually attached to pigsties.
A type of large steel framed aircraft hangar introduced by the Royal Air Force in its Expansion Period with a number of designs between 1934 and 1939, to accomodate heavy bombers.
A stone on which Runes have been inscribed. Often used as memorials though not always associated with a burial.
A workshop used for the manufacture of clay tobacco pipes.
A pit used for containing manure.
A light, open structure for the sale of newspapers, tickets, etc.
A chamber built into the side of a covered reservoir to enable the water level to be inspected.
A store belonging to a cooperative society.
A hall in which public assemblies and meetings can be held.
A pillbox built to a design drawn up the chief engineer of Scottish Command
Engineering works specializing in the production and maintenance of non-passenger carrying railway rolling stock.
Mass produced iron framed shed usually clad in metal sheeting.
A gate on a toll road where travellers had to pay a toll to the toll-keeper.
Religious establishment, founded in Somerset, where free love was practised.
A room containing a boiler, used to provide heating.
A building housing a boiler, often connected to a steam engine house.
A site which has produced evidence of in situ production of items derived from antler.
A cairn used to indicate the limit of an area or a piece of land.
A fountain decorated with shells forming an ornamental feature.
Fixed equipment, such as slides, swings and climbing frames for children to play on. Often found in playgrounds, parks and school grounds.
An establishment where chocolate was available as a beverage.
The line of a flat rod system transmitting power from an engine or waterwheel.
A piece of machinery on which a railway engine, carriage or wagon can be rotated at a railway terminal.
A coastal battery designed for use in short range engagements with enemy vessels, minelayers, blockships ad torpedo craft.

A supermarket for American military personnel, the National Guard and the Reserves and their immediate family, usually sited on a military installation throughout the world. Use term only in conjunction with an American military base.
A low, wide, circular ring or bank of stones surrounding an open, roughly circular area which is (or was initially) free of cairn material. The inner and outer faces of the bank may be kerbed.
A stony mound containing or concealing deliberately deposited human remains. Use specific type where known.
A lock at the end of one company's canal where it joins another company's canal.

A section of the water channel on a canal or river shut off above and below by lock gates provided with sluices to let the water out and in, and thus raise or lower boats from one level to another. Use more specific type where known.

A structure consisting of three stretches of tramline joined by points. The tram is able to go forward, reverse and then go forward again changing line each time until it has turned around completely.
A factory where aircraft are assembled.
A factory where seaplanes are manufactured.
A prefrabicated home sited in parks where a pitch fee is charged. Although technically mobile they usually only make one journey before being permanently installed.
A building or site producing nitrogen-rich fertilizer.
A building or site used for the production of both chemical and organic fertilizer.
A house where the upper storeys rest on projecting floor joists and so create the effect of an overhang.
A jettied house where the overhanging upper storey runs along the entire length of one side.
A chemical works producing mordants for the dying industry.
A post box mounted on a lamp post.

A strategic food store, directly operated by, or on behalf of, the government. The stores were used to store a variety of foodstuffs. They were in operation from the end of the Second World War until the early 1990's.

skos:Concept.skos:altLabel: Asylum For Aged And Decayed Freemasons
skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: A house devoted to the shelter of the poor and endowed by a benefactor for this use.

A Neolithic burial monument comprising a rectangular or trapezoidal stony mound which contains either a passage at one end with or without lateral chambers, or one or more smaller chambers entered from the side of the mound.
A Neolithic burial monument comprising an approximately circular stony mound which contains a stone-built chamber, with or without additional lateral chambers.
A Neolithic burial monument comprising a stone-built chamber within a mound of stones. Use more precise term where known.
A wealden house with only one end being jettied.
A medieval house with central open hall and two storey bays, jettied at first floor level, on either side.
A semi-permanent ahed designed to Air Ministry specification 1136/27 as a quick and cheap hangar for stations overseas
A site associated with Operation PLUTO (Pipe Line Under The Ocean) the operation to supply the allies with fuel following the invasion of Normandy.
A gate used to seal the entrance to a dock to prevent water escaping from a wet dock or entering a dry dock.
Metal cylinder for producing charcoal using the retort method
A former ground surface buried beneath an earthwork or other sequence of deposits. (includes palaeosoils, turf lines)
Use only for features assumed to be archaeological but which cannot be identified more precisely without further investigation .Use more specific term where known
A reinforced concrete block designed to obstruct the progress of a tank or armoured vehicle. Use more specific type where known.

Rectangular slabs of concrete with a sloping top usually with sides of 5 feet by 3 feet and 3 feet high which when placed in rows were intended to form a substantial barrier to enemy armoured divisions in the event of invasion.
A section of a psychiatric hospital or psychiatric ward set aside for children and/or adolescents with mental illness.

A large room, similar to a dormitory, within a hospital, and used for the temporary or permanent accommodation of patients, either waiting for or recovering from operations or undergoing long term treatment.
A hut 51ft long by 20ft wide used to dry, store and pack parachutes.Similar in design to the 2355/25, but constructed in timber instead of brick.
A structure for visually communicating the exact time to ships in anchorage. A ball slides down a mast at the top of the tower, usually at noon or one o'clock exactly.
A tower in a semaphore communication system. Often a three-storey building on a hill in line-of-sight, signal towers provided working and living space, usually for two crewmen with their families.
A factory containing machinery for processing clay for the manufacture of bricks, tiles or pottery.
A dome shaped building, housing training apparatus, including a projector, for training ground gunners in the art of airfield defence. (WWII).
A platform which moves laterally on wheels, by which boats, railway carriages and engines may be moved from one place to another, eg. from one slipway to another parallel to it.
A radar station with sets operating on a wavelength of 10cm or less. They were highly accurate radars and gave better sea level coverage than the earlier Chain Home Low stations.
Buildings and structures inhabited by agricultural workers.
A round hut, similar to a CHARCOAL BURNERS HUT, associated with forest industry. The bark was later used in the tanning process.
A cheap eating establishment traditionally serving jellied eels, pies and mash.
Two or more adjacent locks where the upper gates of one lock serve as the lower gates of the next.
A platform, usually in concrete, on which radar equipment was mounted to assist the targetting of artillery guns. The platform is often the only evidence surviving in the landscape.
A small park or enclosure where animals are kept.
A building where students study theatre and the dramatic arts.
A structure consisting of a vertical mast and a horizontal boom operated by cables on a separate engine or motor. Used for hoisting and moving heavy loads or objects.
A small crane fixed to the wall of a warehouse or similar building.
A large, metal or wooden structure, used for raising, lowering and moving heavy objects. Use more specific type where known.
A dockyard crane permanently mounted on a lighter.
A crane which is driven by a petrol or diesel engine and travels on either crawler tracks or rubber tyres.
A crane mounted on a large metal gantry, used for the lifting of large-scale building materials, etc.
A crane powered by a steam engine.

A crane consisting of a lattice girder carried on a lattice tower forming a T-shaped structure. A hoist is carried along the girder by a 'crab', enabling the crane to perform a variety of tasks eg loading/unloading of ships.
A crane used for the refueling of coal-powered vessels.
A mechanism used for lifting and lowering weights, operated by hand.
A crane in which, during any alteration of radius, an automatic device causes the load to move horizontally.
A crane located on a quayside used for the loading and unloading of goods and materials to and from vessels.
A crane with a projecting arm, usually one that can be raised and lowered.
A crane powered by a treadwheel and used for lifting and lowering, dating from the Roman period. Also used in later periods to assist on building sites, at mines and in ports.
A crane, located in an engineering workshop or similar establishment, which can be moved on rails and thus used anywhere within the workshop.
A hoist suspended from a girder within the roof of a building or workshop.

Rocket projector site with a circular or octagonal concrete holdfast, 1.5m across, surrounded by a 4.6m radius octagonal concrete surround. Six such rocket projectors were arranged in a 3 x 2 grid. Personnel shelters placed midway between each site.
64 Type DFW55373 single projector sites arranged in an 8x8 grid or in 4 groups of 16. 30m between each projector, with hardened personnel and ammunition shelters located midway between each
Factory for the production of Pet Food.
A place where two or more roads meet.
A circular construction at the intersection of two or more roads to aid the passage of vehicles from one road to another.
A road junction where two (or occasionally more) roads cross each other.
A layer underneath the topsoil containing rubble or fragments of building material, e.g. mortar, tile, flint.
An archaeological unit of soil in a horizontal plane which may seal features or be cut through by other features.
A factory manufactoring caravans.
A factory where hemp, the woody stalk of the hemp plant, used for the making of coarse cloth and cordage, was processed.
A hearth constructed specifically for the manufacture of pitch.
A site where tar is manufactured or combined with other substances to produce bitumen, for example.
A house with an open hall whose main span is separated by an arcade from the side aisles.
One or more coils of barbed wire intended to impede the advance of hostile troops.
Barbed wire in the form of a coil which could be extended concertina-like to form a barrier to impede the movement of hostile troops.
Sites and structures, often un-manned, intended to impede or confuse enemy forces.
Rolls of barbed wire with supporting metal posts designed to impede enemy advance.
A series of flat-topped structures, usually made of stone or wood, used to facilitate a person's movement from one level to another.
A set of steps or a framework of bars and steps for crossing over a fence or wall.
An underground passageway for cables, pipes and pedestrians to allow passage beneath an over ground obstacle.
A raised platform or walkway connecting two buildings or a ship with the quay, etc.
An underground foot tunnel primarily constructed to allow for the passage of pedestrians beneath an over ground obstacle.
A road or way along a ridge of downs or low range of hills.
Stones placed in the bed of a stream or on wet ground, to enable crossing on foot.
A narrow bridge for people and animals to cross on foot.
A path across a road, usually marked as a crossing for pedestrians.
Sites and structures associated with pedestrian transport.
A building or site conducting research into communication techniques for use in the Royal Navy.
A building, usually housing electrical or electronic equipment, used for gathering and disseminating information. Use specific type where known.
A model village built by a utopian society or group of artists.
A building housing the instrumentation necessary for the observation and measurement of tremors generated by earthquakes.
A building, group of buildings or installation in which scientific experiments are carried out.
A building, group of buildings or installation in which experiments and observations are undertaken to gather and record information about the weather.
A roadside telephone box for use by motorists in need of assistance.
A freestanding public call box, containing a telephone and usually operated by inserting coins.
A dispersed farmstead where the farm buildings and farmhouse are loosely grouped together within the boundary of the farmstead.
A large site specializing in the manufacture of locomotives.
Sacred Jewish texts and appurtenances buried within a Jewish cemetery.
A building or buildings where explosives are manufactured.
A factory or works principally engaged in the manufacture of the mining explosive sabulite.
A prepared area of grass on which the game of football is played.
The channel of water that provides a current of water to drive a millwheel.
A water channel leading from a water wheel.
A circular concrete platform onto which aircraft would be taxied allowing the ground crew to calibrate, check and adjust the accuracy of the aircrafts compass, usually by rotating the platform.
A mill where flax is processed to make linen, thread and yarn.

Special concrete loading ramps nicknamed 'hards' had been constructed along river banks, beaches and inlets to enable organised embarkation onto various types of landing craft to take place, irrespective of tides.
Based on a typical 18ft span, 40ft long temporary brick hut but with two bay windows in the front elevation, one for the watch office and one for the chief instructor.

An enclosure defined by a single bank and entrance. They occur on every type of ground, although they favour sheltered, valley side locations. Smaller and usually less well defended than hillforts they are thought to be settlements of Iron Age date.
A pit used for the prolonged steeping of the flax plant in water to separate the fibres from the wood.
The dwelling and workshop of a framework knitter.
A building for the storage and drying of hops, often including a hop drying kiln. Usually built as part of a farm.
A ground used for the performance testing of motor vehicles, for example prototype vehicles.
A stone erected to mark a particular spot in the landscape. Can be used for various reasons.
A marker stone showing the extent of a measure of land containing a vein of ore.
A cottage for workers on a country house estate.
Buildings and structures associated with the use of animals to generate power.
A simple machine, worked by horses, to provide a power take-off for driving agricultural machinery.
A building, or buildings, providing accommodation for an infantry regiment.
A barracks including stables and associated buildings housing a cavalry regiment.
A barracks comprising eight barrack blocks accessed via a central corridor. With four blocks on either side of the corridor the whole structure resembled a spider in plan.
A building used to house members of the armed forces.
A residence for military personnel.
A wall and area of ground where the game of fives is played.
A type of engine house creating power by means of compressed air, typically associated with collieries where it is used for raising coal.

A site where flint seams within chalk have been exploited by digging deep vertical shafts, often with horizontal galleries radiating out from the base. Use for Neolithic examples and for Post Medieval gunflint industry.
A workshop containing machinery used to press textiles.
A cottage for workers on a country house estate.
A building situated within the estate of a manor or country house.
Unclassifiable site with minimal information. Specify site type wherever possible.
A site showing some signs of occupation but evidence is insufficient to imply permanent settlement.
Hut for use at Level Crossings that were not adjacent to Signal Boxes.
A gentry house in a town or city, either detached or in a terrace.
An installation used to store ammunition and equipment ready for the mobilization of armed forces in the event of a war.
A building or group of buildings, often enclosed by a system of fortifications, used by an armed force for the storage and distribution of military equipment.

A detached building without an operations block and crew briefing room designed on modern lines similar to, but smaller than WATCH OFFICE (12779/41). Began appearing on new stations from September 1941.
A watch office designed for bomber satellite station comprising a long, temporary brick hut with a watch office, operations room and crew briefing room.
Buildings where gambling takes place.
A place for recreation with electronic game machines and gambling machines.
A place of worship for members of the Church of Scotland which has been Presbyterian since 1690. It is the national Church of Scotland and is free and endowed.

A place of worship for Presbyterians, a movement who started off attempting to reform Anglicanism before breaking away in 1660. Sometimes referred to as moderate puritans, they joined with the Congregationalists to form the United Reformed church in 1972.
A place of worship for Welsh Presbyterians. Formerly known as Calvinistic Methodists, the Presbyterian Church of Wales separated from the established church in 1811.
A bridge which takes a towing path over a branch canal, basin, etc.
The premises of a builders merchant where building materials such as stone, cement, bricks, tiles and timber could be bought.
A wheel which is turned by a horse in order to provide power. Used in mines, manufacturing and farming.
A building used for the dissemination to the public of such items like tourist brochures, travel maps, guide books and other documents, etc.

A spatially discrete scatter of mixed artefactual material found on the ground, seabed or riverbed which may have been deposited over time rather than resulting from one particular event. Index particular types where appropriate.

A spatially discrete, though sometimes extensive, scatter of lithic artefacts recovered from the surface, eg. by fieldwalking, rather than from a particular archaeological context. Use particular types where appropriate.
A spatially discrete, though sometimes extensive, scatter of flint artefacts recovered from the surface, eg. by fieldwalking, rather than from a particular archaeological context.
A house in a terrace consisting of a double row of houses sharing a common back wall, characteristic of industrial cities in the North of England.
A 'through' BACK TO BACK HOUSE - an interlocking L-shaped plan gave each house two street frontages, thus providing better lighting/ventilation.
An abbey or priory of Dominican nuns.
A temporary kiln, in which the pots are stacked and baked in a pit underneath a bonfire.
A factory producing metallic aluminium by an electrolysis process.
A specialist hospital where medical and surgical dental treatment takes place.
A model village built in association with a factory, mill, railway, or any other industrial complex; usually built by the employer.

Inhumation rite in which charcoal is included with the buried corpse, possibly in an attempt to preserve the body. Thought to be associated with high status burials of the early medieval and medieval period.
A post to which ropes are attached to secure vessels at a landing place.
An iron, stone or concrete tower built up from the bed of a reservoir. From it the control valves of the pipes which draw off water at different levels are operated.
A one or two storey reinforced concrete structure, usually associated with two T shaped radio masts. Term is specific to army anti-aircraft control centres operational between 1950-55.
A steep bank or slope. In fortifications, the bank or wall immediately in front of and below the rampart.
An open area of water, usually artificial and enclosed by dock gates or locks, lined with wharves, warehouses and berths to enable vessels to load and unload.
A site where acts of corporal and capital punishment were carried out.
A pond used for the punishment, by ducking in water, of offenders.
A specialist hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of women and children.

A secure, bomb-proof, undergound complex designed to be used by the government in the event of a national emergency such as nuclear war. Usually equipped with communications equipment, emergency rations and water and air filtering plants.
A stand by set house built to Air Ministry drawing number 4238/44.
An expansion period stand by set house designed to drawing number 607/36 and containing a single generator set and switch board. Constructed in reinforced concrete.

A stand by set house built with a steel-framed pitched roof. Built to drawing number 8760/42 it was intended to supersede all earlier designs and was cheaper to produce. Both the transformer and fuel tanks were located outside the main building.
A portable stand by set house built to Air Ministry drawing number 3527/43.
A stand by set house built to Air Ministry drawing number 1039/41.
A stand by set house designed to drawing number 13244/41 and comprising of 4 rooms; a fuel storage room, a transformer chamber, a switchgear chamber and the main engine room with 2 diesel engines.

A stand by set house similar to 13244/41 and designed to drawing number 16302/41 and comprising of 4 rooms; a fuel storage room, a transformer chamber, a switchgear chamber and the main engine room with 3 diesel engines.
A building housing the stand-by generator set and associated equipment which could supply electricity to all essential services in the event of a power cut.
An expansion period stand by set house designed to drawing number 974/35 and containing a single generator set and switch board. Constructed with brick cavity walls.
Field or area of ground where washed new cloth is stretched out to dry.
A self-service dining room, especially for workers/employees; also in institutions, such as schools, hospitals, etc.
Workshop for the manufacture of master parts from working drawings which are then used as patterns for mass manufacture.
A tower, consisting of one or several testing shafts, for testing lifts and for training personnel.
Water spraying tower for cooling coke after it emerges from the furnace.
A factory producing drabbet, a type of linen cloth.
A garden ornament, usually of stone or metal, designed in the the form of a vase used to receive the ashes of the dead.
A factory where preserved food is canned.
The residence of a cloth cutter.

A circular pillbox designed by the Engineering and Metals Company using 'Armco' corrugated iron sheets as the inner and outer skins into which concrete was poured, giving a 12in wall thickness. The design was taken up by DFW and assigned a drawing number.
An artificial area of open water, enclosed by masonry and fitted with dock gates in which ships can be repaired, loaded/unloaded or berthed.
A dock with gates which open for access for some hours before and after high water.
The residence of a priest.
A small, walled fortlet, situated every Roman mile along the length of Hadrian's Wall to defend a gateway allowing the passage of people and as a garrison to accommodate patrol troops.
A fortified Roman site, usually under 1 hectare in area, strategically situated, housing small military patrols, often defended by a rampart, one or two ditches and a gate.
A free standing small turf and timber fortlet, situated every Roman mile along Hadrian's Wall.
A waterwheel in which the incoming water is directed onto the periphery below the top of the wheel.
A waterwheel where the inflow of water strikes the paddles or floatboards well below the axis of the wheel, ie. the water more or less passes under it.

A type of waterwheel where the incoming supply of water leaves a launder near the top of the wheel, and drops onto the paddles or buckets of the wheel which rotates in the reverse direction to that of the incoming flow.
A wheel driven by wind or steam for the lifting of water.
A structure associated with forges, watermills, water-powered factories, etc.
A waterwheel turned by the force of water falling upon the top of the wheel into buckets placed round the circumference.
A piece of land used for the cultivation of hops.
A pit filled with rubble, etc., into which rain or waste water flows in order to disperse into the surrounding soil.
A small enclosure containing cold frames, often of brick and glass construction, usually situated against the exterior of a walled garden's south-facing garden.
A building where motor cycles are assembled.
A stone coffin embellished with sculpture.
A prehistoric coffin made out of a hollow tree trunk.
A chest made of stone, wood or lead, used to enclose a dead body.
A boundary marker for the payment of tax or duty.
A boundary post for the payment of tax or duty.
A medieval high status farmstead, acting as the centre of the estate, directly controlled by the lord and used for the benefit of his household and dependents.
A conical brick structure in which glass articles were made.
Originally, a house of higher social status in a town or port, often with a storage cellar.
A mooring, usually consisting of a concrete plinth, to which a barrage balloon was attached.
A site where a single large balloon was attached by fine wire cables to the ground to form an aerial obstruction to attacking enemy aircraft.
A building associated with a barrage balloon site and intended to provide shelter for the balloon crew from air attack.
A building for housing, maintaining and repairing motor cars. Dating to the 1890s.
Use only for buildings which house motor vehicles. Includes garages for vehicle repair. For petrol sales use PETROL STATION.
A lake, often artifical, in a park or open space, used for the recreational rowing and sailing of boats.
A factory where musical instruments are manufactured.
A factory where musical organs are manufactured.
A storehouse for ore, often found in conjunction with a BLAST FURNACE.
A factory where short wool was spun into woollen yarn to produce cloth.
A woollen mill in which the cloth was passed over rollers covered in short spikes to raise the nap in one direction only.
A building or site used by the armed forces for the storage and issuing of military stores and materials.
The residence of a person entrusted with the management of a great house or castle.
A bed of low-growing foliage plants, all of an even height, arranged in patterns that resemble a carpet both in the intricacy of their design and in the uniformity of surface.
A building where carpets and other floor furnishings were woven.
A handloom weavers workshop where the weaver received yarn from a clothier and manufactured a woven piece of cloth from it.
A light, sometimes ornamental structure in a garden, park or place of recreation, used for entertainment or shelter. Use specific type where known.
A waterside building from which one could fish.
A camp where people who fled from danger or problem whithin their country or across international borders and who are in need of international protection are temporarily placed.
Dummy construction in the form of a battery used during WWII to provide a counterfeit target for enemy aircraft.
A system of lights, controlled fires or dummy constructions, used during WWII to provide a counterfeit target for enemy aircraft.
The standard RFC power house built to Air Ministry drawing number 476/18 and comprising an engine room with a small workshop and driver's room.
A power house built to Air Ministry drawing number 1380/24.

A building housing the permanent electricity generator supply for domestic use or small scale unspecified power generation on an airfield. Unlike stand by set houses, power houses had to cope with both essential and non-essential loads.
A power house built to Air Ministry drawing number 207/17 and comprising four rooms; a driver's room, workshop and store, battery room and engine room containing 2 generator sets.
Site where steel is produced from molten pig iron using a Bessemer Converter, a development from the cementation and crucible steel-making techniques .
