A group of buildings, or part of a works, housing apparatus used in the process of fermentation.

A chemical works engaged in the manufacture of the coal tar derivative, picric acid, often associated with the textile industry where it was used as a dye, but more commonly with the explosives industry where it was used as the shell filling Lyddite.
A hospital where patients would bathe daily in the sea or in indoor salt-water swimming baths.
A type of calcining kiln used in the processing of iron ore.
Ore hearth specifically for the refining of silver.
A small building housing a valve which controls the flow within a water regulation system.

Circular or near circular ditches, usually seen as cropmarks. Use the term where the function is unknown. Ring ditches may be the remains of ploughed out round barrows, round houses, or of modern features such as searchlight emplacements.
A crane located on a quayside used for the loading and unloading of goods and materials to and from vessels.
A crane mounted on wheels and/or rails, used for the unloading of ships' cargoes.
An institution for convicted prisoners held under a regime which strove to reform by means of silent isolation and labour.
Garden area next to public house used for the comsumption of alcoholic beverages.
The public house was a 19th century development, distinctive from the earlier BEER HOUSE by its decorative treatment and fittings.
A public house licensed for the sale of wine and other alcoholic drinks.
A building used for the education of, and as a residence for, chantry priests.
A communal residence of secular vicars whose duties included the education of choristers attached to cathedrals and collegiate churches.
A communal residence of secular priests and/or other clerics sometimes with the condition of learning and education attached.
A complex or network of earthwork or cropmark linear ditches, banks or other features. Use specific type where known.
A timber framed house comprising horizontal and vertical timbers, forming the walls of the building and directly supporting the roof.
A place where members of the British Legion meet.
A small dwelling for the solitary confinement of a pious reclusive religious man or monk, often attached to the north wall of a church. A squint enabled the occupant to witness the Mass.
An anti aircraft battery usually mounting weapons with a larger calibre ammunition such as the QF 3.75 inch (94mm) gun.
A site where guns, mortars or searchlights are mounted. Use specific type where known.
Gun emplacement for static or mobile light anti aircraft artillery.
A site containing one or more artillery pieces and/or rocket launchers for firing at enemy aircraft.
WW2 LAA battery consisting of two or four 40m guns or Bofors guns. Associated structures included tented accommodation, ammunition shelters, a 100 gallon water tank, latrines, wash-house and kitchen.

Heavy anti aircraft battery used from June 1944-May 1945 to combat the V-bomb threat. They are distinct from normal HAA batteries, being laid out in a V-shape, and early on were mainly for mobile 3.7-inch guns.
40mm gun emplacement created between 24th-26th June 1944 as part of the fourth deployment of Diver LAA guns to the Kentish Gun Belt. Each site had an extant searchlight battery.
A command post used to direct the guns of an anti aircraft battery.

Unspecified Second World War anti-aircraft battery. There were three types of battery. The U2P and U20P had different arrangements of DFW55373 projector sites for the 20-barrelled 3" projectors. The U9P mounted 12-barrelled projectors.

A building, often with underground rooms, used to receive all reports of aircraft locations, to assimilate and assess this information in order to provide the most accurate possible picture to the Operations Room of a fighter or bomber Group.
An area of a church, often a free-standing building, in which baptism is administered
A works or factory where shells or projectiles were machined before they were dispatched to a filling factory to be filled with explosives.
Building used for children to play in.
A workshop or factory where brass articles are made by casting molten material into a mould.
A brass manufacturing complex incorporating battery mill furnaces, hammers, etc.
A coastal battery containing one or more artillery pieces for to defend the coast against hostile motor torpedo boats.
A defensive battery positioned facing out to sea enabling the guns to be brought to bear on enemy shipping and amphibious craft.
A place where gold ore is extracted.
A building in which works of art are displayed, permanently or temporarily.
A pit used for the excavation of clay suitable for making bricks.
A place from which clay is extracted.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the extraction of clay.

A pit in which lye is used to clean hides/bones/etc. generally as part of the tanning process to remove excess fat, flesh, hair, etc. from the raw hide. The residue from these pits formed a crude soap which could be used for various cleaning purposes.
An outlying farm or estate belonging to the Augustinian order.
A factory in which is ink is prepared from pigments and additives.
An underground bomb-proof structure used as a command centre for military operations.
A factory used to manufacture fibreglass.
A CRUCK HOUSE where the cruck blades are truncated and joined by a collar beam, above which is a separate roof construction.
A house in which a pair of curved timbers form a bowed A-frame which supports the roof independently of the walls.
A works where cotton waste is stored or processed.
Usually a cotton spinning factory, although some mills have weaving sheds attached, in which case the end product is completed cloth, not yarn only.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the manufacture of lace.
A factory where lace is manufactured.
A building where lace was laid out to dry.
A place where social and other functions such as parties, presentations and meetings can be held.
A hospital department for the medical and surgical treatment of teeth disorders.
A route across a river, or lake. Use only for small inland ferries and index with LANDING POINT/STAGE/STEPS or PIER where known.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the retrieval, refining, processing and storage of petroleum oil.
A works where crude oil is distilled into its fractions or cuts.
Mill for producing a smooth surface and edges on newly sawn timber.
A pumping station used as part of a clean water supply system.
A waterworks pumping station.
A building used to shelter deer hunters.
The residence and office of a chaplain.
A spatially discrete group of pits usually containing artefactual material with little or no accompanying evidence for structural features.
A works used for the production of copperas, a green iron sulphate which is used as a fixative in the dyeing process.
A place where hops are stored.
A long building with a louvred roof in which silver is refined using the Pattinson Process, which had been developed in the 1830s.
A site or building where silver was processed and/or worked and fashioned into objects.

Any building or site in which silver was refined and/or extracted by smelting, cupellation, liquation or by the Parkes Process. IA-C20. Don't use for lead or copper smelters at which silver has been extracted unless silver-related features survive.
A tall chimney terminating a CONDENSING FLUE, used to extract metal from the smoke produced by a lead smelter.
Hut along the coast, which provided shelter for lookouts known as "huers", who kept watch for the pilchard shoals that passed by the coast. Built of stone or wood. Particular common to Cornwall.
A collection of dwelling-houses and other buildings, usually larger than a hamlet but smaller than a town with a simpler organisation and administration than the latter.
A settlement whose plan suggests the aggregation of several formerly distinct settlement nuclei into a single settlement.
A pumping station used as part of a clean water supply system.
A waterworks pumping station.
A building used to pump sewage from the sewers to the filter beds of a sewage works.
An area of ground or water containing explosive mines.
The homestead of a farm consisting of a farmhouse and working farm buildings, with yards, other working areas and usually a garden to the house.
A farmstead where the house and working buildings are attached and in-line. Can include Bastles, Longhouses and Laithe houses.
A building, department or shop where postal business is carried on.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the collection, distribution, sending and reception of mail.
A house by a toll gate or toll bridge where tolls are collected.
A place of worship for followers of Hinduism.
A small body of water, either natural or artificial.
A small cold water bath, often known as a natatio when part of a Roman bath complex.
Sites used for the manufacture of chemicals used as the basis for complex chemical processes or products.

A building used for storing Sulphur, a highly inflammable chemical element used in the manufacture of matches, gunpowder and sulphuric acid. It is also used in bleaching, for vulcanizing rubber and as a disinfectant.

A large steelframed military aircraft hangar designed in 1939, intended for aircraft maintenance on operational stations. It includes side annexes for workshops and offices, provided with a large number of windows. The annexes are of brick or concrete.
A purpose-built dwelling for the supervisor of a factory, mine or other industrial complex.
A factory where worsted, a well-twisted woollen yarn made from long staple wool and used in the manufacture of suits and other garments, was produced.
A place where calcite is extracted using both quarrying and deeper mining techniques. Calcite/limestone is used for making glass, paper, photography, statues, building, and animal food.
A building, on a military airfield or base, in which motor vehicles are housed.
A mill in which textile rags were ground, either to enable the fibres to be respun or to use the pulp in the manufacture of paper.
A stone on which plague victims placed vinegar-disinfected money to pay for food left for them by the townspeople.
The residence of a telegraph keeper, associated with a telegraph station.
A place where watches and timepieces are manufactured and mended.
A small building housing a lavatory.
An office, particularly at a seaport, at which customs are collected.
A building from where marine operations are directed.
A farmstead where mostly detached buildings have developed around two sides of an open cattle yard.
A farmstead where mostly detached buildings have developed around one or more sides of an open cattle yard.
A house in which a member of the Royal Court lives.
A mill used for the preparation of Barilla, an ash of burnt seaweed that was used for the production of soda.
A building containing mechanically powered ore crushers or rollers.

A trench dug through topsoil in an arable field in order to extract underlying clay which was then spread on the field and ploughed in to improve soil fertility. Usually found in peaty soil areas such as the Lincolnshire and Cambridgeshire fenlands.
A deposit that has been burnt and not subsequently disturbed. Refer to Archaeological Science thesaurus for terminology relating to those redeposited from their original location.
A central point for the deposit, collection and recycling of waste materials.
For the disposal of town refuse. Some 19th century plants were linked to a power station. Later ones incorporate INCINERATORS, recycling facilities, etc.
A chute for conveying salt.
A plsce were herbal beers are brewed.
Wind or water-powered mill for land drainage in fens or marshlands.
A building used by an organization or society instituted to promote research.
A hospital where people would pay a subscription in order to recieve treatment when ill.
An establishment providing medical or surgical treatment for the ill or wounded. Use narrower term where possible.

An establishment where alcoholic and non alcoholic drinks are served, food may also be served. May be a an individual room within a larger multi purpose building such as a sports pavilion or a theatre.
A small pumping station.
A room or building where a pump is worked.
An open pit from which coprolites or phosphatic nodules were extracted. Commonly found in the Fens and East Anglia coprolites were ground up and used as fertilizer.
A crane mounted on wheels and/or rails, used for the unloading of ships' cargoes.
A crane which is driven by a petrol or diesel engine and travels on either crawler tracks or rubber tyres.
A building containing the colliery showers. Also often containing first aid and mine rescue facilities.
A school that is established, run and supported by a private, non-governmental body.
A school in which the funds were raised through a system of shareholding whereby parents bought shares in the school and thus paid for their children's education.
Cloth finishing process using machinery to raise the nap of the cloth before shearing.
A kiln used to reduce the shells of shellfish to calcium carbonate.
A courtyard in a prison or workhouse for the inmates to take exercise.
A lock where the gates rise vertically. Rarely found on canals but common on navgable rivers in the Fens, particularly the river Nene.

A structure used to show the time of day by means of the sun shining on a 'gnomon', the shadow of which falls on the surface of the dial which is marked with a diagram showing the hours. Can be freestanding, usually on a pillar, or fixed to a building.
A set of marks found on the wall of a building, thought to be a form of sundial.
A sundial capable of giving an accurate reading of standard time to the minute.
A furnace constructed as a shaft with the fire at the bottom and the fuel and ore added from the top.
A charcoal fired shaft furnace used for the direct reduction of iron ore to produce wrought iron.

An area of land incorporating bodies of water, either natural or manmade for use in water sports activities such as canoeing, rowing and sailing. Usually includes a leisure complex with facilities for the users.
A storehouse associated with rope manufacture (eg. in naval dockyards).
A fountain decorated with shells forming an ornamental feature.

An artificial aperture from which water springs. The water supply usually came from a lake or reservoir higher up in order to ensure the necessary flow and pressure. More recently fountains have been powered by pumps.
An often highly elaborate water fountain, usually found in parks, gardens or urban spaces.
An automata or water device which surprises the unwary onlooker with water. A feature of 16th and 17th century gardens.
An early to mid 20th century school designed to effect maximum ventilation and sunlight for its pupils.
A rectangular shaped area of land enclosed by a boundary ditch, bank, wall, palisade or similar barrier.
An area of land enclosed by a boundary ditch, bank, wall, palisade or other similar barrier. Use specific type where known.
A narrow, open container, usually where food or water for animals is put. Use specific type where known.
A long, wooden, metal or stone vessel holding drinking water for horses.
A long metal or stone vessel for cattle to drink water from.
A long stone or metal vessel for dogs to drink water from.
A room in a library or institution providing periodicals, newspapers, etc.
An area of a building providing reading materials for the benefit of colliery workers.
A land based establishment armed with torpedoes and used to defend the coast from enemy shipping.

A land based installation armed with wire -guided and powered "Brennan torpedoes" which were in operation beween 1890 and 1906. These torpedoes were invented by Louis Philip Brennan. The stations were used to defend the coast from enemy shipping.
The official residence of an abbot.
A substantial house in a town or the country (particularly associated with medieval London). Use more specific monument types where known.
A place from which chalk is extracted.
A bungalow joined to another to form one building.
A building, originally used as a shelter for the duty pilot or officer on watch on an airfield, and later used to direct air traffic. Use more specific type where known.

A control tower constructed on RNAS stations by the Royal Marine Engineers. Built to a common ground floor plan they could be built with one, two or three storeys above this depending on the requirements of the station.
skos:Concept.skos:prefLabel: Royal Naval Air Station Control Tower

skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: The first standardized design for a building for the duty pilot. It took the form of a small bungalow with a bay window on the front elevation.
A high building at an airport from which air traffic is controlled by radio.

A central tower with a single-storey wing either side. The tower contained the watch office on the ground floor, observation room on the second with each wing containing an office for the Chief Flying Instructor or the officer commanding and their aides.
A control tower designed for use on Very Heavy Bomber Station Airfields. Designed to Air Ministry drawing number 294/45 they were the first to be have a Visual Control Room
skos:Concept.skos:altLabel: Very Heavy Bomber Station Control Tower (294/45)

skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: An open metalwork structure supporting either a fabrication shed or the runners for an overhead crane.
A tunnel through which a tramway runs.
A building or site where bloom iron or cast iron is forged into wrought iron.
A building used for the decarburizing of pig iron to produce wrought iron.
A fighter satellite station watch office built to Air Ministry design drawing number 3156/41.
A small single storey structure with just one room containing a pyrotechnic cupboard and built of rendered brick with a flat reinforced concrete roof
A separate residence for guests, a house on a private estate or a monastery building specifically for receiving visitors.
A specialist hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of eye and ear disorders and diseases.
A factory or plant used for the manufacture of electrical machinery or components.
A factory manufacturing electrical equipment, such as engines, transformers and generators for use in industry.
A row of columns supporting an entablature.
A prototype semi-underground silo based launch system specifically designed to hold and fire the Blue Streak Missile. The silo was constructed at RAF Spadeadam in c1959 and abandoned in April 1960.
An area of land which retains distinctive large-scale rectilinear land divisions characteristic of Roman agriculture. Generally aligned with the course of a Roman road.
A structure consisting of a large plastic pipe attached to a high tower and sloping down to a swimming pool. Water flows down the inside allowing people to slide down into the pool below.
School built by the local Education Authority to provide residental schooling at the seaside for children from urban communities.
A structure, composed of oven and hovel, used for the firing of pottery ware.
A large, "bottle-shaped", oven of brick construction used in the baking or firing of pottery.
A type of pottery kiln in which air rises up inside the oven to be forced back down and out through the base of the oven.
A structure in which pottery tiles were baked.
A type of pottery oven in which the air passes from the base of the kiln out through the top.
A low-temperature oven for the firing of metallic-based colour onto pottery after glazing.
A site used for the manufacture of leather products.
A factory for the manufacture of leather goods, such as shoes, saddles, etc. Use TANNERY for the manufacture of leather.
A factory or complex where chamois leather is produced using fish oils as the tanning agent.
The residence of the head or president of a chapter, or community of religious persons.
Residences of religious people and members of the clergy.
A raised step, usually made of concrete, on which supporters stand to watch a game of football.
A finishing process for cloth involving the pounding of the cloth with heavy weights.
The residence of a master ropemaker.

A farmstead with multiple yards which are grouped together and regularly arranged (other than the defined E, F, H, T or Z plans). The yards may relate to one or more buildings or ranges which may be of either loose courtyard or regular courtyard form.

An Iron Age round defended house, found mainly in the north and west of Scotland. Brochs have a tapering profile and thick, usually hollow dry stone walls which contain galleries, cells and a stairway, with guard cells at the entrance.
A furnace or oven used for drying items or materials. Use specific type where possible.
A building found in conjunction with a WATERMILL, used for the drying of corn after harvesting, with a slatted drying floor set above a kiln.
A structure, often sunk into the ground, for the purpose of allowing total bodily immersion in mineral sprinwater or similarly beneficial substances.
A dam and sluice combination, associated with an aqueduct, for the extraction of water from a river to feed a reservoir or water treatment plant.
A dam which can be raised or lowered to regulate the flow of water.
An instrument for measuring and indicating the height of tide.
An engine in which the oscillating motion of the beam is translated via gearing to a rotative motion.
A steam engine with a horizontal beam connecting the piston and crank.
The residence of a keeper of a royal park etc.
A building with malt kilns for the malting of grains and with other similar equipment for brewing work.

In fortification, a detached triangular outwork consisting of two battered faces forming a salient angle. Usually positioned in the ditch in front of a rampart and between two bastions. Term mainly for military architecture from 15th century and later.
A garden devoted to the growth of vegetables.
A factory or works principally engaged in the manufacture of blasing or explosive gelatine.
Mill for fine grinding of tin ore between millstones.
A house built using experimental building techniques and materials.
An enclosure for wild cats such as Lions and Tigers
Including accommodation for animals, birds, reptiles and fish in captivity.
A box or place of confinement for animals, made wholly or partly of wire, wood or bars of metal, so as to admit air and light.
An enclosure, usually within a zoo, designed to represent the natural environment for Lemurs, including shelter.
A town founded as an act of government by charter to house Roman or Latin citizens, usually retired legionaires who had been granted land within a territorium.
The principal stand at a sporting ground, eg. at a racecourse.

Blocks of concrete with four protruding arms so that, whichever way up the caltrop is placed, one arm will always point upward. Used in imitation of the iron caltrops thrown on the ground to impede cavalry.
A small metal bar for the cleaning of dirty footwear before entering a house, etc.
A circular kiln or oven used in the manufacture of bricks. Common in Staffordshire in the 18th century.
A type of temporary transportable aircraft hangar designed in 1936 by N.S. Bellman. It was designed for ease of installation, and was composed of light rolled steel sections.
A place of meeting and worship for Jehovahs Witnesses.
A site where tanks and armoured fighting vehicles can be stored.
A storage facility used for the accommodation and dispersal of vehicles. Often used by the military and emergency services.
A water point with a device to regulate the flow of water.
A point in a village providing water for drinking and washing.

skos:Concept.skos:altLabel: Asylum For Aged And Decayed Freemasons
skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: A house devoted to the shelter of the poor and endowed by a benefactor for this use.
Mark, usually consisting of a horizontal line above an arrow, cut by the Ordnance Survey as part of the survey of Britain and referenced to a known height above mean sea level.
A building used for the shelter and protection of deer, especially in winter.
A platform or other structure for the use of a band of musicians.
A building in which people are held in a state of imprisonment or confinement as punishment. Usually associated with military and political offenders.
A depression in the ground caused by the explosion of a mine or bombshell.
A stone, either in situ or part of a monument, bearing one or more small, roughly hemispherical depressions, generally created by chipping or pecking.
An office used by a qualified pilot, expert in ship-handling and with local knowledge, who assists the captain or master to take a vessel in or out of a harbour or through narrow waters.
A place where tin ore is washed using a stream as the water source.
A site where tin ore is extracted from suspended fire waste in tin mine spoil heaps.
A factory used for the production of acetate.
A mole or pier-like structure situated at the entrance of a harbour, or running out into a lake or the sea, usually used for the landing of craft.
A raised platform for the unloading of coal from waggons or other containers.

Cones of solid concrete usually 3 feet 6 inches in diameter x 2 feet high which, when placed in rows or groups were intended to form a substantial barrier to enemy armoured divisions in the event of invasion.
A pond located at or near a swannery.
A site where copper ore is extracted directly from the surface of the ground.
A church, sometimes circular in plan, founded by the Poor Knights of Christ and the Temple of Solomon, commonly known as the Knights Templar.
A hotel where no alcohol is available.
A place devoted to the cultivation and exhibition of rare trees.
Coastal base for the docking, launch and maintenance of submarines.
The residence of a clothier.
A building in which sheep are sheared.
An inclined plane connecting two different levels, used to accomodate the movement of vehicles, wheeled apparatus,livestock etc.
A ramp or incline between differing levels constructed to allow carriages access.
A place where canal boats are built and maintained.
A mutiple role hangar for aircraft and general storage, manufactured in the USA as a kit for on-site assembly during WWII and post-war. It comprises a steel box frame and a canvas covering.
A winch powered by a small steam engine used to drag barges, boats and other vehicles up an inclined plane.
An engine used for directly winding up coal from deep mines, first used in the 18th century.
A waterwheel where the water enters below the top of the wheel but above the axle.
A slight structure built on an allotment for shelter or storage, or for use as a workshop, by the allotment holder.
A slight structure built for shelter or storage, or for use as a workshop, either attached as a lean-to to a permanent building or separate. Use more specific type where known.

A small tower or bartizan, which was often placed at the angles of a castle, to increase the flanking ability, some only serving as corner buttresses. Also used to describe the small rectangular towers situated between the milecastles along Hadrians Wall.
A small, walled fortlet, situated every Roman mile along the length of Hadrian's Wall to defend a gateway allowing the passage of people and as a garrison to accommodate patrol troops.
A defensive or boundary earthwork.

A system of fortifications constructed along a national frontier to contain the local population, as well as keep out undesirable raiders eg. Offa's Dyke. Use with more specific monument type where known.
A free standing small turf and timber fortlet, situated every Roman mile along Hadrian's Wall.
A building or complex, often associated with a historic site or place of interest, containing interpretation panels and information for visitors to the site or area.
For chemical processes making nylon, rayon, etc.
A farmstead where mostly detached buildings have developed around four sides of an open cattle yard.
A workshop for the manufacture of clothing, eg. tailor's workshop.
The dwelling and workshop of a framework knitter.
A works where cotton waste is stored or processed.
Usually a cotton spinning factory, although some mills have weaving sheds attached, in which case the end product is completed cloth, not yarn only.

A modern building system in which both steel and concrete are utilized together to carry the load in ways that neither material predominates over the other. There are many varieties e. g. a steel frame surrounding a concrete core.
A mill where mustard is produced.
The administrative office of a commercial concern.
A room or building occupied by a person employed to keep accounts of workers' hours of labour.
A mill used for the production of wadding, as opposed to yarn or cloth. Often associated with steam or water power.
A site where unprocessed wood is used to manufacture goods.
Manufacture and use of wood side products, ie. unprocessed wood rather than processed timber.
A structure for visually communicating the exact time to ships in anchorage. A ball slides down a mast at the top of the tower, usually at noon or one o'clock exactly.
A sheltered port for ships.
A harbour constructed from floating pontoons or caissons connected end to end.
A floatable concrete vessel, numbers of which made up the main breakwater of the Mulberry Harbours used to secure beachheads during the allied invasion of Europe in June 1944.
A centre used to train Air Raid Precautions wardens.
An artificial water channel for carrying water over long distances. Use also for bridge-like structures that carry the channel or canal across a valley, river or other obstacle.
A building or site where the carcasses of whales were butchered and rendered into by products such as oil, fenk and whalebone.
A building where ambulances are housed awaiting emergency calls.
A building housing a steam driven ventilation fan used in mines
A heated room or building used to dry yarn after it has been washed.
Use wider site type where known. Only use term where no other part of original building survives.
A vertical, pointed structure usually resembling a pyramid or cone. Use for component of a larger building type where it is now used as a freestanding ornament.
Use as an external architectural feature only.
Use more specific term where known.
A working hospital, often near or associated with a university, where doctors and nurses are trained.
A place where silverware is manufactured.
A crane with a projecting arm, usually one that can be raised and lowered.
A dockside crane with a solid curving jib made out of rivetted iron plates.
A bridge constructed using rockwork to create a craggy, naturalistic appearance. A feature of 18th century rococo gardens and parks.
A building within a transport terminal, often associated with the registration and clearing of incoming and outgoing passengers or freight.
A vane usually combined with crossed rods to show the four compass points. Used to indicate the direction of the wind.
A waterside depot for coals brought from the collieries for shipment, furnished with staging and chutes for loading vessels.
A modern small factory or workshop, often in the form of a prefabricated shed.
A large building where fish are stored before sale.

A prime mover in which a central wheel with curved vanes, enclosed in a chamber, receives water directed onto the curved vanes by a ring of fixed guide vanes, causing the wheel to rotate about its axis.
An impulse water turbine comprising a wheel with hemispherical cups arranged around the circumference using high water pressure to revolve the wheel.
A building housing the services of professionals with an expert knowledge of the law such as the offices of solicitors, barristers and lawyers.
A building containing a range of processes for cleaning and processing metallic ores.
A tower, containing a gate, built into the walls of a town, castle or similar fortification.
A factory where chocolate products are produced.
A factory or site for the manufacture of food stuffs from raw ingredients.
A mill, including a forge and powered hammers where hot metal is shaped by hammering and rolling.
A platform, usually in concrete, on which radar equipment was mounted to assist the targetting of artillery guns. The platform is often the only evidence surviving in the landscape.
A building of unknown purpose found at a military site. Use more specific type where known.

A prefabricated structure consisting of trough shaped asbestos sheets bolted together to form a seven sided building in section with end walls of rendered brick. Manufactured from 1942 by the Universal Asbestos Company for use as airfield accommodation.
A place for strolling, public walks, etc. Usually associated with coastal resorts.

A section of the water channel of a river, shut off above and below by lock gates provided with sluices to let water in and out and thus raise or lower boats from one level to another. Often found situated next to a weir.
A specialized lantern, with a reduced glare, for use in air raids.
A metal pillar with a flashable lamp on top containing an emergency telephone for use by members of the public and by officers of the local police force.
A medieval hospital for lepers, usually consisting of a church and individual shelters for the lepers.
A building housing court rooms and associated offices and cells, in which the Quarter Sessions were held.
A court of summary jurisdiction formally recognized by statute in 1848. Renamed Magistrates Court, following legislation, in 1949.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the production, testing and storage of explosives.
A building in which cordite paste is blended with the solvent acetone and Vaseline to form a cordite dough.

A confusing and baffling network of winding and intercommunicating paths, often bordered by high hedges or walls. Some early examples are believed to have had ritual uses. Use more specific type where known.
A labyrinthine garden feature, common during the 16th and 17th centuries, created by cutting shallow pathways into deep lawns.
A maze used for the act of penitence.
A complex maze incorporating tall hedges. A popular feature of 16th and 17th century gardens.
Small building in which labourers, such as miners and tin workers. They are also associated with gardens where they provide on-site accommodation for gardeners and estate workers.
Place for the Home Guard to store equipment and amunition, either structural or subterranean during the defence of Britain.
A structure, building or room within a building, used by a local authority for the continuance of local government in the event of a military or civil emergency.
A building used as emergency accommodation and food distribution centre for people displaced by a natural disaster or conflict.
A building used for the daily administration of Civil Defence activities.
A garage for the storage and maintenance of motor vehicles, such as ambluances and fire engines, used for civil defence purposes.
A building used to coordinate civil defence in times of war. Can also be utilized as aid centres in times of national emergency.
A building used as the headquarters for the Home Guard during the Second World War.
A reinforced concrete structure, usually sited underground, from where it was intended to conduct the business of government in the event of nuclear war. Date specific late 1950's to early 1970's.

A reinforced concrete structure, usually sited underground, from where it was intended to conduct the business of government in the event of nuclear war. Date specific from mid 1980's to early 1990's.

A reinforced concrete structure, which may be sited above ground or semi-sunken, from where it was intended to conduct the business of government from, in the event of nuclear war. Date specific to the early-mid 1950's.
Sites and buildings used in the coordination of the defence of the civilian population during times of war. Could also be used during times of national emergency.
An observation post used by members of the Home Guard.
An area of cultivated, managed woodland producing wood which is used for a variety of purposes.
A managed small wood or thicket of underwood grown to be periodically cut to encourage new growth providing smaller timber.
An extractive pit or pits, usually 2.5m square by 2m deep dug to extract tin ore in areas where streamworking is not possible. Usually dug along a vein rather than across it.
A site or building where ore is processed to obtain metal.
A kiln used for extracting salt through the evaporation of salt water.
A temporary settlement established as a public protest against an aspect of government policy or more specifically the development of a site.
An informal encampment, usually near a military establishment, set up as a public protest against that establishment or against some aspect of military policy.
A site where clay pipes used for drainage are manufactured.
An air raid shelter, designed to be placed in the garden. Made from prefabricated components, they were often semi-sunken and the structure then covered with soil for added protection.
A cheap eating establishment traditionally serving jellied eels, pies and mash.
A large building used to store tea.
An aircraft hangar designed to be moved from site to site as necessary.
An all-steel end-opening, hangar with canted sides designed for folded-wing aircraft.
A metal girder, usually of iron or steel, embedded in the ground designed to obstruct the progress of hostile tanks or armoured vehicles.
Manmade constructions used to prevent rivers breaking their banks and flooding the surrounding area with water. Often taking the form of a bank or wall.
Gates that can be opened or closed, to admit or exclude water, especially flood water.
A post box mounted on a lamp post.
A hollow pillar, erected in a public place, containing a receptacle for posting letters.
A box in which letters are posted or deposited for dispatch.
A post box mounted in, or on, a wall.
A mill for beating and cleaning cloth, using soap or fullers earth.
A tippler, a machine for loading wagons at a pithead, operated by hydraulic power.
Loading machinery tipping coal into railway wagons usually at a pithead.
A government office used for the collecting of excise tax/duty.

A building used for the preparatory processes in which long and short staple flax fibres were separated by passing through combs. Flax dressing or 'heckling' shops may be located both on and off mill sites.

A rectangular chamber of brick or stone with heavy wooden gates at either end equipped with sluices to let water in and out, thereby enabling a canal boat to be lowered or raised to a different level.
A barrel-making workshop or factory, found in conjunction with a number of industries.

A vertical vein of metallic ore, usually lead, occuring between walls of rock and cutting through the bedding. Often rakes have been worked from early times leaving deep trenches several km long, with adits leading off and shafts sunk at the side.
An arboretum devoted mainly to the growing of conifers.
A calciner dating from the early 17th to early 20th centuries, usually made of brick and without moving parts, consisting of a reverberatory furnace, and used for the extraction of arsenic.
A shop selling a variety of goods and merchandise.
A kiln or furnace for the firing of bricks.
A kiln principally used in brick making which gives a continuous operation.

A missile or aircraft that obtain its thrust from a rocket engine. Some rockets will exist as monuments for example, in the form of gate guardians. Double index with the monument type where appropriate.
A large, watertight enclosure in which the water is maintained at the high-tide level so that vessels remain constantly afloat in them.
A pit used for the excavation of clay suitable for making bricks.
A place from which clay is extracted.
A battery equipped and ready to fire salutes

A nineteenth century stone calciner, similar to a lime kiln, used for extracting arsenic from mined ores, consisting of a solid structure with a central shaft and a drawing-hole at the base for calciner waste.
An abandoned settlement, usually of the Medieval period, often visible only as earthworks or on aerial photographs.
A building with a regulated moderate temperature for the cultivation of plants.
An area for the testing of rockets and guided missiles. Includes all structures associated with both the firing and testing of rockets and missiles.
A building used for the testing of aircraft and aircraft engines.
A medieval house with central open hall and two storey bays, jettied at first floor level, on either side.
A wealden house with only one end being jettied.

The site of a deserted settlement in cases where there is evidence that it has deliberately been relocated in a single planned action, eg. to remove a settlement from an enclosed park, or to create a model community, as opposed to gradual abandonment.
A factory used for the production of red lead used in glass manufacture, or white lead used as the pigment in white paint.
Term for ore store/ore hopper, used particularly in Yorkshire and Derbyshire.
An educational establishment where law is taught.
A monumental burial place, usually for a single person or family.
The residence of a glover.
A pillbox built to a design drawn up by the chief engineer of GHQ home forces.
A dam constructed across a stream to raise its water-level and make it available to power a mill wheel.
A type of updraught intermittent kiln of rectangular plan and battered sides, but with an open top.
A small work shop for nail manufacture, most commonly situated at the back of a nailer's dwelling.
A complex of buildings using Radar or satellite tracking to monitor and detect enemy missile launches early enough to allow a counterattack or defensive measures to be taken.
Buildings, structures and sites for the detection of encroaching enemy forces.
A building housing the acoustic detection equipment for a sound mirror

A site, building or structure used for the detection of approaching hostile aircraft, shipping or missiles early enough to allow a counterattack or defensive measures to be taken. Use more specific term.
A shelter for the storage of bicycles.
A building or site for watching specific military activities or the movement of enemy forces, etc.
An observation post used by members of the Home Guard.
A building, situated on the coast, used for observing the movements of enemy shipping.
Buildings and structures used to monitor the accuracy of bombs dropped on a bombing range
A building with small observation ports used for plotting mines dropped by parachute.
A factory manufacturing billiard tables.
A night fighter station watch office based on the standard design dor Bomber Satellite Station watch offices
A two storey building with a watch office on the ground floor and a control room above. Originally based on drawing number 12096/4.
A marker stone used to demarcate the boundaries of peat cutting grounds and indicate who held the rights for each particular parcel of land.
An engine in which the mechanical force of steam is made available as a motive power for driving machinery.
A steam engine that uses the same steam successively to drive pistons in high and then low pressure cylinders.
A place of worship for followers of Sikhism.
The main hall of worship within a Sikh Temple.
A section of a hospital specializing in the treatment of patients with serious mental disorders.
An outlying farm or estate belonging to the Gilbertine order.
An outlying farm or estate belonging to the Benedictine order.
An outlying farm or estate belonging to the Carthusian order.
An outlying farm or estate belonging to the Augustinian order.
An outlying farm or estate belonging to the Cluniac order.
An outlying farm or estate belonging to the Poor Knights of Christ and the Temple of Solomon, commonly known as the Knights Templars
An outlying farm or estate belonging to the Premonstratensian order.
An outlying farm or estate belonging to the Cistercian order.
An outlying farm or estate belonging to the Order of Tiron.
An outlying farm or estate belonging to the Bridgettine order.

An outlying farm or estate, usually belonging to a religious order or feudal lord. Specifically related to core buildings and structures associated with monastic land holding. Use specific term where known.
A system of lights to aid aircraft when landing at night. When viewed from above the runway lights form an outline of the runway.
A temporary settlement established as a public protest against an aspect of government policy or more specifically the development of a site.
An informal encampment, usually near a military establishment, set up as a public protest against that establishment or against some aspect of military policy.
A stone channel sunk into the ground, employed from the mid-19th century, to carry away gases produced during smelting.
A small, ornate structure in which candles were placed either during masses for the dead or to indicate the position of the cemetery at night .
An outlying farm or estate belonging to the Cistercian order.
An office which administers the affairs of the church.
A laithe with an attached house.
A place where inmates of a workhouse or prison carried out stone breaking.
When secondary product use with major product and MINE, eg. COPPER MINE.
A site with one or more defensive earthworks, often at a river crossing incorporating natural features which define parts of the curtilage.
An area within a building open to the public where light meals and drinks can be purchased and consumed.

A steel pipe driven into the ground at a shallow, oblique angle and packed with explosives. They were intended to be detonated on the approach of a hostile amroured vehicle or tank in order to create an obstacle directly in its path.

A site used for the placing of an explosive, demolition charge. Many types of structures were prepared for demolition in the event of an invasion in order to cause the maximum disruption to the advance of hostile forces. Use more specifc type where known.
A mechanism used to transport minerals or granulated materials.
A cheap eating and drinking establishment usually serving snacks and non-alcoholic drinks.

An establishment originally providing terminals to allow the public to access the internet, usually for a fee. They originally provided snacks and drinks to customers although now this is not always the case.
A press used to extract the juice from apples, which was then used to make cider.
A site used for the manufacture and finishing of querns.
A site where sugar beet was processed before being washed and dried to form granulated sugar.
A building or room used for the exhibition of upholstery for sale.
A large, vertical revolving wheel with passenger cars or pods on the periphery used to give a bird's eye view of the surrounding area.
A special school to train personnel for employment in Air Traffic Control and operation duties.

A nineteenth century stone calciner, similar to a lime kiln, used for extracting arsenic from mined ores, consisting of a solid structure with a central shaft and a drawing-hole at the base for calciner waste.
A type of calcining kiln used in arsenic manufacture.
A site where iron or steel bolts, and often their accompanying nuts, are manufactured. Sometimes referred to as NUT AND BOLT WORKS.
A military camp providing training facilities.
A semaphore signalling tower on a railway.

Sites, buildings, structures & features associated with the transmission & receiving of information. Includes signalling, broadcasting & telecommunications; does not include transport except where there is a specific connection with communication.
A site where the manufacture of glass bottles takes place.
A factory where shirts are manufactured.
A site used for the production of dyes from natural ingredients.
A site used for the production of dyes from controlled chemical reactions. In use from the mid 19th century onwards.
A bed or border in which different species and colours are mixed.
A strip of ground forming a fringe to a garden. Use more specific type where known.
A hospital department for the medical treatment of eye disorders and diseases.
A machine used in a mill to remove bran scales and flour from grits or middlings.
A type of pottery kiln in which air rises up inside the oven to be forced back down and out through the base of the oven.
A purpose built indoor cricket facility for training and playing matches
A specially built building where facilities exist for the playing of a variety of sports.
A site where large sheets of thin metal are manufactured.
A temporary, steel-framed transportable hangar developed by Teesside Bridge and Engineering Company to replace the obsolete Bellman hangars.
A steel framed transportable hangar similar in construction to Type T2 but about half the size. Designed in 1941 and 1942.
A building or site used for the manufacture of small arms and artillery pieces, etc.
A factory used for the manufacture of ordnance including small arms, ammunition, artillery pieces and armoured fighting vehicles.
The position of a fire in a wood-fuelled furnace. All periods from the Iron Age to the 17th century.
A mill used for the preparation and production of Calamine.
A building, usually associated with a port or dock, where seamen could get a meal and a cheap room. Often established by religious groups for the moral betterment of seamen.
A building used for meetings and worship by a religious community trying to propogate its faith in an area.
Iron Age or Roman coastal site producing salt by boiling of seawater in fired clay pans, resulting in characteristic mounds of 'BRIQUETAGE' (see Archaeological Objects Thesaurus).
A place where gypsum is extracted.
An excavation from which stone for building is obtained by cutting, blasting etc.
A site where granite is excavated.
An excavation from which cobble stone is obtained.
A site where cementstone nodules are extracted.
A site where limestone is extracted.
A place where sandstone is excavated.
A place where marble is extracted from the ground.
A site where slate is quarried from the ground.
A place where shale, a laminated clay or silt which has been compressed by the weight of the rocks over it, is extracted from the ground.
Three storey house with a topshop; machinery powered by shafting through the upper floor.
Subsidiary settlement of lay brothers attached to some Carthusian monasteries.
A park for the use of the public for entertainment and relaxation.
A large mounted gun, now disused and placed in a prominent position as a piece of street furniture or as a "feature".
An area of either natural or artificial stone arranged to resemble a rocky outcrop or cliff face within animal cages/enclosures of a Zoo.
The residence of a bridge keeper.
A factory manufacturing timepieces, including clocks and watches.

An underground structure from which operations covering the whole, or part, of the country could be directed in the event of a nuclear attack. Usually equipped with air filtration equipment and supplies for several months.
A floating structure consisting of two walls standing on pontoon tanks, the latter of which can be flooded to receive a vessel and then pumped out until the pontoon deck and the ship are dry.
A pipe, usually of reinforced concrete or metal, which delivers pressurized water from a dam to hydraulic turbines.
An arcade providing shelter for perishable market goods which also provides protection from the elements for the occupants of the adjoining properties.
A 19th century ore processing works which processed the waste material from a mine.
A double lock placed between tidal water and a canal, etc..
An area of ground on which anti tank guns can be placed for testing purposes and to practice firing at targets.
A head of water raised in a conduit system.
A sunken arena used by the Romans for training cavalry horses and recruits.

A building where fish are stored. Often taking the form of a single storey building with one room, but also may provide living accommodation for a fisherman above. Found mainly in the South West of England.
Use with other minerals extracted and MINE where relevant, eg. ZINC MINE.
A site where terracotta, made from weathered clay and grog, was manufactured.
A complex of buildings used for the manufacture of pottery.
Building or structure covering a casting floor or pit.
The residence of a glover.
A wall between two towers or pavilions, usually surrounding a building, and often forming a major part of the defences.

A bridge consisting of a lattice girder spanning the distance between the tops of two towers. Designed to transport vehicles across the gap in a container suspended at road level by ropes under a travelling crane on the girder.
A vessel to contain holy water located near the entrance of a church.
A refreshment house in a public park or country house garden.
A bridge that incorporates one or two spans that tilt at the abutments, to move up and out of the way of shipping. The most famous example of which is Tower Bridge, London.
Shallow ditches and/or poles erected across open land to obstruct the landing of enemy aircraft and gliders.
Submerged obstacles to stop the landing of Seaplanes
An airfield, and associated structures, used by one or more fighter squadrons.
Scaffolding intended to impede the advance of enemy armoured divisions. Often found in association with "one way" anti tank ditches.
A shed used for the maintenance and repair of aircraft.
A specialist hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of children.
Industrial worker's house which has been purpose built by an employer, as opposed to the workshop houses used by artisans.
A small dwelling providing living accommodation for a tin miner.
A rampart or other defensive entrenchment.
A temporary earthwork or fortification constructed by forces laying siege to a castle or town, etc.
A farmstead, often of linear plan, where the working buildings are placed opposite and parallel to the house and attached working buildings with a relatively narrow space between.
A village laid out systematically with spacious and garden-like surroundings.
A settlement built to a pre-determined plan, including housing, infrastructure and associated amenities.
A place of worship for Methodists, a movement founded by John Wesley. Following his death in 1791 there were many secessions.
A place of worship for Primitive Methodists, a group founded in Manchester who broke away from the Methodists in 1806.
An area of grass, marked out for use in the game of cricket.
A building in which the lay sisters resided. Lay sisters were not nuns and as such weren't bound by any vows. They could leave the convent and even marry if they wished.
A residence for a member of a religious community eg. Abbot, Prior, Manciple etc. For multiple occupancy use more specific term eg. DORMITORY.
A building constructed with the minimum amount of combustible materials.
A factory, mill or warehouse constructed with the minimum amount of combustible materials.

An enclosure of Late Neolithic/Early Bronze Age date, related to henges, defined by a circular arrangement of pits, probably none of which originally held posts. More than one circle, concentrically arranged, may be present.
A large, manmade pool, usually lined with tiles, rubber or similar. Can be placed in the open air, eg. a LIDO, or built as part of a covered sports centre.

An unenclosed feature, usually sub-terranean, constructed to contain water for public or private recreation and sporting avtivities. Sometimes part of a LIDO complex. Use INDOOR SWIMMING POOL for pools with a covering structure.

An enclosed feature, usually sub-terranean, constructed to contain water for public or private recreation and sporting activities. Often part of a larger SPORTS CENTRE. Use OUTDOOR SWIMMING POOL for unenclosed pools.
A motor in which rotary motion is produced by steam power.
A site where the baiting of animals took place. Use more specific site type where known.
An enclosure used for baiting bulls.
A pit, sometimes found close to a church or cathedral, where bells were cast in medieval times.
An intricately designed garden in which ground coves, low shrubs or coloured earths are arranged in interlacing patterns resembling knots
A structure used for the drying of food using an indirect source of heat.
A structure used for the roasting or drying of chicory.
A place where worship is offered or devotions are paid to a deity or saint.
A house of Roman Catholic nuns or canonesses.
Use with form of extraction where known. Also use MINE and other ores extracted where relevant, eg. SILVER MINE.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the production of cement.

A mill which ground clinker in the cement production process. During cement production a mixture of lime and clay is burnt which forms a clinker which is then ground into powder. When mixed with water it solidifies to hard cement.
A factory, incorporating power driven machinery from the late 18th century, where cloth was manufactured from threads interlaced at right angles to each other in a loom.
A narrow, open container, usually where food or water for animals is put. Use specific type where known.
A long, wooden, metal or stone vessel holding drinking water for horses.
A long metal or stone vessel for cattle to drink water from.
A long stone or metal vessel for dogs to drink water from.

A building which has been temporarily taken over for use by the military or civilian authorities. During wartime buildings were requisitioned for various purposes, such as temporary hospitals or headquarters.
A building used by an organization or society to promote the study of oriental languages and history through lectures, research, etc.
A house or range of buildings in which dogs are kept, eg. hunting hounds.

An area of managed countryside designated for visitors to enjoy recreations, such as walking specified parks and trails, in a rural environment. Often provides public facilities such as parking, toilets, cafes and visitor information.
A structure, often ornamental, in a garden, park or area of recreation, designed to reflect the style of Indian architecture. The most famous example of which is the Royal Pavilion in Brighton.
A highly defensible gateway, usually of stone with two or more storeys, built into the defensive walls of a town or city.
A place from which clay is extracted.
A pit used for the excavation of clay suitable for making bricks.
A building providing lodgings for members of the police force.
A building or area within a brewery where barrels of ale are stored.
A hospital devoted to the curing or correcting of physical deformities.
A pit filled with rubble, etc., into which rain or waste water flows in order to disperse into the surrounding soil.
A dispersed farmstead where buildings and yards (regular or loose courtyard in their form) are sited alongside a routeway.
A fortified river or river bank forming part of the anti invasion infrastructure.
Steps found at a landing point.
A large wooden structure built alongside the edge of a river where boats may lie for the loading and unloading of goods and passengers.
A building or room for the storage of vegetables, particularly root vegetables, for human consumption.
Any church which bears signs of fortification. Churches on the Welsh and Scottish borders were often fortified, only allowing access to the tower from a single opening in the nave.
An abbey or a priory of Cistercian nuns.
A share or portion of land, allotted to a person, often used for growing, vegetables, fruit, etc.
A roughly square mound of stones which may also contain or conceal a burial.
Reformatory established under the Inebriates Acts 1879-1900 for repeat alcohol related offenders
A building providing business premises to companies or individuals, sometimes for short periods, in exchange for a membership fee.
A single storey building designed so that windows incorporated into the saw tooth roof catch the available light.
A device on an airfield for securing aircrafts when parked outside in order to prevent major movement due to the weather or other conditions.
Buildings incorporating a high degree of protection against damp for the bulk storage of salt.
A structure providing protection against the weather at tram stops.
A large shed for the housing of aircraft, etc.
A hangar for the storage and maintenance of dirigible motor-driven balloons.
A building or site where aircraft can be stored and maintained.
A seperate wing of a large house provide accommodation for guests.
A kiln in which lime is made by calcining limestone or in some areas chalk.
A lime kiln built into a low hillside or slope to facilitate top loading of the limestone.
An area of ground where training in the use of grenades can be carried out.
A chemical works engaged in the production of Ammonium Nitrate, used as a fertilizer or for use in the explosives industry.
A building or site used for the production of both chemical and organic fertilizer.
A building or site producing nitrogen-rich fertilizer.
A building or site where phosphorous-based fertilizers are produced by controlled chemical reactions.
A garden containing trees or shrubs pruned and trained into various geometric, zoomorphic or fantastic shapes.
A threshing barn which also houses farm animals and is somethimes used to stotre grain, house carts and other functions.
A multi-purpose farm building.
A non-conformist minister's house.

A place of worship for members of the Religious Society of Friends, often known as Quakers. The Religious Society of Friends is a denomination founded by George Fox in c.1650 who believed in passivist principles and a rejection of the sacrament.
skos:Concept.skos:altLabel: Religious Society Of Friends Meeting House

skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: A farmstead where mostly detached buildings have developed around one side of an open cattle yard.
A low lying area of land that is usually waterlogged at all times and is flooded in wet weather.
Fairground attraction designed to create optical illusions to give a sense of unbalance and unease.
A windmill with a stationary timber body which contains the grinding machinery, and which supports a rotating cap in which the sails rotate.
A building or part of a building used for the storage of stationery materials.
Large field or yard used to lay fabrics out ready for bleaching.
Mushroom-shaped stones used to raise the floor of barns, granaries etc. above ground level, to prevent vermin gaining access to stored grain and fodder.
An oval or circular structure with seats rising in tiers around a central open space. Used for religious ceremonies, entertainment, training and armed combat contests.
Part of textile mills.
Sites, buildings or structures involved in passive air defence, usually by forcing hostile aircraft to fly high or drop their bombs on the wrong targets. Use more specific term.
A site equipped for passive or active defence against an airborne enemy assault.
A sewer or irrigation channel designed to avoid blockage.
A mill used for the extraction and processing of starch.
A factory engaged in the manufacture of small arms ammunition, especially the metal components and filling with the explosive propellant.
A building or site used for the manufacture of weapons, ammunition and military supplies. Use more specific type where known.
An mill in which manganese was ground to a powder between two horizontal millstones.
A camp for the temporary accommodation of uprooted civilians or foreign ex-service personnel, who had fought for the British forces during WWII (e.g.Polish).
A building or site where boat sails are manufactured from processed cloth.
Container for the storage of unspecified materials.
A tank found on hop farms in which creosote was held, heated from below by a fire with a chimney. The ends of hop poles were dipped in the tar to prevent rotting in soil.
A building or group of buildings, incorporating radio masts, built to intercept radio transmissions from enemy vessels and aircraft during WWI and WWII.

A type of transportable aircraft hangar patented by Miskins and Sons in 1939. The arched hangar was constructed of steel or wooden ribs and generally clad in steel sheets. The hangar did not require any foundations and could be anchored by iron stakes.
A mill for beating and cleaning cloth, using soap or fullers earth.
A building or site from which a lookout can be kept.
A heated room or building used to dry yarn after it has been washed.
A port, dock or harbour where ferries, hovercraft, ocean liners and cargo vessels can load and unload. May include road and/or rail terminals for transportation to the port.
An area of a port, dock or harbour, often including buildings for passport control and customs, where passengers of ocean liners can embark/disembark and where supplies can be taken on board.
A site where iron is smelted or iron goods made.
A piece of ground over which small arms or large artillery may be fired at targets. For rocket and missile firing use ROCKET TEST FACILITY.
A shelter on a firing range from which the wepaons testing can be viewed in safety.
The field or area of ground on which a battle or skirmish was fought.
Site with important historical association.
Sites, buildings, structures, features & areas of land commemorating an historical event, person or animal.
A site where cement is manufactured for the building industry.
A floating bridge, generally temporary, whose decks are supported on low flat-bottomed or hollow floats.
A factory used for the manufacture of scythes.
An often secluded garden set below the level of surrounding ground, usually surrounded with terraces.
Debris consisting of excess construction material used in the building of a nearby site or structure. If unsure of whether debris is from construction or demolition, index with both terms.
A textile-weaving factory housing powerlooms; commonly a one-storeyed shed with wide, north-light roof carried on iron columns.

A prefabricated structure of a steel frame clad in corrugated iron. Semi-circular in section they were used for storage and as workshops, cinemas etc during WWII. Designed at Romney House, London by the Directorate of Fortifications & Works.
A place where a yearly or half-yearly court of record is held by lords of certain manors.
A substantial monument attached to a wall and often standing on the floor.
A military storage aircraft hangar built in the late 1930s. It comprises a semicircular concrete structure with reinforced concrete columns, featuring a curved roof and straight walls.
An often stately or ornate entrance to a railway tunnel.
The entrance to a tramway tunnel.
The entrance to a road tunnel, sometimes of a grand construction.
An often stately and ornate entrance to a canal tunnel.
The entrance to a tunnel. Use more specific type where known.
A tower serving as a reservoir to deliver water at a required point.
A plate-steel water tank on a steel tower designed to hold 80,000 gallons of water. Designed to Air Ministry drawing number 9526/41.

A large, circular, reinforced-concrete tank supported on concrete staging built to Air Ministry drawing number 1178/25 and designed to hold 30,000 gallons of water. The height of the tower varied according to local site requirements.
A plate-steel water tower made with two compartments holding 30,000 gallons of water. Designed to Air Ministry drawing number 20/40.
A barrier, usually of wood or chain, stretched across the entrance to a harbour, port or anchorage, to control entry and/or limit the effect of the weather on the wave action.
A building housing a flight simulator designed to air ministry drawing number 7790/40.
A building in which wrought iron or steel chains were manufactured.
A site where wrought iron or steel chains were manufactured.
A group of, usually three, standing stones forming a square with an open side and often found with a stone circle.
An arrangement of one or more standing stones. Use particularly for isolated recumbent stones, or where original form of monument unclear. Use specific type where known.
Trees, hedges and shrubs planted in the form of a medieval cathedral sometimes used as a memorial.
A forester's cottage.
A distilling or brewing house.

A structure, based on drawing number (3329/41), intended to be the headquarters for the coordination of an airfield's defences. Constructed above ground this design was found to be vulnerable and was superceded by the (11008/41).
A concrete structure designed to be the headquarters for the coordination of an airfield's defences. Constructed partially underground it was only intended to be occupied during an attack.
A column, in the form of a female figure, used to support an entablature.
Use for free standing column.
A group of planted trees or shrubs, generally of uniform age and of a single species.
A building or room where motor vehicles are exhibited for sale.
A canal built as a military obstacle, but also used for the transport of military stores, equipment and personnel.
An artificial navigable waterway used for the transportation of goods. Nowadays also used for recreational purposes.
An office for the administration of town or country estates.
Works producing a refractory clay, kaolin. An essential raw material of porcelain and some types of papermaking.
A fortified wall surrounding a town or city.
1st World War end-opening aeroplane hangar.

A sunken, circular, concrete pillbox used on airfields. They remained flush with the surface to permit the free movement of aircraft but, if attack threatened, could be raised hydraulically or by a counterbalance, and manned to give covering fire.
A building where a stallion is kept.
An instrument used for making a loud sound for information or warning.
A building associated with a spinning mill in which raw material is mechanically spun into yarn or thread.
Graves known to be of shipwreck victims buried close to their site of discovery, as was customary until the 19th century, rather than in consecrated ground.
A building with shelves and/or stands for skeps or wooden hives, and flight holes through the walls for bees.
A place where beehives are kept.
A dark outbuilding or cellar with internal recesses for overwintering skeps of bees.
A large, usually unroofed building with tiers of seats for spectators built in various shapes and enclosing a field used for sports events.
A medieval hospital for lepers, usually consisting of a church and individual shelters for the lepers.
A yard or enclosure attached to a farmhouse, usually surrounded by other farm buildings.
A type of kiln, usually built into banking, with a stone lining that was used to produce white coal which was used as fuel in the lead smelting process.
A site where coal is processed.
A wheel rotated by the treading of persons or animals to power machinery to raise water, etc.
A coin-operated meter receiving fees for parking a vehicle in a street, and indicating time allowed.
A structure providing protection against the weather, situated on railway platforms.
A large scale works for cloth finishing processes.

An earthwork feature used by hunters to trap deer comprising a steep ditch into which the deer are chased with an enclosure to hold them at one end, known from the Isle of Rum and a debateable example in Cumbria.
An enclosure used for corralling deer.
A factory for the production of plastics by chemical processes.
An aircraft maintenance workshop deriving from the use of weather proofing varnish to aircraft canvas called "dope" in order to keep the canvas taut and airtight. From 1912 onwards.
A covered tank in which rainwater is stored for use when required.
A receptacle for the storage of water.
A workshop in which products are made using wood and timber.
A workshop where wooden brushes are manufactured on a small scale.
A school used by the children of settlers at a Chartist Colony.
The residence of a cloth cutter.
A combination of obstructions, used either to stop enemy forces or force them off the road.
A roadblock, usually manned by the Home Guard, where the credentials of civilians and military personnel where checked before allowing them to proceed.
A geometrical planting of trees in the form of the number 5 as represented on a dice.

A section of the water channel of a river, shut off above and below by lock gates provided with sluices to let water in and out and thus raise or lower boats from one level to another. Often found situated next to a weir.
An open metalwork structure supporting either a fabrication shed or the runners for an overhead crane.
A structure composed of two large upright stone supporting a third, lintel stone.
A stone or boulder which has been deliberately set upright in the ground. Use only for isolated stones. Otherwise use specific type where known.
A mill in which barytes concentrates were ground to fine white powder, normally by use of flat millstones similar to those of a corn mill.
Mill for fine grinding of tin ore between millstones.
A building containing mechanically powered ore crushers or rollers.
A mill used for the preparation of Barilla, an ash of burnt seaweed that was used for the production of soda.
A mill for crushing flint. Crushed flint was used in the manufacture of pottery in order to whiten and strengthen the body of earthenware pottery.
A mill used for the preparation and production of Calamine.

A small, defended settlement dating to the Early Iron Age, located on spurs, promontories or hilltops. The defences are marked by single or double trenches which originally held substantial palisades.
An enclosed settlement surrounded by a single or double row of close-set timbers embedded in a foundation trench, without ditches or banks.
A site where cobalt is mined

A small, defended settlement dating to the Early Iron Age, located on spurs, promontories or hilltops. The defences are marked by single or double trenches which originally held substantial palisades.
An enclosed settlement surrounded by a single or double row of close-set timbers embedded in a foundation trench, without ditches or banks.
A building or room where beer is decanted from conditioning tanks, into casks or barrels.

A rectangular chamber of brick or stone with heavy wooden gates at either end equipped with sluices to let water in and out, thereby enabling a canal boat to be lowered or raised to a different level.
A building housing the generator set and associated equipment supplying electricity to a radar station.
A building housing one end of an underwater telegraph cable.
A military base for the training of SOE operatives in the skills and techniques required to survive in enemy-occupied territory.

A complex of buildings, often within an enclosure, housing a pre-Benedictine Reform secular religious community. Now commonly used to describe the main church within such a complex, which over time attained higher status.
An opening or cavity through which a stream or natural watercourse disappears underground.
A closely mown lawn used for the game of croquet.
Narrow, rough tracks often over upland routes used by packhorse trains to carry goods.
Specialized engineering workshop particularly for the production of marine engines or other large components of ships.
A building or site used for the production of anchors.
A heavy framework of parallel beams used to support a ship in dock.
Covered area for making large engineered constructions such as sections of ships or bridges.
Large covered spaces where the steel plate used for ship construction was cut and marked out, prior to being craned onto the hull, etc.
An open metalwork structure supporting either a fabrication shed or the runners for an overhead crane.
A storage rack for sections of steel plate used in the construction of ships.
The unarticulated remains of the body of a human being. If articulated use inhumation.
A rough shelter or dwelling, sometimes used to house cattle.

A pillbox design, assigned a drawing number by DFW branch 3. Although originally believed to be a distinct type, FW3/45 has recently been found to be a design for modifications to existing types. Double index with specific type where known.
A workshop or factory unit where small or light goods are manufacture without the need for large-scale industrial machinery.
A building where milk is deposited and stored before it is despatched to the consumer.
A factory complex consisting of PRINTING SHOPS, COLOUR HOUSES, DYE HOUSES, etc, in which patterns are printed onto calico.
A factory or complex containing machinery for the manufacture of printed materials.
Buildings and sites associated with the manufacture of motor vehicles.
A building or works in which carriages were built. Use RAILWAY CARRIAGE WORKS for sites making railway carriages.
A large site specializing in the manufacture of locomotives.
A house by a toll gate or toll bridge where tolls are collected.
Circular enclosure featuring an enclosing bank with no accompanying ditch. Use specific type where known.
A steep bank or slope. In fortifications, the bank or wall immediately in front of and below the rampart.
A bank or mound of earth used as a rampart or fortification.
Linear or curvilinear construction of earth, turf and stone, often, but not always accompanied by a ditch. Use specific type where known.

An offshore station, equipped with a fixed electronic radio navigation and positioning system such as Hyperfix. The transmission principle are pulsed and phase comparisons systems. Superceded by Global Positioning System in 1994.
A building, usually associated with a port or dock, where seamen could get a meal and a cheap room. Often established by religious groups for the moral betterment of seamen.
Any building, group of buildings, or site at which tungsten ores have been converted to sodium tungstate by means of the Oxland Process. This was first used at Drakewalls Mine, Cornwall, in 1850.
Unspecified landscape feature. Use more specific type where known.
An open circular area where avenues converge.
A building in which the buying of raw cotton and finished goods took place.
A multi-purpose commercial building, used primarily as a trading place for merchants, but also incorporating shops, public offices, guildhalls, etc.
A place where two artificial waterways meet each other.
A railway used for the conveyance of coal and other minerals.
An observation tower located on or near to a bombing range.
A building used to dry teazle heads in. Teazles were used to raise the nap on cloth in teazle shops.
The residence of the supervisor of an inclined plane.
A stall where a cobbler mends shoes.

A recess in a stone or brick wall, usually bounding a garden or orchard, set two to three feet from the ground and facing south to south-east to catch the morning sun, in which a bee skep/beehive is placed. Often found in groupings of three to six.
A pipe through which water is conducted.
A mine for the extraction of iron ore.
A fighter satellite station watch office built to Air Ministry design drawing number 14383/40.
The residence of a chauffeur or driver
A free school for poor children.
A hospital block from where patients are discharged after an operation or other treatment.
A mill for grinding corn. Use with power type where known.
A building housing equipment for the process of distillation.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the process of distilling.
An establishment where tea and other non-alcoholic refreshments and light meals are served.
