A point of public water supply, including conduits, fountains, wells, pumps and standpipes.

A complex of buildings used as a headquarters and training base for Royal Navy personnel. Even though they are buildings on land shore establishments are deemed to be shipsand are designated 'HMS' eg. HMS Dolphin in Portsmouth.
The area of a military base where engineering and maintenance functions are grouped.
A chemical works engaged in the production of Ammonium Nitrate, used as a fertilizer or for use in the explosives industry.
A warehouse, usually under the charge of CUSTOM HOUSE officials, in which goods were stored before the duty had been paid. Often found in dockyards, harbours, etc.

A type of warehouse found in naval victualling yards, used for the storage of rum, a ration of which was given on a daily basis to members of the Royal Navy, up until the 1980s, when this practice ceased.
A jettied house where the upper storey only overhangs the end elevation of the building.
A privately-funded home for the care of the elderly.
A residential home for older people or people with physical and/or mental disabilities who need care provided by registered nurses.
An engineering workshop, often attached to an engine shed, for the running repairs of operational parts, etc.
A building or room used for any type of engineering work. Use more specific type where known.
A Neolithic burial monument comprising an approximately circular stony mound which contains a stone-built chamber, with or without additional lateral chambers.
A building where carpets and other floor furnishings were woven.
A handloom weavers workshop where the weaver received yarn from a clothier and manufactured a woven piece of cloth from it.
A workshop where tapestries were made.
Loading machinery tipping coal into railway wagons usually at a pithead.
A tippler, a machine for loading wagons at a pithead, operated by hydraulic power.
A shop that sells men's clothes, either off the peg, bespoke or both.
A 19th century spa building, usually consisting of a hotel with baths used for water treatment.
A bridge used for carrying liquids, usually water, although sometimes oil, in a pipeline over a river. Mid 19th century onwards.
A church attached to or founded by a college.

A concrete arched military hut constructed by pouring concrete over hessian cloth that had been stretched over a temporary steel framework. Semi circular in section usually with end walls of brick. Designed by the Waller Housing Corp in 1943.
A wooden, stone or iron post for securing things to or for preventing vehicular access to pedestrianized areas.
A workshop where baskets were manufactured.

A 19th century establishment for the provision of work for the unemployed poor of a parish; later an institution administered by Guardians of the Poor, in which paupers are lodged and the able-bodied set to work.

A pass, vulnerable to attack from the enemy but essential for the movement of troops and which, if captured, could divide a defending force. As a result such passes are defended with anti invasion defences such as pillboxes.
A specialist veterinary hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of horses.
A factory where worsted, a well-twisted woollen yarn made from long staple wool and used in the manufacture of suits and other garments, was produced.
A place where radio programmes are produced and broadcast.
Small discreet rural settlements which do not provide the commercial, legal or ecclesiastical services typically found within medieval urban areas.
A building or room where business, administrative or professional activities are conducted. Use specific type where known.
A hospital for the medical or surgical treatment of domestic or wild animals.
A building, range of buildings or site, for the accommodation, rearing and/or treatment of animals, birds and fish, both wild and domestic.
A site intended for use by the Auxiliary Units (or British Resistance Organisation) in the event of an invasion. Use more specific term.
A hideout containing radio equipment to be used by the Special Duties sections of the Auxiliary Units to send information to the control station for relaying to headquarters.

skos:Concept.skos:prefLabel: Auxiliary Unit Special Duties Control Station
skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: An underground hideout containing radio equipment to be used by the Special Duties sections of the Auxiliary Units to co-ordinate information collected by the outstations for relaying to headquarters.

skos:Concept.skos:prefLabel: Auxiliary Unit Special Duties Zero Station
skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: An underground hideout containing radio equipment to be used by the Special Duties sections of the Auxiliary Units to recieve coded information from the out-stations in the surrounding area for relaying to headquarters via direct phone line.

A well concealed structure, usually constructed undergound, intended for use by members of the Special Duties section of the Auxiliary Units (or British Resistance Organization) in the event of invasion.
A purpose-built terrace of shops.
Based on a typical 18ft span, 40ft long temporary brick hut but with two bay windows in the front elevation, one for the watch office and one for the chief instructor.
The residence of an engineer.
A school conducted by members of a convent.
A coupled timber built end-opening First World War aircraft hangar.

A designated area within a town or village with fixed defences such as pillboxes, anti tank ditches and gun emplacements, designed to threaten the flanks of an enemy force which had broken through a stop line.
A mill used to process logwood, the inner red wood of a South American tree used widely in dyeing. Imported in the form of logs and cut and ground into dye by a mechanical process.
A platform or other structure for the use of a band of musicians.
A hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of patients with cancer or related illnesses.
A churchyard or memorial cross set on a long shaft.

An enclosure defined by a single bank and entrance. They occur on every type of ground, although they favour sheltered, valley side locations. Smaller and usually less well defended than hillforts they are thought to be settlements of Iron Age date.
Gun battery built specifically to mount short range weapons to defend a beach against an attempted landing.
A type of WATERMILL, powered by retaining seawater at high tide and then releasing it at low tide via the water wheel.
A bridge on which dwellings or commercial premises have been built.

The earliest side-opening standard type of aircraft hangar designed in 1913 and used in WWI. Originally constructed from wooden trusses and struts, one example has steel frames. It comprised a single or coupled shed with rear workshops.

The earliest side-opening standard type of aircraft hangar designed in 1913 and used in WWI. Originally constructed from wooden trusses and struts, some examples have steel frames. It comprised a single or coupled shed with rear workshops.

skos:Concept.skos:altLabel: Royal Flying Corps Side Opening Aircraft Hangar

skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: A type of carriage house, usually in a churchyard, for storing a hearse.
An outbuilding used for the storage and maintenance of horse-drawn carriages.
A complex of buildings where electricity is produced using steam-powered turbines.
A textile mill where thread undergoes the processes of twisting and doubling to provide material strong enough to be spun and woven.
A mill used for the mechanized processing of silk.
A building in which silk was dried.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the manufacture of silk.
A building wherein silk worm cocoons are boiled to release the silk fibres.
A model village built in association with a factory, mill, railway, or any other industrial complex; usually built by the employer.
A place used for the milking of cows.
A building over a well housing machinery for raising the water. Often consisting of a DONKEY WHEEL or HORSE GIN.
A bridge carrying a railway track across a river, valley, road etc.
A specialized form of truss bridge that extends or cantilevers from both sides of the pier, the inner 'arms' usually supporting a central span.
A bridge made up of many relatively small members joined together in a series of interconnecting triangles.
A large building used for the transaction of the public business of a town, the holding of courts of justice, entertainments and other activities.
The area surrounding a monastic house including conventual buildings, outbuildings, cemetery, fishponds, etc, usually marked out by a bank and/or ditch or precinct wall.
Purpose built accommodation for members of the armed forces and their families.
A long, low-rise building consisting of rows of attached individual suites of rooms used for overnight accommodation by motorists.
A well concealed structure, usually constructed underground, intended for use by members of the British Resistance Organization in the event of invasion.
A small workshop, employing up to 10 men, working on hand-operated carding engines and hand jennies, spinning yarn for handloom weavers.
A gate leading to water, either a river or the sea. Used as a means of supplying castles, for example, with goods brought by water transport.
A holding tank/pen on a river or seashore for raising and preserving fish and/or for catching them easily.
An area where fish are naturally present, eg. part of a river.
A multi-level structure designed to simulate tall buildings to allow firefighters to practice firefighting and rescue techniques
A civic building housing fire engines and a permanent fire-fighting force.
A fire station built for use by the Auxiliary Fire Service, established in 1938 to supplement existing local brigades.
A building or room where items of pottery are manufactured. Includes handcrafted and machine made pottery.
A factory where tweed, a twilled woollen fabric with an unfinished surface, is manufactured.
The area beneath a natural overhang at the base of a cliff or crag. This may have been used for occupation, burial, etc. Index with site type where known.
A platform, sometimes floating, for the landing of passengers and goods from vessels.
An area of land, usually on a slope, which has been built up to provide a flat surface for the cultivation of crops.
A building for the storage, repair and maintenance of chains for lighthouses, lightships and lightbouys.
20th century plant for separating minerals using variations in water-repellent properties under controlled chemical conditions. Survives as ruins of buildings or tanks.
A factory used for the production of red lead used in glass manufacture, or white lead used as the pigment in white paint.
A workshop used for the decoration of fired pottery or ceramics. Usually part of a larger complex.
A levelled area of ground, circular in shape, used as the base on which a monument was built.Sometimes raised, a platform is often the sole surviving evidence for a monument.

A site where a building once stood as identified by a level area of ground, often compacted or made from man-made materials. Use only where specific function is unknown, otherwise use more specific term.
A raised platform or stage for public speaking or conducting an orchestra. Also a platform for supporting cameras during filming.
Platform or structure used for viewing performances.
Unspecified. Use specific type where known.
A simple form of stone slab bridge, particularly associated with South West England.
A non-specialist hospital dealing in general medical and surgical treatment.
A marked path along which aircraft taxi to or from a parking area, runway, etc.
A substantial area of ground surrounded by slight univallate earthwork often interpreted as stock enclosures or as sites where agricultural produce was stored.

A small, defended settlement dating to the Early Iron Age, located on spurs, promontories or hilltops. The defences are marked by single or double trenches which originally held substantial palisades.
A covered area of ground attached to a building.
A paved area, generally found at the back of a house.
A low, hemispherical cairn surrounded by a freestanding, continuous circle of boulders.
A pillow-shaped, flat topped rectangular mound often surrounded by a shallow ditch used to farm rabbits.
In the glass industry this is bench-like structure within the melting-furnace on which crucibles are placed.
A mill for grinding corn. Use with power type where known.
A building temporarily requisitioned for use as an auxiliary hospital administered by members of the Voluntary Aid Detachment during the First World War.

A building temporarily requistioned for use as a hospital. Auxiliary hospitals treated the less seriously wounded and were less strict than military hospitals although they remained under military control.
A workshop with equipment for the making and repair of ships' rigging.
A bridge for carrying a road or railway over another.
A building, usually within the grounds of a school and often containing dormitories, used by pupils who board.
A hospital where people with learning disabilities receive medical treatment.
An enclosure where ewes are kept at the time of lambing.

A building used for the preparatory processes in which long and short staple flax fibres were separated by passing through combs. Flax dressing or 'heckling' shops may be located both on and off mill sites.
A lime kiln built into a low hillside or slope to facilitate top loading of the limestone.
A kiln in which lime is made by calcining limestone or in some areas chalk.
Any earthworks, walling, bastion or fortified outwork, or combination of these, generally with ditch or moat.
A hangar for the storage and maintenance of dirigible motor-driven balloons.
Vertical screens made of wood or steel framing mounted on concrete blocks were built to protect airships from cross winds when entering or leaving the airship sheds.
A building or site used for the production of naphtha, a volatile petroleum-derived product used in the manufacture of solvents, cleaning fluids etc.
Accommodation designed for the elderly, disabled, etc, as individual units.
A narrow bridge for people and animals to cross on foot.
A shallow outdoor pool, usually rectangular in shape filled with water which when frozen was used for the sport of Curling.
The official residence of a dean.
A radio station set up to broadcast signals aimed at 'bending' or altering German navigation transmissions.
A hotel where no alcohol is available.
A pound for the accommodation of livestock.
Small engineering works specialising in the production of items such as ploughs and threshing machinery.
A manor or estate owned and run by an order of knights and governed by a preceptor.
skos:Concept.skos:altLabel: Preceptory Of The Knights Of St Lazarus

skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: An estate or manor of a subordinate community of the Knights of the Order of the Hospital of St John of Jerusalem. Includes the mother house, the Priory of St. John, Clerkenwell.
A storage area usually for naval weapons and stores.
A massive structure, usually of stone, serving as a pier or breakwater, or joining two places separated by water.
Non-military maritime flood and erosion defences.
A structure providing accommodation for poultry.
A place where (young) holiday-makers and hikers can be put up cheaply for the night.
A building used as a temporary form of accommodation during a holiday, which includes self-catering.
A type of clothier's house, consisting of TOPSHOP and dwelling, used for hand-weaving of textiles.
A water-filled hole used for the disposal of aggregate originally used as ballast in ships.
A place used to clean the fleece of sheep before shearing. This could be a watercourse temporarily dammed in order to wash sheep.
A pen for holding sheep waiting to be washed.
A place where sheep are washed in a chemical bath to control the parasites of sheep. To conserve the poisonous chemicals the bath is usually small and are not allowed to enter any watercourse.
A place or building where animals can be washed. Often in the form of a pool with a walled funnel-like structure enabling animals to be guided into the pool.
A college founded for the education and betterment of the working classes. Lectures usually being held after the end of the working day.
A pit in the ground from where minerals are dug.
A site where coal is processed.
Used where an existing building is designated as the residence of an official.
A house with an aisle on one side only.
Use where the intervening arcade is closed but timber-framed.
A site, usually including fuel tanks, pipe works and control buildings, where flaming petroleum was intended to be used as a weapon against a hostile invasion.
An anti-personnel device consisting of a 40 gallon fuel drum placed on top of an explosive charge and detonator. When detonated the barrel would explode sending burning fuel over the intended target.
A kiln for roasting ore.
A type of calcining kiln used in the processing of iron ore.
A place where scrap metal is collected.
A building in London belonging to one of four legal societies having exclusive right of admitting persons to practise at the English bar.
A manufacturing complex incorporating furnaces, calciner and condenser flues. Use SMELTERY for more modern type of plant.

Blocks of concrete with four protruding arms so that, whichever way up the caltrop is placed, one arm will always point upward. Used in imitation of the iron caltrops thrown on the ground to impede cavalry.
A building used for the decarburizing of pig iron to produce wrought iron.
A building or site where bloom iron or cast iron is forged into wrought iron.
Permanently moored historic maritime craft preserved and converted into a museum and open to the public.
An enclosure containing a dock, boat yard, warehouse, etc, in which canal vessels are built and repaired, and all sorts of stores and merchandise for transportation brought together.
A building used by a group of people who meet socially to participate in activities, usually related to a particular interest or occupation.
A place where ambulances are serviced and maintained.
A factory engaged in the manufacture of small arms ammunition, especially the metal components and filling with the explosive propellant.
Obstacles like concrete cubes, cylinders or pimples erected in the defence of Britain.
A metal girder, usually of iron or steel, embedded in the ground designed to obstruct the progress of hostile tanks or armoured vehicles.
A piece of land used to grow vegetables to be sold at markets.
A lock at the end of one company's canal where it joins another company's canal.
One of a line of blocks on the floor of a building slip on which the keel of the ship to be constructed is laid. Also used in dry docks to rest a ship when a dock is pumped dry.

A factory or group of buildings engaged in the manufacture of acetone. A variety of processes may be used to manufacture acetone including the use of destructive distallation of wood and fermentation technology.
A storage rack for sections of steel plate used in the construction of ships.
A slaughterhouse for horses.
A kiln principally used in brick making which gives a continuous operation.
A small, steel shelter designed for use as a firewatchers post during an air raid.

A building or structure used to provide protection to an Air Raid Warden or firewatcher during an air raid, thus enabling the identification of the locations of fires caused by incendiary bombs in comparative safety.
A door, gate, doorway or gateway of grand or elaborate construction. Use specific type where possible.
Manmade constructions used to prevent water flooding the surrounding area. Often taking the form of a bank or wall but may be more elaborate e.g. the Thames Barrier.
A channel dug, or built up, to carry away surplus water from a river or waterway to prevent it bursting its banks and flooding.
A club where predominantly rhythm and blues style music is played, analagous to a jazz club.
A small eating and drinking establishment or refreshment bar at a railway station for the use of passengers.
A small eating and drinking establishment or refreshment bar.

Blocks of solid concrete, in the form of cylinders usually 2 feet across x 2 feet 6 inches or 3 feet high. Cylinders were mainly used in road blocks intended to impede enemy movement in the event of invasion.
A school attended by children between the ages of eleven and sixteen.
A school attended by children between the ages of eleven and sixteen offering a vocationally orientated curriculum.

A house within a row. At first floor level a gallery which runs through the front of the building. Access to the gallery was gained by steps set at intervals along the row. Commonly found in the city of Chester.
A building complex with hangars and slipways built adjacent to a body of water where seaplanes can be stored and maintained.
A chemical works engaged in the production of the coal tar derivative phenol, a chemical used for the manufacture of explosives during WWI.
A barrier of concrete or earth, etc, built across a river to create a reservoir of water for domestic and/or industrial usage.
A dam constructed across a stream to raise its water-level and make it available to power a mill wheel.
A garden designed to display sculpture, publicly or privately.
For the production of clay tobacco pipes.
An establishment with automatic washing machines available for public use.

A curved dam usually built of concrete and designed with the curve upstream so that the force of the water compresses the structure and strengthens it as it pushes it into its foundations. Arch dams are best suited to narrow gorges
A barrier of concrete or earth, etc, built across a river to create a reservoir of water for domestic and/or industrial usage.
A garden building or greenhouse, containing pools in which Water Lilies are grown.
A house which bears signs of fortification. These often include crenellated battlements and narrow slit-like windows.
A fortified house of two or three storeys, the lower floor being used to house animals and the upper for domestic use.

A chemical works engaged in the manufacture of the coal tar derivative, picric acid, often associated with the textile industry where it was used as a dye, but more commonly with the explosives industry where it was used as the shell filling Lyddite.
A column set on a pedestal and decorated with the bows of warships to celebrate naval victories. Originally a Roman form, it was revived in 17th and 18th century decoration.
The residence of a signalman.
A house, enclosure or large cage for the keeping and breeding of birds.
The limit line of a parish.
A printer's workshop in the newspaper/publishing industries.
A mooring, usually consisting of a concrete plinth, to which a barrage balloon was attached.
A building associated with a barrage balloon site and intended to provide shelter for the balloon crew from air attack.
A site where a single large balloon was attached by fine wire cables to the ground to form an aerial obstruction to attacking enemy aircraft.
A site where chalk is extracted from the ground.
A furnace used for the smelting or reheating of lead.
Cottage provided for guests to a country house.
A building, or first-floor room in a building, for the dry and secure storage of grain after it has been threshed and winnowed.
A body of water placed in such a way as to reflect a building or landscape feature.
A place of accommodation for a stablehand.
A building or settlement enclosure with a thick drystone wall, generally circular or oval in plan, usually sited in an elevated position.
A site where machine tools, machines designed to remove surplus material from a work piece by accurately guided cutting tools, are manufactured.
House owned by the church, often used for meetings.
An inn temporarily used for the performance of plays and other public entertainment.
A wayside inn for livestock traders.
A public house offering lodgings to the passengers, and stabling for the horses of stage coaches.
An inn, with an integral courtyard, for the lodging and entertainment of travellers. Often with open galleried wings overlooking the courtyard.
A public house for the lodging and entertainment of travellers, etc.
A farmstead where mostly detached buildings have developed around two sides of an open cattle yard.
A factory used for the manufacture of ordnance including small arms, ammunition, artillery pieces and armoured fighting vehicles.
A wall for growing fruit, dating in England from the mid-18th century, whose curving lines gave added strength, thus doing away with the need for buttressing.
A kiln in which stone is burnt as it falls through a heated and slightly inclined steel tube.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the manufacture of plaster.
A building in which apparatus measuring the amount of water supplied/used is housed.
A crane mounted on wheels and/or rails, used for the unloading of ships' cargoes.

Building block (often a temporary brick structure or Nissen hut) comprising office accommodation for flight commanders and flight sergeants as well as pilots' rest rooms, storerooms and locker rooms. Some flight offices have central corridors.
A fortified tower found at the angle of a castle wall.
A market building, pre-19th century, incorporating other function rooms, eg. theatres, courtrooms, schoolrooms.
A building or group of buildings owned and operated by a governing body and often occupied by a government agency. Use specific type of building where known.
A complex of buildings producing power derived from nuclear energy.
An area of land which has been drained or cleared for habitation and/or cultivation.
A small, Iron Age/Romano-British enclosed settlement found in South West England.
A rotating, domed, steel turret set over a circular pit used as a gun emplacement.
Working area for rag sorting and grading.
A building where horses are rubbed down after training.
A building used for the storage and distribution of civilian respirators and Air Raid Precautions equipment.
A piece of stone, usually shaped, of uncertain origin or use.
A small area of managed woodland, created to provide cover for deer and other game.
A protected parachute store built with permanent brick cavity walls and a roof of reinforced concrete slabs in two heights separated by lantern lights.
A hospital for convalescents or consumptives.
A basin or harbour, which is open to the tides. Vessels can only enter and leave at high tide and are stranded at low tide.
A woollen mill in which the cloth was passed over rollers covered in short spikes to raise the nap in one direction only.
A channel carrying overflow water past a dam. Early 19th century onwards.
A building or complex where animal hair is processed, using a variety of means, for use in products such as brushes, mattresses etc.
The cleaning and sorting of horse hair mainly for use in the upholstery trade.
A canal built as a military obstacle, but also used for the transport of military stores, equipment and personnel.
A model village established by the chartists.

A factory used for the production of artificial limbs. They were often located within the precincts of a hospital, to enable fittings to take place and help the amputee to get used to wearing the limb.
The official residence of a bishop.
An official residence of a bishop used during the summer months.
A house constructed with a basic timber framework; between the members are panels which can be infilled with timber, wattle and daub, plaster, brick or other materials.
A house in which a pair of curved timbers form a bowed A-frame which supports the roof independently of the walls.
A timber framed house comprising horizontal and vertical timbers, forming the walls of the building and directly supporting the roof.
Area of land set aside and managed for the preservation of flora, fauna, their natural habitats and physical features.
A large, rectangular pillbox based on the FW3/28 with the addition of a small infantry chamber to one side of the main gun chamber.
Similar in design to the Callender Hangar but with a reduced height of 17ft. Built to Air Ministry drawing number 17346/40.

A transportable hangar designed by Callender Cable and Construction to Air Ministry drawing number 6633/37. A steel box-girder framework with corrugated iron cladding and canvas doors it had a clear door height of 25ft.
A railway at a dockyard used for the transportation of goods to and from the dock side.
A workshop used in the manufacture and preparation of textiles.
A workshop used in the manufacture and preparation of cotton
A place where paper, frequently printed in ornamental designs, used for covering the interior walls of buildings, is manufactured.
A windmill with a rotating cap containing the windshaft, and a stationary body in the form of a tower.
A building in which the ingredients of an explosive charge are weighed into their correct proportions and mixed prior to incorporation.
A usually large school providing courses for children of all abilities, between the ages of eleven and sixteen.

A transportable hangar designed by Callender Cable and Construction to Air Ministry drawing number 6633/37. A steel box-girder framework with corrugated iron cladding and canvas doors it had a clear door height of 25ft.
Similar in design to the Callender Hangar but with a reduced height of 17ft. Built to Air Ministry drawing number 17346/40.
A factory used for the manufacture of ordnance including small arms, ammunition, artillery pieces and armoured fighting vehicles.
A building or site used for the manufacture of small arms and artillery pieces, etc.
An industrial facility concerned with the manufacture of magnesium from magnesium hydroxide derived from sea water. Magnesium was used in the manufacture of aircraft.
A mechanism used for lifting and lowering weights, operated by hand.
An artificial steep-sided earthen mound on, or in, which is set the principal tower of a castle.
A temporary castle built to house and protect troops beseiging another castle or town.
A castle without a motte.
An enclosure within a bailey which contained a keep and sometimes took the place of a motte.
A fortress and dwelling, usually medieval in origin, and often consisting of a keep, curtain wall and towers etc.
A castle erected without permission, ie. without a royal licence to crenellate.
Castles constructed between 1481 and 1561 for defence using heavy guns.
A castle surrounded by two or more lines of walled fortifications.
A castle built on a simple, rectangular plan, usually with a tower at each corner. This design became common in England after 1300.
An early form of castle consisting of a flat-top steep-sided earthen mound, supporting a wooden tower, and a bailey.
A defensive bank and ditch, circular or oval in plan, surrounding one or more buildings.
Site associated with the testing of nuclear material or its containers.
A building where motor cycles are assembled.
The channel of water that provides a current of water to drive a millwheel.
Water channel leading to water wheel.
A water channel leading from a water wheel.
A pair of SHEER LEGS mounted on shore or on a SHEER HULK, used as a crane to hoist a mast and lower it into place on a ship.
A building or structure from which observation is kept of the approach of danger.
A mechanically operated lift used to transfer rolling stock from one level of track to another.
A structure consisting of a box or platform for carrying goods or passengers from one level to another. Use specific type where known.
A building used to house peacocks.
An abbey or priory for nuns ofthe Benedictine order.
A building or complex where skins are prepared, with their hair still on, to make fur products.
A pillbox built to a design drawn up by the commander of the Royal Engineers for the Colchester Garrison.
A dwelling cut into the rockface of a cliff or hillside, often with a built frontage. Many date from the Medieval period and are still in use in some areas of the country.
Long parallel soil ridges in excess of 5 metres across separated by furrows, formed by using a heavy plough capable of turning the soil.
A ridge and furrow produced by a plough drawn between two steam engined vehicles, or a steam engined vehicle and a moveable windlass, standing on opposite headlands.
A series of long, raised ridges separated by ditches used to prepare the ground for arable cultivation. This was a technique, characteristic of the medieval period.
Long parallel soil ridges less than 5 metres across separated by furrows, formed by using a heavy plough capable of turning the soil.

A long, narrow, irregularly constructed and generally unstructured mound of stones. Normally a by-product of field clearance for agricultural purposes, though prehistoric examples may include burials and other deposits.
An irregularly constructed, generally unstructured, mound of stones. Often, but not necessarily, circular. Normally a by product of field clearance for agricultural purposes.
A mound or structure on which targets are placed for archery practice or competition.
Sites and structures associated with the manufacture of bricks and tiles. Includes sites associated with earth extraction and preparation.
A pit used for the containment of clay whilst it is mixed to the right consistency for brickmaking.
A factory for the production of missiles
A store for keeping undressed meat.
A small building in which game is hung up and kept cool.

A timber building based around a sunken hollow, the floor of which may have been suspended above the hollow to counteract dampness. Grubenhauser are believed to date from the 5th to 8th centuries AD but may be earlier. Use Grubenhauser as plural.
Shelter on military airfield to provide night time accommodation for airmen during WWII.
A house where the upper storeys rest on projecting floor joists and so create the effect of an overhang.
A building where the upper storeys rest on projecting floor joists and so create the effect of an overhang.
A building constructed with a basic timber framework; between the members are panels which can be infilled with timber, wattle and daub, plaster, brick or other materials.
Place where ships and boats are dismantled.
The rigging mast of a sailing ship erected as a monument. Used for naval displays.
Factory where yarn is made from paper.
A building containing machinery for the spinning of yarn.
An artificial area of open water, situated on a river, enclosed by masonry and fitted with dock gates in which ships can be repaired, loaded/unloaded or berthed.
A settlement showing evidence for one or more hut circles, enclosed by a distinct boundary ditch, wall, earth rampart or similar barrier. Characteristic of the later prehistoric period.

A two-storey, structure with a brick ground floor and a reinforced concrete upper floor with balcony and large windows to the watch office and control room. This became the most common building design for air traffic control in the Second World War.
A site used for the production of items derived from animal bones.
A large-scale site where medicinal drugs are maufactured.
A factory used for the industrial manufacture of chlorophyll for medical purposes.
An oval or circular structure with seats rising in tiers around a central open space. Used for religious ceremonies, entertainment, training and armed combat contests.
An apparatus for weighing people, animals or things.
A dam with a watertight upstream side, which may be flat or curved, supported by a series of buttresses on the downstream side.
A building used to dry flax.
A covered shopping street, sometimes with galleries, dating from the late 18th/early 19th century.
A processed used to increase the thickness of the natural oxide layer on the surface of metal parts. The part being treated forms the anode of an electrolytic cell.
The course or channel of a river or stream preserved as a geological feature.
Posts with hooks attached to allow drying new cloth to be stretched out between them.
Engineering workshop intended either for final adjustments of new machinery or the fitting of replacement parts to machinery under repair.
A building or room used for any type of engineering work. Use more specific type where known.
A bridge carrying a tramway.
A building or structure in which processed cloth is dried.

A series of parallel railway sidings on which goods wagons originating from different locations can be sorted or re-sorted into new trains before being despatched to their next destination or sorting points.
A site in which one or more searchlights were positioned to locate enemy aircraft or surface vessels for the benefit of batteries and night fighter aircraft.
An emplacement mounting a small, portable electrically-powered searchlight.
A site in which one or more searchlights and their accompanying structures were positioned to locate enemy aircraft or surface vessels for the benefit of batteries and night fighter aircraft.
A site where iron is smelted or iron goods made.
A building in a military complex (eg. naval dockyard, castle, etc.) for preparing gunpowder.
A house or range of buildings where domestic dogs and cats can be kept for a period.
A hospital which primarily cares for patients injured in accidents.
A long, narrow mound of earth or stone and of uncertain date and function. Use more appropriate term where possible.

A small tower or bartizan, which was often placed at the angles of a castle, to increase the flanking ability, some only serving as corner buttresses. Also used to describe the small rectangular towers situated between the milecastles along Hadrians Wall.
A track of two parallel ruts deliberately cut in the ground or living rock for the guidance of two-wheeled carts when the way was obscured by darkness or water.
A pathway, not necessarily designed as such, beaten down by the feet of travellers.
A path, barred to vehicles, reserved for riding horses.

Rocket projector site with a circular or octagonal concrete holdfast, 1.5m across, surrounded by a 4.6m radius octagonal concrete surround. Six such rocket projectors were arranged in a 3 x 2 grid. Personnel shelters placed midway between each site.
64 Type DFW55373 projector sites arranged in and 8x8 grid or in 4 groups of 16. 30m between each projector, with hardened personnel and ammunition shelters located midway between each
A site containing slipways and associated buildings used specifically for the repair of ships and larger ocean-going craft.
A water pump situated at the side of a road or track for use by travellers and their animals.
An alignment of trees planted as part of a designed landscape. For a belt lining a road use TREE AVENUE.
A building, often converted from its original use, for use as a temporary accommodation by members of the Women's Land Army during the First and Second World Wars.
A garden maintained by, and for the benefit of, a community.
A spoil heap consisting mainly of slag, pieces of refuse material separated from a metal during the smelting process.
A conical or flat-topped tip of waste discarded from a mine or similar site.
A garden in which flower beds are the primary focal point.
A garden, often geometrical in layout, or area for the cultivation of roses.
A wall, usually of reinforced concrete, designed to obstruct the progress of a tank or armoured vehicle
A place where sails are manufactured.
A representation of the crucifixion of Christ or related scenes as a sculpture in a churchyard, etc.
The official residence of an archbishop, eg. Lambeth Palace.
A small house, usually on the estate of a country house, forming part of a widow's dower and intended as her residence.
A small building used as a shelter by a constable of the watch responsible for patrolling the streets at night to safeguard life and property.
A place where osiers (willows) are grown for basket-making.
A settlement located on or near to the shores of a lake. Buildings associated with lake villages are usually raised on piles to prevent them from being flooded.
Building or structure housing a form of ore crushing device associated with tin mines.
Mill for fine grinding of tin ore between millstones.
A mill used for the processing of tin ore by crazing, stamping or smelting.
A hut provided as accommodation for hop pickers and may also be know as a Hop Pickers' Hut
A board indicating the name of the railway station.
The residence of health workers. Includes single dwellings of doctors, nurses etc. but not multiple dwellings eg.NURSES HOSTEL
Buildings and structures associated with the creation and use of hydraulic power.
A hydraulic machine used to magnify the stroke of a hydraulic piston. The pulleys and chains of a crane or other device are attached to the jigger.
A place where people recovering from illnesses or accidents are helped to recover their physical and/or mental capabilities.
An artificial mound, generally conical, placed within a garden or park to provide a viewing point to overlook the garden or park. It may also serve as a visual focus in the garden or park layout.
An artificial hill constructed in Tudor gardens, especially, to provide a good view.
A workshop used by a joiner; a craftsman working with wood and producing more ornate work than that of a carpenter.
Building or structure housing a buddle.
A cleansing house associated with Jewish burial ceremonies
A coastal site producing salt by scraping up salt-impregnated sand and silt, leeching out the salt to produce a concentrated brine, then boiling in 'saltcotes' (small huts containing lead pans)
A building used to house railway engines.
A mill for shredding cloth, for use in flock paper, etc.
Small mobile steam engine.
An engine in which the mechanical force of steam is made available as a motive power for driving machinery.
An engine in which a vertical piston rod supplies energy via a crankshaft directly to the flywheel suspended above the cylinder. Extensively used as mine winding engines.
A steam engine with a horizontal beam connecting the piston and crank.
A steam engine that uses the same steam successively to drive pistons in high and then low pressure cylinders.
A piston mounted horizontally supplying power via a valve gear directly to a crankshaft or flywheel.
A mill used for the production of cardboard and other similar products.
A construction designed to look like a pillbox in order to deceive or confuse the enemy.
A residence of two or three monks of the Premonstratensian order dependent on a foreign mother house.
Cloth finishing process using machinery to raise the nap of the cloth before shearing.
Place where a smith works iron. May be for small scale local use or within a larger industrial complex.

A two-storey, all-concrete construction with a watch office and additional rooms given over to the meteorological section, including a forecast room and met store. A concrete parapet all around the roof differentiates it from 5845/39.
Mine for the extraction of bismuth, which usually occurs in small quantities in the ores of other metal ores, particularly lead, and some copper ores.
A building providing lodgings for police constables.
A mill in which strands of yarn are twisted together to produce a strong thread with a uniform thickness.
An installation used for the storage of ammunition.
An area of hardstanding on which ammunition is stored.
A structure sited within the grounds of a fire station used for drying hoses.
A wide ditch surrounding a building, usually filled with water. Use for moated sites, not defensive moats. Use with relevant site type where known, eg. MANOR HOUSE, GARDEN, etc.
A separate hospital building, or block of an asylum, where new arrivals were segregated from old inmates for a defined period. This system was developed from the mid-19th century onwards.
A flour mill using both stones and rollers to produce flour and, perhaps mainly from the stones, animal feed from grains other than wheat.
A building where documents such as title-deeds, charters, etc, were kept as evidence of rights or privileges.

A place of worship for members of the United Methodist Free Church. Formed in 1857 by the amalgamation of the Methodist Reform Church and the Wesleyan Association they later became part of the United Methodist Church in 1907.
A man-made trough or valley through a hill, carrying at its base a railway.
A building or site where aircraft can be stored and maintained.
A large shed for the housing of aircraft, etc.
A pile of rough stones and soil used for the growing of ferns and other plants.
Workshop used in the the production of tripe.
A large, undergound watercourse.
A gate leading to water, either a river or the sea. Used as a means of supplying castles, for example, with goods brought by water transport.
A small timber one-roomed dwelling where holiday makers could rest after a day spent sunbathing, swimming and playing on the beach.
A hilltop enclosure bounded by one or more substantial banks, ramparts and ditches. Use more specific type where known.
A hilltop enclosure bounded by a single rampart, usually accompanied by a ditch.
A site where sugar beet was processed before being washed and dried to form granulated sugar.
A civil and administrative area incorporating a town of medieval origin.
A bridge whose trusses or girders form parapets on either side of the deck.
A dry ditch or sunken fence which divided the formal garden from the landscaped park without interrupting the view.
A designated area of land, usually closed to the public, used for military exercises and training purposes.
An area of ground where training in the use of grenades can be carried out.
A prefabricated structure of a light timber frame with external weather boarded walls and a timber felt covered roof. They were used as barrack blocks during WWII. Manufactured by Magnet Limited.
A large park for keeping deer. In medieval times the prime purpose was for hunting.

Area in a deer park where a single deer was chased by dogs over a set distance, with bets made on the outcome. It usually includes a stand (for viewing) and can also include three distance markers, a finishing post and a ditch behind the last post.
A building complex with hangars and slipways built adjacent to a body of water where seaplanes can be stored and maintained.
A factory built as a pattern for improved design.
An inlet in the banks of a navigable river, often lined with brick and gated, into which boats can be drawn for repair etc.

A hexagonal pillbox with an interanl anti-ricochet wall. The rear wall was lengthened to take two rifle loopholes in addition to the five light machine gun. Both 15in and 42in thick walls are common. Designed by DFW branch 3.
A prominent structure situated on land specifically as a guide to navigation for travellers or as an aid/warning to sailors out at sea.
Buildings and plant used for the extraction and purification of arsenic oxide into various forms of pure arsenic.
A library for use of the public.
A building, room or suite of rooms where books, or other materials, are classified by subject and stored for use by the library's members.
A light, ornamental building or structure built to incorporate, or in association with, a mineral spring.
Building housing apparatus for testing chain links.
A mill in which oilcloth (a heavy cotton or linen cloth with a linseed oil coating) was produced.
A garden of regular, linear or geometrical design, often associated with the traditional Italian, French and Dutch styles.
A school associated with a cathedral or college originally intended to provide a general education for their choristers.
A formal garden consisting of lawns, walks and borders belonging to a college or university, eg. Oxford or Cambridge.
A chemical works engaged in the production of Ammonium Perchlorate, a product used in the explosives industry.
A factory where lengths of soft, woollen cloth, loosely woven to retain heat, used as a bed covering, were manufactured.
A small, often weatherboarded, roadside house in which cab drivers could rest and take refreshments. Late 19th century onwards.
Purpose built workers' accommodation comprising single rooms with communal eating and washing facilities. Usually for short stay accommodation only.
A type of bridge which completely encloses the traffic using it.
A mill where mustard is produced.
A building where civilians are enlisted to join the military forces.
A municipal pawnshop.
A pawnbrokers shop or place of business.
A building or site used for the production of frameworks of beds.
Wind or water-powered mill for land drainage in fens or marshlands.
A place where wheels and wheeled vehicles were manufactured, originally from wood.
An aerial lift in which cabins are suspended from a continuous cable between two towers which hold the winding mechanism. The cable may be supported by towers or pylons.
A means of transportation where cars, chairs or cabins are carried above the ground by means of one or more cables suspended between towers or pylons.
A building, often close to a churchyard, used for the entertainment of poor people on their wedding day.
A building in which newly made bricks are laid out to dry.

A steel aircraft hangar evolved from the German "Lamellendach", a segmental roof design of the 1920s using a diamond shaped web of pressed steel producing a hangar with a shallow curving profile. Used for both military and civil purposes.
A building at the entrance to an factory manufacturing explosives where a person was searched for matches, prior to entering the workplace.
A building or structure to house railway wagons.
Building housing the machinery for the shredding and grinding of wood in running water and pressing of the resulting fibres into a pulp.
A small building, often inhabited by a gatekeeper, gamekeeper or similar. Use specific type where known.
A kiln used to reduce the shells of shellfish to calcium carbonate.
A district, suburb or quarter of a town or village adjacent to a fort, with the lowest legal status accorded to a built up area.
Form of dam, usually associated with ponds supplying water for blast furnaces.
A building for the storage of all stores supplied for naval service other than victualling and armament.

Traditionally a mew was a building housing hawks when they were moulting, however since the C16th the term has been used for a series of stables grouped around an open yard or alley, often with rooms above. Use only for stables otherwise use FALCONRY.
A specialist hospital for the medical treatment of skin diseases.
An inland settlement such as Runcorn, Ellesmere Port or Stourport, that combines docks and terminal facilities at the interface between land and canal transportation systems.
A settlement area that combines a harbour and terminal facilities at the interface between land and water transportation systems.
A planned, self-contained, community incorporating green open spaces and containing housing, industrial and agricultural zones.
Pipes used to carry water or hydraulic fluid for power transmission within a hydraulic system.
A settlement site enclosed within a timber palisade.
A building, on an airfield, used to house a fire engine.
The carriage house or garage for a fire engine - especially those built by insurance companies or industrial concerns.
A factory that manufactures toys.
A hairdressing establishment for men.
A ditch that indicates the limit of an area or a piece of land.
A ditch which is not continuous but instead is made up of segments which may vary in length and width.
A long and narrow hollow or trench dug in the ground, often used to carry water though it may be dry for much of the year.
A ditch associated with a palisade.
A medieval hospital for lepers, usually consisting of a church and individual shelters for the lepers.
A barn in which a central space is separated from a side aisle by posts and braces.
A workshop or factory for casting metals.
A workshop or factory where bells are made by casting molten metal into moulds.
A purpose built trench designed to prevent the successful landing of enemy glider-borne and airborne forces.
A specialist hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of fistular and rectal disorders and diseases.
skos:Concept.skos:prefLabel: Hospital For Fistula And Rectal Diseases

skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: A structure used for the lifting of boats and other water craft.
A commercial building used primarily as a trading place for wool merchants.
Prayer hall at burial ground, especially a small walk-in memorial devoted to a deceased Hasidic rabbi.

A type of military building associated with military airfields, where air crews were briefed for missions. The room could be a seperate building or part of an operations block and are built of varying types of temporary brick or nissen hut constructions.
A curved structural span which is supported at the sides or ends. May vary in shape from the horizontal flat arch through semicircular and semielliptical forms.
A specialist hospital treating patients with chest disorders and diseases, can be pre sanatoria.
An uncommon form of a regular courtyard farmstead where the buildings are arranged in a Z-shaped form.
A building, site or structure associated with the playing of racket sports.
An indoor play area for the game of badminton.
Reheating of iron from a finery, for rolling or slitting.
A wealden house with only one end being jettied.
A medieval house with central open hall and two storey bays, jettied at first floor level, on either side.
A Roman cremation burial in which the human cremated remains are placed inside or adjacent to a wooden casket, frequently decorated with lion-headed mounts and studs.
A non residential building providing recreational, social and other facilities, especially for the elderly and those with special needs.

A prefabricated temporary structure made of lightweight timber framed panels clad externally with corrugated iron sheets. Used during WWII as officers quarters. Possibly manufactured by Boulton and Paul Limited.
A place where ambulances are serviced and maintained.
An establishment where the art of sword fencing is taught.
A raised platform for the unloading of coal from waggons or other containers.
A mole or pier-like structure situated at the entrance of a harbour, or running out into a lake or the sea, usually used for the landing of craft.
Includes crests, hatchments and supporters.
A place in which turpentine is produced.
A building designed to house a lifeboat, usually with a stone ramp to launch the boat into the sea.
A building specifically built to house life saving apparatus used when conditions prevented the lifeboat from deploying.
A hospital where Air Force personnel and their families receive medical and surgical treatment.
A platform on which corpses are placed and allowed to decompose in the open air, so as to leave only the bones for subsequent burial.
A village laid out systematically with spacious and garden-like surroundings.

A multi-storey, fortified hall house with one of the crosswings being raised in the form of a crenellated tower. Permanently occupied, they date from the mid 14th to the 17th century and are found mainly in the border counties of the North of England.
Machinery for raising and lowering men and materials to and from the surface of a mine.

A building, usually associated with, or found within the grounds of, a cemetery and used for the storage of coffins prior to burial. Reception houses were introduced as a result of concerns around the implcations for public health of C19 burial practices.

A place of worship for Bible Christians, a group who split from the Wesleyan Methodists to form their own church in the South West of England. They were amalgamated into the United Methodist Church in 1907.
A place where pigs are reared.
A chemical works engaged in the production of the coal tar derivative phenol, a chemical used for the manufacture of explosives during WWI.
The cleaning and sorting of horse hair mainly for use in the upholstery trade.
A large building, situated by or near a dock, canal, road or railway and used for the temporary storage of goods or merchandise awaiting transportation.
A large store for the temporary accommodation of goods awaiting transportation to or from the sea.
A place where sand is extracted from surface workings.
A site associated with the extraction, from the ground, of sand and gravel. Use more specific type where known.
A kiln in which the contents are protected from the fire, usually by a lining of tiles or refractory bricks.
A training establishment for gunnery personnel.
A mill used for the manufacture of narrow strips of woven fabric used in the closing or fixing of garments, or for binding the edges of fabric goods.
Building housing machinery used in the production of wooden pulley blocks for the rigging of sailing ships.
A group of buildings in which local sewage is filtered and purified in large rectangular or circular tanks.
A naval base that builds, repairs, docks or converts warships, and is manned by civilian engineers and workers and administered by engineer duty officers.
A chemical works producing mordants for the dying industry.
A factory where nails are manufactured.
A hostel used to accommodate members of the Womens Land Army who undertook essential agricultural work during the Second World War.

Buildings used for the accommodation, welfare and recreation of servicemen, especially those serving in the Royal Air Force. Use only for buildings associated with military installations. For non-military, use DOMESTIC class and its narrower terms.
An institution for the imprisonment of felons and debtors.
A coastal battery constructed at short notice usually mounting a variety of artillery pieces.
A defensive battery positioned facing out to sea enabling the guns to be brought to bear on enemy shipping and amphibious craft.
A kiln for drying hops in a brewery or maltings complex, as distinct from the OASTHOUSES found on farms.
A factory used for the manufacture of screws.
The residence of a canal worker.
A specialist hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of foot disorders and diseases.
A house with a range at the end of it, at right angles to the main range.
An outdoor theatre for the staging of dramatic productions.
A building used primarily for the performing of plays.
A coastal gun/watch tower built as part of the anti-invasion defences during the Napoleonic Wars.
A watch office with additional rooms given over to the meteorological section, including a forecast room and met store.
An all timber constructed watch office with meterological section. Similar in design to 2328/39 and 5845/39. There were only two known examples built in the UK at Wick and St.Eval.
An artificial mound, generally conical, placed within a garden or park to provide a viewing point to overlook the garden or park. It may also serve as a visual focus in the garden or park layout.
A school for the teaching of poor children, often the recipients of Poor Law relief.
A residential home for children with physical or learning disabilities, sensory impairment and/or mental health issues but who do not necessarily need medical attention.
An area off the coast where ships anchor.
Stone used for grinding or polishing during the manufacture of lithic implements

A site which has produced evidence of in situ working of stone for the manufacture of tools, weapons or other objects. Such sites will usually, but not always, be of prehistoric date. Use object material where known.

Source from which stone utilized for the manufacture of non-flint artefacts, including axes, was obtained. Applied only to sources exploited during the Neolithic and earlier Bronze Age. Do not use for flint mining or knapping sites.
A machine producing mechanical power by the internal combustion of gas.

A small, defended settlement dating to the Early Iron Age, located on spurs, promontories or hilltops. The defences are marked by single or double trenches which originally held substantial palisades.
An enclosed settlement surrounded by a single or double row of close-set timbers embedded in a foundation trench, without ditches or banks.
A stone which has a socket for an unknown function. Use specific term where known.

An area of a port, dock or harbour, often including buildings for passport control and customs, where passengers and vehicles using ferry services can embark/disembark and where supplies can be taken on board.
A small dwelling for the solitary confinement of a pious reclusive religious woman or nun, often attached to the north wall of a church. A squint enabled the occupant to witness the Mass.
A school for parentless children.
Cubicles for housing rams, resembling pigsties with their own yard but slightly larger.
A workshop used for the manufacture of statues, either cast or carved.
A road block formed by placing rails or girders in an upright position in sockets in the road surface, forming a moveable barrier.
A purpose built tower used for the testing of helicopter rotor blades.
A place where wheels and wheeled vehicles were manufactured, originally from wood.
Component. Use wider site type where known.
A tall multi-storey block of flats, slender with a square plan.
A floating, fixed marker used to indicate to a navigator a sea area to approach or avoid.
Large semi-subterranean feature often packed with straw for the storage of potatoes and other root crops.
A hospital where elderly people receive medical treatment, but not overnight accommodation.
A dockyard crane permanently mounted on a lighter.
An outer wall of a castle or similar fortification.
An artificial stretch of water, usually rectangular in shape, used decoratively, particularly in formal gardens, eg. Long Water, Hampton Court. Occasionally used to supply water to cascades.
A high-humped, narrow, cobbled bridge used by trains of packhorses, often located in upland areas where the bulk of goods were carried by horses.
A gate or mechanism designed to allow animals which are being raced to start at the same time.
A share or portion of land, allotted to a person, often used for growing, vegetables, fruit, etc.
An imprecise term used to describe large Iron Age settlements of town-like proportions.
A site with one or more defensive earthworks, often at a river crossing incorporating natural features which define parts of the curtilage.
A large space in an underground tunnel, usually wider than the tunnel itself, used for storage, etc.

An anti aircraft battery armed with 3 inch rockets with a ceiling of 22,000 feet. Both single and multiple launchers were designed. Single launchers being used to defend vulnerable points such as coastal batteries with multiple launchers defending town.
An employment exchange for unemployed labourers, servicemen, etc.
A coastal battery containing one or more artillery pieces for to defend the coast against hostile motor torpedo boats.
A farmstead where the working buildings are arranged around a yard.
A government employment agency for those out of work offering advice on jobs, training and retraining.
A double-span aircraft hangar designed by Boulton & Paul of London and Norwich. Mainly used on aircraft factory sites and at Armament Training Schools.
A building or buildings used for the production of pens.
A circular kiln or oven used in the manufacture of bricks. Common in Staffordshire in the 18th century.
A kiln or furnace for the firing of bricks.
An all-steel end-opening, hangar with canted sides designed for folded-wing aircraft.
A building or site used for the exercise and training of military personnel.
Industrial worker's house which has been purpose built by an employer, as opposed to the workshop houses used by artisans.
A small dwelling providing living accommodation for a tin miner.

A detached building without an operations block and crew briefing room designed on modern lines similar to, but smaller than WATCH OFFICE (12779/41). Began appearing on new stations from September 1941.
A watch office designed for bomber satellite station comprising a long, temporary brick hut with a watch office, operations room and crew briefing room.
A small enclosure built onto the perimeter of a Roman fortress or fort.
A building where artefacts, scientific specimens, antiquities and similar objects of interest could be examined through microscopes by members of the public.
Expanding storage tank for gas, often includes a meter for measuring the amount used.
Storage tank for coal gas and possibly other types of gas .
A refreshment house in a public park or country house garden.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the production, testing and storage of gunpowder.
A building containing presses for the compaction of mill cake gunpowder as part of the gunpowder manufacturing process.
A major fortified place, often a town, capable of containing a large force. If Roman use LEGIONARY FORTRESS.
A large, fortified permanent Roman military base, made of timber and stone, surrounded by a rampart and ditches.
A camp where people who fled from danger or problem whithin their country or across international borders and who are in need of international protection are temporarily placed.
A works or factory principally engaged in the manufacture of dynamite
A small yard attached to the rear of a house or other building.
Large storage structure for powdered cement.

Component part of a Flint Mill where flint is calcined before it is brittle enough to be ground in the mill. Ground, burnt flint is used in the production of earthenware pottery, which whitens and strenghens the body.
A prepared slope on which rails are laid to enable early tramroads and railways to negotiate a steep gradient.
An embankment or cutting on a railway system, surfaced at a uniform gradient, up or down which materials were hauled by rope.
A prepared slope with rails on which boats can be transferred from one canal to another at a higher or lower level. The boats can either be floated in a caisson or carried in a cradle or sling.
A site containing a tennis court, changing facilities and a club house.
A covered gateway, at the entrance to a churchyard, where during a funeral a coffin could be set down until the vicar arrived.
A building equipped with facilities for bathing, and occasionally public baths.
A building or site used for the maintenance and repair of motor vehicles.
A site or establishment for the casting and refining of metallic copper.
A post to which ropes are attached to secure vessels at a landing place.
A hospital department which treats patients without keeping them in overnight or for a longer period.
A building or site used for the production of anchors.
A small store building at a railway station for the storage of equipment and other stores associated with the railway.
A house for the keeper of a level crossing on a railway.
A conduit or pipes, used primarily for conveying petroleum from oil wells to a refinery, or for supplying water to a town or district, etc.
Traditionally the chief residence of a land owner. Now used specifically to describe the residence of the Lord Mayor of London.
Factory or workshop making bits, spurs and other small metal objects associated with horse harness.
A wall built to give shelter to sheep.
A textile factory where the process of doubling, the twisting together of two spun yarns, takes place.
A fortified keep in the form of a tower, used as a last refuge or defence. If a component of a larger site, use KEEP.
The major tower of a fortification, often acting as its last defence.

A prefabricated structure of reinforced concrete posts and beams with infillings of pre stressed concrete planks and felted slabs. Initially used for military barracks in WWII and later for civilian housing. Manufactured by the Orlit Company.
A scientific laboratory where marine life is studied and researched.
Use only where stone is natural or where there is no indication of function.
A stone, of unidentified function, showing evidence of great heating at some point in the past, leading to vitrification.
A tower in which shot is made from molten lead poured through sieves at top and falling into water at bottom.

A square pillbox with loopholes for four light machine guns with 18 in thick walls. Probably designed by DFW branch 3 although it may have been adapted from an external source as Southern Command correspondence refers to the type as 'Stento'.
A site available to the public for the pursuit of leisure and recreational activities.
A large board found at sporting events, erected so as to be seen by the spectators, on which the score of a game is kept.
An educational establishment where the art and theory of building and construction is taught.
The grounds of an institution for higher education eg. a university, including the educational buildings, entertainment and sports facilities and student's halls of residence.
A group of planted trees or shrubs, generally of uniform age and of a single species.
A post, usually of iron or concrete, used to support a street lamp.
A natural ditch the depth and/or width of which has been increased so as to prevent the progress of a tank or armoured vehicle.
A man made ditch designed to obstruct the progress of a tank or armoured vehicle. Ditches were often reveted with concrete or wood.
Stop-line against invading tanks in form of a ditch during the defence of Britain.
Purpose-built lodgings for assize court judges. Early 19th century.
A position or place that allows a wide or favourable overall view of a scene or situation.
A church, the plan of which is based on that of a Roman basilica.
A type of pottery oven in which the air passes from the base of the kiln out through the top.
An area of the sea or coastline where vessels have been abandoned.
A lime kiln where the fuel is not mixed with the limestone but burnt below it.
A site with accommodation buildings and ancillary facilities for Royal Air Force personnel.
A place where money is coined under public authority.
A mill for crushing flint. Crushed flint was used in the manufacture of pottery in order to whiten and strengthen the body of earthenware pottery.

Component part of a Flint Mill where flint is calcined before it is brittle enough to be ground in the mill. Ground, burnt flint is used in the production of earthenware pottery, which whitens and strenghens the body.
Obstacles such as scaffolding, barbed wire and concrete blocks or cylinders placed on a beach to impede the progress of enemy soldiers, vehicles or watercraft landing from the sea.
Scaffolding erected on a beach and in the surf so as to prevent hostile forces from landing.
Obstacles, including scaffolding and anti tank blocks designed to impede an enemy's attempts to land forces onto open beaches.
A building or site used for the production of naphtha, a volatile petroleum-derived product used in the manufacture of solvents, cleaning fluids etc.
A place where watches and timepieces are manufactured and mended.
A mill in which poor quality woollen cloth was made from fibres produced by grinding light woollen rags.

Component part of a mungo and shoddy mill, where non-wool fibres from shredded material are destroyed by either soaking rags in an acid solution or rotating them in drums in a hot acidic gas followed by heat. The result is an all-wool product.
A path across a road marked with black and white stripes where pedestrians may cross.
A path across a road, usually marked as a crossing for pedestrians.
A place for sharpening metal objects like tools and weapons.
A defensive or boundary earthwork.
A linear earthwork, usually a bank accompanied by a ditch, which runs across rather than along an area or ridge of higher ground.
A building used by teachers for in-service training.
A hall licensed for musical performances, singing, dancing and other entertainments, exclusive of dramatic performance.
Temporary accommodation for war evacuees.
A garden where yew and other coniferous trees are grown.
House, where destitute Jews converted to Christianity after the expulsion. Latin for "House of Converts".
An engineering works producing items for the railway other than rolling stock, such as signals, tracks, points, etc.
A type of stock exchange for tin which replaced the stannary courts in the mid 19th century.
A mill where china stone is grinded.
A complex of buildings with the purpose of providing and storing food and drink supplies (esp. for the navy).
An earthwork used as a boundary marker.
A building found in conjunction with a WATERMILL, used for the drying of corn after harvesting, with a slatted drying floor set above a kiln.
A furnace or oven used for drying items or materials. Use specific type where possible.
A kiln where gypsum was dried to a state where it could be used as plaster of Paris or for the production of cement.
A kiln used for the drying of wood.
A road or pathway raised above surrounding low, wet or uneven ground.
A lodging house for apprentices learning a trade or profession. This accommodation was often provided in lieu of wages.
The residence of a ford keeper.
A chemical works engaged in the production of the coal tar derivative phenol, a chemical used for the manufacture of explosives during WWI.
A building used for the testing of weapons for quality, accuracy and explosive power.
A chamber attached to the sewer of a building to facilitate the removal of any blockage.
A garden with one or more platforms with walks, often on different levels, usually close to the house.
A place where padlocks and rim locks for doors are made from iron and brass.
A site containing plant and machinery for the manufacture of steel.
Site where steel is produced from molten pig iron using a Bessemer Converter, a development from the cementation and crucible steel-making techniques .
Production of high quality steel by reheating cementation steel in a refractory crucible.
Production of steel by reheating wrought iron in charcoal filled containers.
A building used for the testing of steel.
A building or site used for the production of acids by a range of chemical processes.
A radio station set up to broadcast signals aimed at 'bending' or altering German navigation transmissions.
A building or group of buildings containing equipment capable of transmitting and receiving radio signals. Use BROADCASTING RADIO STATION for broadcasting establishments e.g. BBC Radio stations.
An establishment where musical performances take place.
A boundary post for the payment of tax or duty.
Purpose built or modified structure used for scenery in a film.
A building or complex of buildings where cinematographic films are produced.
A house with an open hall whose main span is separated by an arcade from the side aisles.
An artificial water channel for carrying water over long distances. Use also for bridge-like structures that carry the channel or canal across a valley, river or other obstacle.
An area attached to a house, or part of an estate used for pleasure and recreation.

A light timber framed building usually with brick panels which rests on a timber frame with jacking points; should ground subsidence occur the structure could be jacked to a level position. Usually found in the Cheshire Salt Field.
A hut, usually containing lead pans, in which salt water is boiled to produce salt.
A siren used to warn of an impending attack by enemy aircraft.
A garden created within woodland where imported species such as camellias, magnolias and rhododendrons are grown.
A type of buddle used as an ore-cleaning device for seperating metallic ore from waste material by washing the dirty ore in a continuous flow of water.
A processed used to increase the thickness of the natural oxide layer on the surface of metal parts. The part being treated forms the anode of an electrolytic cell.

A type of temporary military aircraft hangar introduced in 1940; of steel welded and bolted construction typically clad in galvanized corrugated iron sheets. The T2 became the standard temporary hangar for the RAF in World War Two.
A settlement carefully planned from its inception and usually constructed in an area which was previously undeveloped. Many new towns were developed following the New Towns Act 1946.
A protective earthen mound, often the main defence of a fortification.
A flat bottomed ditch flanked by mounds running to the south of Hadrian's Wall for much of its length, marking the boundary of the military zone.
An engine house which used air pressure to power trains on the experimental atmospheric railways of the 1840s.
A site where clay is extracted from the surface of the ground.

A prefabricated structure of cellular hollow plywood 'aero' beams and columns clad with timber framed units of flat asbestos facing sheets and a felt roof. Designed as airfield accommodation that could be reused as post WWII emergency housing.
A hospital for the reception of women during their confinement.
An area of ground on which anti tank guns can be placed for testing purposes and to practice firing at targets.
A piece of ground, or a building, on which artillery may be fired at targets.
A bridge which has had mines placed within its structure to enable it to be destroyed in the event of an invasion.
A car park situated beneath the surface of the ground.
A car park on the roof of a building.
A place where cars and other road vehicles may be parked and left.
A car park, on two or more levels.
A building or site for the manufacture of livestock fodder.
Watch Office with operations room designed to Air Ministry drawing number (13079/41)
A hotel adjacent to a railway terminus. Railway hotels were often owned by a railway company.

A structure comprising of two walls of stone or wood with nets or fish traps attached. Located in coastal waters, on shelving coastlines or in river estuaries they form large enclosures with a V or L shaped plan. The narrow point on the seaward side.
A fence or row of stakes, often with nets attached forming an enclosure within a river or harbour and used for catching, or holding, fish.
An earthen bank indicating the limit of a plantation.

Accommodation used as an alternative to the workhouse following several Poor Law Acts. Modelled on continental examples and first erected at the end of the 1860s, it is based on the idea of a "village" of small houses accommodating a small group.
A road surface made out of wooden blocks or planks. It was much used in English cities before 1940, but the cost of wooden blocks eventually made it uneconomical.
A type of Roman lodging house, frequently sited near the town gate.

A funeral rite in which the human body is burnt, usually on a pyre, leaving fragmentary charred or completely combusted remains. Often found buried, occasionally in a container associated with grave goods.
Urn containing a cremation. Where component use with wider site type.
A small dwelling providing living accommodation for a tin miner.
Industrial worker's house which has been purpose built by an employer, as opposed to the workshop houses used by artisans.
A site incorporating all of the production processes for the manufacture of plaster.
A distinctive magistrates court established by legislation in 1980, dealing with civil family proceedings.
A factory containing machinery for processing clay for the manufacture of bricks, tiles or pottery.
An establishment where the art of sword fencing is taught.
A place where silverware is manufactured.
A centre where patients suffering from venereal and associated diseases receive treatment.
A fortifed position, often including fieldworks or defensive structures, designed to keep enemy forces engaged to allow reinforcements to be mobilized.
