An entrance chamber from tide water to basin, with gates at each end and means of pumping up or lowering the level of water to suit.

A curved dam usually built of concrete and designed with the curve upstream so that the force of the water compresses the structure and strengthens it as it pushes it into its foundations. Arch dams are best suited to narrow gorges
A room or building housing the controls to a mechanized system, eg. in a power station, airport, etc.
A specialist hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of kidney disorders and diseases.
A walk or path lined with lime trees.
A cutting through a wood to open up a view or establish an allee.
A winding walk, common in early 18th century Rococo gardens and parks.
A walk, common in 18th century gardens, providing a view across the surrounding countryside.
A place for strolling, public walks, etc. Usually associated with coastal resorts.
A winding path in a garden or park, common in the late 17th and early 18th centuries.
A place or path for walking in a park or garden. Use more specific type where possible.
A garden walk lined with yew trees and hedges.
A walk bordered by trees or clipped hedges in a garden or park. Made of gravel, sand or turf, it is different from a path or avenue.

A monument consisting of a small (generally less than 100m diameter) subcircular enclosure with a narrow approach way consisting of parallel ditches (thus banjo shaped). Believed to be associated with stock management in the Later Prehistoric period.
A stone found on route to a churchyard on which the coffin is rested during transportation.
A structure, often within a CHURCHYARD or LYCH GATE, on which a coffin could rest prior to burial.
A site or building used for the manufacture of goods made from pewter, an alloy of tin and lead.
Usually a small, two or three man trench, dug as an isolated fieldwork rather than as part of a defensive system. A WWI and WWII feature.
An excavation used as a means of concealment, protection or both.

Blocks of solid concrete,in the form of truncated pyramids usually 3 feet square x 2 feet high which could be placed in rows to impede enemy movement in the event of invasion. Pimples were recommended for use on soft ground.
The part of a road intended for vehicular traffic.
An area of a carriageway, usually delimited by road markings, for the sole use of bicycles.
Unenclosed wasteland, forest and pasture used in common by the community.
A works engaged principally in the manufacture of the explosive bellite.
A site where machine tools, machines designed to remove surplus material from a work piece by accurately guided cutting tools, are manufactured.
A site where lime (calcium carbonate) is made.

Component part of a mungo and shoddy mill, where non-wool fibres from shredded material are destroyed by either soaking rags in an acid solution or rotating them in drums in a hot acidic gas followed by heat. The result is an all-wool product.
A mill for the manufacture of low grade cloth made from ground-up heavy woollen rags.
A series of steps designed to enable fish to ascend a fall of water or a dam.
A factory used for the production of thick, flat glass used for shop window panes, etc. Plate glass is produced by rolling and casting rather than traditional blowing.
A site where all the processes for the production of glass and objects made from glass are carried out.
A factory where knitted fabrics are manufacterd using knitting machines.
A building or compound housing a permanent establishment of members of a religious organization to do missionary work.
A surface interpreted as a buried cultivation layer, for example an agriculturally cultivated field.
A mine used for the extraction of tungsten bearing ore. Use with other mineral ores extracted and MINE, eg. TIN MINE.
A camp used for the accommodation of members of the Womens Auxiliary Air Force who undertook a variety of essential roles within the RAF to enable their male counterparts to fight more effectively.
Mill for grinding bark usually for use in the tanning industry. Use with power type(s), eg. WATERMILL where known.

skos:Concept.skos:prefLabel: Hospital For People With Learning Difficulties
skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: A hospital where people with learning difficulties receive medical treatment.

Nowadays a hospital where patients suffering from psychiatric disorders receive medical care and treatment. Traditionally they were often places where psychiatric patients were kept confined away from society receiving minimal medical care or attention.
An aircraft hangar designed by T. Bedford Consulting Engineers usually erected on aircraft factory sites rather than operational airfields.

A large type of military repair hangar mainly used on WWII bomber bases, constructed using steel stanchions and clad in corrugated iron. B 1 hangars were part of a series of prefabricated buildings intended to supplement existing hangars on bases.
Aircraft hangars designed by T. Bedford Consulting Engineers to meet the requirement to repair damaged heavy bombers in situ on their airfields.
A works used for the production of parchment from animal skin.
Ornamental wrought iron screen associated with gate lodges or entrance lodges.
A factory where biscuits are manufactured.
An all timber constructed watch office with meterological section. Similar in design to 2328/39 and 5845/39. There were only two known examples built in the UK at Wick and St.Eval.
The residence of a ford keeper.
A hospital where Royal Naval personnel and their families receive medical and surgical treatment.
A site containing a forge for the manufacture of cutlery.
A building that housed humans and cattle under one roof, with a shared entrance providing access to the cattle housing (usually downslope) and the dwelling area.
A cross, erected on a highway or in an open place, at which monks and others used to preach.
Block, often made of concrete, to secure smaller maritime craft. Many were made during the Second Wold War to secure craft which were to be used in the D-Day landings.
A section of roadway attached at one end to a harbour or dockside and ending at a landing stage, rising and falling with the tide, for the loading and unloading of vehicles and pedestrians.
The central part of a road between the pavements or the verges.
A factory for the production of plastics by chemical processes.
Sites where controlled chemical reactions are employed to help manufacture domestic products.
A structure used for the drying of food using an indirect source of heat.
A structure used for the roasting or drying of chicory.
A building or room, purpose built for the teaching, rehearsing and playing of music.
The public house was a 19th century development, distinctive from the earlier BEER HOUSE by its decorative treatment and fittings.
A public house licensed for the sale of wine and other alcoholic drinks.
A gate which allows water to pass into a dock, etc, at flood tide, and by which it is retained during the ebb tide.
The horizontal beam on a lock gate.
A chemical works engaged in the production or refining of toluene, a substance extracted from coal tar or specific types of crude oil, and used in the production of explosives during WW1.
An area of land used for camping. Often includes facilities for washing, catering and entertainment.
An area of land used for producing renewable energy, which can comprise a solar farm, wind turbines or biomass facility
Mill for fine grinding of tin ore between millstones.
A friary of the Order of the Friar servants of the Blessed Virgin Mary or Servites. The Servite Fathers came to England in 1864.
A hut used by a person who makes items from wood. Often found in a woodland setting.

A large octagonal pillbox, with a projecting entrance, equipped with loopholes for eight light machine guns and a light anti-aircraft mounting sited in a central well which was accessed from inside the pillbox. Designed by DFW branch 3.
A church, usually found in East Anglia, of early Medieval and/or Medieval date with attached or detached round tower.
Plant for the processing of uranium ores, such as pitchblende. Uranium is the principal extract, but radium may also be recovered as a by-product
A tall stack used to disperse foul air from the bottom of a mine.
A tall chimney terminating a CONDENSING FLUE, used to extract metal from the smoke produced by a lead smelter.
Chimney used on an industrial or commercial site.
An educational establishment, often privately funded, for young women.
Structure used for viewing deer hunt.
A facility where the exterior of a motor vehicle can be cleaned.
A factory in which logs are converted to timber by running them through a series of saws.
A room or part of a church where the vestments, vessels and records are kept.
The rear part of a Roman fort, where barrack accommodation, stables and stores were situated. Use with wider site type where known.
A building in which purified charcoal was produced by distillation of wood in sealed cast-iron retorts heated in fire-boxes. Tarry by-products were sometimes recovered by condensation flues.
A works using sealed retorts to produce charcoal. Wood distillates may be produced as byproducts of this process. They may be found at separate works or comprise part of a gunpowder works.
An enclosed area of parkland used almost exclusively for the hunting of deer.
Stone for holding ox yokes.
A mechanism used to turn a tram around.
A designated area, usually sited at a strategic crossroads, with fixed defences such as pillboxes, anti tank ditches and gun emplacements, designed to act as a rallying point for defenders.
A system of petrol burners, pipework and pump houses on an airfield used to 'burn' away fog so that aircraft may take off and land safely.
A building or site used for the storage and distribution of the essential logistical requirements of an armed force.
Sorting offices constructed during the Second World War designed to rapidly move goods from the vulnerable docks and ports via the rail network.
A land based establishment armed with torpedoes and used to defend the coast from enemy shipping.

A land based installation armed with wire -guided and powered "Brennan torpedoes" which were in operation beween 1890 and 1906. These torpedoes were invented by Louis Philip Brennan. The stations were used to defend the coast from enemy shipping.
A shaft or pit dug in the ground over a supply of spring-water.
A well with a superstructure, either partially or wholly enclosed with an access door, designed to protect the water source.
A place of worship for Protestant Methodists, a group who broke away from the Methodists to form their church in Leeds in 1828.
A protected chamber for investigating the controlled detonation and burning of explosive compounds, typically associated with a protected control room and high speed visual recording facilities.
A building or site used for the production of acids by a range of chemical processes.
An outdoor trail that has keep fit equipment with supporting information plaques intermittently positioned along its route
A village cemetery where cinerary urns were buried in large numbers during the Bronze Age.
A cemetery comprising exclusively cremated human remains, some or all of which may be contained within pottery vessels.

A cemetery of later prehistoric date comprising exclusively cremated human remains, some or all of which may be contained within pottery vessels. The cemetery area is partly or wholly surrounded by an earthwork bank and/or ditch.
An enclosure used for the cultivation of fruit trees.
Usually a servants' dining room.
A searchlight battery, which points out to sea, used to locate enemy shipping
The residence of a lacemaker.
A specialist hospital where medical and surgical dental treatment takes place.
A monument featuring an artificial circular shallow depression surrounded by a bank which runs around the rim of the depression.
The rectangular pit in which the lower part of a waterwheel revolves.
A building or large scale site for the manufacture and/or storage of weapons, ammunition and equipment.
A pipe or channel for conveying water or other liquids.
A multiple, parallel arrangement of linear earthwork ditches, usually accompanied by banks, and often of considerable territorial extent. Usually of later prehistoric or Roman date.
A substantial bank and ditch forming a major boundary between two adjacent landholdings. Most date from the late Bronze Age and Iron Age.
An open space or area, usually square in plan, in a town or city, enclosed by residential and/or commercial buildings, frequently containing a garden or laid out with trees.
An open area, often paved or cobbled, surrounded by buildings and accessible to the public.
An area within a building used for the storage of cheese.
A place where meat and fruit, etc, is preserved by salting and/or drying.
A building of varying designs intended for directing military aviation operations. Normally associated with military airfields.
A building or room, originally equipped for gymnastics or indoor sports but also, more recently, equipped with cross-training machines and free-weights for members to improve their physical fitness.
A lime kiln where the fuel is not mixed with the limestone but burnt below it.
A crane powered by a treadwheel and used for lifting and lowering, dating from the Roman period. Also used in later periods to assist on building sites, at mines and in ports.
A refuse heap of discarded shells.
A refuse heap.
A building used for broadcasting radio programmes for public entertainment. Often includes recording studios, transmitters and offices. Use RADIO STATION for non-broadcasting uses eg. Military.
A command post used to direct the guns of a coastal battery.
A military building from which the guns of a battery were directed.
A hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of patients with cancer or related illnesses.
A specialist hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of children.
A vertical or inclined excavation giving access to an underground mine.
Horizontal tunnel opening from the surface used for haulage or access to a mine. It can also be used for drainage.
An area of a port, dock or harbour, often including buildings for passport control and customs, where passengers of ocean liners can embark/disembark and where supplies can be taken on board.
A round or polygonal building containing a wheel turned by an ox to provide power.

A pit lined with the bony cores of animal horns. Thought to date from the 17th/18th centuries and believed to have been used in the tanning industry although some may have been used for casting cannon.
A site used for the production of items derived from animal horns.

A building as part of a workhouse, prison or hospital, often including porter's lodge, baths, clothes store, washrooms, casual cells, rooms etc, for receiving inmates/patients. Use term from Components thesaurus if it is part of a building complex.
Purpose-built structure with thick walls used to store clay before transportation.
A glasshouse used to grow and display tender decorative plants. May be either an extension to a house or freestanding.
A place where processed cloth is cut for use as garments or soft furnishings, etc.
A specialist hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of heart disorders and diseases.
A specialist hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of urinary disorders and diseases.
A building or buildings used for the manufacture of shoe and leather polish, etc.
A place where patients have X-Rays taken to highlight an illness or irregularity.
A house, enclosure or large cage for the keeping and breeding of birds.
A route across a river, or lake. Use only for small inland ferries and index with LANDING POINT/STAGE/STEPS or PIER where known.
An engineering site where railway carriages are manufactured.
A building that housed humans and cattle under one roof, with a shared entrance providing access to the cattle housing (usually downslope) and the dwelling area.
A building used by an organization or society instituted to promote technology through lectures, research, etc.
A structure used for the transmission and interception of radio signals. Usually composed of a number of different elements such as aerials, receiving equipment and supporting pylons.
A mine used for the extraction of zinc bearing ore. Use with other metal ores extracted and MINE where necessary, eg. LEAD MINE.
A brewing or baking house attached to a vernacular building, 16/17th century.
The residence and office of a chaplain.
A place where injured or endangered animals are kept and looked after.
Bleach works or bleach house for bleaching of textiles, etc.

Device for extracting juice from apples, usually crab apples, for use in cooking and medicine. Consists of a stone base carved with channels in the upper surface which was used with an upper weight, often secured with a wooden beam wedged into position.
A building on a river or canal in which the water levels are controlled.
1st World War end-opening aeroplane hangar.
An area of a barn, paved or boarded, on which corn was threshed by hand flailing. Use broader site type where known.
A dam constructed on the reaches of a canal or river designed to retain the water and to regulate its flow.
An outfall from a canal, river or reservoir.
A workshop where baskets were manufactured.
A place where oysters are bred for consumption.
A building or structure in which processed cloth is dried.
A double lock placed between tidal water and a canal, etc..
A bridge, usually resting on raised arches, carrying a road across low-lying land or water.
A factory or group of buildings used for the production of plated goods. Plating is the process whereby one metal object is coated with a thin layer of another metal.
An observation post used by Air Raid Precautions wardens to watch for aircraft and bomb strikes.
A building where official archives are kept for public inspection.
A specialist hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of women and children.
A hospital devoted to the curing or correcting of physical deformities.

An area of a port, dock or harbour, often including buildings for passport control and customs, where passengers and vehicles using ferry services can embark/disembark and where supplies can be taken on board.
A chemical works engaged in the production or refining of toluene, a substance extracted from coal tar or specific types of crude oil, and used in the production of explosives during WW1.
An artificial lake, often made by damming a stream. A common feature of landscape parks.
A hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of military personnel and/or their families.
A hilltop enclosure bounded by one or more substantial banks, ramparts and ditches. Use more specific type where known.
Hillslope forts with wide spaced ramparts.
A hospital where elderly people receive medical treatment, but not overnight accommodation.
A tunnel with strengthened construction, used as an emergency exit from a civil defence building.
A tunnel built to allow internees (in a camp, prison etc.) to escape.
An underground channel with a vaulted roof. Use specific type where known.
A factory or plant used for the manufacture of electrical machinery or components.
A factory manufacturing electrical cables.
A factory manufacturing electrical equipment, such as engines, transformers and generators for use in industry.
An outdoor theatre for the staging of dramatic productions.

Area or zone of sea where a battle, skirmish or action was fought between naval ships or warships and privateers. Not to be used for enemy action upon mercantile ships or a sudden strike by mine/torpedo against an enemy warship.
A factory used to make packaging equipment.
The residence of a clothier.
A flower bed, usually circular and convex in form, edged with wicker basketwork, iron hoops or terracotta.
A site where the manufacture of glass bottles takes place.
A piece of ground used for motor racing.
A factory in which varnish is manufactured.
A coastal battery used for delivering fire at long distance thus forcing a warship threatening or bombarding shore installations to withdraw out of range.
A factory making baize for snooker and gaming tables.
A vault or crypt under a church or chapel. Use wider site type where known.
An ornamental garden feature, sometimes with an associated bath house.

A building, with adjacent open areas, in which buses are maintained, usually having an extensive area free from upright columns or stanchions to permit overnight storage, repair bays, stores and an office.
An enclosure, usually private, used for burial. Often found within a cemetery.
A building or site used for the production of bricks and other items, from a clay with refractory properties.
Use for the remains of a cargo which have been accidentally lost at sea, or purposefully dumped, and which consist the only physical evidence of a vessel.
Small revolving wooden chalets that could be turned with their backs to the prevailing wind so that hospital patients could recline in them on long chairs in all weathers.
A roadside telephone box for use by motorists in need of assistance.
A freestanding public call box, containing a telephone and usually operated by inserting coins.
A bridge that crosses over a railway.

A large steelframed military aircraft hangar designed in 1939, intended for aircraft maintenance on operational stations. It includes side annexes for workshops and offices, provided with a large number of windows. The annexes are of brick or concrete.
A building, on an airfield, used to house a fire engine designed to Air Ministry drawing number 5342/42.
An electricity-producing power station fired by oil.
A building or structure used for the storage of sugar.
A naval base that builds, repairs, docks or converts warships, and is manned by civilian engineers and workers and administered by engineer duty officers.
An enclosure in which ships are built and repaired, and all sorts of ships' stores are brought together.
A concrete, circular concave dish 30 feet in diameter used as an acoustic listening device to detect approaching enemy aircraft.
A light anti aircraft position, usually open-walled and built of concrete, brick or sandbags used to emplace one or more machine guns mounted on pintels.
The main dwelling-house of a farm, it can be either detached from or attached to the working buildings.
A factory where hats are manufactured.
A circular pillbox designed by the Croft Granite, Brick and Concrete Company, with six loopholes. With no roof or door access was gained through the roof.
64 Type DFW55373 projector sites arranged in and 8x8 grid or in 4 groups of 16. 30m between each projector, with hardened personnel and ammunition shelters located midway between each
A purpose built pit, usually below a gatehouse or barbican, into which the counterweight of a drawbridge could be lowered, thus enabling the bridge to be raised.
Term applied to a pit trap itself and also a walled enclosure containing one or more pit traps.
A textile building where the process of combing, a preparatory process for long wools, takes place.
A site where merchandise and goods are temporarily stored before or after transportation by rail.
A place where coal is mined.
A place where goods are sold in bulk, rather than by retail.
A centre providing emotional and practical support to those living with life-threatening illnesses.
A street lamp in which the light is produced by the burning of coal gas. More recently natural gas has been used.
A light, often suspended from a lamp-post, to illuminate a street or road.
A long, wooden, metal or stone vessel holding drinking water for horses.
A narrow, open container, usually where food or water for animals is put. Use specific type where known.
A long metal or stone vessel for cattle to drink water from.
A long stone or metal vessel for dogs to drink water from.

A curved military aircraft hangar produced in 1939. The frame is steel which is then clad with steel sheeting and reinforced concrete and typically covered with a thin layer of concrete, earth and turf.
A pit which shows evidence for having been used for cooking. Often contains charcoal, burnt bone fragments etc.
A road which has had mines placed within its structure to enable it to be destroyed in the event of an invasion.

Manmade structure for bathing or swimming that is located on the beachfront and filled by tidal waters. Similar to a LIDO, with the main difference being the extent of the built up complex around the pool.
A building or group of buildings used for the making, processing, storing and selling of milk and other dairy products.
A factory where cars are manufactured.
A monument consisting of an area enclosed by a ditch, bank, wall, palisade or similar barrier, where the barrier follows a circular course, but is not regularly laid out.
A circular shaped area of land enclosed by a boundary ditch, bank, wall, palisade or similar barrier.
An oval shaped area of land enclosed by a boundary ditch, bank, wall, palisade or similar barrier.
A monument consisting of an area of land enclosed by a ditch, bank, wall, palisade or similar barrier, where the boundary follows an irregular curving course.

A site consisting of, usually two, sub-circular enclosures linked by a linear ditch running tangentially to the enclosure boundaries. Characteristic of the later prehistoric period in the Wessex region.
An area of land, in the shape of a D, enclosed by a boundary ditch, bank, wall, palisade or similar barrier.
A building used by an organization or society instituted to promote science through lectures, research, etc.
A subscription club, usually with a library and newspaper room, established from c.1815-1860, their educational function gradually taken over by the public libraries in the later 19th century.
A type of public building common in the 18th and 19th century, serving as an educational and/or learned society institute.
A building in which an organization or society is instituted to promote literature through lectures, study and research, etc.
A town laid out systematically with spacious and garden-like surroundings.
A place where dockyard craftsmen both design and build ships.
Obstacles, often semi permanent, which are placed on railway lines to prevent the enemy from using them. Set up during the defence of Britain.
The receptacle at the top of a rain-water pipe which gathers the water from one or more outlets or gutters on the roof.

A lighthouse whose lantern is sufficiently high to be seen at a long range and above low lying cloud or fog. In locations where varying weather conditions occur a High Light is usually accompanied by a LOW LIGHT built alongside or nearby.
Buildings in London formerly used as hostels for law students.
A pumping station for draining a mine or colliery.
Buildings and plant used for the extraction and purification of arsenic oxide into various forms of pure arsenic.
A rectangular pillbox with an enclosed square plan section for three light machine guns and an adjacent open area housing a mounting for a light anti-aircraft weapon. Designed by DFW branch 3.
A house consisting of a single storey hall with two storey domestic ranges attached to either one or both ends.
A structure for producing power through a rotary motion achieved by the weight of men or animals treading on a succession of moving steps or a belt that forms a kind of continuous path.
An appliance for producing motion by the stepping of men on movable steps on a revolving cylinder. Used as a form of punishment in prisons.
A building or complex in which visitors to a prison can meet with the inmates under the supervision of the prison staff.
Large covered spaces where the steel plate used for ship construction was cut and marked out, prior to being craned onto the hull, etc.
A workshop, associated with a tannery, in which the fleece is removed from the skin prior to the tanning process.
A hospital where patients can rest and recover after an operation or illness. Medical facilities for treatment are also available.
Purpose built or modified structure or building used for scenery in a television program.
A building or series of rooms specially designed for the recording and transmission of live or taped television programmes.
A long seat, usually made of stone or wood, with or without a back.
A site inhabited by a modern order of nuns, founded in 1900 at Lanherne, Cornwall, following Carmelite traditions.
A building in which hoops (for masts) were heated.
Large concrete letters representing the ground-to-air airfield code. It has been used to show pilots in WWII the name of the airfield they were above e.g. DW for Dunkeswell.
A small building used by a gatekeeper.
A wall or masonry construction built for the purpose of retaining or supporting a bank of earth, wall, rampart etc.
A wall constructed for the purpose of confining or supporting a mass of earth or water.
A landing circle marked out in white used as the airfield symbol.
An airfield with associated hangars and control buildings used for the storage, maintenance and deployment of military aircraft and airships flown by the Royal Naval Air Service.
A landing and taking-off area for military aircraft. Often includes ancilliary structures and buildings for the maintenance and storage of aircraft, etc.
An enclosure created by constructing one or more lines of ramparts across a promontory which projects into the sea.
A defensive enclosure created by constructing one or more lines of ramparts across a neck of land, in order to defend, or restrict access to, a spur or promontory, either inland or on the coast.
Saxon rectangular burial chamber comprising a large sunken 'room' lined with wood. 6th and 7th century AD.
A grave marker in the form of a casket.
A site where wrought iron or steel chains were manufactured.
Building housing apparatus for testing chain links.
A place where gold is worked into articles or products.
A building housing computers and information technology equippment e.g. for a business, factory or other instituion.
A building at an airport from where passengers embark and disembark from an aircraft.
A building within a transport terminal, often associated with the registration and clearing of incoming and outgoing passengers or freight.
A Palaeolithic or Mesolithic occupation site, excluding occupations of caves and rock shelters. Evidence for occupation may include traces of hearths and other structures.
When secondary product use with major product and MINE, eg. COPPER MINE.
Originally partially covered baths shaped somewhat like a slipper, now usually a number of single baths of the modern domestic style installed for hire at public baths.
A group of buildings or works where the evaporation and crystallization of sodium aluminium sulphate solution is performed.
A large tank used for soaking alumina-bearing shale in water and chemicals, the initial stage in the alum-making process.
An area of land, often enclosed, used for cultivation or the grazing of livestock.
A field covered with herbage for the grazing of livestock.
A complex of buildings where barytes is processed for industrial use.
A spa building to which water was pumped from springs or wells; usually also serving a social function as an ASSEMBLY ROOM, eg. as at Bath.
A complex maze incorporating tall hedges. A popular feature of 16th and 17th century gardens.
A mechanical device consisting of a system of signal lights operating in sequence, placed at road intersections and pedestrian crossings to regulate traffic.
Textile mill producing calico, ie. coarse, unbleached cotton cloth.
The residence of a well keeper.
Based on a typical 18ft span, 40ft long temporary brick hut but with two bay windows in the front elevation, one for the watch office and one for the chief instructor.
A building housing a whim, a machine worked by a horse, used for raising ores, etc, from a mine.
A hospital for the treatment of diseases of the nerves and nervous system.
A Swiss-styled house, usually with steeply pitched and projecting roof.
A dam constructed across a stream to raise its water-level and make it available to power a mill wheel.
Traditionally a dock where cambering, the bending of beams for shipbuilding, took place. Now used for a small dock.
An artificial navigable waterway used for the transportation of goods. Nowadays also used for recreational purposes.
A canal that can accommodate ocean-going ships, usually built across an isthmus or to give access to a river port e.g. Manchester ship canal
A school where theological subjects are taught.
A building for the storage and drying of hops, often including a hop drying kiln. Usually built as part of a farm.
A school where the applied sciences and the mechanical arts are taught.

A chemical works engaged in the manufacture of the coal tar derivative, picric acid, often associated with the textile industry where it was used as a dye, but more commonly with the explosives industry where it was used as the shell filling Lyddite.

A row of houses linked at first floor level by an open continuous gallery which runs through the front of the buildings. Access to the gallery was gained by flights of steps. Commonly found in the city of Chester.
A row of buildings built during different periods, as opposed to a TERRACE.
A shopping complex, usually indoors, comprised of a number of separate retail outlets surrounding an open space. Often on more than one level.
A heavy framework of parallel beams used to support a ship in dock.
A room or building used for curing fish or meat.
A passage or road closed to traffic at one end.
An airfield with associated hangars and control buildings used for the storage, maintenance and deployment of military aircraft and airships flown by the Royal Naval Air Service.
A landing and taking-off area for military aircraft. Often includes ancilliary structures and buildings for the maintenance and storage of aircraft, etc.
A type of bridge which was designed for temporary use and then capable of being moved to another site. Use for temporary bridges which have remained in situ since erection.
A floating bridge, generally temporary, whose decks are supported on low flat-bottomed or hollow floats.
A place of worship specifically for mariners and their families.
A hilltop enclosure bounded by a double line of ramparts.
A tunnel running under a river or a hillside through which a railway line runs.
A tunnel carrying a railway beneath the surface of the ground.
A core part of a town or city that has or had a particular set of characteristics; for example an area of high status residences or an area where a particular industry/trade was centred.
A lighted pillar or LIGHTHOUSE, eg. Dunston Pillar, Lincs., erected in 1751 to guide travellers over the heath.
A kiln principally used in brick making which gives a continuous operation.
Workshop for the painting of vehicles, machines, etc.
A building where pins are manufactured.
A trench cut around a building or structure to prevent the spread of fire.
A temporary castle built to house and protect troops beseiging another castle or town.
A house with no row of posts between the central space and the aisles.
An area in a town where traffic is prohibited, often containing shops.
A building situated next to a horse racing course with facilities for participants and spectators.
A building or site where the carcasses of whales were butchered and rendered into by products such as oil, fenk and whalebone.

A mill for the processes of grinding, balling, couching, drying and packing of woad. The mill can be demountable, enabling it being located close to the fields, as woad crop has to be rotated and move to new fields as soon as the ground is exhausted.
The residence of a sailor.
A sculptured, carved or moulded representation of an imaginary creature with a human head and breast combined with the body of a lion.
A workshop for the manufacturing of furniture.
A port situated on a river, often associated with a town or overland goods transport facilities.

A type of tower mill, either with turbine-type sails able to take wind from any direction, or with sails working with shrouds to direct wind from one direction. The sails directly drove millstones set beneath them.
A building for the storage and drying of hops, often including a hop drying kiln. Usually built as part of a farm.
A place where abrasive mediums such as sand-paper and grinding wheels are manufactured.
A house with no row of posts between the central space and the aisles.
A factory where carpets are manufactured.
A building where artisans could learn more about their craft, and the scientific and theoretical principles behind it, by attending lectures and the use of the reading room facilities.
A factory for the manufacture of leather goods, such as shoes, saddles, etc. Use TANNERY for the manufacture of leather.
A factory or complex where chamois leather is produced using fish oils as the tanning agent.
A road or way for riding on horseback within a park or estate.
A site, building or factory where seawater is used in the production of salt.
A site, building or factory where geologically-derived brine is used for the production of salt.
A site, building or factory used for the production of salt.
A building used for the care of the sick. Only to be used where part of a complex, eg. a workhouse. In such cases use with appropriate monument type.
A house consisting of a single storey open hall with a two storey domestic range attached to both ends forming an H shape.
An optical instrument for making distant objects appear nearer and larger, often found on the promenade or pleasure pier at a seaside resort or at a site of scenic beauty.
An often highly elaborate water fountain, usually found in parks, gardens or urban spaces.
A small-scale garden.
A type of clothier's house, consisting of TOPSHOP and dwelling, used for hand-weaving of textiles.
A workshop in which textile fibres were spun into yarn by hand.
A building, department or shop where postal business is carried on.
The residence of a bridge keeper.
A site where lime (calcium carbonate) is made.

A mill used for the production of mortar; a combination of sand, lime and water, used to make the joints between courses of bricks in buildings. In more recent times cement has replaced lime to create a quicker drying mortar.
Place where food or money was handed out to the poor.
Used for boiling sections of willow for basket making, etc.
A large, watertight enclosure in which the water is maintained at the high-tide level so that vessels remain constantly afloat in them.
A place where military personnel parade, practice marching, assemble or muster for a march or any other special purpose.
A factory where food is preserved either by freezing, salting or pickling
Small furnace, used to create an upward draught of air in mine workings.
A floatable concrete vessel, numbers of which made up the main breakwater of the Mulberry Harbours used to secure beachheads during the allied invasion of Europe in June 1944.
A harbour constructed from floating pontoons or caissons connected end to end.
When a secondary mineral, use term for product type, eg. LEAD MINE.
A works or factory where shells or projectiles were machined before they were dispatched to a filling factory to be filled with explosives.
A building where advice and aid appertaining to physical and economic wellbeing of disadvantaged members of a community are made available.

A building containing a series of seats for use by the clergy during services. The seats are usually placed in the church and as such this is a very rare monument type, being purpose-built. An example being St. Germoe's Chair in Germoe, Cornwall.

A concrete structure, based on drawing number (11008/41), intended to be the headquarters for the coordination of an airfield's defences. Constructed partially underground it was considered less vulnerable than the (3329/41).
A mill for the processing of rice for use in food products.
The court or enclosed space at the front of a building or structure.
The residence of a ferrykeeper.
Oven for roasting coal to drive off chemical constituents and reduce it to almost pure carbon, ie. coke.
A large building, situated by or near a canal, used for the temporary storage of goods or merchandise awaiting transportation to or from the canal.
A place for sharpening metal objects like tools and weapons.
A building used as a social venue by people interested in, and involved with, the sport of hunting.
Two or more adjacent locks where the upper gates of one lock serve as the lower gates of the next.
A railway at a dockyard used for the transportation of goods to and from the dock side.
A device with a funnel-shaped entrance designed for catching eels.
An accounts office, especially within an industrial or commercial complex.
A building used for drilling out the bores of cannon and other military pieces.
A horse-powered winding engine used at mining sites.
The residence of a lifeboatman.
The residence of an admiral of a port.
An establishment from which food is distributed to the public during wartime or similar states of emergency.
A type of pottery kiln in which air rises up inside the oven to be forced back down and out through the base of the oven.
A hot steam bath introduced from the East, in which heavy perspiration is followed by soaping, washing, massage and cooling.
A manor house, which was granted a royal licence to crenellate.
A farmstead, often of linear plan, where the working buildings are placed opposite and parallel to the house and attached working buildings with a relatively narrow space between.
A type of Roman lodging house, frequently sited near the town gate.
A light, ornamental structure in a garden, park or place of recreation built in the Chinese style.
A building housing a double inlet fan that was used for the ventillation of mine shafts
A place where people can recover from illnesses or health problems through controlled eating and programmes of exercise, etc.
A site or establishment for the casting and refining of metallic copper.
A place where saltpetre, the chief component of gunpowder, is kept.
A piece of ground on which athletes race.
A sports arena with a steeply banked oval track for bicycle racing. There are outdoor as well as indoor velodromes.
An open metalwork structure supporting either a fabrication shed or the runners for an overhead crane.
A building or other establishment used for the retail, making and repairing of jewellery.
A tall, hollow pipe, usually cast-iron, resembling a lamp-post. Used to ventilate sewer systems.
A place where meat and fruit, etc, is preserved by salting and/or drying.
A place where lead ore is extracted from an open cast mine.
A pit dug to protect a small group of infantry men.
Circular structure, normally indicated by one or more rings of post holes and/or a circular gulley, and usually interpreted as being of domestic function.
A dockyard crane permanently mounted on a lighter.
A site containing a forge for the manufacture of cutlery.
A place where a product is given any finishing processes before being despatched to the user.
A tract of land with trees, sometimes acting as a boundary or barrier, usually smaller and less wild than a forest.
Factory for the production of safety fuses used in the ignition of gunpowder for blasting.
Accommodation in a monastery for new monks.
A channel which carried processed alum as liquid from the alum quarry/works to the alum house
A controlled point with warning lights and gates or barriers where a road crosses a railway line.
A level crossing designed to allow the passage of aircraft to and from a runway which has a railway or road running through it.
A fighter satellite station watch office built to Air Ministry design drawing number 18441/40.
A settlement without any obvious evidence for a boundary. Use specific type where known.

A settlement with evidence for several hut circles but clearly lacking an obvious boundary. Where it is not certain whether a boundary existed or not, use HUT CIRCLE SETTLEMENT. Characteristic of the later prehistoric period.
A place where knitted fabrics and legware garments were manufactured.
A room or building for hand knitting garments on simple hand frames.
A building in which potatoes can sprout and germinate.
A wide ditch surrounding a building, usually filled with water. Use for moated sites, not defensive moats. Use with relevant site type where known, eg. MANOR HOUSE, GARDEN, etc.
A board, wall painting or other structure displaying advice, giving information or directions
A plaque attached onto, or a line incised into, a wall face or other surface to indicate the height of flood water inundation.
A river canalized for shipping.
A works where bleach is manufactured.
A specialist hospital for the medical treatment of patients suffering from epilepsy. Originally epilepsy was seen as a mental illness.
A kiln used for the production of any of the soda group of alkalis by the heating of plant remains or salt.
A bridge built to enhance or compliment the surrounding landscape. Mainly found on estates or in parkland and usually 18th and 19th century.
A bridge decorated with shells forming an ornamental feature.
A bridge constructed using rockwork to create a craggy, naturalistic appearance. A feature of 18th century rococo gardens and parks.
The foremost church within a parish.
Hut along the coast, which provided shelter for lookouts known as "huers", who kept watch for the pilchard shoals that passed by the coast. Built of stone or wood. Particular common to Cornwall.
A grave lined with slabs of stone or slate and covered by a large slab of stone. Commonly found on the Isle of Man.

Generally rectangular structure normally used for burial purposes, and formed from stone slabs set on edge, and covered by one or more horizontal slabs or capstones. Cists may be built on the surface or sunk into the ground.
A place where letters and parcels are sorted before being distributed. Usually found at a large general post office.
A garden with real or supposed Swiss features, including buildings and plantings.
A factory where tobacco pipes made of clay are manufactured.

A permanent military RAF aircraft hangar type, designed in 1924. It features a steel frame (with longitudinal ridge and valley trusses for the roof) reinforced concrete and brick infilling for the walls. Typically 122 foot span by 249 foot in length.
An aircraft hangar built to Air Ministry design number 454/43. Mainly constructed on aircraft factory aerodromes
Railway constructed specifically for the movement of coal around the pithead of a coal mine.
A building used for the storage of explosives of a non-military function, eg. mining explosives, signal explosivres etc.
A protected building used for the storage of explosives and other pyrotechnic equipment and designed to Air Ministry drawing number 2647/37.
A high status Iron Age grave in which a two or four wheeled vehicle accompanies a frequently richly furnished inhumation burial. A barrow may overlie the grave.
A building used to store fodder for deer.
A waterside depot for coals brought from the collieries for shipment, furnished with staging and chutes for loading vessels.
A building, usually associated with a port or dock, where seamen could get a meal and a cheap room. Often established by religious groups for the moral betterment of seamen.
A building used for meetings and worship by a religious community trying to propogate its faith in an area.
An endowed school providing a liberal education for such as can afford it.
A workshop or foundry where iron articles are made by casting molten material into moulds.

A rectangular arena, rounded at one end designed for chariot racing. The racetrack circled a central barrier (spina) constructed between two turning posts (metae). The only known example found in Britain, so far, is in Colchester.
An engineering works that produces tufting machinery especially for use in the manufacturing of carpets.
Open-air area often terraced on which a range of ore processing operations are carried out.
An establishment serving coffee and other refreshments and inexpensive foods. Between the 17th and 18th centuries they were also meeting places for political discussions.
A hall used by the members of a trade union for meetings and social functions.
A large building, situated by or near a dock, canal, road or railway and used for the temporary storage of goods or merchandise awaiting transportation.
A large store for the temporary accommodation of goods awaiting transportation to or from the sea.
A large building, situated at a railway terminus, used for the temporary storage of goods or merchandise awaiting transportation to or from a railway.
A large building, situated by or near a canal, used for the temporary storage of goods or merchandise awaiting transportation to or from the canal.
A hall, apartment or large room, designed or used primarily for festive or state functions.
A naval dockyard building used for the manufacture of flags.
The dwelling place of a farm worker.
Purpose built area, incorporating water supply, for the cleaning of carriages, carts, etc.
A mill where flax fibres were woven into linen cloth.
A manufacturing site producing weaving shuttles for the textile industry.
A Norman keep, in the form of a circular or polygonal enclosure surrounded by a wall.
Forms of ride which are designed for entertainment.
A type of fairground or seaside amusement, often a permanent structure, where carriages travel at high speeds on an undulating track raised some distance from the ground.
A depression in the ground caused by the impact of a falling object, such as a crashed aircraft.
A place, where a corpse could be laid whilst being carried on its way to a burial, to allow the bearers to rest.
A place where vehicles can be filled up with petrol, oil, water, etc.
A free-standing building or a room used as a storage place for valuable objects.
An enclosure used for corralling deer.
A pen, often circular and stone-walled, for rounding up livestock.

An earthwork feature used by hunters to trap deer comprising a steep ditch into which the deer are chased with an enclosure to hold them at one end, known from the Isle of Rum and a debateable example in Cumbria.
A man made ditch designed to obstruct the progress of a tank or armoured vehicle. Ditches were often reveted with concrete or wood.
Stop-line against invading tanks in form of a ditch during the defence of Britain.
A building offering accommodation to people who are visiting a town or locality renowned for its mineral springs.
A deep gutter, drain or sink.
An artificial watercourse for the conveyance of water.
6 DFW55373 projector emplacements spaced in a 3x2 rectangular gid, but each spaced 35m apart. No blast protection was provided at the shelters, which were placed between the projector emplacements.
An engineering works producing items for the railway other than rolling stock, such as signals, tracks, points, etc.
A man made terrace, often constructed in concrete, built to allow spectators a view of organized outdoor events or activities.
A building for the housing of trams.
A house of friars of the Augustinian order. Also known as Austin Friars
A factory or site where wooden clogs are manufactured.
A trench dug to contain a sill beam, a horizontal timber beam used as a foundation for the wall of a building. Use wider site type where known.
A building or a room for accounts.
A giant figure of a man, animal or symbol carved on chalk hillsides mainly in southern England.
A non-profit making restaurant administered by a Local Food Committee which provided customers with good quality and wholesome food which could be purchased without ration coupons.
A place where refreshments or meals may be obtained.
A building from which the firing of torpedoes can be controlled and evaluated.
A designated area of water in which the perfromance of torpedoes can be evaluated.
A factory built for the production of breakfast cereals.
An aircraft hangar designed to Air Ministry specifications (drawing number 2243/41). Constructed from prefabricated A-frames and clad in corrugated iron.
A mine used for the extraction of zinc bearing ore. Use with other metal ores extracted and MINE where necessary, eg. LEAD MINE.
The residence of a coastguard.
A stone with a cross carved into the surface.
A farmyard or enclosure containing regularly built stacks of hay, corn, peas etc.
A place of worship specifically for mariners and their families.
A house or shelter for the storage and/or launching of boats.

A tower situated above the rampart walkway and in between the angle towers along a defensive structure, such as a castle wall. They were used as lookout towers, roofed strongpoints or platforms from which missiles could be discharged or artillery fired.
An intrusive feature cut for the purpose of containing a cremation burial within it.
A factory used for the manufacture of serge, a heavy woollen cloth.

A decoy site designed to replicate the layout of an RAF satellite airfield, complete with dummy aircraft, simulated runways and simple structures intended to fool enemy aircraft during daylight raids.
The approximate location at which stray finds of artefacts were found. Index with object name.
A modification of WATCH OFFICE (12779/41) where the original large windows were removed and smaller frames fitted, the gap being filled with straight-joint brickwork.

A type of aircraft hangar from the closing years of WWI either of steel or wood utilising a type of lattice work roof support known as a Belfast Truss, which features diagonally interlaced pieces of thin pine. The roof appears as a smooth curve.
A building used as a control centre for the Air Raid Precautions network, responsible for issuing air raid warnings and coordinating fire and rescue services.
A group of buildings containing machinery for the production in bulk of butter or related dairy products.
A shore establishment for the teaching of maritime theory and practical skills.
A water feature intended to play a trick on a visitor by drenching them unexpectedly. The device would be triggered by the visitors foot or remotely. Italian for 'water jokes'.
The residence of a master shipwright.
A building where milk is deposited and stored before it is despatched to the consumer.
A notional line of resistance defined by anti tank obstacles, pillboxes and gun emplacements.
An open yard or place where timber is stacked or stored.
A coastal gun/watch tower built as part of the anti-invasion defences during the Napoleonic Wars.
A pit from which marl, a mixture of clay and carbonate of lime, is excavated. Marl is used as a fertilizer.
A building, either purpose-built or modified, used for the co-ordination of the Fire Service.
A chemical works engaged in the production or refining of toluene, a substance extracted from coal tar or specific types of crude oil, and used in the production of explosives during WW1.

A two-storey, brick construction with a watch office and additional rooms given over to the meteorological section, including a forecast room and met store. A brick parapet on the roof differentiates it from 2328/39.
The dwelling place of a farm worker.
A factory or works used for the forging and sharpening of a variety of tools including scythes, spades, etc.
A factory used for the manufacture of scythes.
A site used for all the processes associated with the manufacture of roof, floor or decorative tiles.
A garden or collection of potted plants on the flat roof of a house or other building.
A works site making and/or maintaining drive belts for industrial power.
A military storage aircraft hangar built in the late 1930s. It comprises a semicircular concrete structure with reinforced concrete columns, featuring a curved roof and straight walls.
A single-span aircraft hangar designed by Boulton & Paul of London and Norwich (drawing number 4178/44). Mainly used on aircraft factory sites and at Armament Training Schools.
An aircraft hangar built to Air Ministry design. Mainly constructed on aircraft factory aerodromes.
A building where distillation, a chemical process used in the production of a range of different chemicals, took place.
A steep-sided pit formed by, and for, the extraction of gravel.
A structure housing machinery for crushing coal. Usually found at the pithead of a colliery or coal mine.
A structure used for the roasting or drying of chicory.
A structure used for the drying of food using an indirect source of heat.
A farmstead where the house and working buildings are attached and in-line. Can include Bastles, Longhouses and Laithe houses.
An outbuilding where a horse-drawn carriage is kept.
A pedestrianized shopping street, or a more complex arrangement of shopping 'squares' and walkways.
Engineering workshop intended either for final adjustments of new machinery or the fitting of replacement parts to machinery under repair.
A stone or metal post that indicates the limit of an area or piece of land.
A pit used for the containment of clay whilst it is mixed to the right consistency for brickmaking.
A public music or dancing establishment often with facilities for gambling.
A one-storey house.
A bungalow joined to another to form one building.
A factory where lace is manufactured.
A facility used for the storage and distribution of fuel for transportation. Often associated with dockyards and railways.
A type of guildhall belonging primarily to the London livery companies, but also found elsewhere in the country, so called because of the livery worn by members of the guild.
A religious house governed by an abbot or abbess. Use with narrow terms of DOUBLE HOUSE, MONASTERY or NUNNERY.
A small outlying farm building, especially common in southern England, used to store ash (which was used as a fertilizer).
The official residence of a dean.
A loft for the drying of thread or cloth.
A large self-service store selling foods and some household goods.
A jettied house where the upper storey only overhangs the end elevation of the building.
A building or site used to assess the mechanical state of a vehicle.
The residence of a master shipwright.
Use with wider site type where known.
A building where clothes are washed.
A laundry built in conjunction with a PUBLIC BATHS.

A small rectangular or sub circular area or areas bounded by an earthwork, ditch or similar boundary, where one side is formed by an existing linear boundary, forming a pattern reminiscent of clothes hanging from a washing line.
A brewery building where malt is mixed with hot water to form wort.
A building or site used in the production of japanned goods. Japanning was the process of covering a material with a hard, black lacquer in imitation of Japanese lacquer work.
A stone or brick wall enclosing a park.
A site, usually consisting of a bowling green and pavilion, frequented by lawn bowlers.
A dam with a watertight upstream side, which may be flat or curved, supported by a series of buttresses on the downstream side.
A type of temporary bridge designed by Sir Donald C.Bailey during the Second World War.
Scaffolding erected on a beach and in the surf so as to prevent hostile forces from landing.
A vertical structure, sometimes made of steel, often used in the manufacture of cement. Material is loaded at the top, burnt in the middle and removed at the bottom.
A twin-shafted kiln, circular or oval in plan, consisting of a fire chamber, pre-heater and cooling chamber.
Early form of powered hammer, usually wooden, used primarily in the iron industry.
A machine in which a heavy block of metal is used for beating, breaking or driving something.
An establishment used to serve ice cream to the general public.
An open-sided building known to have been used for sheltering animals other than cattle.
The residence of a lacemaker.
An enclosure created by constructing one or more lines of ramparts across a promontory which projects into the sea.
A defensive enclosure created by constructing one or more lines of ramparts across a neck of land, in order to defend, or restrict access to, a spur or promontory, either inland or on the coast.
A frame containing glass tiles or bricks set into a pavement to allow the lighting of basement areas.
Building with underfloor kiln used for drying China Clay slurry prior to packing and transportation. Central feature of China Clay Works.

Component part of a mungo and shoddy mill, where non-wool fibres from shredded material are destroyed by either soaking rags in an acid solution or rotating them in drums in a hot acidic gas followed by heat. The result is an all-wool product.
A mill for the manufacture of low grade cloth made from ground-up heavy woollen rags.
A tunnel running under a river or through a hill along which vehicles may travel.
A building in which railway wagons can unload local goods.
Finishing process for cloth, especially linen, running the cloth between heavy rollers.
A place of worship for followers of the Wesleyan Reform Union, a movement formed in 1859 by those members of the Methodist Reform Church who did not join the Wesleyan Association.
A mine used for the extraction of uranium bearing ores.
A purpose-built fisherman's house, eg. a house with a first floor dwelling and ground floor fish store, or a house with a watch tower for spotting shoals.
A golf course, clubhouse and ancilliary buildings.
A straight mine entrance, driven on a constant downwards slope.
A military storage aircraft hangar designed in 1937. It has a curved profile and is constructed from steel ribs supporting a concrete skin. The roof is covered with earth and turf.
A school design consisting of single-storey buildings with classrooms entered from a verandah.
A tunnel running under a river or a hillside through which a railway line runs.
A tunnel carrying a railway beneath the surface of the ground.

A subrectangular earthen enclosure defined by a ditch, usually with an internal bank, assumed to have been used for the primary exposure or burial of human remains in the Neolithic period prior to secondary burial elsewhere.
A building where patients or inmates of a hospital or workhouse were disinfected and their clothes washed or burnt to prevent the spread of infectious diseases or other ailments.
A gatehouse bridging a canal.
A building or buildings where soap is manufactured.
A building used by organizations or societies for the promotion of a particular profession through lectures, research, etc.
A place with organized amusements for people on holiday.
Purposely built camp with recreational facilities and individual chalets for accommodation.
An internal combustion engine powered by the combustion of vapourized oil.
A post set up, to which offenders were tied to be whipped.
A night fighter station watch office based on the standard design dor Bomber Satellite Station watch offices
A two storey building with a watch office on the ground floor and a control room above. Originally based on drawing number 12096/4.

An institution created with the merging of Gaols and Houses of Correction in 1865. Nowadays term used for a prison to which people are sent whilst remanded in custody before trial or direct from court after conviction.
A site used for the separation of oil into its constituent parts by heating in an enclosed vessel(s).
A manmade barrier built across a river in order to increase the depth of water.
A coupled timber built end-opening First World War aircraft hangar.
Term applied to both the pit trap itself, and the walled enclosure containing pit trap(s).
A room to display various items of hardware and ironmongery.
Seats or benches covered in turf, built against a wall, tree or fountain, were a common feature of medieval enclosed gardens.
A type of GARDEN HOUSE, usually in the form of an open-fronted shelter with seat.
A library for use of the public.
A residence of two or three monks of the Order of Tiron dependent on a foreign mother house.
A specialist hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of ear, nose and throat disorders and diseases.
A stone edge-runner grinding machine or mill used for mechanically grinding and mixing the ingredients of gunpowder.
A vehicle or aircraft placed at the entrance to a site as a symbolic guardian.

Used by Ordnance Survey to record high accuracy height above Ordnance Datum Newlyn. Marked by a low concrete pillar, and maybe surrounded by railings, they comprise an underground chamber protecting the reference point, built directly onto stable bedrock.
Buildings and structures associated with the processing and storage of natural gas.

A facility where natural gas is made smaller in volume, to facilitate its distribution through the National Transmission System. Term can also be used for a station, which recompresses the gas to the required pressure.
A glasshouse used for the cultivation of tropical plants.
A factory manufacturing sports equipment.
A factory manufacturing billiard tables.
A structure consisting of a vertical mast and a horizontal boom operated by cables on a separate engine or motor. Used for hoisting and moving heavy loads or objects.
A pillbox built to a design by the commander of the Royal Engineers for the Colchester Garrison.
An educational establishment where dentistry is taught.
A boat roofed over and fitted up as a home for living in permanently or temporarily.
A wall for growing fruit, dating in England from the mid-18th century, whose curving lines gave added strength, thus doing away with the need for buttressing.
A usually south-facing wall used for the cultivation of fruit plants.
A shop selling household furniture.
A factory where jute (plant fibres), was used to make products such as hessian, sacking, cordage and backing materials for carpet and linoleum.
Buildings associated with the extaction of uranium from its pitchblende or copper ores.
Three storey house with a topshop; machinery powered by shafting through the upper floor.
A stable used for riding horses or those used to pull coaches, gigs, etc.
A covered stall at a market or fair, etc.

A place of worship for members of the United Reformed Church, a group formed in 1972 by the amalgamation of most of the Congregational Churches in England and Wales with the Presbyterian Church in England.

A place of worship for members of the Congregational Church. These churches, the first of which was founded in 1616 in Southwark, practised self government. Most of them were merged to form the United Reformed Church in 1972.
An offshoot of the Wesleyan movement founded in 1838 by John Banyard at Rochford, Essex. In 1956 it changed name to the Union of Evangelical Churches. There are 17 chapels in Essex and London.
A venue, with a boxing ring and associated facilities, which is used to train for and undertake amateur or professional boxing.
An area of ground used for the game of quoits.
A brass plaque, usually on the ground rather than a wall fixture, commemorating a person or event.
A factory used for the manufacture of scythes.
An area of hardstanding to allow movement of farm transport in all weathers.
A place of worship for Roman Catholics.

A prefabricated structure of reinforced concrete posts supporting a pitched roof frame with an infilling of concrete panels. Produced by during WWII as barrack accommodation and as emergency housing. Similar in style to Maycrete huts.
The bottom of a dock.
An isolation hospital for infectious diseases and leprosy, sometimes known as a Pest House; commonly situated on the edge of a town.
An oven used in the coal industry for the recovery of gas, tar and other by-products of the coking process. Late 19th century-20th century.
A surgery where patients who pay for medical treatments are seen and treated.
A room or office at a general practitioners' or veterinary practice, where patients or animals are seen and medicine dispensed.
A standard latine block on RAF airfields.
A large, deep, manmade pool, usually with accompanying diving boards/platforms and forming part of a swimming pool complex.
An area where builders keep building materials such as brick, stone, planks and cement.
Garden or open-air enclosure, usually connected to commercial premises, where tea and other refreshments are served to the public.
An iron frame placed over a coffin or at the entrance to a grave to act as a deterrent against resurrectionists.

A prefabricated structure of cant sided lightweight timber wall sections bolted together. Externally the walls were clad with plasterboard covered with felt. Designed for use as barrack accommodation during WWII.
A hostel owned by a Christian association which provides cheap accommodation for young people.
A place where boats or ships are built or repaired.

Traditionally a mew was a building housing hawks when they were moulting, however since the C16th the term has been used for a series of stables grouped around an open yard or alley, often with rooms above. Use only for stables otherwise use FALCONRY.
Manmade constructions used to prevent rivers breaking their banks and flooding the surrounding area with water. Often taking the form of a bank or wall.

A mound of fire-cracked stones, normally accompanied by a trough or pit which may have been lined with wood, stone or clay. Assumed to be locations where heated stones were used to boil water primarily for cooking purposes.
A specialist hospital where the elderly receive medical treatment.
A chemical works engaged in the production of Ammonium Perchlorate, a product used in the explosives industry.
Part of textile mills.
A two-storey watch office, built to Air Ministry drawing number 1959/34. It became the standard design for watch offices with a large, almost square, ground plan with a central observation tower.
A building and open area from which buses, usually those working local or regional services, begin or end their journeys.
A shed for storing fishing bait.
A place where boats or ships are built or repaired.
A hospital department where heat, light, sound, electricity, etc, is administered to patients suffering from muscular or skeletal disorders.
A separate hospital building, or block of an asylum, where new arrivals were segregated from old inmates for a defined period. This system was developed from the mid-19th century onwards.
A terrace or row of dwellings, with a NAIL SHOP attached to each house.
A small Anglo-Saxon cross-slab buried on the breast or beneath the head of a corpse.
A bridge in which the load is carried by a single beam, or beams, spanning the space between two supports.
A simple form of stone slab bridge, particularly associated with South West England.
Where secondary product use with major product and MINE, eg. LEAD MINE.
A mill manufacturing bobbins for the textile industry.
Gates that can be opened or closed, to admit or exclude water, especially flood water.
A kiln for drying hops in a brewery or maltings complex, as distinct from the OASTHOUSES found on farms.
A hollow pillar, erected in a public place, containing a receptacle for posting letters.
A detached fort covering a strategic point.
A structure, often built undergound, used for defence and co-ordination of military activity.
A textile mill where crepe is manufactured.Crepe is a fine cloth particularly silk or mixture of silk and cotton.
A terrace house sharing a common wall with its neighbours.

A house within a row. At first floor level a gallery which runs through the front of the building. Access to the gallery was gained by steps set at intervals along the row. Commonly found in the city of Chester.
A building or part of a building used for the storage of shoes or boots.
A house with windows and doors on one side only; often built facing inwards onto a burgage plot, or sometimes on a steep slope, with no apertures on the uphill side.
An establishment or works where the distilling of spirits is carried out.
The outlet or mouth of a sewer where it dispenses into the sea, lake, etc.
A large drain or conduit for carrying away wastes.
A room or building in which riding tackle is stored.
An area within a building open to the public where light meals and drinks can be purchased and consumed.
A flat, level area of ground within a garden. Often raised and accessed by steps.

Traditionally, dating from the medieval period, this was an area on the north bank of the Thames where the Merchants of the Hanse conducted their business. Now includes a similar establishment in a provincial town.
A type of clothier's house, consisting of TOPSHOP and dwelling, used for hand-weaving of textiles.
A tower at the mouth of the harbour to defend the end of the harbour boom.

A stone building with external access to the domestic accommodation via a permanent stair. The ground floor is normally used as a byre in rural contexts, but in an urban setting it may be intended for one of a number of other non domestic uses.
A manufacturing site producing weaving shuttles for the textile industry.
A factory where paper is made. Use with power type where known.
A temporary brick and timber watch office based on the all-timber 2423/39. Built after 1941 on many Operational Training Unit airfields the design was superseded by 8936/40.
A structure consisting of combustible material, typically wood, on which a body is placed and then cremated, sometimes with accompanying grave goods. Use only when evidence of structure exists.
A lock at the point where two waterways join together.
A workshop or factory where statues are made by casting molten material into moulds.
Traditionally a place where meat and fish were sold.
An artificial water channel for carrying water over long distances. Use also for bridge-like structures that carry the channel or canal across a valley, river or other obstacle.
A house with an aisle on one side only.
A terrace or row of dwellings, with a NAIL SHOP attached to each house.
A building or buildings used for the manufacture of crucibles.
A works where cotton waste is stored or processed.
A cable, usually erected between posts, used to prevent the landing or hostile aircraft.
A naval base that builds, repairs, docks or converts warships, and is manned by civilian engineers and workers and administered by engineer duty officers.
An enclosure in which ships are built and repaired, and all sorts of ships' stores are brought together.
A stable located at a railway station or goods yard. Horses were necessary both for freight and passengers to continue their journey beyond the railway.
Small engineering works specialising in the production of items such as ploughs and threshing machinery.
A factory where tapestries were manufactured.
A building or subterranean structure used for the storage of spirits.
A post set up alongside a canal to mark the miles to and from a place.
Residential area built to house athletes and their coaches at the Olympic Games. The buildings are generally reused as public housing after the contest.
A largely residential area on the outskirts of a town or city.
A single line, or pair of roughly parallel lines, of pits set at intervals along a common axis or series of axes. The pits are not thought to have held posts.
A pit alignment accompanied by a linear bank (or banks) running parallel and adjacent to the line(s) of pits.
The establishment of an undertaker who is responsible for the management of the ceremony connected with the burial or cremation of a dead body.

An establishment where alcoholic and non alcoholic drinks are served, food may also be served. May be a an individual room within a larger multi purpose building such as a sports pavilion or a theatre.
A building housing washing facilities and toilets. The term occurs mainly in a military context.
Outdoor site for domestic washing, etc.
A building or site where lead is obtained from ore.
A building in which wrought iron or steel chains were manufactured.
A supporting structure for drilling machinery used in the extraction of or prospecting for mineral oils.
The ground immediately surrounding a place, particularly a religious building.
A house provided for the treasurer of a cathedral, palace or similar.
A layer of remains left by a single culture, from which the culture can be dated or identified.
A room or building for hand knitting garments on simple hand frames.
A residential home for children with physical and/or learning disabilities, sensory impairment and/or mental health issues who need medical intervention and/or care provided by registered nurses.
A site used for the sport of badger baiting using fighting dogs.
A building or structure of unknown function found on a railway. Use more specific type where known
A building in which textile rags are sorted according to fibre types.
Building used for the display of inscription panels and memorials to those buried in the underlying catacomb.
A place where photographs are displayed for sale.
A building, often located in a park, where players can change and store equipment and from where spectators can watch the game.
A building, usually at a sports ground, with facilities for players and spectators.
A small hut erected over a mine shaft.
A Neolithic burial monument comprising a stone-built chamber within a rectangular or trapezoidal earthen mound.

A rectangular or trapezoidal earthen mound of Neolithic date, usually accompanied by flanking or encircling ditches, and normally associated with human remains. Mound construction and associated features vary considerably in type and complexity.
A form of Neolithic long barrow comprising an oval, rather than rectangular or trapezoidal mound.
1st World War end-opening aeroplane hangar.
Position often screened by earth, stone or wood from which game is shot.
A building or wing of a large house in which the servants would live and carry out some of their duties.
Grinding mill for producing dyes and pigments from natural materials.
A separate residence for guests, a house on a private estate or a monastery building specifically for receiving visitors.
A factory or site where wooden clogs are manufactured.
A pit used to trap game. Often originally covered and consealed, and sometimes with sharpened stakes in the base.
A house in a terrace built on top of another, with access at high and low level to either side.
A block for mounting a horse.
A structure erected for the processing of shale, to extract oil through heating.
A building housing filters for sewage. Usually associated with a sewage pumping station.
A place where metal knives and edge cutting tools were manufactured.
A place where watches and timepieces are manufactured and mended.
A workshop with a forge for the melting and working of white metal, ie. low-melting alloys. Also used for a smith specializing in decorative or finely finished wrought iron work.
A place where padlocks and rim locks for doors are made from iron and brass.
A place where an anti-corrosion coating of zinc is added to iron and steel products to prevent them from rusting.
A terrace or row of dwellings, with a NAIL SHOP attached to each house.
A workshop used by a craftsman who works in base or precious metals.
A workshop used for the manufacture of items of jewellery and/or timepieces from precious metals and precious or semi-precious stones.
Place where a smith works iron. May be for small scale local use or within a larger industrial complex.
A mill used for the preparation of raw fleece etc, for spinning by a coarse form of carding.
A place in which gunpowder and other explosives are stored in large quantities.
A building used for the storage of explosives of a non-military function, eg. mining explosives, signal explosivres etc.
