A wayside inn for livestock traders.
A place where metal knives and edge cutting tools were manufactured.
A building or complex producing umbrellas, parasols and canes.
A house with a pitched roof with a double slope and gables on the side elevations of the building.
A small house built out of rough logs.
A sewer or irrigation channel designed to avoid blockage.
A factory or site where wooden clogs are manufactured.
A fortified house of two or three storeys, the lower floor being used to house animals and the upper for domestic use.
A medieval house with central open hall and two storey bays, jettied at first floor level, on either side.
A wealden house with only one end being jettied.
A place where photographs are taken of people or things on a commercial basis.
A mill for the removal by mechanical means of the dried wood and seeds of the flax and cotton plants after retting. The resulting 'tow' is then spun into linen and cotton respectively.
A purpose-built triangulation point used for the metrical survey of Britain carried out by the Ordnance Survey.
A purpose-built triangulation pillar used for the metrical survey of Britain carried out by the Ordnance Survey.
A heated stone, brick or iron chamber used for drying corn.
An underground room or building with an arched roof, often used as a burial chamber. Use wider site type where known.
A post set up alongside a canal to mark the miles to and from a place.
A post or pillar set up alongside a road to mark the miles from or to a place.
A shelter, sometimes camouflaged, for the observation of birds and animals at close quarters.
A narrow strip of land where a plough and team could turn. This usually remains higher than the ploughed land.
Traditionally, the hall of a crafts, trade, or merchants' guild. Nowadays, often used to describe a TOWN HALL.
Garden area next to public house used for the comsumption of alcoholic beverages.
A hospital where more 'natural' means of treatment are used rather than conventional methods.
A kiln that is octagonal in plan. Use with functional kiln type where known.
An embankment or cutting on a railway system, surfaced at a uniform gradient, up or down which materials were hauled by rope.

An Iron Age round defended house, found mainly in the north and west of Scotland. Brochs have a tapering profile and thick, usually hollow dry stone walls which contain galleries, cells and a stairway, with guard cells at the entrance.
The residence of a station master.
A marker stone erected to indicate a claim to the rights, usually mineral, of an area.
An inclined concrete ramp on which cars can move from one level to another.
A beacon, firmly embedded on the sea floor, consisting of an iron mast, with ladder steps leading up to the refuge cage considerably above high-water mark, and capable of holding several people.
Underground passage with storage chambers found in South West England.
A works where cotton waste is stored or processed.
A factory where ribbons are manufactured.
The residence or official premises of a consul, the official appointed by a state to protect its citizens and commercial interests in a foreign state.
A large site specializing in the manufacture of locomotives.
An area, often a village, with fixed defences such as pillboxes, anti tank ditches and gun emplacements, designed to stop the advance of an enemy force and to hold out for an agreed period of time.
A vault used for the storage of cider.
A small carved figure, usually female in appearance, probably representing fertility charms, found on Romanesque churches in the West of England, eg. Kilpeck.
Component: Use wider site type where known.
A processing house or room in a brewery.
A factory manufacturing timepieces, including clocks and watches.
A site where scientific and technical instruments such as microscopes are assembled.
A small park or enclosure where animals are kept.
A site, including hangars, moorings and ancillary buildings, used for the storage, maintenance, take off and landing of airships.
A factory where gloves are manufactured.
A coal-burning power station where domestic electricity for an area is produced, eg. Battersea Power Station, London.
A building or room in which wood is stored.
A type of kiln, usually built into banking, with a stone lining that was used to produce white coal which was used as fuel in the lead smelting process.
A specialist hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of eye disorders and diseases.

A structure or building used in the manufacture of the explosive cordite. After the cordite had been pressed to extract moisture it was placed on racks within the stove prior to being taken to the reeling house for winding.

A Neolithic burial monument comprising a rectangular or trapezoidal stony mound which contains either a passage at one end with or without lateral chambers, or one or more smaller chambers entered from the side of the mound.

Approximately circular or oval setting of spaced post holes indicating the former presence of a free-standing arrangement of upright timber posts. Often regarded as a wooden equivalent of the better known stone circles.
A building used for the finishing, drying and storage of lace.
A crane fixed to a quay, used for the unloading of ships cargoes.
An instrument for gauging the amount of rain which has fallen over a stated period.
A grotto or shrine dedicated to the nymphs, composed of fountains designed to imitate a natural grotto.
A shady cavern built as a garden feature. In the 18th century it usually took the form of an artificial rocky cave or apartment decorated with stalactites and shells in a wild part of the grounds.
A place where pieces of stone are crushed and ground.
A building manufacturing bandages.
A cheap restaurant.
A scientific laboratory where marine life is studied and researched.
A group of buildings or rooms equipped with apparatus for scientific experiments or other research, testing and investigations.
An ore works at which gold was separated from the ore by the addition of mercury.
A free-standing cross made of stone in the form of a cross with a ring surrounding the intersection. Often used as a grave marker
Regular courtyard farmsteads where the buildings are arranged around all four sides of the yard.
A structure, partly underground, for the preservation of ice for use during warmer weather.
An attic workshop for textile manufacture, usually weaving.
Regular courtyard farmsteads where the buildings are arranged as two ranges at right angles to each other.
A large scale works for cloth finishing processes.
An establishment open at night for refreshment and entertainment.
A site used for the production and/or working of metallic lead.
A building where the bones of the dead were stored.
A meeting hall, sometimes equivalent to a GUILDHALL, but also associated with some early mining industries.
An engineering site where railway carriages are manufactured.
A modern building in which the load is carried by a metal girder framework and infilled with a light curtain wall.
A farmstead where mostly detached buildings have developed around three sides of an open cattle yard.
Garden area next to public house used for the comsumption of alcoholic beverages.
A round or polygonal building containing a HORSE ENGINE. Commonly found on farms next to the threshing barn, where it is used to power the machinery.
A house with a pitched roof with a double slope and gables on the front and rear elevations of the building.
A hole dug to provide a firm base for an upright post, often with stone packing. Use broader monument type where known.
A small detached building used to accommodate patients with tuberculosis.
A bridge whose upkeep and repair was financed by the exaction of a toll.
A purpose-built fisherman's house, eg. a house with a first floor dwelling and ground floor fish store, or a house with a watch tower for spotting shoals.
A gallery or building in a garden, usually south facing, used for the growing of oranges and other fruit.
A pit from which sand is excavated.
A tread-wheel by which a crane was formerly worked.

A complex of buildings at a seaport, comprising of a terminal building, landing pier and hangars, used for the embarkation of passengwers and/or freight on flying boat services during the 1930's-50's.
An edging of stone forming the kerb of a path.
A plain four walled court used to play the game of racquets on.
A command post used to direct the guns of a coastal battery.
A defensive gun battery positioned to face out to sea to fire on enemy ships and amphibious craft.
Garden comprising rockwork features including grottoes, cascades and arches, often in different architectural styles ie. Gothic, Chinese and rustic. In use from the mid C18.
Open sided barn for the storage of wood produced by the periodic cutting of small trees.
The principal house of a manor or village.
A Cornish Medieval amphitheatre used for the performance of mystery plays and sports.
A crude shelter for persons engaged in the production of pure carbon by the controlled burning of wood and other organic materials.
A building with malt kilns for the malting of grains and with other similar equipment for brewing work.
A pipe or channel for conveying water or other liquids.
A mill where flax fibres were woven into linen cloth.
A building containing equipment used for the polishing of grains of gunpowder and extraction of the resulting dust.
An area speciallly developed to accommodate commercial buildings.
An area including buildings dedicated to scientific research for commercial purposes. Often associated with, or operated by, a university or higher education institution.
A trench dug in order to receive the foundations of a structure such as a stone wall etc.
A construction trench dug to receive a line of posts for a wall, with associated packing.
An establishment from which food is distributed to the public during wartime or similar states of emergency.
An enclosed area of ground immediately surrounding a cathedral.
The slab or place on which a fire is made.
An building, often including recreational facilities, provided for the relaxation of serving Royal Air Force Personnel.
A long bed containing rose plants.
A site where scientific and technical instruments such as microscopes are assembled.
A factory manufacturing timepieces, including clocks and watches.
An artificial pond or pool constructed for the purpose of watering livestock, particularly in prehistory.
Workshop for producing crates, particularly for the packing of pottery.
A building housing machinery.
An enclosure used for the cultivation of fruit trees.
A site where canvas, coarse, unbleached cloth, made from hemp or flax, was manufactured.
A housing for racing pigeons usually situated in allotments of back yards.
Cloth finishing process using machinery to raise the nap of the cloth before shearing.
A school where handicrafts are taught.
A building that housed humans and cattle under one roof, with a shared entrance providing access to the cattle housing (usually downslope) and the dwelling area.
A small, defensive settlement, usually consisting of one dwelling and ancillary buildings, surrounded by a palisade.
A stone or brick wall either in, or enclosing, a garden.
A wall for growing fruit, dating in England from the mid-18th century, whose curving lines gave added strength, thus doing away with the need for buttressing.
Regular courtyard farmsteads where the buildings are arranged as an H-shaped plan, commonly with cattle housing to two or more cattle yards.
A factory where putty, used as a means of securing windows and for setting plumbing fixtures, is produced from a combination of whiting and oil.
A school run by a Christian church.
A piece of forest land converted into arable.
The entrance to a tramway tunnel.

A poorly understood Neolithic monument comprising a very long, narrow earthen mound. They may be of single-phase construction, or represent the addition of a linear extension to the bank of an existing Long Barrow.
A room or building where a pump is worked.
A small pumping station.
The meeting hall of a secular or ethical society.
Workshop for producing crates, particularly for the packing of pottery.
A site with one or more defensive earthworks, often at a river crossing incorporating natural features which define parts of the curtilage.
An imprecise term used to describe large Iron Age settlements of town-like proportions.
A factory where knitted fabrics are manufacterd using knitting machines.
Stadium housing a track and associated buildings and structures for the public racing of greyhounds.
A group of buildings, or part of a works, housing apparatus used in the process of distilling.
An office where the administrative duties of a university are performed.
A movable bridge that swings or rotates around a central pier, or one that is pivoted only at one end, to provide a passageway for navigation.
A building used in the preparation of manure.
A dedicated room for housing the organ feeder bellows, can be an underground chamber or a free-standing building.
A room or building where clothing and other fabrics are washed, mangled, steamed and ironed.
A small settlement, usually consisting of one dwelling with ancillary buildings.
A shop selling tea, butter, flour, sugar, spices, tinned foods and miscellaneous household stores.
A large, watertight enclosure in which the water is maintained at the high-tide level so that vessels remain constantly afloat in them.
Roman coastal forts fortified with large walls and a ditch, introduced to cope with raids from across the English Channel and North Sea.
A church established by a religious community to propogate its faith.
A pillbox constructed for use in training exercises forming part of a simulated defensive position
Block of flats within which the individual dwellings are accessed by narrow external balconies.

A stone building with external access to the domestic accommodation via a permanent stair. The ground floor is normally used as a byre in rural contexts, but in an urban setting it may be intended for one of a number of other non domestic uses.
A threshing barn, usually timber framed which is raised on staddle stones.
A building where distillation, a chemical process used in the production of a range of different chemicals, took place.
A tower used to store grain in.
A prepared area used for the game of baseball.
A type of temporary bridge designed by Sir Donald C.Bailey during the Second World War.
A site used for the extraction of peat.
Accommodation for the warrener(s) usually located within the boundary of the Rabbit Warren. They also provided a place to store nets, traps and other necessary equipment.
A monument featuring a bank or mound constructed primarily of stone. Use specific type where known.
Long alignment of cairns lying between two large cairns; first recognized as a site type on Sourton Tor, Dartmoor.
A system of individually enclosed fields.
A library where books may be consulted but not taken away.
A structure comprising two upright spars, joined at the top to form a triangle, with a hoisting tackle suspended from the apex. Used to lift cargo or other weights.
Regular courtyard farmsteads where the buildings are arranged around three sides of a yard which is open to one side.
A building where masts are made and stored.
A small roofed shelter for cattle without tethering point or stalls, but with a small yard attached. It is often detached from the main range of farm buildings.
A place where gold is worked into articles or products.
A settlement where previous house sites are now unoccupied, but often visible as earthworks, crop or soil marks.
Small vernacular building used by fishermen for the preparing of nets and storage of equipment.
A tread-wheel by which a crane was formerly worked.
A dispersed farmstead where buildings and yards (regular or loose courtyard in their form) are sited alongside a routeway.
A piece of forest land converted into arable.
An establishment serving coffee and other refreshments and inexpensive foods. Between the 17th and 18th centuries they were also meeting places for political discussions.
A coastal battery containing one or more artillery pieces for to defend the coast against hostile motor torpedo boats.
A place in which turpentine is produced.
A site or building where barrage balloons are manufactured. Consider double-indexing with the term WAR PRODUCTION FACTORY if appropriate.
A building used, as a meeting place and administration block, by an organization run for the benefit of students at a school, college or university.
A factory engaged in the manufacture of small arms ammunition, especially the metal components and filling with the explosive propellant.
A hospital where people with learning disabilities receive medical treatment.
A purpose-built residence for an artist, containing a studio.

A nineteenth century stone calciner, similar to a lime kiln, used for extracting arsenic from mined ores, consisting of a solid structure with a central shaft and a drawing-hole at the base for calciner waste.
An inhumation, usually Roman, which has been covered by tiles to form a tent-like structure over the body; the apex is covered by ridge tiles.
A site where iron oxide and iron sulphates, used as brown pigments, are excavated.
A bridge whose deck is hung from above by large cables, chains or pinned iron or steel bars hanging from towers.
A sculpted cross, or a cross incised into stone or trees, to mark a parish boundary.
Pit for mixing raw materials with water in the preparation of a clay body.
A stone (including standing stones, natural boulders and rock outcrops) decorated with carved motifs.
A garden for the cultivation of herbs used for medicinal or culinary purposes.
A place where telephones and their components are manufactured
An enclosed piece of land adjoining a house.
A building or school where music is taught.
A factory for processing rubber or manufacturing rubber goods, such as tyres.
A workshop or foundry where iron articles are made by casting molten material into moulds.
The rural residence of a country gentleman.
A mill, on two or more levels.
An outlying farm or estate belonging to the Poor Knights of Christ and the Temple of Solomon, commonly known as the Knights Templars
An area, often including a platform, used for boxing competitions.
A building in which apparatus registering the amount of gas consumed is housed.
A timber framed house comprising horizontal and vertical timbers, forming the walls of the building and directly supporting the roof.
A house in which a pair of curved timbers form a bowed A-frame which supports the roof independently of the walls.
A house constructed with a basic timber framework; between the members are panels which can be infilled with timber, wattle and daub, plaster, brick or other materials.
A site or establishment for the casting and refining of metallic copper.
For the production of clay tobacco pipes.
A barn in which a pair of curved timbers form a bowed A-frame which supports the roof independently of the walls.
A barn which is constructed with a timber framework; between the members are panels which are infilled with timber, wattle and daub, plaster, brickwork, stone or other materials.
A block for mounting a horse.
A prison site for the containment of servicemen captured in war.
A kiln used for the slow burning of vegetable matter to produce potassium carbonate.
A depot for the transfer of town refuse to river barges before transportation to the REFUSE DEPOT.
A hospital for the treatment of diseases of the nerves and nervous system.
A place where stained glass is manufactured, traditionally for church windows.
A tank or pond containing a layer of sand etc, for filtering large quantities of liquid.
A residential home for adults with learning difficulties and/or physical disabilities.
An upright post with projecting arm from which the body of a criminal would be hung in chains after execution.
Seaside structure, usually consisting of a manmade retaining wall that keeps a relatively large area of the tidal water partitioned off for controlled boating or swimming.
A small brewery, often situated in a public house, producing limited quantities of beer, for consumption locally and/or on the premises.
A planned administrative capital for local government which provided amenities for the Roman and peregrine (non-Roman) inhabitants of the town.
A glasshouse used for growing pineapples.
A place where the popular gambling game of bingo is played.
Small vernacular building used by fishermen for the preparing of nets and storage of equipment.
An emplacement mounting a small, portable electrically-powered searchlight.
A site in which one or more searchlights and their accompanying structures were positioned to locate enemy aircraft or surface vessels for the benefit of batteries and night fighter aircraft.
A burial in which the body is placed in, or covered by a boat, which is then covered with earth. Use with barrow type where relevant.
Originally a fence against which trees and shrubs were grown. Later used to describe a row of trees and shrubs forming a hedge clipped into a green wall.
A workshop for printing textiles in a CALICO PRINTING WORKS.
A platform for storing winter fodder.
A place where swans are bred and reared.
A type of pottery oven in which the air passes from the base of the kiln out through the top.

Originally an area planted with evergreens or winter-flowering plants for winter display, they can also be large glasshouses built for public entertainment where the original purpose of displaying plants has either disappeared or been minimalised.
A water-filled structure for experimental research.
A tree named after a person or event associated with it, e.g. Byron's Oak at Newstead.
A purpose built theatre with a central open yard, dating to the Elizabethan period. Famous examples include The Globe and the Swan.
Material, stone or wood, lining the inside of a grave.
A temporary settlement or shanty-town erected by railway construction workers or "navvys".
A factory or works used for the production of turpentine, wood alcohol and similar chemicals by the distillation of pulped wood.
A bridge, often over a canal or road, allowing access between two parcels of land.
A residential home for children with physical or learning disabilities, sensory impairment and/or mental health issues but who do not necessarily need medical attention.
An area of a port, dock or harbour where cargo vessels can load and unload large storage containers. May include a rail terminal for containers which have been transported to the port by rail.
A site where wrought iron or steel chains were manufactured.
A building in which wrought iron or steel chains were manufactured.
The dwelling of a blacksmith, nailer, sword cutler, etc, often adjacent to, or containing, a BLACKSMITHS WORKSHOP.
An establishment where tea and other non-alcoholic refreshments and light meals are served.
A room or suite of rooms used as dwellings, eg. in private houses, hotels or tenement houses.
A farmstead where the main range of working buildings are attached in-line and form a long row often facing a series of yards.
A path, or marked lane, designated for use by cyclists.
An area of a carriageway, usually delimited by road markings, for the sole use of bicycles.
A building, usually part of a textile mill complex, where warp yarn is sized prior to weaving. Sizing is the application of a starch solution to warp threads to add strength and protection.
A shed used for the maintenance and repair of aircraft.
An enclosure where the boundary consists of a line of discrete pits, as opposed to a continuous ditch. Use with a term that describes the shape of the monument.
A garden created to commemorate a person or event.
A crude, stone-built shelter for persons involved in lime production and the processing of lime burning.
A factory or works principally engaged in the refining or manufacture of TNT.
A site where barytes (barium sulphate) is mined. Barytes is also commonly worked from the waste tips of lead mines.
A barrier, usually of wood or chain, stretched across the entrance to a harbour, port or anchorage, to control entry and/or limit the effect of the weather on the wave action.
A handloom weavers workshop where the weaver received yarn from a clothier and manufactured a woven piece of cloth from it.
A building where carpets and other floor furnishings were woven.
A workshop where tapestries were made.
A factory where shirts are manufactured.
A public house where no alcohol is sold.
A small shelter used by a man employed to carry links (torches) to light people along a street.
A specialist hospital treating patients with chest disorders and diseases, can be pre sanatoria.
A facility for the kitting out and induction of recruits before being sent on for training.
Building housing machinery used in the production of wooden pulley blocks for the rigging of sailing ships.
A law court builidng established during the 1970's accommodating offices and courtrooms fro the Crown and County Courts.
A place where furs are made into finished products.
A protected building used for the storage of explosives and other pyrotechnic equipment and designed to Air Ministry drawing number 2647/37.

A metal, wooden or concrete box containing a telephone for use by the public, limited accommodation for use as a temporary cell, and a lamp on top that could be used to attract the attention of a passing patrol.
A building containing a weighing machine for weighing goods; sometimes found in markets, ports, etc.
Bridge for carrying pipes between buildings or working areas.
A light, mostly wooden errected structure serving as workshop for the building, storage, repair and maintenance of boats.
A hospital where people with learning difficulties receive medical treatment.
skos:Concept.skos:prefLabel: Hospital For People With Learning Difficulties

skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: A large bed surrounded by an earthwork and filled with composing vegetable matter and animal waste. This was used to produce Nitre, a constituent of gunpowder.
An artificial mound of earth outside a ditch or wall intended to deflect or absorb cannon fire.

A building or part of a building, sometimes attached to a religious community, where religious activities such as worshipping, meetings, teaching about the faith and conferences take place. It can also provide accommodation.
A component of salt works containing flues and drying areas where salt blocks are dried before being crushed and bagged.
A small protective fortification, such as an earthwork.
A field system which appears to have developed in an organic, or piecemeal, fashion over time.

A monument comprising an irregularly circular enclosing ditch, interrupted by several causeways, surrounding a central circular area used for funerary activities, often concealed originally beneath an earthen mound. Index with barrow type where known.
A small hut, dwelling or cave, usually in a secluded spot, in which a hermit lived. Hermits chose to live solitary lives often due to religious motives.
A fortified tower designed to house a number of artillery pieces and a small garrison. Artillery towers first appear in England in the 16th century.
A prepared area of ground, often enclosed, used for the game of basketball.
Factory making slippers.

Cones of solid concrete usually 3 feet 6 inches in diameter x 2 feet high which, when placed in rows or groups were intended to form a substantial barrier to enemy armoured divisions in the event of invasion.
An enclosure for cattle.
A residential establishment for retired armed servicemen and women.
A building containing machinery for the spinning of yarn.
Factory where yarn is made from paper.
An oven used in the coal industry for the recovery of gas, tar and other by-products of the coking process. Late 19th century-20th century.
A farmstead where the main range of working buildings are attached in-line and form a long row often facing a series of yards.
A non-profit making restaurant administered by a Local Food Committee which provided customers with good quality and wholesome food which could be purchased without ration coupons.
A place where refreshments or meals may be obtained.
The main dwelling-house of a farm, it can be either detached from or attached to the working buildings.
A building or part of a building used specifically to store items of hardware and ironmongery.
A site where all the processes for the production of glass and objects made from glass are carried out.
A factory used for the production of thick, flat glass used for shop window panes, etc. Plate glass is produced by rolling and casting rather than traditional blowing.

A system of defensive works such as anti-tank obstacles, ditches and pillboxes, designed to stop the advance of an enemy. Defence lines were constructed across and around strategic areas of ground and sites such as industrial towns.
A building or site from which a watch can be kept to prevent the illegal import/export of goods.
A structure, into which a cart can be drawn, to enable it to be loaded from above.
Building housing machinery used in the production of wooden pulley blocks for the rigging of sailing ships.
A road, used traditionally for the transportation of a corpse to a place of burial.
A place in which gunpowder and other explosives are stored in large quantities.
A building or site from which a lookout can be kept.
A short piece of track lying parallel to the main railway line enabling trains and trucks to pass one another. Sidings can also be used to park trains which are not in use.
A mill used for the preparation and production of Calamine.
A mill for crushing flint. Crushed flint was used in the manufacture of pottery in order to whiten and strengthen the body of earthenware pottery.

Component part of a Flint Mill where flint is calcined before it is brittle enough to be ground in the mill. Ground, burnt flint is used in the production of earthenware pottery, which whitens and strenghens the body.
A bridge that crosses over a railway.
A type of updraught intermittent kiln of rectangular plan and battered sides, but with an open top.
A wealden house with only one end being jettied.
A medieval house with central open hall and two storey bays, jettied at first floor level, on either side.
A roomspace within an abode which combines the specific functions of several of the more traditional roomspaces into a singular unified space.
A mill for the processing of rice for use in food products.

A glass sphere in a metal frame standing on a small pillar. A card is placed behind the sphere which focuses any sunlight, marking the card and thus indicating how many hours of sunlight there was on that day.

A flour mill which uses one or more pairs of horizontal millstones to grind wheat into flour which millers call a ï¿½sudden deathï¿½ process; within not more than 90 seconds complete wheat grain becomes wholemeal flour.
A factory where flour was produced for use in food products.
A steam-powered factory.
A kiln used to calcine the component parts of cement to remove excess water and other ingredients.

The main office of a telegraph company containing rows of tables set with Morse sounders, keys, relays and pigeon holes from where MORSE coded messages were transmitted and received and telegrams dispatched.
A cross channel telegraph office.
An enclosed field for horses.
A passageway, duct or pipe used for the conveyance of heat, gasses, smoke or air.
A shaft allowing access to an area. Often used as an additional escape route to the main shaft in a mine or as an air shaft.
Use only if function unknown, otherwise use specific type.
A purpose-built dwelling for the manager of a factory, works, textile mill, etc, often found within the complex itself.
A site or building used for the manufacture of goods made from pewter, an alloy of tin and lead.
A factory where rock gypsum is ground into a powder used in the production of plaster.
A prefabricated timber structure similar to Sectional hutting that was used by the Air Ministry for accommodation at airfields during WWII. Manufactured by Gerrard and Sons from 1939 to 1941.
A hall built as a memorial to a particular person or event.
A building for a society formed for the promotion of some branch of learning or science.

Part of the WWII air defence radar system, whereby in 1939 a chain of radar stations were established along the south and east coast of Britain. The equipment was based upon apparatus developed for ionospheric research.
A radar station with sets operating on a wavelength of 1.5m. Chain Home Low Stations were intended for use in locating low-flying aircraft but was also capable of detecting high-flying aircraft.
A crane powered by a steam engine.
Pens for housing cattle awaiting transportation.
A building in which engineered metal products are finished and polished.
Gates that can be opened or closed, to admit or exclude water, especially flood water.
A cast-iron or stone boundary post, obelisk or plate found on roads, railways, canals etc around London marking the boundary within which a duty was payable on coal.
skos:Concept.skos:altLabel: City Of London Coal Duties Boundary Marker

skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: A light, mostly wooden errected structure serving as workshop for the building, storage, repair and maintenance of boats.
A series of cages in which hens are confined for intensive egg laying.
A dump for wasters; pieces of pottery spoiled in the manufacturing process.
A house consisting of a single storey hall with two storey domestic ranges attached to either one or both ends.
A building or area where stone is stored for industrial or agricultural use.
Shallow ditches and/or poles erected across open land to obstruct the landing of enemy aircraft and gliders.
Submerged obstacles to stop the landing of Seaplanes
A single storey mill used in the textile industry.
A road or way for riding on horseback within a park or estate.
A greenhouse for the growing of figs.
A double lock placed between tidal water and a canal, etc..
A hole dug in the ground to act as a, usually temporary, communal toilet facility.
A hoist suspended from a girder within the roof of a building or workshop.
A crane suspended from running rails in the roof of an engineering workshop or similar establishment.
A pond or pool with arms covered with nets into which wild birds, are lured and then caught. Monument type includes water feeder channels.
A building or buildings where soap is manufactured.
A jettied house where the upper storey only overhangs the end elevation of the building.
Shallow ditches and/or poles erected across open land to obstruct the landing of enemy aircraft and gliders.
Submerged obstacles to stop the landing of Seaplanes
A hospital where patients can rest and recover after an operation or illness. Medical facilities for treatment are also available.
A kiln in the form of a pit dug into the earth which was used for the the production of white coal prior to the Industrial Revolution.
A room in a monastery used by monks or nuns as a day room.
A processing house containing equipment for sieving caked gunpowder to produce graded granules.
A building where people pay to see films and 'moving pictures'.
The residence of a marsh keeper.
A works, including an extractive site, producing a clay of high plasticity and firmness, used as a basic raw material for porcelain.
A model village built by a utopian society or group of artists.
A single storey mill used in the textile industry.
Purpose-built housing for railway workers.
A factory where explosives and the components of munitions of all types are brought together for assembly.

A kiln in which lime is made by calcining limestone. This type of kiln usually consists of a circular bowl surrounded by pennanular banks with a funnel exit on the lower side. They normally survive as an earthwork. Superseded by Flare Kilns.
A works engaged principally in the manufacture of ammonal explosives.
A building or group of buildings situated close to the sea used by coastguards to enable them to monitor the coastline.
Open yard for keeping cattle in during winter. Used from the mid-14th century in drier, Eastern, arable counties.
A pit where domestic waste material is deposited.
A building temporarily requisitioned for use as an auxiliary hospital administered by members of the Voluntary Aid Detachment during the First World War.

A building temporarily requistioned for use as a hospital. Auxiliary hospitals treated the less seriously wounded and were less strict than military hospitals although they remained under military control.
A pier of brick, masonry, etc, to which the hinges of a gate are attached.
A wooden frame with holes, through which the head and hands of an offender were thrust, in which state they would be exposed to public ridicule and assault.
Graves known to be of shipwreck victims buried close to their site of discovery, as was customary until the 19th century, rather than in consecrated ground.
A factory, incorporating power driven machinery from the late 18th century, where cloth was manufactured from threads interlaced at right angles to each other in a loom.
An establishment for the storage of food for use during wartime or similar states of emergency.
A factory where chocolate products are produced.
A building or structure for the storage of processed minerals, chemicals or agricultural products, etc. Use more specific type where known.
A monument consisting of an area of land enclosed by a ditch, bank, wall, palisade or similar barrier, where the barrier consists of several straight or near straight sections.
A single ditched 3-sided rectilinear enclosure.
A factory used for the production of red lead used in glass manufacture, or white lead used as the pigment in white paint.
A building or buildings where electronic components or devices are designed, developed, manufactured and assembled.
Boarding school for children of Travellers and Romany Gypsies while their parents were away on agricultural work

Traditionally an amber-coloured globe lamp atop a tall black and white pole, acting as a signal to road users that there is a pedestrian crossing. Modern beacons may also include an outer ring of flashing LED lights.
A small concrete turret placed on top of a standard 4 ft. diameter concrete pipe sunk into the ground. Intended for use in defending road junctions, airfields and beach exits.
A gun battery used to signal warnings to ships during bad weather.
An engineering workshop for the manufacture and repair of springs.

A rectangular chamber of brick or stone with heavy wooden gates at either end equipped with sluices to let water in and out, thereby enabling a canal boat to be lowered or raised to a different level.
A large building used for the storage of leather goods or processed animal skins.
Finishing process for cloth, especially linen, running the cloth between heavy rollers.
A stone, terracotta, wooden or metal receptacle used to grow flowers in.
A site, containing installations and machinery, used for measuring the power of explosives.
A building for the weighing or testing of metals, eg. at a mine site.
A house to receive boat landings.
Where several minerals produced, use with other products and MINE, eg. ARSENIC MINE.
An outlying farm or estate belonging to the Bridgettine order.
An inclined plane built to allow tanks to be loaded and unloaded between rolling stock on the railway network and vehicular low loaders.
A boat, ship or other vessel either whole or in part. Watercraft often survive as commemorative monuments or have been reused as floating restaurants, museums, hotels etc.
A circle of wooden stakes or stake holes in the ground.
An alignment of stakes or stakeholes of unknown function
A hospital department where surgical and medical dental treatment takes place.
A place where railway engines are kept.
Form of ore crushing machinery associated with tin mines often wooden and water-powered.
A garden incorporating fountains and pools in which aquatic and other water-loving plants are grown.
A device for catching fish, may be a portable or permanent structure, often a fence or row stakes made in a river, harbour, etc
An engine in which the oscillating motion of the beam is translated via gearing to a rotative motion.
A commercial building used primarily as a trading place for breweries and hop merchants.
Traditionally the chief residence of a land owner. Now used specifically to describe the residence of the Lord Mayor of London.
A reservoir or tank used to hold a supply of water for fire-fighting purposes in the event of the main supply being damaged or cut off.
A miniature railway on which targets can be placed to provide moving targets on a firing range.
An area of ground used for the testing of, and practicing with, weapons against fixed and moveable targets.

A shaft which appears to have been dug for, or which contains objects apparently deposited for, reasons other than storage, disposal or extraction (eg. of stone, water, etc). Index with principal object types.
An outlying farm or estate belonging to the Premonstratensian order.
A wooden stake fence, often associated with deer hunting.
A place of worship for Unitarians, a movement which does not believe in the Trinity but only in the Unity of Christ. Christ was to them just an exalted human teacher.
A three-storey RNAS control tower, incorporating meteorological office on the ground floor and an air watch office on the second floor.

Feature, typically a ship, boat, aircraft or vehicle, deliberately sunk for recreational and diver educational purposes in inland bodies of water used as dive centres, such as lakes and water-filled quarries, or offshore as artificial reefs.
An establishment where patients can rest and recover after an operation or illness.
A building or buildings used for the manufacture of candles.
A large wooden gate, positioned at either end of a canal or river lock, equipped with sluices to let water through.
A point in a village providing water for drinking and washing.
A small circular enclosure defined by a turf or earthern bank.
A circular kiln or oven used in the manufacture of bricks. Common in Staffordshire in the 18th century.
A kiln or furnace for the firing of bricks.
A kiln principally used in brick making which gives a continuous operation.
Usually a rural hospital with up to 25 beds. Can include small pre-Cranleigh institutions, eg: dispensaries with in-patients.
Usually a rural hospital with up to 25 beds. Can include small pre-Cranleigh institutions, eg: dispensaries with in-patients.
Detached block comprising one or more storeys of wards.
A school where Jewish children are educated.

A rectangular chamber of brick or stone with heavy wooden gates at either end equipped with sluices to let water in and out, thereby enabling a canal boat to be lowered or raised to a different level.
A stone-lined pit in which seaweed was burnt. The calcined ashes were used in the manufacture of soap and glass, amongst other things.
A structure used for the lifting of boats and other water craft.
A mill used for the production of cardboard and other similar products.
A system of trenches dug by troops for practice purposes.
A place of worship for followers of the Methodist New Connexion, a movement founded in 1791 when Alexander Kilham led the first group to split from the Methodists.
A functioning clock designed to serve also as an ornamental feature or sculpture.
A clock with special mechanisms and dials to display astonomical information.
A site where iron oxide and iron sulphate is extracted.
A covered passageway projecting into or across a ditch of a fortified place to provide flanking fire to the ditch in which it stands or for the purpose of sheltering communication with outworks.
A trench, usually linking two or more rows of trenches, enabling the conveyance of messages or equipment safely from one trench to another.
A cairn erected to mark a particular spot in the landscape. Can be used for various reasons.
Starshaped cairn with three radial arms of equal length, a monument unique to upland Northumberland. (Late Neolithic or early Bronze Age).
A post or pillar set up alongside a road to mark the miles from or to a place.
A post set up alongside a canal to mark the miles to and from a place.

A building used by the society, fraternity or order organized under this name with initiatory rites, mystic signs of recognition and various degrees of dignity or honour, for social or benevolent purposes.
A factory or complex where chamois leather is produced using fish oils as the tanning agent.
A factory manufacturing insulation material for electrical cables.
When secondary product use with major product and MINE, eg. COPPER MINE.
A building in which pack animals could shelter.
A reinforced concrete structure, often sited underground, used as a shelter from the threat of nuclear attack.
A space in a Buddist building that is used for teaching Dharma/Dhamma - the teachings of Buddha.
An establishment for the testing of eyesight, making up of optical prescriptions and the sale of spectacles.
The office or headquarters of a local police force, or of a police district.
An area of land, with associated buildings and targets, used for practicing the dropping of bombs and other aspects of air warfare.
Any structure or object, used for the purpose of practice bombing.
A grouping of retail warehouses and supermarkets with associated car parking.
Site or building constructed or adapted for indoor and/or outdoor leisure and sport activities, for example archery, team-building and "outward-bound" activities based on military training.
A building or site used for the production of anchors.
A factory where seaplanes are manufactured.
A circle of spaced upright boulders emerging from a low, hemispherical, stony mound. The boulders may lean outwards due to pressure from the cairn material.
A balance engine used to replenish the water levels of a river by transferring water from a reservoir or other supply.
An often light and airy garden building in the Moorish style used for recreational purposes.
A wall containing apertures to allow a weapon to be fired through it.
Site for the disposal of unexploded ordnance, possibly attached to a bombing range.
A site where concrete and concrete products are manufactured from a mixture of cement and aggregate.
Residues from ore-processing operations; intact tips and deposits may preserve considerable evidence on the processes used. A high rpoportion have been destroyed by reprocessing.
A coastal battery designed for use in short range engagements with enemy vessels, minelayers, blockships ad torpedo craft.
A channel carrying overflow water past a dam. Early 19th century onwards.
A school in which instruction is given on a Sunday, especially such a school for children connected with a parish or congregation.

A prefabricated structure of cellular hollow plywood 'aero' beams and columns clad with timber framed units of flat asbestos facing sheets and a felt roof. Designed as airfield accommodation that could be reused as post WWII emergency housing.
An area of arable land with common rights after harvest or while fallow. Usually without internal divisions (hedges, walls or fences).
A building where an officer of a county, district or municipality acting as a representative of the Crown holds inquests, including deaths through violence or accident and treasure trove.
A furnace for the manufacture of glass. Includes glass cones, open hearth and oil-fired furnaces.
A furnace for the calcining and roasting of a mixture of sand and fluxes as a preparatory stage in glass-making.

Land which has been temporarily taken over for use by the military or civilian authorities. During wartime land was requisitioned for various purposes, such as for argriculture or for military training/events etc.

The first transportable aircraft hangar developed by the RFC/RAF, which comprised a kit of timber and canvas that could be assembled in 48 hours. The canvas doors open one end only. Also known as Type H hangar.
A turbine driven by gas flow or the gas from combustion.
A rotary prime mover. Turbines may be steam, water or gas operated.
A motor in which rotary motion is produced by steam power.
A large, luxuriously appointed building used as an official residence by a member of royalty.
A camp used to accommodate members of the Womens Land Army who undertook essential agricultural work during the Second World War.
A distinctive, clerestory-roofed building of five 10ft bays, used for the drying, storage and packing of military parachutes and built to Air Ministry drawing number 17865/39.
The residence of a prison governor.
Specialist hospital treating patients with physical disabilities.
A structure found on lighthouses, piers, etc, capable of emitting a loud noise to warn shipping in foggy weather.
A medicinal or mineral spring often with an associated building.
A way, path or road through a cutting.
Any church of the Anglican Communion.
A stone-faced enclosure, with entrance closed by a floatable caisson or by gates, which can be pumped dry for inspection, maintenance, or repair of the hull or underwater fittings of a ship or ships.
A hangar used for the storage of barrage balloons.
A pier where passsengers can embark and disembark and goods can be transferred to and from vessels.
A hut used by a person who makes items from wood. Often found in a woodland setting.
A semi-permanent ahed designed to Air Ministry specification 1136/27 as a quick and cheap hangar for stations overseas
An inscribed marker stone found on Hadrian's Wall.
A stone commemorating the date of a specific event.
A stone commemorating a person or event.
A commemorative stone inscribed with a dedicatory inscription to a person or event.
A kiln with a pyramid roof and capped vent in which barley is dried. Found on the site of a malt house.
A building used to coordinate movement of railway engines and rolling stock in the event of war.
A building used to house calves.
Bank to let deer cross ditches, fences or roads, into, but not out of, a deer park.
A manmade chamber cut into a rockface.
A place for keeping vestments and sacred vessels.
A factory where putty, used as a means of securing windows and for setting plumbing fixtures, is produced from a combination of whiting and oil.
A place where tobacco is made into cigarettes, cigars, etc.
A house or centre used for meditation, contemplation and/or prayer.
A place where the homeless are accommodated, permanently or temporarily.
A residence of two or three monks of the Gilbertine order dependent on an English mother house.
A mutiple role hangar for aircraft and general storage, manufactured in the USA as a kit for on-site assembly during WWII and post-war. It comprises a steel box frame and a canvas covering.
An industrial manufacturing complex producing bricks.
A building containing pans in which salt water or brine was boiled to produce salt.
A metal pillar with a flashable lamp on top containing an emergency telephone for use by members of the public and by officers of the local police force.
A mill used to dress ore by means of a jigging machine.
A kiln for drying hops in a brewery or maltings complex, as distinct from the OASTHOUSES found on farms.
A court of summary jurisdiction established, following legislation, in 1908 for the trial of offenders below the age of legal reponsibility.
A strong, fortified dwelling, of between two and four storeys. Occupied only in times of trouble built mainly in the border country of the North from the mid 14th to the 17th century.
A factory manufacturing personal hygiene and beauty products
A road/carriage way giving access from the main road to the house, stables.
A deep gutter, drain or sink.
Artificial water channel, usually leading to a mill.
A channel or pipe providing water to a canal or other body of water.
An artificial watercourse for the conveyance of water.
A reinforced wall designed to reflect the blast from an explosion. Often found associated with powder magazines, pillboxes and air raid shelters.
A defensive construction situated in the sea, designed to protect the land from seabourne attack. The term applies mainly to those monuments built from around 1860 onwards.
A place where perfume is sold, as well as manufactured.
A monument consisting of parallel banks, normally accompanied by ditches, which appears to mark out an approach to another monument or monuments.

A prefabricated structure of a steel frame clad in corrugated iron. Semi-circular in section they were used as accommodation for the armed forces and, during WWII, as emergency housing for bombed out civilians. Also used for storage.
A site used for the manufacture of lasts, shoemaker's models of the foot for shaping and repairing footwear. Lasts can be from a variety of materials, such as wood or iron.
A building or site where boat sails are manufactured from processed cloth.

An establishment used for the manufacture of reeds and healds, which are components of a textile loom with related functions, in that they move and control the threads, and similar wire-based construction.
An establishment where the theory and practice of medicine is taught.
A path running by the side of a canal or navigable river for use in towing vessels.
A dock with gates which open for access for some hours before and after high water.
An engineering works that produces machinery specially for use in shoe making.
A medieval hospital for lepers, usually consisting of a church and individual shelters for the lepers.
A large tank where particles suspended in water, or other liquids, are allowed to sink to the bottom forming a sediment.
Debris derived from the demolition of buildings or other structures. If unsure of whether debris is resulting from construction or demolition, index with both terms.
A place, often including a BAKERY, where sweetmeats and pastries are sold.
A subterranean feature entered from a hillside, cliff face, etc. A cave may have been used for occupation, storage, burial, refuse, or as a hide-away. Index with site type or objects where known.

Rectangular slabs of concrete with a sloping top usually with sides of 5 feet by 3 feet and 3 feet high which when placed in rows were intended to form a substantial barrier to enemy armoured divisions in the event of invasion.
A chapel for followers of Benjamin Ingham after he left the Moravians prior to joining the Sandamanians.
A place where metal knives and edge cutting tools were manufactured.

A building with a range of facilities for the exclusive use of its all-male membership. Rooms were often provided as offices or short term accommodation, and the club could be used for business or social gatherings.
A path in a garden.
The residence and small-scale workshop of a hosier.
A specialist hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of ear disorders and diseases.
A site where a periodical gathering of buyers, sellers and entertainers, meet at a time ordained by charter or statute or by ancient custom.
General term describing any defence work where no more specific term is applicable.
A walkway on the top of a defensive wall, providing access to the parapets and towers.
A civilian settlement outside a Roman fort.
A closely mown lawn used for the game of croquet.

A prefabricated structure consisting of six curved asbestos cement sheets that were bolted together, without a frame, creating a hut semi-circular in section. Used on airfields during WWII and manufactured from 1942 by the Turner Asbestos Company.
An instrument for measuring magnetic forces, especially the strength of terrestrial magnetism.
A place of worship for members of the United Methodists Church, a group formed in 1907 by the amalgamation of the United Methodist Free Church, the Methodist New Connection and the Bible Christians.
A mill or factory in which raw cotton, wool, nylon or other material is spun into yarn or thread.
An alignment of posts or postholes of unknown function
A military base normally between 20 and 30 acres in size, containing legionary and auxiliary battle units, which served as stores depots and winter quarters during campaigns.
A factory complex consisting of PRINTING SHOPS, COLOUR HOUSES, DYE HOUSES, etc, in which patterns are printed onto calico.
A factory complex consisting of PRINTING SHOPS, COLOUR HOUSES, DYE HOUSES, etc, in which patterns are printed onto textiles.
A purpose-built trench used to test chemical warfare weapons.
Site or building used for paintballing.
A building, usually part of a textile mill complex, where warp yarn is sized prior to weaving. Sizing is the application of a starch solution to warp threads to add strength and protection.
A railway worked by the propulsive force of compressed air or by the formation of a vacuum.
A building or subterranean structure used for the storage of beer.
A residence of two or three monks of the Cistercian order dependent on a foreign mother house.
A road, sometimes raised as a causeway, which serves as an approach road to a building or bridge.
An earthen mound, usually within an ornamental garden, on which a tree was planted.
A signpost, usually placed at a juntion or crossroads, bearing a number of individual signs radiating outward from the post to indicate locations in several directions.
A post bearing one or more signs indicating the direction, and often the distance, to specified locations or routes.
6 DFW55373 projector emplacements spaced in a 3x2 rectangular gid, but each spaced 35m apart. No blast protection was provided at the shelters, which were placed between the projector emplacements.
A long, wooden, metal or stone vessel holding drinking water for horses.
The premises of a police officer for a parish or township who was appointed to act as a conservator of the peace within the district.
Platform, usually stone-built, which holds the winding gear of a mine shaft.
A fountain erected specifically to supply drinking water.
A group of related buildings, primarily with a domestic function, which is arranged along a principle axis such as a main road or routeway.
Shed for grinding rags, eg. for use in mungo and shoddy mills.

A calciner commonly used between 1870 and circa 1900 for extracting arsenic from mined ores and featuring a slightly inclined rotating iron tube with a firebox at the bottom and an ore feed at the top.
Water channel leading to water wheel.
A single line, or two or more roughly parallel lines, of standing stones set at intervals along a common axis or series of axes.
A port on the sea, rather than on river or estuary.
A hilltop enclosure bounded by a double line of ramparts.
A place of accommodation at a college for staff and students.
The residence of a coachman.
An artificial area of open water, situated on a river, enclosed by masonry and fitted with dock gates in which ships can be repaired, loaded/unloaded or berthed.
An area of ground which has been cleared of plants and other obstruction.
Emergency deceleration lane.
A water tank, often raised on stilts, used to supply water to steam trains.
A factory where general hardware, fittings, items of ironmongery are produced.
A depot used for the unloading of coal.
A bell mounted on an anchored vessel, buoy, headland, rock etc and rung as a warning to mariners in foggy weather.
Reinforced concrete blocks, walls or ditches designed to obstruct the progress of a tank or armoured vehicle.
An area of ground on which a house is built. A platform is often the sole surviving evidence for a house.
The residence of a piermaster.
A building or site used for the production of naphtha, a volatile petroleum-derived product used in the manufacture of solvents, cleaning fluids etc.
A pillbox built to a design drawn up by the chief engineer of GHQ home forces.
Building used for field studies and outdoor pursuits in the countryside and in an urban context.
A county judicial building where the Quarter Session and the Assizes for the County were held.
An area for the testing of guided missiles.
A place where trams are maintained and refitted, etc.
A building or room where items of pottery are manufactured. Includes handcrafted and machine made pottery.
A purpose built indoor cricket facility for training and playing matches
A place of law to which debtors were taken for the recovery of monies by their creditors.
A vessel, usually made of stone, which contains the consecrated water for baptism. Use a broader monument type if possible.
A cheap restaurant.
A building where ambulances are housed awaiting emergency calls.
A building or group of buildings in which communications signals, usually intercepted fro military purposes, are analysed.
An enclosure for the containment of a bull.
A path across a road marked with black and white stripes where pedestrians may cross.
A dock with gates which open for access for some hours before and after high water.
A room or building used for recording and broadcasting radio programmes.
A marker, of stone, wood or metal, used to delineate the limits of a stretch of highway, river or canal subject to a toll charge.
A site where large sheets of thin metal are manufactured.
A mark erected on or near danger or on shore as an aid to pilotage.

A room where surgical operations are performed. Originally in the form of a room with a raised table surrounded by tiered seating from where students could watch an operation or disection be performed.
A site used for the production of sodium bicarbonate, soda ash or caustic soda.

A building used as a social venue by people interested in, and involved with, the sport of rowing. An area of the building may be used for the storage of canoes, sculls etc. Often situated by a river.
A site including a pitch, stands and other ancillary buildings associated with the game of football.

A square pillbox with walls up to 48in thick, designed to emplace a 2 pounder anti-tank gun. A large opening in the back allowed the gun to be wheeled into position at the large embrasure in the front wall. Designed by DFW branch 3.
A building adjoining a cricket pitch with facilities for players and spectators.
A cross erected within a town, usually funded by the inhabitants.
A hospital for the care of patients with incurable illnesses.
A plant for bottling manufactured goods, as opposed to a BOTTLE WORKS where bottles were made.
A building or site where boat sails are manufactured from processed cloth.
A coastal battery constructed at short notice usually mounting a variety of artillery pieces.
A pillar housing a transformer to convert AC electricity supply, for use by electrified transport systems or for domestic purposes.
A factory for the manufacture of heels for the shoe making trade.
A council-owned single apartment.
A priory of double order of Fontevrault nuns and brethren.
A manor house, which was granted a royal licence to crenellate.
A coastal battery used for delivering fire at long distance thus forcing a warship threatening or bombarding shore installations to withdraw out of range.
A kiln used for the production of any of the soda group of alkalis by the heating of plant remains or salt.
A small, usually inexpensive, restaurant with a limited menu of light meals served at counters or tables.
An industrial manufacturing complex producing bricks.
A commercial premises supplying ships with provisions.
A shop housing the business of a grindery dealer. Grindery are the tools and materials used by shoemakers and other leather-workers.
A distinctive, clerestory-roofed building of three 10ft and two 12ft bays, used for the drying, storage and packing of military parachutes and built to Air Ministry drawing number 10825/42.
The dwelling and workshop of a framework knitter.
An educational building where examinations are held.
A long ridge of earth, rocks or gravel primarily constructed to carry a roadway.
A jettied house where the overhanging upper storey runs along the entire length of one side.
Temporary accommodation for war evacuees.

A tunnel built alongside a canal tunnel to enable a horse to be unhitched and led through the hillside to meet the barge when it emerged from the tunnel. Mainly built prior to the development of the towpath tunnel.
A depot used for the unloading of coal.
A supply of water used to keep canals that were vulnerable to water shortage topped up.
A large natural or artificial body of water, sometimes covered, used to collect and store water for a particular function, eg. industrial or public use.

A northern term for water reservoirs at steam powered industrial sites that are part of the steam raising plant and are used for recirculating condenser cooling water. The lodge had to be large enough to supply the condenser with cool water for a day.
A house or range of buildings in which dogs are kept, eg. hunting hounds.
Canal docks where the freeboard of a boat was marked. By placing increasing ton weights at 4 points around the boat, its displacement could be marked for toll purposes.
An artificial area of open water, situated on a canal, enclosed by masonry and fitted with dock gates in which ships can be repaired, loaded/unloaded or berthed.
A place where silicate rock was extracted to be shaped for use as whetstones. Examples can be found in Derbyshire and the Blackdown Hills in Devon.
A scientific laboratory where marine life is studied and researched.
A jettied house where the upper storey only overhangs the end elevation of the building.
A complex of buildings used for the manufacture of radio valves or similar electronic components.
A large board, often attached to the side of a building, on which advertisements can be displayed. Use for external structures only.
A barn in which a pair of curved timbers form a bowed A-frame which supports the roof independently of the walls.
A building or room used for the repair and maintenance of machinery in a large complex, such as a hospital, school or factory.
A closely mown piece of ground used for the game of lawn bowling.
A structure used for the roasting or drying of chicory.
A pit containing burnt ashes.
An establishment where deaf people receive education, training and social support.
A specialist hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of fistular and rectal disorders and diseases.
skos:Concept.skos:prefLabel: Hospital For Fistula And Rectal Diseases

skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: A specially marked ground used by children for the game of hopscotch.
A factory manufacturing fireplaces.

A concrete structure, based on drawing number (11008/41), intended to be the headquarters for the coordination of an airfield's defences. Constructed partially underground it was considered less vulnerable than the (3329/41).
A site where petroleum is drawn.
A specialist hospital where water treatment is given to patients suffering from muscular-skeletal complaints, etc.
A flour mill using both stones and rollers to produce flour and, perhaps mainly from the stones, animal feed from grains other than wheat.
Traditionally a dock where cambering, the bending of beams for shipbuilding, took place. Now used for a small dock.
A double-span aircraft hangar designed by Boulton & Paul of London and Norwich. Mainly used on aircraft factory sites and at Armament Training Schools.
A place where products are manufactured from wood.
A plate, usually of wood or metal, used to indicate the limit of an area or piece of land.
A factory where fish are processed into food products.
A building used to dry flax.
Former terrestrial landscape of any kind now submerged through erosion, as at Dunwich, or historical inundation processes, eg. post-glacial submersion of the North Sea landscape ("Doggerland").
A forest killed by rising sea-level. Nowadays only tree stumps survive.
A works, including an extractive site, producing a clay of high plasticity and firmness, used as a basic raw material for porcelain.
A building where merchandise and goods are temporarily stored before or after transportation by rail.
A circle made out of stones, which is used for making wheels.
Factory where yarn is made from paper.
A building containing machinery for the spinning of yarn.
A flatbed lorry with a concrete defensive position fitted on the back enabling the "pillbox" to be driven to where it was most needed in the event of an airborne force landing on the airfield.
A building in which wrought iron or steel chains were manufactured.

A metal, wooden or concrete box containing a telephone for use by the public, limited accommodation for use as a temporary cell, and a lamp on top that could be used to attract the attention of a passing patrol.
A fortified building or site with purpose built emplacements for artillery pieces.
A building licensed for the sale of beer.
An establishment used for the custody of money received from, or on behalf, of its customers.
A bank which specializes in accepting savings deposits. Originally established to help the poor.
A site or building used for the manufacture of goods made from pewter, an alloy of tin and lead.
An open area, often paved or cobbled, surrounded by privately owned buildings and inaccessible to the public.
A structure for adding coal to railway locomotives usually by gravity from a higher level.
Place where tanned leather is dressed and coloured.
A large warehouse or store for upholstery.
A castle erected without permission, ie. without a royal licence to crenellate.
A garden surrounded by a substantial wall.
A large kitchen garden enclosed by a substantial wall, not usually adjacent to its associated house.
Covered area for making large engineered constructions such as sections of ships or bridges.

A curved dam usually built of concrete and designed with the curve upstream so that the force of the water compresses the structure and strengthens it as it pushes it into its foundations. Arch dams are best suited to narrow gorges
A steam-powered machine used for raising ore or water from a mine.
A residential home for adults with learning difficulties and/or physical disabilities.
An artificially raised level of ground.
A site where large sheets of thin metal are manufactured.
A wall in a flower or kitchen garden, containing conduits or pipes for heating the wall.
A bridge carrying a tramway.
A basement or cellar, usually within a house, leased as a separate dwelling.
A factory or building where furniture is upholstered.
A specialist hospital for the medical treatment of skin diseases.
A specialist hospital where women receive medical and surgical treatment.
A pit dug into the ground or a simple construction made of stone, brick or metal. Designed to contain a fire and prevent it from spreading, but can also be used to heat stone for breaking.
A small workshop, employing up to 10 men, working on hand-operated carding engines and hand jennies, spinning yarn for handloom weavers.
An apparatus around which cables or hawsers are wound for hoisting anchors, lifting weights, etc.
A transportable hangar designed by A & J Main of Glasgow.
A group of buildings and machines, usually situated close to the pithead, enabling the rapid, mechanized loading of goods wagons with coal.

A small underground chamber from where it was intended to monitor radioactive fallout in the event of nuclear attack. The majority were built between 1956 and 1964, although construction continued into the early 1970s.
An establishment where books, periodicals, music, etc, are produced from original manuscripts and distributed to booksellers, dealers and the public.
Seaside structure, usually consisting of a manmade retaining wall that keeps a relatively large area of the tidal water partitioned off for controlled boating or swimming.
A commercial building, or buildings, used for the production of soft drinks.

A stone wall, often of considerable length, built to divide an area of land. Most occur as part of extensive walled field systems. This is a regional term specific to Dartmoor and should not be used in other parts of the country.
A stall, often within a cow house, where cattle are kept individually.
A stall where animals are kept individually.
A building or building complex where municipal offices and other public buildings are situated.
A site used for the production of anaesthetic gas.
A crane suspended from running rails in the roof of an engineering workshop or similar establishment.
A structure used for execution by hanging. Usually two uprights and a cross-piece, from which the offender is suspended by the neck.
A place where hops are stored.
An outdoor meeting place.
A straight road lined with trees along either side, also straight lines of trees found in parkland usually leading to a landscape feature.
A building used for a variety of administrative purposes, usually at a naval dockyard.
A channel which feeds water from a reservoir into a canal when the water level gets low.
A purpose-built, or modified, building where organizations and associations meet for presentations and consultation.
A mill used for the mechanized processing of silk.
An engineering works producing items for the railway other than rolling stock, such as signals, tracks, points, etc.
A point where water issues naturally from the rock or soil onto the ground or into a body of surface water.
Artificial water channel, usually leading to a mill.
A lightweight prefabricated structure of corrugated galvanized steel having a semicircular cross section. The design was based on the Nissen hut developed by the British during the First World War.
A site used by a carrier to accommodate his horses and vehicles and store goods awaiting transportation, etc.
A place of worship for the followers of Jainism
The residence of a clothier.
An outbuilding containing brewing equipment, as opposed to a large commercial BREWERY. Often found in conjunction with public houses, country houses etc.
A factory where preserved food is canned.
A building used for the preparation of animal skins and hides prior to the tanning process.
A mill which is powered by a turbine.
A bishop's court for ecclesiastical causes and offences, formerly having wider jurisdiction in matters of moral discipline.
A bridge, usually resting on raised arches, carrying a railway across low-lying land or water.
A sculptured likeness, portrait or image, often found on a tomb or other memorial.
A military camp providing training facilities.
A section of roadway attached at one end to a harbour or dockside and ending at a landing stage, rising and falling with the tide, for the loading and unloading of vehicles and pedestrians.
A small dwelling providing living accommodation for a tin miner.
A group of buildings containing machinery for the production in bulk of butter or related dairy products.
A building or site where lead is obtained from ore.
A castle built on a simple, rectangular plan, usually with a tower at each corner. This design became common in England after 1300.
A tower at the mouth of the harbour to defend the end of the harbour boom.
A waterwheel where water enters below the axle but above the bottom of the wheel.
A form of inhumation in which the skeleton is interred, usually on its side, with hip and knee joints bent through an angle of less than 90 degrees.
A processing house where surplus water is removed from gunpowder after incorporating.
A building or site used to produce alkaline chemicals by controlled reactions.
A small dye works, often associated with a CALICO PRINTING WORKS.
Oven for roasting coal to drive off chemical constituents and reduce it to almost pure carbon, ie. coke.
A rescue station serving a number of mines in the immediate area.
Grounds, usually associated with a country house, laid out so as to produce the effect of natural scenery.
A specialist hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of eye and ear disorders and diseases.
Machine, frequently horse powered, for mixing raw clay into brick earth.
A piece of land, sometimes man-made, completely surrounded by water.
A small island, especially within a river.
A form of inhumation in which the skeleton is interred, usually on its side, with the knees brought up against the chest. This is a more extreme form of crouched inhumation.
A pit for the extraction of fullers earth (a hydrous silicate of alumina), which was used for cleansing, and finishing, cloth and wool.

A type of aircraft hangar from the closing years of WWI either of steel or wood utilising a type of lattice work roof support known as a Belfast Truss, which features diagonally interlaced pieces of thin pine. The roof appears as a smooth curve.
A building for the storage, repair and maintenance of chains for lighthouses, lightships and lightbouys.
A residence of two or three monks of the Benedictine order dependent on a foreign mother house.
A large room within a hospital set aside for emergency patients.
A platform, sometimes floating, for the landing of passengers and goods from vessels.
A terrace, balcony or room exposed to the rays of the sun which were thought to be beneficial to recovering from an illness.
A place where furs are made into finished products.
A pit dug in the prospect of finding valuable minerals, coal, metal ores, etc, beneath the ground surface.
A building or site used for the storage and distribution of food.
A large, manmade pool, usually lined with tiles, rubber or similar. Can be placed in the open air, eg. a LIDO, or built as part of a covered sports centre.

An enclosed feature, usually sub-terranean, constructed to contain water for public or private recreation and sporting activities. Often part of a larger SPORTS CENTRE. Use OUTDOOR SWIMMING POOL for unenclosed pools.

A prefabricated structure of reinforced concrete posts and beams with infillings of pre stressed concrete planks and felted slabs. Initially used for military barracks in WWII and later for civilian housing. Manufactured by the Orlit Company.
A prominent structure situated on land specifically as a guide to navigation for travellers or as an aid/warning to sailors out at sea.
A pit dug for the extraction of brine.
A place of worship for Protestant followers of Hussite doctrines which accept the Bible as the only source of faith.
A building used for drilling out the bores of cannon and other military pieces.
A building containing a machine tool for boring out large cylindrical holes in items such as steam engine cylinders, pump barrels, etc.
A stone circle featuring a stone which lies lengthways between two of the upright standing stones.
A fighter satellite station watch office built to Air Ministry design drawing number 17658/40.
Any wall enclosing a building or complex of buildings, eg. prisons, dockyards, factories, etc.
A building housing the brakes for an incline railway or tramway.
A tall, tapering pillar with a pyramidal top, generally square on plan. Used in England from the late 16th century as a public, funerary or garden monument.
The residence and small-scale workshop of a hosier.
A building in which coal slurry, produced in the coal washing process, is recovered.

Court where sessions were held periodically in each county in England, for the purpose of administering civil and criminal justice. Presided over by itinerant judges acting under certain special commissions. Abolished 1971 and in 1972 replaced by Crown C.
A strong, fortified dwelling, of between two and four storeys. Occupied only in times of trouble built mainly in the border country of the North from the mid 14th to the 17th century.
A plot of earth used for the raising of plants.
A heavy framework of parallel beams used to support a ship in dock.
A steam powered winding gear used at a colliery or other mine.
