A building used to accommodate hippopotami.
Mechanism for turning around vehicles in a confined space.
A row of balusters, usually made of stone, surmounted by a rail or coping.
An 18th century garden building, designed in the form of a classical Doric temple, used for standing or sitting in.
A jettied house where the upper storey only overhangs the end elevation of the building.
Recovery and removal of grease (lanolin) from raw wool.
A building used for the accommodation of sick and wounded members of the armed forces.
Small mobile steam engine.
One of 12 roadside crosses erected by Edward I in memory of his wife, Eleanor of Castile, the most famous being Charing Cross in London.
A building used for drilling out the bores of cannon and other military pieces.
A building containing a machine tool for boring out large cylindrical holes in items such as steam engine cylinders, pump barrels, etc.
A mill in which textile rags were ground, either to enable the fibres to be respun or to use the pulp in the manufacture of paper.
An area within a hospital where children are accommodated during the period of their medical or surgical treatment.
A place where the homeless are accommodated, permanently or temporarily.
A bridge with two or more decks allowing it to carry various modes of transport at the same time.
An elevated table or podium on which to place or sacrifice offerings to the deities.
A shaft cut to facilitate the extraction of salt from halite deposits by pumping water into the deposit and pumping out brine from which the salt is later extracted.
A building or site used for the manufacture of whiting either from crushed chalk, limestone, marble or through chemical preparation.
A dispersed farmstead where buildings are arranged around scattered yards which can be loose or regular in their form.
A residence of two or three monks of the Cistercian order dependent on an English mother house.
A site including a pitch, stands and other ancillary buildings associated with the game of rugby.
A mixed house of Augustinian nuns, canonesses and canons.
A workshop in which saggars - fire clay boxes to protect ware from direct action of flame and gases during firing - were manufactured.
A coastal site producing salt by boiling of unconcentrated seawater in a PANHOUSE, normally using coal fuel. Foreshore BRINE TANKS may also be present

Based on the previous all-timber design 2423/39 and the temporary brick and timber design 518/40, the 8936/40 was built with pre-cast concrete slabs replacing the timber floors and staircases with only the balcony and watch office roof in timber.
A type of malt house.
A small circular enclosure defined by a turf or earthern bank.

Traditionally a building or site where stage coaches were built. Nowadays the term is applied to buildings used for the manufacturing of the body work and furnishings of motor vehicles and railway carriages.
A pit from which marl, a mixture of clay and carbonate of lime, is excavated. Marl is used as a fertilizer.
A bowl-shaped cavity or depression created in the subsoil by the long term presence and growth of tree roots or when a large tree is blown over or has its stump pulled out.
A mill or factory in which raw cotton, wool, nylon or other material is spun into yarn or thread.
A building used for the storage of rope made from the fibrous stems of the hemp plant.
A garden consisting primarily of rocks and rock plants.
A cemetery containing more than one burial type eg cremations and inhumations.
An area of ground belonging to a church, often used as a burial ground.
A mine in which access is gained by a straight entrance driven on a constant downward slope. Use with product(s) extracted and MINE where known, eg. COAL MINE.
A man-made passageway, which is built through a sea- or riverbed.
A building used for housing, and protecting from the weather, carts, waggons and farm implements, often open-fronted.
A channel which carried processed alum as liquid from the alum quarry/works to the alum house
A building used for the crystallization process in alum making.
A large tank used for soaking alumina-bearing shale in water and chemicals, the initial stage in the alum-making process.
A group of buildings or works where the evaporation and crystallization of sodium aluminium sulphate solution is performed.
A factory where brushes are manufactured. Use for all types of brush.
A site where iron or steel bolts, and often their accompanying nuts, are manufactured. Sometimes referred to as NUT AND BOLT WORKS.
A watertight reservoir or tank that receives sewage, and by sedimentation and bacterial action effects a process of partial purification.
A site where copper or copper based alloys are produced by smelting copper ore.
Building or buildings used for the production of Gas Masks. Consider double-indexing with the term WAR PRODUCTION FACTORY if appropriate.
A place providing social, recreational, and educational facilities for a neighbourhood.
A place where ropes are made.
A site or building used for processing shale. Shale can be fashioned into goods or, if bituminous, distilled to produce oil, naphtha or tar.
A building equipped with instruments and a flight simulator used to teach members of bomber crews how to correctly identify targets for bombing.
Block for the treatment of separate diseases.
Any military base where the depot battalion of a regiment is based. Depot battalions maintain the stores and records of a regiment and train new recruits.
A storehouse in 16th and 17th century houses.
Range used by the Navy with reinforced observation huts which housed quadrant equipment to record accuracy and damage.
A house or centre used for meditation, contemplation and/or prayer.
A building where reptiles are accommodated at a zoo or wildlife park.
A bridge, carrying a footpath or road, usually across marshy or waterlogged ground.
A glass-house or hot-house constructed for the cultivation of a grapevine.

A decorative emblem stating the name of a village or town and depicting aspects of the place's history of culture. Most signs are mounted on a post and usually errected in a central position near the church or village green.

A two-storey, all-concrete construction with a watch office and additional rooms given over to the meteorological section, including a forecast room and met store. A concrete parapet all around the roof differentiates it from 5845/39.
A building or buildings where soap is manufactured.
Central functional building of a gas works. Coal is roasted in retorts producing gas and coke.
Permanently moored historic maritime craft preserved and converted into a museum and open to the public.
A group of cairns occurring within close proximity to each other. Use for instances where the majority are clearance cairns. Also index specific types where known.
A coastal site producing salt by solar evaporation of seawater in a series of PONDS, without any boiling stage
Triangular concrete pyramids with 6 feet long sides and 5 feet high, intended to impede enemy movement in the event of invasion. Thought to be confined geogaphically to Southern Command.
Buildings and sites associated with the manufacture of cotton.
A stopping place on an underground railway system where passengers can board and disembark from a train.
A place where railway trains regularly stop for taking up and setting down passengers or for receiving goods for transport.
A building or site used for the storage and distribution of fuel.
A storage rack for sections of steel plate used in the construction of ships.
A levelled area of ground on which a barn is built. A platform is often the sole surviving evidence for a barn.
A factory principally engaged in the manufacture of the propellant explosive cordite.
A hospital where more 'natural' means of treatment are used rather than conventional methods.
The residence of a coastguard.
An establishment where beauty treatments and associated therapies are provided by professional practitioners.
A group of buildings and satellite dishes used to transmit and receive signals relayed by satellites.
An apparatus around which cables or hawsers are wound for hoisting anchors, lifting weights, etc.
A building adjacent to a monastery where alms were distributed to the poor.
The residence of a piermaster.

Originally an area planted with evergreens or winter-flowering plants for winter display, they can also be large glasshouses built for public entertainment where the original purpose of displaying plants has either disappeared or been minimalised.
A small, single storey building used as the Pilots' room on fighter stations and as the watch office on bomber stations.
A place where pheasants are reared and kept.
A works or factory where nitroglycerine is manufactured.
A small, single storey building used as the Pilots' room on fighter stations and as the watch office on bomber stations.
A mine yielding rock salt.
A site, in which salt is obtained by boiling and evaporating salt brine or seawater in large pans. Often the only surviving evidence are the mounds formed from the waste produced by the process.
A small eating and drinking establishment or refreshment bar at a railway station for the use of passengers.

A type of prefabricated house erected, to 11 approved designs, as part of the Temporary Housing Programme, between 1944 and 1948. This scheme was devised to relieve the post-war housing shortage at a time when conventional materials were unavailable.
Accommodation and facilities for aircrew away from the main RAF airfield.
A structure, usually well concealed, used to store explosives intended for use by the Auxiliary Units (or British Resistance Organization) in the event of an invasion.
A calciner dating from the early 17th to early 20th centuries, usually made of brick and without moving parts, consisting of a reverberatory furnace, and used for the extraction of arsenic.
A running track used for athletic practice and competition.
A path covered in a layer of water-worn or pounded stones.
A mill for the removal by mechanical means of the dried wood and seeds of the flax and cotton plants after retting. The resulting 'tow' is then spun into linen and cotton respectively.
A purpose-built dwelling for the supervisor of a factory, mine or other industrial complex.
A matzevah from the Ashkenazi group of Jews descended from medieval Jewish communities of the Rhineland and Eastern Europe. Characterised by upright headstones with Hebrew Inscriptions
Finishing process for cloth, especially linen, running the cloth between heavy rollers.
A house by a toll gate or toll bridge where tolls are collected.
A site used for the production of dyes from controlled chemical reactions. In use from the mid 19th century onwards.
A site used for the production of dyes from natural ingredients.
A building used for the administration of a squadron.
An administrative building used to organize and co-ordinate the activities of members of the armed forces.
A site or factory where waste slag from ironworking if further processed for use in manufacturing.
A long bed planted with perennial flowers and plants.
A place where gardening tools, plants, etc, are sold.
An enclosed observation tower, usually made of brick or concrete and raised on four legs, associated with WW2 bombing ranges.
A building in which photographers, taken for aerial reconnaissance purposes, are analysed and interpreted to provide intelligence on enemy activities.
Non-specific building type associated with an airfield.
A building or site used to produce alkaline chemicals by controlled reactions.
A shop selling ironmonger's goods, household tools and utensils.
A factory or works which has been temporarily turned over to the manufacture of goods for the war effort.
An existing factory that was converted for use as aircraft works in the run up to or during the Second World War.
A building where people could bathe in salt water. Salt water was believed to have medicinal properties.
An open area of water, usually artificial and enclosed by dock gates or locks, lined with wharves, warehouses and berths to enable vessels to load and unload.
The residence of a coachman.
A place where processed cloth is cut for use as garments or soft furnishings, etc.
A transportable hangar designed by A & J Main of Glasgow.
An area within a hospital concerned with the care and medical treatment of expectant mothers.
An ancilliary building within a larger works, as distinct from a SMELT MILL.
A stone, usually found in a schoolyard, either built into a wall or forming part of a free standing structure, on which pencils can be sharpened. Although increasingly rare examples do survive.
A structure, often concrete or brick, used as a shelter by members of the British citizen army during watch or patrol duties, or air raids, in wartime.
An area of land and associated buildings where vines are cultivated. The grapes produced are then used to make wine.
A place where tree trunks were sawn into planks by hand.
A HORSE GIN used for domestic cider manufacture, especially on farms.
The field or area of ground on which a battle or skirmish was fought.

Area or zone of sea where a battle, skirmish or action was fought between naval ships or warships and privateers. Not to be used for enemy action upon mercantile ships or a sudden strike by mine/torpedo against an enemy warship.
A factory for the manufacture of heels for the shoe making trade.
A structure used for the storage of coal.
A public building where regular dances were held.
Pit for mixing raw materials with water in the preparation of a clay body.
A building where artefacts, scientific specimens, antiquities and similar objects of interest could be examined through microscopes by members of the public.
A room in which a judge sits to hear cases and undertake other official proceedings which are not of a sufficient importance to be brought into court.
A garden in which bees are kept.
A furnace used for the refining of precious metals. eg. the separation of silver from argentiferous lead.
A multi-purpose farm building in an outlaying area of a farm.
A factory where pianos are manufactured.
Cluster of dwellings of medieval or later date (Scots)
A channel which carried processed alum as liquid from the alum quarry/works to the alum house
A group of buildings or works where the evaporation and crystallization of sodium aluminium sulphate solution is performed.
A building housing an engine, usually with an attendant boiler house and chimney. Used for winding from a pit.
A garden specifically planted with sweet smelling, fragrant plants.
A kiln with a pyramid roof and capped vent in which barley is dried. Found on the site of a malt house.
A mill where flax fibres were woven into linen cloth.
A hilltop enclosure bounded by a single rampart, usually accompanied by a ditch.
For reheating of worked metal or glass to make it malleable or to harden it after use for toolmaking, etc.
A small building built over the end of a water conduit or spring.
The area of water retained above a mill dam for driving a mill.
A section of road that provides a passage beneath another road or railway.
A factory or complex of buildings where creosote oil is produced. Creosote oil is distilled from coal tar and used as a wood preservative.
Underground chambers and stone passages of Iron Age date found in South West England.
A place where specific skills are taught on short courses.
A stone used to instruct a coachman to unhitch a horse, previously taken on to help pull the coach up a steep gradient.
A building or room used for the practice and study of dance.
An alloy of tin, antimony and copper used as a replacement for pewter.
A loft over a stable or barn used for storing hay.
A structure which allows aircraft fitted with radar equipment to 'home' in on an airfield in the dark or in poor visibility, and land safely. Radar beacons can also be used as navigation aids.
A site or structure on which a signal, especially a fire, could be placed as a warning or means of communication. Use for beacon sites or surviving beacon structures.
A foreshore structure to prevent barges from sinking in the river mud. Made by placing chalk on fascines of brushwood, which is in some cases retained by a timber revetement.
A crane for lowering loaded coal waggons onto a ship.
A decorative garden, often landscaped, laid out with intricate flower beds and hedges, and often containing ornate sculptures, fountains and garden ornaments.
A specialist hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of ear, nose and throat disorders and diseases.
A house used to accommodate camels, often found at a zoo or wildlife park.
A hearth used for the reheating of metal slag to extract further metal.
A working hospital, often near or associated with a university, where doctors and nurses are trained.
A building or group of buildings situated close to the sea used by coastguards to enable them to monitor the coastline.
An establishment where chocolate was available as a beverage.
Hillslope forts with wide spaced ramparts.
A workshop or factory where bronze articles are made by casting molten metal into moulds.
The residence of a storekeeper of naval ordnance.
A group of trees planted as part of a designed landscape.
A place where the science of historical and comparative language is taught.
An outlying farm or estate belonging to the Order of Tiron.
A medieval high status farmstead, acting as the centre of the estate, directly controlled by the lord and used for the benefit of his household and dependents.
A cairn featuring a mound of small diameter (normally less than 6m), which is surrounded by a kerb of stones which are considerably taller than the mound.
A cultivated plantation of watercress, usually situated near springs or small running streams.
Covered area for making large engineered constructions such as sections of ships or bridges.
A place of worship for Calvinistic Methodists, Welsh Methodists who split from the established church in 1811.
A building used for the accommodation of a military guard and/or the detainment of prisoners.
An inlet in the banks of a navigable river, often lined with brick and gated, into which boats can be drawn for repair etc.
The place where a house stood or had once stood, often adjoining a garth or croft.
A complex of buildings and earthworks constructed for the storage of bombs and pyrotechnics.
A temporary airfield in use during the build-up to D-Day. They consisted of a natural earth or grass surface reinforced with wire mesh.
A wall between two towers or pavilions, usually surrounding a building, and often forming a major part of the defences.
A mobile piece of equipment used by the Royal Observer Corps to track the movements of enemy aircraft.
A site where jet is extracted from the surface of the ground.
A garden incorporating Egyptian architectural features such as sphinxes and tomb-like features, etc.
Residence of a leading land-holding family within the district.

Traditionally a building or site where stage coaches were built. Nowadays the term is applied to buildings used for the manufacturing of the body work and furnishings of motor vehicles and railway carriages.
A pillbox which varies from standard designs.
A site occupied by people who have no legal right to the land or buildings on it.
A medicinal or mineral spring often with an associated building.
A farm building in which cattle are housed before slaughter.
A concrete, cylindrical pedestal on which a spigot mortar was mounted. The pedestal is often the only evidence for a Spigot Mortar emplacement to survive.
An official residence of an abbot during the summer months.
A building or subterranean structure used for the storage of wine.
A lime kiln built into a low hillside or slope to facilitate top loading of the limestone.
A building where the study and practice of preparing, preserving, compounding and dispensing drugs is performed.
A building in which hoops (for masts) were heated.
A building for miners to change their clothes.
A hall used for the promotion and selling of agricultural produce and practice.
A club founded to provide education, relaxation, and recreation for working men.
A place where current and former members of the armed services meet for social and recreational activities.
A coke-filled tower used for the dissolving and neutralising of acid produced by alkali-making processes.
A chemical works engaged in the production of the coal tar derivative phenol, a chemical used for the manufacture of explosives during WWI.
A pit which appears to have been dug for, or which contains, objects apparently deposited for reasons other than storage, disposal or extraction. Index with principal object types.
A site where jet is extracted from the surface of the ground.
Earthworks of uncertain date and purpose, consisting of cross-shaped banks sometimes with an accompanying ditch. Their distribution is largely confined to North Yorkshire.

A chemical works engaged in the manufacture of the coal tar derivative, picric acid, often associated with the textile industry where it was used as a dye, but more commonly with the explosives industry where it was used as the shell filling Lyddite.
An area of land, usually planted with creeping plants and turf, laid out in a woodland landscape to produce the natural effect of a clearing.
A place of meeting and worship for followers of the Church Army, a body of trained lay evangelists devoted to evangelism and social work.
A building in which cows are milked.
A strip of cultivated land situated against the exterior of a walled garden's perimeter, so placed to maximise usable wall space.

An operations room, built to drawing number 367/41, to control the lighting arrays of the DREM type of bombing decoy in use during the Second World War. Unlike earlier designs it was surface built and then covered in earth to protect against flooding.

An operations room, built to drawing number 3395/40, to control the lighting arrays of the 'T' type of bombing decoy in use during the Second World War. It was semi-sunken for added protection and then covered in earth
A decoy site designed to simulate the flarepath lighting of permanent RAF stations, to lure attacking night bombers away from legitimate targets.
An establishment used for gambling.
Machine, frequently horse powered, for mixing raw clay into brick earth.
A house joined to another to form one building.
A friary belonging to the Friars of the Sack also known as Friars of Penance or Penitentia.
skos:Concept.skos:prefLabel: Friary Of Friars Of The Sack

skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: Area in a brewery used for the production of beer by the Burton Union method.

A type of military aircraft hangar of the Cold War, hardened and therefore protected against the effects of nuclear weapons. It comprises a semi-circular structure built of corrugated-steel supporting a reinforced-concrete skin. Three NATO designs.
A kiln for drying hops in a brewery or maltings complex, as distinct from the OASTHOUSES found on farms.
A site associated with the large scale construction of buildings or items manufactured by the building industry.
A building where jazz music is performed. Often situated in small venues to afford the intimacy of the musicians performing in close proximity to the audience.
A small paved area attached to a building.
A dam with a watertight upstream side, which may be flat or curved, supported by a series of buttresses on the downstream side.

Traditionally an amber-coloured globe lamp atop a tall black and white pole, acting as a signal to road users that there is a pedestrian crossing. Modern beacons may also include an outer ring of flashing LED lights.
A beacon used for coastal navigation. Many date from the Medieval period.
Model village built as a holiday resort.
A signalling station which used a series of shutters to indicate various messages.
A room or small building kept at low temperatures for the storage of perishable items, particularly food.
A receptacle used as a home for bees, traditionally made of thick straw-work in the shape of a dome, but sometimes made of wood.
A portable beehive, often made of straw.
A building or room for the distribution of medicines, eg. in a hospital or clinic.
A house or range of buildings in which dogs are kept, eg. hunting hounds.
A piece of grassland, often near a river, permanently covered with grass which is mown for use as hay.

A structure to which a net filled with mail bags is attached. Situated next to railway lines, it allows mail to be collected by a train without it stopping, the bag being 'caught' by the train as it passed. Can also be used to 'catch' mail.
The horizontal beam on a lock gate.
A site where lime (calcium carbonate) is made.
A building where tallow is produced, ie. solid animal fat that has been separated by heating, usually for making candles.
Use with other minerals extracted and MINE where relevant, eg. ZINC MINE.
A barn in which a central space is separated from side aisles by posts and braces.
A barn in which a central space is separated from a side aisle by posts and braces.
A large cauldron used in the making of a preservative from the bark of spruce, fir or other conifers. The preservative was used to treat nets, sails and other fishing gear.
Roman coastal forts fortified with large walls and a ditch, introduced to cope with raids from across the English Channel and North Sea.
A mill used for the mechanized processing of silk.
A coastal battery designed for use in short range engagements with enemy vessels, minelayers, blockships ad torpedo craft.
A crane whose winding mechanism was operated by hydraulic jiggers.
A hydraulically-powered crane constructed from open box girders.
An enclosure for pigs that includes a covered pen and yard.
64 Type DFW55373 single projector sites arranged in an 8x8 grid or in 4 groups of 16. 30m between each projector, with hardened personnel and ammunition shelters located midway between each
A piece of machinery used to raise oil from a well.
A building or site used for the production of acids by a range of chemical processes.
A school in which students are taught according to the beliefs of the muslim faith.
A lime kiln in which coal is burnt, as distinct from a flame-free kiln in which wood or peat is used.
An engine in which the power is provided by electricity either in the form of batteries or direct from the mains supply.
Works producing a refractory clay, kaolin. An essential raw material of porcelain and some types of papermaking.
A building or site used for the production of bricks and other items, from a clay with refractory properties.
A decorated, hanging sign, bearing the name and also often a pictorial representation of the inn or public house to which it is attached.
A large, "bottle-shaped", oven of brick construction used in the baking or firing of pottery.
A pit from which sand is excavated.
A building or works in which carriages were built. Use RAILWAY CARRIAGE WORKS for sites making railway carriages.
A seaside pier used as a promenade and amusement park.
A structure used for music, dance, ceremonial or civic events.
A C20th military building used to test the efficiency of gas protection equipment provided for drivers of all forms of vehicles.
A simple wind-driven machine used for a variety of purposes.
A wind-powered pump for land drainage.
An apparatus designed with a large vaned wheel rotated by the wind in order to generate electricity.

A circular or octagonal building at the base of a post mill to provide storage space and to give protection to the superstructure. The roundhouse is not attached to the mill itself. Some roundhouses were later converted for domestic purposes.
A group of electricity-producing windmills or wind turbines.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the production and use of wind power.
An artificial mound of earth indicating either the former site of a windmill or built as the base of a post windmill.
A type of WATERMILL, powered by retaining seawater at high tide and then releasing it at low tide via the water wheel.
A tunnel running under a river or through a hill along which vehicles may travel.
Watch Office with operations room designed to Air Ministry drawing number (7345/41
A building, originally used as a shelter for the duty pilot or officer on watch on an airfield, incorporating an operations room.
Watch Office with operations room designed to Air Ministry drawing number (13079/41)

A place of worship and meeting hall for members of the Salvation Army, an evangelical sect founded by William Booth in Nottingham in 1865 and derived from Wesleyan Methodism. They rejected the sacraments and adopted a quasi-military rhetoric and style.
A platform scale, flush with the road, for weighing vehicles, cattle, etc.
Housing provided for refugees. Similar to refugee camp but with the reuse of existing buildings rather than a temporary camp.

A site, complex or building which has been converted for use as the headquarters for the civilian authorities in the event of a nuclear attack or major natural disaster destroying the seat of government.
A purpose-built or adapted structure intended as a headquarters for an air raid precautions warden.
A Cornish Medieval amphitheatre used for the performance of mystery plays and sports.
A building used as a meeting place by a synod, an assembly of the clergy.
A building or buildings used for the production of paints, varnishes, colours and distemper.

Regular courtyard farmsteads where the buildings are arranged as an E-shaped plan around two cattle yards. Cattle housing and stabling typically extend as three ranges from the longer main range which includes a barn or mixing house.
A workshop where wooden brushes are manufactured on a small scale.
A mechanically operated display board used in greyhound racing, which showed the state of the Tote, or cumulative betting on individual greyhounds.
Water channel leading to water wheel.
The channel of water that provides a current of water to drive a millwheel.
A steam driven winding engine house for raising coal to the surface.
A site which has been bombed but where there is no crater, eg. bombed buildings.
A small building housing a valve which controls the flow within a water regulation system.
A pit for the reception of night-soil and refuse.
A covered pit into which raw sewage is discharged.
A garden in which a variety of plants are grown to encourage butterflies.
Vertical or horizontal levels driven into a hill slope to assess the viability of mineral resources but never fully exploited.
The residence of an employee with the duty of maintaining a section of a railway or road.
A mill used for the production of wadding, as opposed to yarn or cloth. Often associated with steam or water power.
A hospital block where patients come for day-care medical treatment.
An island, partly or wholly artificial, built up by dumping timber, earth and stones onto a lake or river bed. Often revetted with timber piles or palisade.

A building or buildings ranged around a courtyard on at least three sides. They occur in the Iron Age, as well as being an influential plan type of house from the 15th century onwards. Index with appropriate period.
An office, particularly at a seaport, at which customs are collected.
A court of criminal, and limited civil, jurisdiction in England and Wales. Established in 1972 to replace the Assize Court, following legislation in 1971.
A site where tin ore is extracted from suspended fire waste in tin mine spoil heaps.
A place where tin ore is washed using a stream as the water source.
An enclosed encampment, often featuring temporary or semi-permanent structures, used for the detention of prisoners of war, refugees or other civilians detained on political or social grounds.
A site used for the production and/or working of metallic iron.
A steep-sided pit formed by, and for, the extraction of gravel.
The name of a class of excavations, found in chalk formations in England, consisting of a shaft sunk to the chalk, and there widening out into one or more chambers.
Large covered spaces where the steel plate used for ship construction was cut and marked out, prior to being craned onto the hull, etc.
A meeting place for freemasons.
Steps found at a landing point.
A building or site used by the armed forces for the storage and issuing of military stores and materials.
A hall, apartment or large room, designed or used primarily for festive or state functions.

A small rectangular or sub circular area or areas bounded by an earthwork, ditch or similar boundary, where one side is formed by an existing linear boundary, forming a pattern reminiscent of clothes hanging from a washing line.
A structure with semaphore arms and/or coloured lights used as a means of warning on railway systems.
A weekend retreat for Royal parties and others, when hunting in the Royal forests, or as a viewing station for the chase.
A room used for directing military operations and exercises.

Name given to a workhouse after 1929. The Local Government Act of 1929 abolished Poor Law Unions and Guardians, and control passed to public assistance authorities run by county boroughs and county councils. Lasted until 1948 when poor laws were repealed.
A furnace for smelting ore in which the fuel and ore are mixed.
A building in which raw pottery is finished by dipping it in glaze.
Ornamental wrought iron screen associated with gate lodges or entrance lodges.
An observation post, usually well concealed, intended for use by the Auxiliary Units (or British Resistance Organisation), in the event of an invasion, to watch enemy movements without being seen.
Narrow ridges representing the surviving surface traces of later prehistoric cultivation.
An apparatus for burning refuse to ashes.
An appliance for producing motion by the stepping of men on movable steps on a revolving cylinder. Used as a form of punishment in prisons.
A simple wind-driven machine used for a variety of purposes.
A side-opening steel framed shed. A smaller version of the SEAPLANE SHED (TYPE F) they were built from 1916 on RNAS seaplane bases
A framework, often made of steel, supporting a crane or similar structure, or for supporting a platform or stage.
A building where people congregate to undertake sustained mental contemplation or religious or spiritual reflection.
A bridge over a canal.
A floating structure consisting of two walls standing on pontoon tanks, the latter of which can be flooded to receive a vessel and then pumped out until the pontoon deck and the ship are dry.
Gun battery built specifically to mount short range weapons to defend a beach against an attempted landing.

Manmade structure for bathing or swimming that is located on the beachfront and filled by tidal waters. Similar to a LIDO, with the main difference being the extent of the built up complex around the pool.

An unenclosed feature, usually sub-terranean, constructed to contain water for public or private recreation and sporting avtivities. Sometimes part of a LIDO complex. Use INDOOR SWIMMING POOL for pools with a covering structure.

A funerary site, either totally or partially underground, for the depositing of the dead. Often found in cemeteries in the form of a circular or semi-circular sunken area comprising of several galleries with vault entrances built into the side.
The residence of a herder.
The residence of a drover.
A house or shelter used by drovers, herders or shepherds during the seasonal moving of livestock from the highlands to the lowlands. Use more specific type where known.
A small building used as a shelter by a shepherd.

A square shaped area of land enclosed by a boundary ditch, bank, wall, palisade or similar barrier. Small square enclosures (with sides of less than c.20m) have been interpreted as the remains of square barrows of Iron Age date.
A large metal pylon structure used to tether airships.
A public house licensed for the sale of wine and other alcoholic drinks.
A building or workshop where fine furniture, often veneered, is made.
An early Medieval commemorative monument in the form of a stone which has been inscribed with symbols.
A small, defensive settlement, usually consisting of one dwelling and ancillary buildings, surrounded by a palisade.
A piston mounted horizontally supplying power via a valve gear directly to a crankshaft or flywheel.
A workshop used for the manufacture of statues, either cast or carved.
The building attached to a cathedral or collegiate church where the dean, prebendaries or monks and canons met for the transaction of business.
A component of another building, often a house, used for storing nets.
A small stone structure, usually at a spring or bog, in which dairy products were kept cool on slate shelves.
A mill or factory in which raw cotton, wool, nylon or other material is spun into yarn or thread.
Living and working quarters for the cellarer who was in charge of provisions and the running of the cellar.
A market hall where cloth merchants can show their wares and conduct business.
A mill used for grinding textile rags.
An aircraft hangar designed to Air Ministry specifications (drawing number 2243/41). Constructed from prefabricated A-frames and clad in corrugated iron.
The official residence of the chief officer of the municipal corporation of a city or borough in England.

A type of goose pen with stone-clad compartments, built into the base of a Cornish hedge near the periphery of a farmstead. Aspect is often towards entrance track or driveway since geese were used in similar role to guard dogs. Particular to Cornwall.
An enclosure or pen for confining geese.
A factory used for the production of red lead used in glass manufacture, or white lead used as the pigment in white paint.
An abbey or priory of Gilbertine Nuns.
A workshop where tapestries were made.
A type of pottery oven in which the air passes from the base of the kiln out through the top.
A site where the process of combing, the preparatory process for long wools, takes place.
An area of flattened or compacted ground used for charcoal burning.
An outlying farm or estate belonging to the Carthusian order.
A gate used to seal the entrance to a dock to prevent water escaping from a wet dock or entering a dry dock.
An engineering workshop, often attached to an engine shed, for the running repairs of operational parts, etc.
A frame used to lift unco-operative horses off the ground during shoeing.
An engineering works that produces machinery specially for use in textile making.
A modification of WATCH OFFICE (12779/41) where the original large windows were removed and smaller frames fitted, the gap being filled with straight-joint brickwork.
A small building housing a mechanism used for winding a cable.
A workshop with a forge for the melting and working of white metal, ie. low-melting alloys. Also used for a smith specializing in decorative or finely finished wrought iron work.
A mill where mustard is produced.
A house for the keeper of a level crossing on a railway.

Unspecified defensive structure like a mound of earth, a rampart, an embankment or a wall-like fortification. Also used as an early term for a bastion or blockhouse. Use more specific term where known.
A factory where security safes are manufactured.
A factory where lengths of soft, woollen cloth, loosely woven to retain heat, used as a bed covering, were manufactured.
A building used by members of the Womens Institute, an organization which meets regularly and engages in various social and cultural activities.
A factory complex consisting of PRINTING SHOPS, COLOUR HOUSES, DYE HOUSES, etc, in which patterns are printed onto calico.
A factory, incorporating power driven machinery from the late 18th century, where cloth was manufactured from threads interlaced at right angles to each other in a loom.
A garden where woodland and meadow flowers grow in an apparently natural way.
The residence of a Royal Navy or Merchant Navy officer.
A mound or structure on which targets are placed for archery practice or competition.
A mound or structure on which an archery, musketry or artillery target is erected. Use specific type where known.
WWII secret bases, sometimes partially underground, intended for use by the British resistance in the eventuality of a foreign invasion.
A mill in which sets of rollers were used to roll metal to set thicknesses or shapes such as rails, beams or rods.
A hotel adjacent to a railway terminus. Railway hotels were often owned by a railway company.
Site used for the maintenance of aircraft.
A monument commemorating an animal.
A depression in the ground caused by the explosion of a mortar shell.
A place where metal-cutting hand files were made.
A mill in which sets of rollers were used to roll metal to set thicknesses or shapes such as rails, beams or rods.
A fighter satellite station watch office built to Air Ministry design drawing number 18441/40.
A bridge that incorporates a span that moves upwards vertically to provide a passageway for navigation.
A dam and sluice combination, associated with an aqueduct, for the extraction of water from a river to feed a reservoir or water treatment plant.
A small latrine or toilet, usually built into the thickness of the wall of a castle or great house, with the waste dropping into a cess pit or straight to the outside.
A building in which an organization or society is instituted to promote foreign languages in England such as French and German, etc.
A building or range of buildings used to accommodate race horses.
Use for complexes where services (eg. restaurants, shops) are provided in addition to facilities for buying petrol.
A shallow artificial pond, usually found on the coast, in which sea water is allowed to evaporate leaving behind the salt.
A hospital for the treatment of venereal disease.
A building, similar to a cart shed, but used to house traps, gigs and coaches.
Casing for electrical connections: an enclosed and protected box inside which electrical circuits are interconnected or branched for distribution.
An office at which the registration of marriages, births and deaths are recorded, and in which marriage ceremonies may take place.
Prehistoric structure consisting of three or more standing stones in close proximity to each other, forming an unroofed approximately rectangular structure open in one direction.
A place of worship and residence for Anglican nuns.
A hospital where Royal Naval personnel and their families receive medical and surgical treatment.
A central office dealing with financial accounts.
A site for the sale or hire of agricultural machinery.
A mill where flax is processed to make linen, thread and yarn.
A small area of managed woodland, created to provide cover for foxes.
A two-storey watch office similar in design to drawing number 1959/34 but constructed completely from concrete. A large, almost square, ground plan with a central observation tower.
The residence of the supervisor of an inclined plane.
An establishment for the theoretical and practical training of nurses.
A building or set of rooms where a newspaper is compiled and produced, before being printed. May include facilities for printing.
A concrete marker placed to indicate the direction of a target on a bombing range to aircraft.
A range marker allowing bombers to locate the bombing range.
An area of land, roughly shaped like a trapezoid and enclosed by a boundary ditch, bank, wall, palisade or similar barrier.

A lighthouse whose lantern is sufficiently low to be seen below low lying cloud. In locations where varying weather conditions occur a Low Light is usually accompanied by a HIGH LIGHT built alongside or nearby.
A semaphore signalling tower on a railway.

The residence of a preceptor, officials and servants, etc, supervising the estates of the Knights Templars military order. Includes the mother house styled the Temple, London. The Order was suppressed in 1312.
A Palaeolithic or Mesolithic temporary site where there is evidence to suggest animal butchery. Evidence may include animal remains and a specialized tool assemblage.
A toilet or toilets for public use.
A hospital which primarily cares for patients injured in accidents.
Any structure or object, used for the purpose of practice shooting by aerial, seaborne or land mounted weapons.
A place where public sales of goods are made by competitive bidding.
A house in which a passage runs across the building, usually adjacent to a hall, between front and back entrance doors.
A departmental building within a college or university where a particular subject is taught and administered.
A building in which a judicial court is held.
A hospital which has been built either wholly, or partially, underground in order to protect it from attacks by enemy aircraft.
A substantial structure supporting or surrounding a gate. May be ornate or monumental, and have associated structures such as lodges, tollbooths, guard houses etc.
A Hall where billiards was played.
An instrument for measuring and indicating the height of tide.
A pillbox built to a design drawn up by the commander of the Royal Engineers in Southern Area (Taunton Line).
A building for the storage and drying of hops, often including a hop drying kiln. Usually built as part of a farm.
A garden incorporating features of traditional Japanese gardens - a pool, an island, stepping stones or a bridge, cherry trees and other shrubs and flowering plants grown with the emphasis on line.
A building where beer was sold or displayed.
A chair fixed to the end of a plank, in which scolds or dishonest people were tied and ducked in water as a punishment.
An instrument for measuring and indicating the height of tide.
A building for the crushing of stones and minerals.
A building used to store navigational buoys.
A building or site used for the manufacture of swords.
A large bath used for Jewish ritual ceremonies.
A furnace composed of two fire brick boxes: the fire was in the lower box and the upper box held the crucibles. Used in the manufacture of steel.
A building or room within a granary used to dry grain. Often consisting of an oven with a refractory-brick drying floor above, on which the grain was placed.
An arena for bull-baiting, not a tethering ring.

A prefabricated structure of reinforced concrete posts supporting a pitched roof frame with an infilling of concrete panels. Produced by during WWII as barrack accommodation and as emergency housing. Similar in style to Maycrete huts.
A factory where jute (plant fibres), was used to make products such as hessian, sacking, cordage and backing materials for carpet and linoleum.
A lid for a well. Well covers are often ornate and can be made of various materials.
A mine used for the extraction on tin bearing ore.
A stone or brick wall enclosing a park.
A circular kiln or oven used in the manufacture of bricks. Common in Staffordshire in the 18th century.
A canal built as a military obstacle, but also used for the transport of military stores, equipment and personnel.
A warehouse used for the storage of fruit and/or vegetables.
A building in which a parliament meets and conducts the business of government.
A factory, or group of buildings, containing apparatus used to extract specific properties, e.g flavour or scent, from natural ingredients.
A hut used for the accommodation of members of the armed forces.
A room or building used for the making of films, television or radio programmes and musical recordings (CDs, LPs, etc).
A textile mill where felt is produced.
A structure found on lighthouses, piers, etc, capable of emitting a loud noise to warn shipping in foggy weather.
A crude, stone-built shelter for persons involved in lime production and the processing of lime burning.

A cable repeater station for the undersea telephone and telegraph cables. Repeater stations compensated for the inadequacies of 1920's and 30's equipment over long distances, by repeating the signal every 200 miles.

A building, similar in style to a telephone exchange but smaller. They were used to compensate for the inadequacies of 1920's and 30's equipment over long distances, by repeating the signal every 200 miles.
A mechanized gate or barrier at a level crossing used to prevent road vehicles crossing a railway line when a train is approaching.
A school for instruction in the art of horsemanship.
A crane fixed to a quay, used for the unloading of ships cargoes.
A non-vertical kiln where the shaft and burning zone is horizontal to the ground thereby allowing material to be fed in.
A pipe through which water is conducted.
A stepped, roadside platform, usually of stone on which a sedan chair was placed to allow the porters to lift the chair without having to bend.
A small, steel shelter designed for use as a firewatchers post during an air raid.
A local civil court first established during the 17th Century by local Acts of Parliament to deal with minor cases of debt. Based on a model established during the reign of Henry VII.

A round house indicated by the presence of a low, roughly circular bank of turf, earth or stone, which formed the base of the walls. Characteristic of the later prehistoric period. Where several occur together use HUT CIRCLE SETTLEMENT.
A site where clay pipes used for drainage are manufactured.
An airfield with associated hangars and control buildings used for the storage, maintenance and deployment of military aircraft and airships flown by the Royal Naval Air Service.
A place where paper, frequently printed in ornamental designs, used for covering the interior walls of buildings, is manufactured.
The residence of a lacemaker.
Pasture to which animals were driven for grazing, with associated temporary huts for domestic or agricultural use.
Wooden board marking a grave.
A place where fish are processed after being caught.
A building associated with the legal administration of a forest, eg. Forest of Dean.
The outer boundary of an airfield.
A temporary kiln, in which the pots are stacked and baked in a pit underneath a bonfire.
A factory making flame retardant materials.
A building used by an organization instituted to promote the needs and rights of the blind.
An Anglo-Saxon fortified town or other defended site, not necessarily urban.
A place where hats are made and sold.
An enclosure surrounded by a wooden stockade. A rare site type of Neolithic date.

A wall within a lead mine surrounding a dressing floor, where waste from mining and smelting is deposited, to protect livestock from entering and consuming contaminated material and becoming poisoned, or 'bellanded'.

A building within a gunpowder works complex, where the mill cake (pulverised and incorporated ingredients of gunpowder) was broken down. It was crushed or broken down by passing it between pairs of revolving gunmetal rollers in a breaking-down machine.
A site used for the manufacture of gunpowder.

A building within the gunpowder works complex. During the gunpowder production process, the mill cake was broken down, pressed and then corned. The remaining dust was removed from the corned powder by tumbling it in gauze-covered revolving cylinders.
The courtyard of a castle, ie. the area enclosed by the rampart or curtain. Use with wider site type where known.
A site, usually including hardstandings and associated buildings, where ambulances can be parked and stored.
Use for stationary railway carriage being used for a purpose it wasn't originally intended for - office, shelter, etc.
The remains of a vessel which has either sunk or suffered structural damage to the extent where it can no longer function.
A stone on which a monarch traditionally sat during the coronation ceremony.
An independent school for children up to the age of 11 or 13 in which pupils are prepared for entry into a public school.
A crane used for the refueling of coal-powered vessels.
A hospital department for the identification and treatment of skin tissue disorders.

A prefabricated structure of a steel frame clad in corrugated iron. Semi-circular in section they were used as accommodation for the armed forces and, during WWII, as emergency housing for bombed out civilians. Also used for storage.
A grotto decorated with shells, sometimes a room in a house, sometimes a detached building.
A covered trench, often in a zig zag form, made for the purpose of approaching a beseiged place under fire of the garrison.
A building used by an organization instituted to promote the needs and rights of the blind.
A factory complex consisting of PRINTING SHOPS, COLOUR HOUSES, DYE HOUSES, etc, in which patterns are printed onto calico.
A house with no row of posts between the central space and the aisles.
A house with an aisle on one side only.
Use where the intervening arcade is closed but timber-framed.
A quarry for the extraction of Soapstone (also known as steatite or soaprock), a metamorphic rock largely composed of the mineral talc and rich in magnesium.
A steam whistle or siren used for signalling purposes.
A stone that indicates the limit of an area or piece of land.
The residence of health workers. Includes single dwellings of doctors, nurses etc. but not multiple dwellings eg.NURSES HOSTEL
Small stone hearth set up in a shallow pit. Burns vegetation and coppiced twigs to produce potash.
A multi-level structure designed to simulate tall buildings to allow firefighters to practice firefighting and rescue techniques
A crude, stone-built shelter for persons involved in lime production and the processing of lime burning.
A factory where hemp, the woody stalk of the hemp plant, used for the making of coarse cloth and cordage, was processed.
A type of temporary transportable aircraft hangar designed in 1936 by N.S. Bellman. It was designed for ease of installation, and was composed of light rolled steel sections.

A large circular defence work surrounded by a brick revetted ditch and sunken below a glacis. Usually built out of brick with the embrasures lined with granite blocks. Armed with ten or elven guns. Early 19th century as part of coastline defence.
A steam-powered factory.
A rectangular pillbox with an enclosed square plan section for three light machine guns and an adjacent open area housing a mounting for a light anti-aircraft weapon. Designed by DFW branch 3.
The residence of a ferrykeeper.
Triangular concrete pyramids with 6 feet long sides and 5 feet high, intended to impede enemy movement in the event of invasion. Thought to be confined geogaphically to Southern Command.

An offshore station, equipped with a fixed electronic radio navigation and positioning system such as Hyperfix. The transmission principle are pulsed and phase comparisons systems. Superceded by Global Positioning System in 1994.
A specialist hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of ear disorders and diseases.
A place where gold ore is extracted.
Horse powered ore crusher, consisting of a stone wheel running over a circular iron or stone bed.
A small narrow rectilinear enclosure with high hedges boundaries for the cultivation and shelter of flowers, particularly Daffodils and Narcissi.
A wall structure built to direct a current into the desired channel in a harbour, river etc.
A factory where packaging products, such as cardboard boxes, are produced.
A wall used in the game of handball.
A water channel leading from a water wheel.
A place where a group of people live together sharing accomodation and goods, forming their own community based upon common ideals.
A layer of stone, brick or boards, etc, on which people tread. Use broader site type where known.
Floor cover in Roman time, where small cubes (tesserea) of one or more colours were laid in a geometric pattern.

A place of worship for the Knights of the Order of the Hospital of St John of Jerusalem, a military order dedicated to the provision of hospitality for pilgrims, to the care of the sick and to the protection of the Holy Land.
An area within a hospital where patients receiving privately-funded medical and surgical treatment are accommodated. Often includes separate rooms.
A workshop for combining flax or hemp as a preparatory stage of rope making.
A building where distillation, a chemical process used in the production of a range of different chemicals, took place.

A horizontal surface separating the base of a rampart or earthwork from an associated ditch or moat. Can also refer to a continuously sloping bank of earth against a wall, as in a fortified city wall.

A garden or park, with ancilliary buildings, in which young and domesticated animals are kept for public exhibition, especially for children. Children are given the opportunity to come into close contact and handle animals.
A garden or park, with ancilliary buildings, in which wild animals are kept and reared for public exhibition.

A place of worship for the sect known as 'Cokelers', formed circa 1850 by John Sirgood. Most aspects of Dependent belief are fairly orthodox within the Arminian traditions of Protestant dissent. Chapels can be found in Sussex, Surrey, London and Kent.
Workshop, as part of a gunpowder works complex, in which explosive is loaded into shells. Also used for expense magazine, where powder was stored between work processes.
An aircraft hangar designed by T. Bedford Consulting Engineers usually erected on aircraft factory sites rather than operational airfields.
A specialist hospital where the elderly receive medical treatment.
A 19th century spa building, usually consisting of a hotel with baths used for water treatment.
A prison used for temporary detention. The typical village lock-up was a one-storeyed, one-celled building, sometimes of round or polygonal plan.
Engineering works dedicated solely to the manufacture and repair of boilers.
Mediaeval-17th century mining method which involved exploiting an exposed surface vein. Rarely associated with waste.
A North country memorial imitating a wattled hut decorated with formalized bears or snakes.
A wall containing apertures to allow a weapon to be fired through it.
A large, "bottle-shaped", oven of brick construction used in the baking or firing of pottery.
A mine used for the extraction of tungsten bearing ore. Use with other mineral ores extracted and MINE, eg. TIN MINE.
Not a round barrow ploughed out at one end, but a specific type, the flat edge being additionally defined by stone slabs.
A building, either purpose-built or modified, used for the co-ordination of the Fire Service.
A kiln with a pyramid roof and capped vent in which barley is dried. Found on the site of a malt house.
A matzevah from the Sephardi group of Jews descended from medieval Jewish communities of the Iberian Peninsular and Northern Africa. Characterised by flat slabs with Hebrew Inscriptions
An inclined ramp of earth, stone or brick used to deliver fuel to the firing hole of a kiln. Mediaeval and later.
An area where birds are protected and bred.
A body which has been interred in boggy or marshy ground or other similarly waterlogged environment. Interment may have been deliberate or accidental.
An extant settlement which shows evidence of a shift in focus, eg. towards a new road, generally in the form of abandoned buildings or earthworks on the margin furthest from the new focus.
A table made of stone, found in streets, parks, etc.
A building in a zoo or wildlife park used to accommodate giraffes.
A building containing a number of areas for bathing, some of which are naturally heated by thermal springs.
A building used to manufacture Producer Gas. Producer Gas is a mix of gases formed by passing compressed air through hot coke.

A site where a cable was fired into the air, with parachutes attached to either end, to present an aerial obstruction to bring down, through contact, fouling and general drag, or obstruct the passage of an aircraft. Usually found as one of a group.

A forcing house used for various types of fruit which first appeared in the 19th century. Lean-to houses were used for wall-grown fruit and free-standing houses for fruit grown in pots or for trees planted in the ground.
A building or room used for the storage of pottery moulds.
A small house or cottage at the entrance to a cemetery, usually occupied by a caretaker or gardener, etc.
A large storehouse where wholesale goods are stored.
A building or buildings used for the production of whistles.
A kiln where gypsum was dried to a state where it could be used as plaster of Paris or for the production of cement.
A place of worship for members of the Methodist Reform Church. This group was the result of a secession from the Methodists in 1849. They remained until joining with the Wesleyan Association in 1857.
A building or room within a monastery in which the monks were allowed to warm themselves. The warming house was often the only place where a fire was allowed.
A building used to house apes and monkeys.
A pit containing the waste product form iron working.

A communication system in which cylindrical containers are propelled through a network of tubes either by compressed air or partial vacuum. They are used for transporting solid objects, as opposed to conventional pipelines, which transport fluids.
A defence work, either a detached fieldwork or an outwork built as part of a fortification as a last defensive position.
The residence of a signalman.
A site used for the extraction of metallic zinc by a variety of processes.
The area of a town or city, such as a harbour or dockyard, alongside a body of water.

A hole in the ground which has been created by driving or hammering an upright stake into the ground. As a feature of some archaeological sites they may often represent the only surviving evidence for the former presence of an above-ground structure.
A room or building used as a store, usually for documents, works of art, books etc.
A building used for the safe storage and public display of jewellery, eg. the Jewel House at the Tower of London.
A cover consisting of a plate for covering over or closing in a chamber or receptacle.
The residence of a miller, often attached to a mill.
A hall, often associated with a synagogue, used for studying the Torah and other religious texts.
The residence of a lifeboatman.
A building housing a set of bellows used to provide the blast of air to a blast furnace or similar installation.
A protective structure, often made of sandbags with reinforcement, designed to protect aircraft at airfields from enemy attack.
A zoo building containing artificial ponds or tanks in which aquatic plants and animals are kept alive for purposes of observation and study.
A room used by those who have to wait at railway or bus stations, etc.
A building where threads of different qualities and colours are mixed together.
A small monastery or nunnery of the Augustinian order dependent on a larger mother house.
A factory where buttons are manufactured.
An apartment, usually with a north-light, used by artists.
A kiln used for the slow burning of vegetable matter to produce potassium carbonate.
A 19th century structure of various shape or material for the protection of troops in an emergency.
A kiln used for the slow burning of vegetable matter to produce potassium carbonate.
A building or room where nets are made
A battery mounted in the flank of a bastion from which flanking fire is directed across a curtain wall.
An area used for crushing mineral ore or stone. Often includes mechanically powered ore crushers.
A building or site incorporating sonar equipment used for detecting the presence of enemy ships or submarines.
An artificial fall of water often taking the form of a water staircase.
A hall used for the promotion and selling of horticultural produce and practice.
A wall enclosing a precinct.
A building or subterranean structure used for the storage of wine.

A type of transportable aircraft hangar patented by Miskins and Sons in 1939. The arched hangar was constructed of steel or wooden ribs and generally clad in steel sheets. The hangar did not require any foundations and could be anchored by iron stakes.
A building or group of buildings, incorporating radio masts, built to intercept radio transmissions from enemy vessels and aircraft during WWI and WWII.
A building used for the testing of steel.
A hospital department where research and treatment into the causes and nature of diseases or abnormal bodily conditions is carried out.
A nunnery of nuns belonging to the Order of the Servants of the Blessed Virgin Mary or Servites.
A specialist hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of kidney disorders and diseases.
A workshop or factory where the barrels of cannon are cast.
A rectangular pillbox with an enclosed square plan section for three light machine guns and an adjacent open area housing a mounting for a light anti-aircraft weapon. Designed by DFW branch 3.
A kiln that is octagonal in plan. Use with functional kiln type where known.
A dam and sluice combination, associated with an aqueduct, for the extraction of water from a river to feed a reservoir or water treatment plant.

A temporary structure used for the firing of bricks or tiles. Unfired bricks or tiles were stacked upon a layer of fuel (usually wood) and then surrounded by a wall of old bricks and covered by a layer of mud or clay. The clamp was then fired.
A structure consisting of a large, metal framework holding a skyward facing dish. Used for transmitting and receiving signals which are relayed by satellite.
A house having four rooms of equal height on each of two floors; in larger houses there are often two parallel and equal roofs.
A commercial premises where clocks are sold and repaired.
A factory or group of buildings used for the production of plated goods. Plating is the process whereby one metal object is coated with a thin layer of another metal.
A mill in which strands of yarn are twisted together to produce a strong thread with a uniform thickness.
A gun battery used to signal warnings to ships during bad weather.
A small building housing pilot's and locker rooms with flight offices and a watch office. The only known example was built at Tangmere.
The site of the formal burial of cremated bone, sometimes 'urned' in a vessel or casket of glass, wood or, more commonly, ceramic.
A building or site producing nitrogen-rich fertilizer.

A lighthouse whose lantern is sufficiently high to be seen at a long range and above low lying cloud or fog. In locations where varying weather conditions occur a High Light is usually accompanied by a LOW LIGHT built alongside or nearby.
A target range used for rifle and small arms practice and recreational purposes.
A bridge crossing under railway property.
A laundry situated within the estate of a manor or country house.
A mill used to process logwood, the inner red wood of a South American tree used widely in dyeing. Imported in the form of logs and cut and ground into dye by a mechanical process.

A roughly circular monument featuring a low, more or less level platform of stones surrounded or retained by a low stone kerb. Some may feature a small central open area, thus resembling a ring cairn.
A building where nurses live.
The entire playing area and associated buildings upon which the game of cricket is played.

A type of steel framed transportable British military aircraft hangar developed from 1941onwards. The hangar had a steel frame, some versions used commercially available sheeting for cladding. It was similar to but smaller than the arcraft hangar type T2.
A small, open air bowl-shaped furnace, in which the flames are fanned by bellows. Used for both ferrous and non-ferrous smelting.
A bridge whose upkeep and repair was financed by the exaction of a toll.
A site where cement is manufactured for the building industry.
A marker stone showing the extent of a measure of land containing a vein of ore.
A site where canvas, coarse, unbleached cloth, made from hemp or flax, was manufactured.
A residence of two or three monks of the Benedictine order dependent on an English mother house.
The residence of a verger, typically a layperson who assists in the ordering of religious services within the Anglican church.
An old opencast iron ore site, which has been abandoned.
A site where metal springs are manufactured.
A place where architectural ornaments such as stone vases and urns are manufactured.

A term for a type of house, with varying definitions according to period. Roman villas were high-status and usually associated with a rural estate, whereas Georgian and later period villas were often semi-detached, town houses.
A tunnel with a canal running through it.
A canal tunnel built with one or more integral towpaths
A tower with one or more horizontal platforms extending out over deep water for use in diving competitions.
A building, factory or works which was engaged in the manufacture of refining saltpetre. Often part of a gunpowder works.
A telegraph pole, tree trunk or similar erected on the side of a road, or in an open space, to prevent the landing of hostile aircraft
The residence of a sailor.
A building to house waterwheels, attached to a WATERMILL or water-powered factory.
A large building or structure where coal is washed, sized and graded before being sold.
A factory which produces artificial imitations of mineral water, such as soda water.
A pedestal terminating in a head or bust of Hermes or some other deity.
A hospital where Air Force personnel and their families receive medical and surgical treatment.
A small garden building used to store equipment used in the game of croquet.
A site or establishment for the casting and refining of metallic copper.
A building or cage in which parrots are bred and kept.
A wooden or stone plinth for depositing milk churns on.
A site where fluorspar or fluoride of calcium, often used as a flux by copper-ore smelters, is extracted from an open cast mine.
A permanent Roman fort enclosed by a number of ditches and ramparts, used to house a garrison of auxiliaries.
A mill, including a forge and powered hammers where hot metal is shaped by hammering and rolling.
A movable bridge that swings or rotates around a central pier, or one that is pivoted only at one end, to provide a passageway for navigation.
A modern fodder store on a farm.
A gateway with one or more chambers over the entrance arch; the flanking towers housing stairs and additional rooms. Use with wider site type where known.
A building where violins are manufactured and the art of violin making is taught.
Garden or open-air enclosure, usually connected to commercial premises, where tea and other refreshments are served to the public.
A commercial building used for the production of detailed, often technical, drawings.

Blocks of solid concrete,in the form of truncated pyramids usually 3 feet square x 2 feet high which could be placed in rows to impede enemy movement in the event of invasion. Pimples were recommended for use on soft ground.
A site used for the butchery of animals.
A multi-storey building in which individual blocks of flats cluster around a central service core.
An ornamental, commemorative tablet. Use with materials field when indexing.
An open flat gound where the sport of shooting with bow and arrows is pursued. The ground can be equipped with targets mounted on butts and various fixed distance marker.
A large building, situated at a railway terminus, used for the temporary storage of goods or merchandise awaiting transportation to or from a railway.
A temporary overnight camp enclosed by a shallow ditch and palisade, constructed by Roman troops on campaigns or manoeuvres.
A circular building for housing and repairing railway locomotives.
A kiln in which the prolonged heating or roasting of materials to drive off water, volatiles and sulphur so that they may be reduced to a powder, was performed.
Pit for the depostion of ore sediment from waste water collected from ore washing.
A house, the inhabitant of which keeps an official register e.g. a registrar's house near a cemetery would keep an official record of deaths and burials.
A chemical works engaged in the production of Ammonium Nitrate, used as a fertilizer or for use in the explosives industry.
A building containing a bier; a movable stand on which a corpse, often in a coffin, is placed prior to burial.
A widening in a canal to allow boats to turn around.
An underground hideout containing radio equipment to be used by the Auxiliary Units to relay information gained from the various out-stations back to headquarters.
A hall used for the promotion and selling of agricultural produce and practice.
A chemical works producing mordants for the dying industry.
A Roman market hall principally selling meat and poultry but also other provisions.
A building where onions are laid out to dry.

Structural elements (parts of hull etc.) or fixtures and fittings (masts, etc.) lost during a naval engagement without incurring the actual loss of a ship. May also be used as a monument type for expended ammunition (e.g. shells, cannonballs).
A type of back to back house built on a hillside, of four storeys and with entrances at different levels.
A factory used for the processing of isinglass, a product obtained from the swim bladders of sturgeon and used in the brewing industry as part of the process for clearing wine and beer.
A place where the game of squash is played.
A supported, roof structure covering all, or part, of a railway platform.
Power station using domestic refuse as its principal fuel.
A bridge carrying a railway track across a river, valley, road etc.
Works for the extrusion of aluminium and for creating aluminium products.
1st World War end-opening aeroplane hangar.
A place where the game of skittles is played.
A building in which cordite dough is stored before extrusion.
A horse-powered winding engine used at mining sites.
The residence of a lock-keeper.
A tower used for surveying, especially in civil engineering projects such as bridges.
Steps found at a landing point.
A tunnel through which a tramway runs.

A pit dug to extract Sarsen stones from the superficial geology in which they occur. They range in size from one dug for the extraction of a single boulder to pits from which multiple boulders are extracted & date from the Neolitic to the mid 20th century
A long, low-rise building consisting of rows of attached individual suites of rooms used for overnight accommodation by motorists.
A centre for the teaching of crafts.
Power generation by releasing stored water through a turbine driving a generator.
A garden seat covered in clipped, camomile plants which release a fragrant smell when sat upon.

A pit used for the re-burial of disarticulated human remains from many individuals, occasionally displaying sorting of remains, eg. grouping of skulls or long bones. Distinct from mass burials which contain articulated skeletal remains.
A building containing soft play equipment for children.
The dwelling and workshop of a framework knitter.
A factory making laminate flooring.
A depot or warehouse for the storage, distribution and repair of shoe making machines.
A freestanding public call box, containing a telephone and usually operated by inserting coins.
A roadside telephone box for use by motorists in need of assistance.
Unenclosed wasteland, forest and pasture used in common by the community.
A factory built for the production of breakfast cereals.
A building equipped with facilities for bathing, and occasionally public baths.

A building designed specifically for handling tobacco. This may be a bonded warehouse containing facilities for removing tobacco leaves from the hogsheads in which they were imported, and pressing them.
A structure, usually of earth and concrete, and usually, although not always, subterranean, designed for protection against explosives.
An unroofed structure, found on military airfields, protected by brick walls and earth banks for shelter during air raids.
A factory where paper is made. Use with power type where known.
A power station used to produce electricity, fired by coal gas.
A circular kiln or oven used in the manufacture of bricks. Common in Staffordshire in the 18th century.
A system of overhead cables from which cars or containers are suspended (usually driven electrically).
A residence of two or three monks of the Premonstratensian order dependent on an English mother house.
A 17th century garden in the Dutch style: usually flat and compact, with an emphasis on small canals, hedges, topiary, lead statuary and flowering shrubs and bulbs.
A wall structure built to direct a current into the desired channel in a harbour, river etc.
A site where gypsum and anhydrate is mined.

A building or part of a building, sometimes attached to a religious community, where religious activities such as worshipping, meetings, teaching about the faith and conferences take place. It can also provide accommodation.
A building or subterranean structure used for the storage of beer.
A stone edge-runner grinding machine or mill used for mechanically grinding and mixing the ingredients of gunpowder.

A hexagonal pillbox, with an internal anti-ricochet wall and loopholes for fives light machine guns and one rifle. Originally designed to have 15in bulletproof walls many were built with 42in thick shellproof walls. Designed by DFW branch 3.
A farm with a pond, river, lake or tanks where fish are kept and bred for commercial purposes.
The residence of a lightkeeper.
A bridge supported by large beams or girders, originally of wood or iron, now usually of steel or reinforced concrete.
A small transportable hangar built by the Teesdie Bridge and Engineering Company. Mainly used on RNAS airfields for folding wing aircraft.
A building on a railway system housing levers used to regulate trains on the tracks using signals and to change the points to enable a train to transfer from one track to another.
An apparatus around which cables or hawsers are wound for hoisting anchors, lifting weights, etc.
A monument erected as a permanent reminder of a military victory. The design usually includes images of the spoils of the battle.
A structure in which pottery tiles were baked.
A building or room where food is prepared and cooked.
An abbey founded in 1415 for nuns of the Bridgettine order.
A hospital for the reception of women during their confinement.
A specialist school for the teaching of blind people.
A school for pupils with physical or learning difficulties.
A specialist school for the teaching of deaf people.
A pipe, usually of reinforced concrete or metal, which delivers pressurized water from a dam to hydraulic turbines.
A stone on which flax stems were beaten with wooden mallets, a process known as beetling.
A house in a terrace built on top of another, with access at high and low level to either side.
A factory for the assembly of components. Usually associated with the manufacture of vehicles: cars, lorries, etc.
A fairground ride, often a permanent structure, consisting of a tower with an internal staircase and an external spiral shaped slide.
The main dwelling-house of a farm, it can be either detached from or attached to the working buildings.

An operations room, built to drawing number 3395/40, to control the lighting arrays of the 'T' type of bombing decoy in use during the Second World War. It was semi-sunken for added protection and then covered in earth
A farmstead where the farmhouse and working buildings are attached and in-line. They can comprise the extension of linear farmsteads.

A lighthouse whose lantern is sufficiently low to be seen below low lying cloud. In locations where varying weather conditions occur a Low Light is usually accompanied by a HIGH LIGHT built alongside or nearby.
