A form of blast furnace. Steel is smelted in an open hearth while the waste gases are used to preheat the air blast.
A magistrates court sitting for the purpose of holding trials for children and young people. Replaced the juvenile court, following legislation, in 1991.

A short-term storage centre of goods or special parts to facilitate the rapid processing of orders and supply of goods to customers; unlike a warehouse, the emphasis is on the moving of goods rather than on a long-term storage.
A factory where fruit and seed oil is produced by an oil machine.
A lime kiln in which coal is burnt, as distinct from a flame-free kiln in which wood or peat is used.
A library which lends books (and sometimes other materials) to its members.
A works producing gelatine from animal products for use as a culinary setting agent and in the photography, dyeing, brewing and glue industries. For explosives use GELATINE WORKS (EXPLOSIVE)
A stone or timber lined channel for conveying ore out of a working.
A building for the manufacture of condensed milk.
An anti tank wall constructed specifically to be used for training purposes.
A road block formed by placing rails or girders in an upright position in sockets in the road surface, forming a moveable barrier.
An isolation hospital for infectious diseases and leprosy, sometimes known as a Pest House; commonly situated on the edge of a town.
Specialist hospital treating patients with physical disabilities.

A type of steel framed transportable British military aircraft hangar developed from 1941onwards. The hangar had a steel frame, some versions used commercially available sheeting for cladding. It was similar to but smaller than the arcraft hangar type T2.
A factory where metal wire is manufactured.
A water-powered forge or wire mill which manufactured metal wire combs for use in the textile industry.

A pillbox design, assigned a drawing number by DFW branch 3. Although originally believed to be a distinct type, FW3/45 has recently been found to be a design for modifications to existing types. Double index with specific type where known.
A wooden or metal structure covering a shipbuilding slip way.
The residence of a miller, often attached to a mill.
A depot for the depositing, storage and dispatch of plant or other resources associated with the delivery of local government public services.
A building containing machinery for operating sluices.
A temporary, usually roofed, wooden structure placed on the ramparts or walls of a castle to improve the defenders field of fire along the length of a wall.
An 18th century cottage with a pottery kiln attached.
A chamber attached to the sewer of a building to facilitate the removal of any blockage.
A settlement used for trading.
An ornamental receptacle to catch rainwater for birds to drink from and bathe in. Sometimes mounted on a column or plinth.
A bridge that incorporates one or two spans that tilt at the abutments, to move up and out of the way of shipping. The most famous example of which is Tower Bridge, London.
A defensive embankment with three or more ditches.
A building or area where processes like bleaching, dressing, etc, are conducted under one roof.
Use where the intervening arcade is closed but timber-framed.
A house with an aisle on one side only.
A house with no row of posts between the central space and the aisles.
Mill for producing a smooth surface and edges on newly sawn timber.
An impulse water turbine comprising a wheel with hemispherical cups arranged around the circumference using high water pressure to revolve the wheel.

A prime mover in which a central wheel with curved vanes, enclosed in a chamber, receives water directed onto the curved vanes by a ring of fixed guide vanes, causing the wheel to rotate about its axis.
A building providing accommodation, dining facilities and recreation for non commissioned officers.
A channel or pipe providing water to a canal or other body of water.
A mill for grinding or crushing bones, in the process of making bone china, for example.

A rectangular or trapezoidal non-megalithic stony mound of Neolithic date, with human remains in cists rather than a large chamber. Mound construction and associated features vary considerably in type and complexity.

A Neolithic burial monument comprising a rectangular or trapezoidal stony mound which contains either a passage at one end with or without lateral chambers, or one or more smaller chambers entered from the side of the mound.
A kiln used for the drying of wood.
A district, suburb or quarter of a town or village adjacent to a fort, with the lowest legal status accorded to a built up area.
A high pole, painted with spiral stripes of different colours and decked with flowers, erected on an open space, often the village green, for merrymakers to dance around on May Day.
A cross erected in a village.

A monument consisting of a small (generally less than 100m diameter) subcircular enclosure with a narrow approach way consisting of parallel ditches (thus banjo shaped). Believed to be associated with stock management in the Later Prehistoric period.
A bridge carrying a road over land or water.
A short or long term residential home for people not requiring medical intervention or nursing care, usually for older people.
A hiding place for a (Roman Catholic) priest.
Chamber built into underside of a structure to exercise demolition.
A chemical works engaged in the production of Ammonium Perchlorate, a product used in the explosives industry.
A place where silica or silicate, the most common mineral component of rock, is extracted from the ground.
A three-sided structure for the production and storage of silage.
An institution for the imprisonment of vagrants and misdemeanants.

Feature, typically a ship, boat, aircraft or vehicle, deliberately sunk for recreational and diver educational purposes in inland bodies of water used as dive centres, such as lakes and water-filled quarries, or offshore as artificial reefs.
A works where bleach is manufactured.
A hearth for roasting metallic ore, usually non ferrous, before smelting.
Three storey house with a topshop; machinery powered by shafting through the upper floor.
A natural ditch the depth and/or width of which has been increased so as to prevent the progress of a tank or armoured vehicle.
A non-conformist minister's house.
A crane in which, during any alteration of radius, an automatic device causes the load to move horizontally.
A site with one or more defensive earthworks, often at a river crossing incorporating natural features which define parts of the curtilage.
An imprecise term used to describe large Iron Age settlements of town-like proportions.
A fighter satellite station watch office built to Air Ministry design drawing number 17658/40.

An emplacement housing mobile sound locating acoustic dishes/horns for the detection of incoming enemy aircraft and the triangulation of their positions so that they could be targeted by Anti aircraft guns.
A house consisting of a single storey open hall with a two storey domestic range attached to both ends forming an H shape.
An artificial mound created by the disposal of aggregate originally used as ballast in ships.
The residence of a canal worker.
A mill used to dress ore by means of a jigging machine.
A kiln used for the production of any of the soda group of alkalis by the heating of plant remains or salt.

A structure over an opening usually formed of wedge-shaped blocks of brick or stone held together by mutual pressure and supported at the sides; they can also be formed from moulded concrete/ cast metal. A component; use for free-standing structure only.
A factory where collars, for shirts and other garments, are manufactured.
A strong, fortified dwelling, of between two and four storeys. Occupied only in times of trouble built mainly in the border country of the North from the mid 14th to the 17th century.
A vault, often located under a chancel or chancel aisle, containing an altar and usually used for burial.
A labyrinthine garden feature, common during the 16th and 17th centuries, created by cutting shallow pathways into deep lawns.
A site containing slipways and associated buildings used specifically for the repair of ships and larger ocean-going craft.
An establishment for the preparation and selling of food to be consumed off the premises.
A site where large sheets of thin metal are manufactured.
A factory where hemp, the woody stalk of the hemp plant, used for the making of coarse cloth and cordage, was processed.
An ancilliary building, usually to provide gas for lighting a particular building (eg. railway stations, factories, etc) as opposed to public GAS WORKS.
A factory manufactoring caravans.
A building or buildings used for the manufacture of metal boxes or cases.
A rural school serving a number of villages, built in Cambridgeshire in the 1930s.
A farmstead where mostly detached buildings have developed around one side of an open cattle yard.
A channel for taking a rapidly flowing stream of water away from a canal lock, or away from the canal itself.
A factory where fruit and seed oil is produced by an oil machine.
The residence of a glover.

An anti aircraft battery armed with 3 inch rockets with a ceiling of 22,000 feet. Both single and multiple launchers were designed. Single launchers being used to defend vulnerable points such as coastal batteries with multiple launchers defending town.
A type of temporary bridge designed by Sir Donald C.Bailey during the Second World War.
An area of ground in which horses can be exercised.
A large store where wool is stored.
A building in which works of art are displayed for sale.
Horizontal masonry or timber work at the entrance to a dock.

An establishment where alcoholic and non alcoholic drinks are served, food may also be served. May be a an individual room within a larger multi purpose building such as a sports pavilion or a theatre.
A building on a river or canal in which the water levels are controlled.
A specialized form of truss bridge that extends or cantilevers from both sides of the pier, the inner 'arms' usually supporting a central span.
A site where gypsum and anhydrate is mined.
A table found in a garden, often made of stone.
A range of buildings used to house abandoned or stray dogs.
A building, within a gas works, housing a gas purifier.
A kiln in the form of a pit dug into the earth which was used for the the production of white coal prior to the Industrial Revolution.
A factory for processing rubber or manufacturing rubber goods, such as tyres.
A miniature railway on which targets can be placed to provide moving targets on a firing range.
A building or site used for the storage and distribution lighter than air gases for use in barrage balloons.
A building in which oxen are accommodated.
A building, on an airfield, used to house a fire engine designed to Air Ministry drawing number 12563/40.
Building for testing the condition and strength of textiles.
A cast iron hammer used for shingling iron or making heavy forgings.
A non-specialist hospital dealing in general medical and surgical treatment.
A small building used as a shelter by a shepherd.
A site where alum (hydrous sulphate or salt and alumina) is quarried.
A centre used by the Air Raid Precautions network to co-ordinate reports of air raids in an area.
A sacred area of a building or a consecrated piece of land.
An area of land consisting of the lord's demesne and of lands from whose holders he may exact certain fees, etc.
A manmade barrier built across a river in order to increase the depth of water.
A building combining a cow-house with crop storage space.
A heavy framework of parallel beams used to support a ship in dock.
A centre used by the Territorial Army, the volunteer reserve of the British army.
A mill in which barytes concentrates were ground to fine white powder, normally by use of flat millstones similar to those of a corn mill.
A building housing a Russian-style steam bath or banya.
A building, usually in a rural setting, with a range of facilities for the use of members.
A treadwheel using a donkey as motive power. Usually found operating wells.

A section of the water channel of a river, shut off above and below by lock gates provided with sluices to let water in and out and thus raise or lower boats from one level to another. Often found situated next to a weir.
A camping place set aside for the use of caravans.
A mill in which strands of yarn are twisted together to produce a strong thread with a uniform thickness.
An abbey of the Bridgettine double order of nuns and religious men.

A monument within a church or cathedral representing one of the stations of the cross. Usually images or pictures of successive incidents of the Passion, they are intended to be visited for meditation and prayer.
A barrier which rotates on an axis and is usually so arranged as to allow a person to pass through an opening only in one direction.
A house consisting of a single storey open hall with a two storey domestic range attached at one end, forming a T shape.
An explosive-proof vaulted chamber used for the storage or ordnance.
An often ornately decorated theatre for the performance of opera.
Use for complexes where services (eg. restaurants, shops) are provided in addition to facilities for buying petrol.
A stone slab, raised on stone or wooden piers, used for the display of fresh fish. Usually found in market places.
A defensive cattle enclosure added to fortified towers.
A place at a school where children receive medical advice, health checks and treatment.
An arrangement of railway tracks, stations and other buildings that together form a railway transport system.
A place where lead ore is extracted from an open cast mine.
A component of a salt works housing iron pans where the brine was evaporated above a furnace and flue. Such houses were lightly built in order to allow the heat and steam to escape.
Residence for retired people, often in the form of an apartment complex, differing from a nursing home as the residents live independently.
A large building used for the storage of grain.
Any building, group of buildings, or site in which antimony was smelted. Mainly 18th century.
A factory where tobacco was ground to form snuff.
A machine gun post designed by James Ruck constructed from hollow blocks and prefabricated concrete sheeting with loopholes allowing for a garrison of eight.
A 19th century glasshouse built specifically for the fostering of camellias.
A Roman sanctuary, devoted to the Graeco-Roman cult of Mithras.
A place of burial for members of the Religious Society of Friends, often known as Quakers.
skos:Concept.skos:altLabel: Religious Society Of Friends Burial Ground

skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: A building providing shelter for sheep and storage for fodder and shepherding equipment.
A building or site from which a watch can be kept to prevent the illegal import/export of goods.
A workshop or factory where the barrels of cannon are cast.
A private garden established primarily for growing vegetables and herbs for domestic consumption.
A large kitchen garden enclosed by a substantial wall, not usually adjacent to its associated house.

Standard dwelling of the non-ruling classes of Japan until the mid twentieth century. Minkas are timber-framed houses with mud-plastered panels and thatched roofs. The design varies from region to region. Minkas served as home as well as workplace.
A building or site used for the production of bricks and other items, from a clay with refractory properties.
A bell-shaped pit used in early coal mining. Use with functional type if known, eg. COAL WORKINGS.
Factory producing asbestos sheeting and or asbestos fibre.
A structure which protects a beach or harbour by breaking the force of the waves.
A floating structure designed to resist the force of waves.
A dwelling for the keeper of a canal wharf.
A site used for the extraction of metallic zinc by a variety of processes.
An often ornate wrought-iron bracket used to hang lamps outside public houses, shops, hotels and restaurants, etc.
An engine house used to pump water to the top of an ACCUMULATOR TOWER.
A site, including buildings and hardstandings, used for the storage and distribution of ammunition.
A stable found at a coaching inn where horses are housed.
A dedicated room for housing the organ feeder bellows, can be an underground chamber or a free-standing building.
A room containing copper or steel vessels in which hops are added to the basic beer mixture.
The residence and office of an archdeacon.
A building or area where stone is stored for industrial or agricultural use.
An inclined plane built to allow tanks to be loaded and unloaded between rolling stock on the railway network and vehicular low loaders.
A lodging house for apprentices learning a trade or profession. This accommodation was often provided in lieu of wages.
A building with a range of educational and recreational facilities for the exclusive use of its all-female membership.
A factory or works housing machinery used to produce stockings and socks, using mechanized knitting processes.

A concrete hut produced by the Ministry of Works as a cheaper alternative to the BCF Hut as any suitable wall cladding could be employed in its construction. Usually used to form barrack blocks on airfields from 1944 onwards.
A pool and ancilliary buildings used for the housing of dolphins.
Stone, brick or wooden steps or stairs found in a garden.
Garden steps covered in turf.
A long, narrow yard used for jousting.
A building housing transformers to convert AC electricity supply to DC supply for use by tramcars.
A type of windlass for drawing up ore.
A prepared area used for the game of netball.
A building or subterranean structure used for the storage of meat.
A protected parachute store similar in design to the 6351/37 except constructed wholly from reinforced concrete.
A small building used by the keeper of a castle, park, etc.
A factory or plant for the manufacture of ice using mechanized refrigeration techniques.
A site or establishment for the casting and refining of metallic copper.
A shaft, separate to the main working shaft, used to pump water out of the mine workings.
A building, usually associated with a hospital, where doctors live. Include blocks of self-contained flats.
A mill or works where needles were manufactured.

A two-storey, brick construction with a watch office and additional rooms given over to the meteorological section, including a forecast room and met store. A brick parapet on the roof differentiates it from 2328/39.
A toilet or toilets for public use.
A pumping station used in the production of hydraulic power, eg. in warehouse complexes, goods depots on railways, etc.
Mill incorporating water-powered hammers for beating brass sheet, etc. into vessels, pots, etc.
A factory for the assembly of bicycles.

Component part of a mungo and shoddy mill, where non-wool fibres from shredded material are destroyed by either soaking rags in an acid solution or rotating them in drums in a hot acidic gas followed by heat. The result is an all-wool product.
A mill in which poor quality woollen cloth was made from fibres produced by grinding light woollen rags.
A small structure comprising of a 'shelf' of wood or metal sitting on pillars and erected for the benefit of porters to allow them to rest their burdens.
A building or group of buildings designed for the breeding and rearing of animals, including fish and birds. Often include incubators and heated rooms.
A factory or works engaged in the manufacture of the explosive guncotton. They may be found as separate factories or form part of a cordite factory.
A purpose-built hall (usually 19th century) which was available for public hire and could be used for a variety of activities, eg. lectures, meetings, balls and concerts.
A bollard made from, or in the form of, a cannon barrel.
A hospital for the care of patients with incurable illnesses.
For the collection of money by charities, churches, etc.
A small building housing pilot's and locker rooms with flight offices and a watch office. The only known example was built at Tangmere.
A building or part of a building used for the storage of furniture or furniture related materials.
A stone-faced enclosure, with entrance closed by a floatable caisson or by gates, which can be pumped dry for inspection, maintenance, or repair of the hull or underwater fittings of a ship or ships.
Areas used for potato-growing.
A coin-operated meter receiving fees for parking a vehicle in a street, and indicating time allowed.

A structure to which a net filled with mail bags is attached. Situated next to railway lines, it allows mail to be collected by a train without it stopping, the bag being 'caught' by the train as it passed. Can also be used to 'catch' mail.
A structure indicated by the presence of post holes and of uncertain interpretation.
An elevated platform on which a criminal is executed.
A library which lends books (and sometimes other materials) to its members.
A prefabricated structure of reinforced concrete posts supporting a pitched roof frame with an infilling of sawdust concrete panels. Produced by Maycrete Ltd during WWII.
A mechanism used to turn a trolleybus around.
A place where two or more railway lines meet.
A machine used for the loading and unloading of grain to and from a warehouse

A glass sphere in a metal frame standing on a small pillar. A card is placed behind the sphere which focuses any sunlight, marking the card and thus indicating how many hours of sunlight there was on that day.
Small stone hearth set up in a shallow pit. Burns vegetation and coppiced twigs to produce potash.
A pond used for the rearing, breeding, sorting and storing of fish.
A private chapel for a royal court.
A steam powered winding gear used at a colliery or other mine.
An instrument of punishment, in which the offender was placed in a sitting position in a timber frame, with holes to confine the ankles and wrists between two planks.
A CRUCK HOUSE where the cruck blades are truncated and joined by a collar beam, above which is a separate roof construction.
Grassland fertilized by allowing floodwater to cover it in winter.
Textile mill producing calico, ie. coarse, unbleached cotton cloth.
An institution for the detention of prisoners, surrounded by a wall and/or fence as a barrier to escape. The level of security depends on the category of inmate detained.
A building containing a small stone cylindrical furnace, eg. used for tin smelting in Cornwall.
Central two-storeyed tower surmounted by an octagonal glazed control room giving a 360 degree view. Flanked by single-storey wings.
Works where yarn is prepared prior to spinning.
A crane mounted on wheels and/or rails, used for the unloading of ships' cargoes.
Engineering workshop housing specialized machinery such as lathes, presses, etc., for making machines.
A house occupied by an employee of a waterworks. Usually found in association with a pumping station or waterworks.
A path that is roofed over.
A mill for grinding or crushing bones, in the process of making bone china, for example.

Nowadays a hospital block where patients suffering from psychiatric disorders receive medical and surgical treatment. Formerly a place where psychiatric patients were primarily segregated from other patients in a hospital.
A building in which goods were kept prior to being cleared by customs officers.

An artificially constructed wall with recessed and projecting grips for hands and feet and places to attach ropes. Used for practising rock climbing. If the wall is situated within a sports centre use term from Components thesaurus.
A pit where calcium oxide (Quicklime) has been hydrated to produce calcium hydroxide, known as slaked lime.
A road block formed by placing curved rails, "hairpins", in sockets in the road surface.
A building housing a number of power looms.
A site where the process of combing, the preparatory process for long wools, takes place.
A place where gold is worked into articles or products.
A natural or man-made gap in vegetation or other combustible material that acts as a barrier to slow or stop the progress of a fire.

A well or spring, possessing religious or otherwise ritualistic significance, around which a structure, such as a niche, wall or shelter, has been constructed. In the case of the water source being a natural spring, double-index with SPRING.
A pulley block and metal ring used to guide a line or rope and cause it to run easily without chafing.
An Anglo-Saxon fortified town or other defended site, not necessarily urban.
A priory of the female Order of Knights Hospitallers.
A golf course, usually situated on or near the coast, consisting of sand dunes with few trees or water obstacles.
A prepared area of ground used to play the game of golf on.
An establishment used for the manufacture of jacquards and dobbys, which are textile loom components that control the weaving of complicated or figured patterns.
A meeting hall, or sale room in a town, for manufacturers and traders.
A lock at the point where two waterways join together.
A building used for storing tree bark.
A stone on which plague victims placed vinegar-disinfected money to pay for food left for them by the townspeople.
A hospital where people would pay a subscription in order to recieve treatment when ill.
A site where terracotta, made from weathered clay and grog, was manufactured.
A complex of buildings used for the manufacture of pottery.
A Neolithic monument comprising an irregularly circular enclosing ditch, interrupted by frequent causeways, and often accompanied by an internal bank, also causewayed.
A fort with projecting bastions, which came into use from the 16th century onwards.
A works or factory where shells or projectiles were machined before they were dispatched to a filling factory to be filled with explosives.
A building or structure from which observation is kept of the approach of danger.

A subsidiary enclosure externally attached to an enclosure of known or unknown date and function. The annexe is generally smaller than, and secondary to, the main enclosure. Use more specific site type where known. Do not use for Roman military sites.
A vertical structure, sometimes made of steel, often used in the manufacture of cement. Material is loaded at the top, burnt in the middle and removed at the bottom.
A twin-shafted kiln, circular or oval in plan, consisting of a fire chamber, pre-heater and cooling chamber.
A training college where workers can attend classes in vocational subjects. The classes are often day-release and sanctioned by the employer.
A structure extending into the sea for the purpose of preventing further movement of washed up sand and shingle.
A place of worship for Christadelphians, a fundamentalist sect founded in America in the late 1840s who rejected the trinity and awaited the second coming of Christ.
A structure inclined towards the water on which a ship may be built or lowered into the water.
The residence and small-scale workshop of a hosier.
A common type of lock in the form of a chamber with gates on either side.
A building used for a variety of administrative purposes, usually at a military base.
A building used for the treatment of victims of chemical, gas or other forms of contamination.
A firm beach or foreshore used for landing and loading of ships and other vessels. In more recent times hards have been reinforced with concrete.
Buildings and works around a mine shaft with an artificial embankment on which the winding gear etc, is located.
A commercial bakery or bread factory. If domestic use BAKEHOUSE.
A friary belonging to the Pied Friars also known as Friars of Blessed Mary or St Mary de Arens.
A mound used to elevate buildings associated with a fishery e.g. smoke houses, above the level of a flood plain.
A place where boats are built and stored.
A house consisting of a single storey open hall with a two storey domestic range attached at one end, forming a T shape.
A factory in which logs are converted to timber by running them through a series of saws.
Use with form of extraction where known. Also use MINE and other ores extracted where relevant, eg. SILVER MINE.
An oven used in the coal industry for the recovery of gas, tar and other by-products of the coking process. Late 19th century-20th century.
A large free-standing arch erected to commemorate a triumph or victory.
A factory or works principally engaged in the manufacture of the explosive Gelignite.
A building or set of rooms, primarily of the 18th century, in which social gatherings and balls were held.
A purpose-built dwelling for the supervisor of a factory, mine or other industrial complex.
A hand operated mechanism used to raise and move water, liquids, compressed gases etc.
Building or buildings housing equipment for generating heat for a building complex.
A place from where rescue missions are co-ordinated and casualties treated after an accident, offensive action or disaster.
A yard for pigs.
A fortified keep in the form of a tower, used as a last refuge or defence. If a component of a larger site, use KEEP.
A building where radium is used in the treatment of cancer.
A training school where ballet is taught.
When a secondary mineral, use term for product type, eg. LEAD MINE.
A building containing apparatus for the removal of large pieces of detritus from a water supply.
A sign used by the Air Raid Precautions network to assist in identifying vital equipment and resources in the event of an air raid or to aid movement during blackouts.
A public institution for the care and protection of children without parents.

An institution for the imprisonment of prisoners who can be trusted to serve their sentence without likelihood of escape and of being a threat to the public. There is no physical barrier designed to prevent absconding.

A Roman under-floor heating system in which hot air heated by a stoked furnace, flowed through channels, created by either raising the floor on pillars of brick and tile or cutting channels into the concrete floor and tiling over them.
A pedestrianized shopping street, or a more complex arrangement of shopping 'squares' and walkways.
A dam and sluice combination, associated with an aqueduct, for the extraction of water from a river to feed a reservoir or water treatment plant.
A kiln for roasting ore.
A type of calcining kiln used in the processing of iron ore.
The premises of an agricultural merchant where agricultural equipment, animal feed and fertilizers can be bought.
A prepared area, traditionally grass, where tennis is played.
A site where metal springs are manufactured.
A site used for all the processes associated with the manufacture of roof, floor or decorative tiles.
A cross found in a market place.
A lime kiln where the fuel is not mixed with the limestone but burnt below it.
A place where ceramic tiles are manufactured.
A building where masts are made and stored.

The room housing the looms in a domestic handloom weavers cottage. In general, wool loomshops were above the living quarters, whereas cotton loomshops were often below in a cellar, since the floor was usually kept damp to aid the weaving of the cotton.
A place where silverware is manufactured.
A large wooden structure built alongside the edge of a canal where narrow boats may lie for the loading and unloading of goods.
A drainage structure that extends across and beneath roadways, canals or embankments.
A shop where fish and chips are sold.
A head of water raised in a conduit system.
Three storey house with a topshop; machinery powered by shafting through the upper floor.
A bridge in which one leaf may be retracted in a horizontal plane, passing on rollers over or under the adjacent fixed leaf.
A device on an airfield for securing aircrafts when parked outside in order to prevent major movement due to the weather or other conditions.
A factory where cars are manufactured.
A friary belonging to the Franciscan order. Includes houses of both Friars Minor and Friars Observant or Capuchins.
A mixed house of nuns and religious men of the Benedictine order.
A tower built to display a large clock.
A brass manufacturing complex incorporating battery mill furnaces, hammers, etc.
A workshop or factory where brass articles are made by casting molten material into a mould.

A strategic food store, directly operated by, or on behalf of, the government. The stores were used to store a variety of foodstuffs. They were in operation from the end of the Second World War until the early 1990's.
A steam driven winding engine house for raising coal to the surface.
A man made ditch designed to obstruct the progress of a tank or armoured vehicle. Ditches were often reveted with concrete or wood.
A processing house where surplus water is removed from gunpowder after incorporating.

A structure, often sited underground, from where it was intended to conduct the business of government in the event of nuclear war. Sub RSGs were introduced between the RSGs and local authorities to allow the RSGs to focus on strategic direction.
A site incorporating all of the production processes for the manufacture of plaster.
Small settlement with no ecclesiastical or lay administrative function.
A temporary hostel built for industrial or transport workers; for example, railway workers' hostels were provided for engine drivers.
An establishment where deaf people receive education, training and social support.

A multi-storey, fortified hall house with one of the crosswings being raised in the form of a crenellated tower. Permanently occupied, they date from the mid 14th to the 17th century and are found mainly in the border counties of the North of England.
A bridge in which one leaf may be retracted in a horizontal plane, passing on rollers over or under the adjacent fixed leaf.

A building or site used to train civilians and members of the services in the skills designed to protect the civilian population during times of war. Could also be used during times of national emergency.
Establishments responsible for the research into and the design, development and manufacture of chemical weapons
A communal dining room, especially in schools, colleges and monasteries.
A site where weapons and/or explosives are tested experimentally, or are routinely tested as part of a manufacturing quality control process.
A factory where brushes are manufactured. Use for all types of brush.
A double lock placed between tidal water and a canal, etc..
A light, ornamental building or structure situated close to the sea.
A building containing a number of single roomed cells used for detaining prisoners.
A mill used for the sizing and drying of warp threads before they were wound onto warp beams as part of the power-weaving process.
An artificial, sometimes temporary, platform on which helicopters can take off and land.
An informal garden attached to a cottage where flowers, vegetables and fruit trees are grown.
A factory for the manufacture of heels for the shoe making trade.
A pillbox built to a design drawn up by the Air Ministry. Usually found on or near airfields.
A building or structure in which bricks are made.
The residence of a master ropemaker.
A freestanding staff upon which a flag is hung.
A common type of lock in the form of a chamber with gates on either side.
A military storage aircraft hangar designed in 1937. It has a curved profile and is constructed from steel ribs supporting a concrete skin. The roof is covered with earth and turf.
A building used for the administration of a squadron.
Place for people who underwent regular blood letting.
A barrel-making workshop or factory, found in conjunction with a number of industries.
A site used for the manufacturing of steel. Use more specific type where known.
A specialist hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of urinary disorders and diseases.
A specialist hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of heart disorders and diseases.
A place of worship for Particular Baptists, a Calvinistic Baptist denomination who believe in predestination.

A place of worship for Strict Baptists, a sect who broke away from the Particular Baptists and kept up the practice of denying communion to non members after the union of General and Particular Baptists was formed in 1891.
A prison for the confinement of people who owe money.
An open grating of wrought iron, bronze or wood, forming a screen to a door, window or other opening, or used as a divider.
A purpose built trench designed to prevent the successful landing of enemy glider-borne and airborne forces.
A two-storey watch office similar in design to drawing number 1959/34 but constructed completely from concrete. A large, almost square, ground plan with a central observation tower.

In the glass industry, a furnace of Lorraine Type, comprising a central rectangular melting furnace with ancillary structures at each corner, adjacent to the fires. Post-Mediaeval until superceded by coal-fired furnaces.
A factory where matresses are made.
A factory where pencils are manufactured.
A factory or works used for the production of turpentine, wood alcohol and similar chemicals by the distillation of pulped wood.
A radar station with sets operating on a wavelenght of 1.5m established to provide radar plotting of both shipping and aircraft movements.
skos:Concept.skos:prefLabel: Coast Defence Chain Home Low Station

skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: Temporary settlement relating to the construction of railways, viaducts, dams, etc.
A factory where hats are manufactured.
A form of lock on a river, which increased the depth upstream and had a gated opening.
Non-pavilion type of attached ward block.
A waterwheel where the water enters at the same level as the axle.
A settlement showing evidence for one or more hut circles, enclosed by a distinct boundary ditch, wall, earth rampart or similar barrier. Characteristic of the later prehistoric period.
A textile mill where crepe is manufactured.Crepe is a fine cloth particularly silk or mixture of silk and cotton.

An operations room, built to drawing number 367/41, to control the lighting arrays of the DREM type of bombing decoy in use during the Second World War. Unlike earlier designs it was surface built and then covered in earth to protect against flooding.
A small workshop, employing up to 10 men, working on hand-operated carding engines and hand jennies, spinning yarn for handloom weavers.
A fence that indicates the limit of an area or a piece of land.
An alloy of tin, antimony and copper used as a replacement for pewter.
A raised platform from which an officer can address or review his troops.
A building where mineral jelly was stored. Mineral jelly was used as a stabilizer in the manufacture of the explosive, cordite.
A type of concrete bridge, developed in the 20th century, that consists of reinforced concrete deck slabs that sit on the supporting bridge piers and/or abutments.
A machine used to raise and lower miners to and from the pit bottom.
A searchlight battery used to light a beach.
A circular bank of stones and turf, sometimes accompanied by a ditch, surrounding a natural outcrop of rock, usually a tor, or an earthfast boulder.
A wall, usually of reinforced concrete, designed to obstruct the progress of a tank or armoured vehicle
An earthwork or structure on a rifle range used to mark a set distance from the rifle butts (usually at 50 or 100 yard intervals).
An airfield, and associated structures, used by one or more bomber squadrons.

A type of prefabricated house erected, to 11 approved designs, as part of the Temporary Housing Programme, between 1944 and 1948. This scheme was devised to relieve the post-war housing shortage at a time when conventional materials were unavailable.
A shallow place in a river or other stretch of water, where people, animals and vehicles may cross.

A natural spring located within a, usually small, man-made structure, such as a niche or a box. The structure is so placed to accomodate use for a specific non-religious function, such as communal bathing.
A laithe with an attached house.
A grain grinding mill in which the meal is ground into flour between revolving metal rolls.
A site where copper ore is extracted directly from the surface of the ground.
A settlement, usually enclosed, on a sloping hillside containing a number of oval or circular scopped house floors separated by walls or unexcavated ridges.
A building adjacent to a monastery where alms were distributed to the poor.

An earthwork feature used by hunters to trap deer comprising a steep ditch into which the deer are chased with an enclosure to hold them at one end, known from the Isle of Rum and a debateable example in Cumbria.
A factory or works used for the production of turpentine, wood alcohol and similar chemicals by the distillation of pulped wood.
An area of agriculturally used land, which is divided into small, elongated, rectangular fields running parallel to each other.
Small tower projecting from a castle wall, or other fortified wall. Allows defenders to fire along the length of the wall.
A specialist hospital where women receive medical and surgical treatment.
A place where wigs, hair-pieces and hair extensions are made and sold.
A detached block within a hospital complex used as sleeping accommodation for patients.
The masonry beneath a lock gate, sometimes projecting several feet from the gate.
A place where metal-cutting hand files were made.
A place where graphite is extracted.
A water pump situated at the side of a road or track for use by travellers and their animals.
A hiding place for stores, often underground, used by smugglers.
Circular spoil heap surrounding a wide central depression, the entrance to a mine shaft.
A building where animals are slaughtered.
A building or site used to produce alkaline chemicals by controlled reactions.
A medieval court established for the administration of forest law.

A small dispersal WWII military aircraft hangar featuring an "A" shaped steel frame clad with corrugated iron; end doors were supported by outriggers when open.Typically used on aircraft storage units or satellite landing grounds. Variations in size.
A horticultural site where trees, shrubs and plants are grown for sale and transplanting elsewhere.
An open area of prepared ground used for practising putting with golf clubs.
An area where the sport of wrestling takes place.

A four-storey RNAS control tower. The first floor contained offices for the commander flying and meteorological offices and the upper two floors, in the form of a central tower, provided offices for air traffic control.
A structure used for the roasting or drying of chicory.
An area on post-war military airfields for parking aircraft on quick reaction alert to allow immediate access to the runway. Abbreviation ORP.
A massive structure designed to transfer canal boats between different canal or river navigations, eg. Anderton boat lift.
A building or room used for holding, viewing, identifying or examining dead bodies prior to burial or cremation.
A hospital building of uncertain function. Use more specific type if known.
A farmstead where the farmhouse and working buildings are attached and in-line. They can comprise the extension of linear farmsteads.
A tunnel carrying a railway beneath the surface of the ground.
A calciner used in arsenic production from the 1820s to the 1950s featuring a distinctive, slowly rotating hearth.
A two-storey watch office, built to Air Ministry drawing number 1959/34 but with slight design modifications as detailed in drawing number 1960/34.
An extractive pit or pits, usually 2.5m square by 2m deep dug to extract tin ore in areas where streamworking is not possible. Usually dug along a vein rather than across it.
A building, factory or works which was engaged in the manufacture of refining saltpetre. Often part of a gunpowder works.
A building where miners could improve their knowledge by attending lectures and using the reading room facilities.
A shallow pond containing salt water and used for the manufacture of salt through the evaporation process. For metal vessels associated with the DIRECT BOILING and SLEECHING SALT WORKS use SALT PAN.
A type of textile mill found in Lancashire in the 19th century. Small businesses paid the owner rent for space for their machines, and power from the mill engine or waterwheel.
A farmstead where mostly detached buildings have developed around four sides of an open cattle yard.
Levelled or terraced area of ground presumed to have been the site of a house or hut.
The space enclosed between the gates and side-walls of a lock.
A building in which moist guncotton is dried by warm air for use in nitroglycerine manufacture.
A large building where iron is stored.
A place of worship for the followers of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter Day Saints
An establishment providing care for the terminally ill.
An engineering workshop for the manufacture and repair of springs.
A wall in a flower or kitchen garden, containing conduits or pipes for heating the wall.
A building or complex where soft skins are produced by tanning with alum.
An area within a hospital used for the isolation of patients. Patients were isolated if they had an infectious disease or suffered from a psychiatric illness.
A large wooden gate, positioned at either end of a canal or river lock, equipped with sluices to let water through.
A Neolithic burial monument comprising a stone-built chamber within a rectangular or trapezoidal earthen mound.
A Neolithic burial monument comprising a stone-built chamber within an earthen mound. Use more precise term where known.
A Neolithic burial monument comprising a stone-built chamber within a circular or sub-circular earthen mound. See RELIGIOUS, RITUAL AND FUNERARY Class List for context.
A site where methane gas, released by coal mining, is collected and processed.
A building where non-commissioned aircrew are housed.
A bridge whose deck is directly supported from pylons by straight cables without vertical suspenders.
A public recreational complex centred around an open-air swimming pool. Use SWIMMING POOL as a component of LIDO.
A meeting hall, or sale room in a town, for manufacturers and traders.
A flat slab of stone used to provide a level surface from which to measure the height of racehorses at a meeting, as part of the handicapping and anti fraud systems.
Originally built as a family house. Converted into flats during the 19th or 20th century.
Pairs of canal gates (also called Brindley gates) designed to rapidly shut off a section of a canal to prevent flooding
A component part of a treadmill crane, the shed is used to enclose the treadwheel.

A building designed specifically for handling tobacco. This may be a bonded warehouse containing facilities for removing tobacco leaves from the hogsheads in which they were imported, and pressing them.
Moorings for a seaplane not part of a seaplane base.
A purpose-built dwelling for the supervisor of a factory, mine or other industrial complex.
A calciner used in arsenic production from the 1820s to the 1950s featuring a distinctive, slowly rotating hearth.
An area of land enclosed by two parallel ditches. Use with specific shaped enclosure where known.
An area of land enclosed by one or several boundary ditches. Double index with a term to indicate the shape of the enclosure where known.
A structure providing protection against the weather at tram stops.
A canal tunnel built with one or more integral towpaths
A tunnel with a canal running through it.

The first transportable aircraft hangar developed by the RFC/RAF, which comprised a kit of timber and canvas that could be assembled in 48 hours. The canvas doors open one end only. Also known as Type H hangar.

Usually dating from the early 20th century these cabinets, sited alongside public highways, were used for the distribution of electricity for street lighting control and later for domestic use. In Wolverhampton these boxes also serviced the tram system.
An imprecise term used to describe large Iron Age settlements of town-like proportions.
A site with one or more defensive earthworks, often at a river crossing incorporating natural features which define parts of the curtilage.
An ancilliary workshop used for repairs, etc.
An 18th century garden building, designed in the style of a classical Ionic temple, used for standing or sitting in.
A decorative garden ornament, usually of stone, in the form of a wide, shallow dish.
A site used for the extraction of metallic zinc by a variety of processes.
A tree-lined way or approach where the trees have been cut into various forms and shapes.
A laithe with an attached house.
The residence of a storekeeper of naval ordnance.
A room designed or suitable for dancing.

Area in a deer park where a single deer was chased by dogs over a set distance, with bets made on the outcome. It usually includes a stand (for viewing) and can also include three distance markers, a finishing post and a ditch behind the last post.
A mill with machinery used to cut slabs of metal into rods, or thin sections, for use in nail making or wire drawing.
A house with windows and doors on one side only; often built facing inwards onto a burgage plot, or sometimes on a steep slope, with no apertures on the uphill side.
A ditch constructed to surround a town for defensive purposes.
A form of lock on a river, which increased the depth upstream and had a gated opening.

An area of a port, dock or harbour, often including buildings for passport control and customs, where passengers and vehicles using hovercraft services can embark/disembark and where supplies can be taken on board.

A solid concrete or stone base on which a machine (often an engine and therefore called the engine bed, forming part of an engine house) was mounted to power an industrial process. Dates from the 19th century.
A workshop where tapestries were made.
Use for speculatively built 19th century "model dwellings", rather than those built by a philanthropic society.
A house built by a local authority.
A type of back to back house built on a hillside, of four storeys and with entrances at different levels.
Covered area for making large engineered constructions such as sections of ships or bridges.

A curved military aircraft hangar produced in 1939. The frame is steel which is then clad with steel sheeting and reinforced concrete and typically covered with a thin layer of concrete, earth and turf.
A pit or tank where the chemicals used in tanning are washed from the animal hides.
A commercial premises supplying ships with provisions.
A wall with niches in a CREMATORIUM to display the urns containing ashes. Use only when related to funerary site.
A factory where rock gypsum is ground into a powder used in the production of plaster.
A group of cairns in close proximity which are predominantly funerary or ritual in nature.
A system of artificial or natural drains and ditches used to drain off surplus water.

A four-storey RNAS control tower. The first floor contained offices for the commander flying and meteorological offices and the upper two floors, in the form of a central tower, provided offices for air traffic control.
A hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of sailors and/or their families. For Royal Naval seamen use ROYAL NAVAL HOSPITAL.
A place where tin ore is washed using a stream as the water source.
Also use with other metal ores extracted and MINE where relevant.
A large tank used for soaking alumina-bearing shale in water and chemicals, the initial stage in the alum-making process.

A building where fish are stored. Often taking the form of a single storey building with one room, but also may provide living accommodation for a fisherman above. Found mainly in the South West of England.

A building or tower used to communicate information to shipping or other stations using signals such as flags, fires or lights. Roman signal stations took the form of a stone tower surrounded by a ditched enclosure and were used to warn of Saxon raids.
A building within a transport terminal, often associated with the registration and clearing of incoming and outgoing passengers or freight.
A free-standing house, not joined to another on either side.
A linear earthwork, usually a bank accompanied by a ditch, which runs across rather than along an area or ridge of higher ground.
A workshop used by a joiner; a craftsman working with wood and producing more ornate work than that of a carpenter.
A metal structure supporting high powered lights.
An inclined plane with a cradle designed to lift a ship from the water onto a slip.
A balance engine used to replenish the water levels of a river by transferring water from a reservoir or other supply.
An underground vertical cylindrical structure for the storage and launching of ballistic missiles.
A site where traditional public shows, in which the display of exotic animals, combined with feats of agility and comedy, were held.
A site where clay is mined from the ground.
A modified Nissen hut, based on drawing number (2900/43), used for the repair packing and storage of inflatable liferafts.
A factory where furniture is manufactured.
A garden featrue where several allees radiate from a single point (usually the house). French for 'Goose Foot'
A reinforced wall designed to reflect the blast from an explosion. Often found associated with powder magazines, pillboxes and air raid shelters.
The residence of a herder.
A building housing washing facilities and toilets. The term occurs mainly in a military context.
A type of GARDEN HOUSE situated on an island in a garden lake or canal or, more generally, by any waterside.
Workshop for placing handles on mugs, teapots, etc.
Building housing apparatus for testing chain links.
A hut provided as accommodation for hop pickers and may also be know as a Hop Pickers' Hut
A factory, where preserves such as jam and marmalade, are manufactured.
A small dye works, often associated with a CALICO PRINTING WORKS.
Works producing a refractory clay, kaolin. An essential raw material of porcelain and some types of papermaking.
Building housing the machinery for the shredding and grinding of wood in running water and pressing of the resulting fibres into a pulp.
A court established in England and Wales by Parliament in 1846 to decide minor civil disputes.
A circular arrangement of spaced stone uprights set within a high bank, often interrupted by a formal entrance gap.
A wide street, traditionally lined with trees.
A cluster of piles for mooring a vessel.
A centre attached to a prison where families and friends can visit with the inmates.
Reformatory established under the Inebriates Acts 1879-1900 for repeat alcohol related offenders
A building found in conjunction with a WATERMILL, used for the drying of corn after harvesting, with a slatted drying floor set above a kiln.
A kiln used for the drying of wood.
A house of friars of the order of St Dominic. Also known as Friars Preachers or 'Black Friars'.
A place where processed cloth is cut for use as garments or soft furnishings, etc.
Mill for grinding bark usually for use in the tanning industry. Use with power type(s), eg. WATERMILL where known.
A factory that manufactures watches.
A factory where pencils are manufactured.
A garden building, octagonal in plan, designed in the style of a classical temple, used for standing or sitting in.
Ore hearth specifically for the refining of silver.
A zinc smelting furnace patented by William Champion of Bristol in 1738 for the reduction of zinc from zinc oxide by means of condensing.
A training college for the instruction of military trainees in the theory and practice of warfare.
A prepared slope with rails on which boats can be transferred from one canal to another at a higher or lower level. The boats can either be floated in a caisson or carried in a cradle or sling.
A common type of lock in the form of a chamber with gates on either side.
An institution for the detention of prisoners considered to be a major threat to public safety and/or to the security of the nation.
An uncovered area, surrounded or partially surrounded by buildings.
A cable railway with ascending and descending cars counterbalanced.
A workshop or factory unit where small or light goods are manufacture without the need for large-scale industrial machinery.
A building designed to house insects.
A site used for the production and/or working of glass.
A building containing celestial telescopes in which astronomical or meteorological phenomena may be observed.
A temporary brick building, based on drawing number (2901/43), used for the repair, packing and storage of inflatable liferafts.
A pumping station used as part of a clean water supply system.
A hospital for the treatment of venereal disease.
A series of locks usually with short reaches between them allowing boats to travel up and down a steep incline.
A building where the administrative functions of a Trade Union are carried on.
Use only where evidence is specific, ie. copper/tin alloy. For working of copper based alloys of unknown composition use COPPER WORKING SITE.
An underground chamber, store room or passage.
Underground chambers and stone passages of Iron Age date found in South West England.

A multi-storey, fortified hall house with one of the crosswings being raised in the form of a crenellated tower. Permanently occupied, they date from the mid 14th to the 17th century and are found mainly in the border counties of the North of England.
An inn temporarily used for the performance of plays and other public entertainment.
A building for the storage of ammunition and other military stores.
An existing factory that was converted for use as aircraft works in the run up to or during the Second World War.
A light anti aircraft position, usually open-walled and built of concrete, brick or sandbags used to emplace one or more machine guns mounted on pintels.
A cross erected by the side of the road.
A brick, stone or iron receptacle for baking bread or other food in.
A factory where cars are manufactured.
An indoor court where the ancient and complex sport of real tennis is played, eg. the court at Hampton Court Palace.
A settlement site enclosed within a timber palisade.
Sorting offices constructed during the Second World War designed to rapidly move goods from the vulnerable docks and ports via the rail network.
A site or building used to co-ordinate Air-Sea Rescue operations.
A stone set up on a road or path to mark the miles from or to a place.
A building housing a flight simulator designed to air ministry drawing number 10040/41.
A site, usually including hardstandings and associated buildings, used for the storage of military vehicles.
A large, rectangular open space at the centre of a Roman town, incorporating public spaces and a market area.
A circular bank surrounding an area where burials were placed.
A training establishment for gunnery personnel.
A hospital where patients would bathe daily in the sea or in indoor salt-water swimming baths.
A building used for the daily administration of that branch of the RAF dealing with training pilots.
A factory where musical organs are manufactured.
A covered area used for the drying of animal hides.
A framework used as a support upon which fruit-trees or climbing plants are trained.
A vault shaped trellis on which climbing plants are trained.

A well or spring, possessing religious or otherwise ritualistic significance, around which a structure, such as a niche, wall or shelter, has been constructed. In the case of the water source being a natural spring, double-index with SPRING.
A factory where seaplanes are manufactured.

A fairly regular system of small rectangular fields. Examples may date from the middle Bronze Age to the Roman period. The word 'Celtic' carries no chronological or cultural connotations in this context.
A bridge that incorporates one or two spans that tilt at the abutments, to move up and out of the way of shipping. The most famous example of which is Tower Bridge, London.
A small crane fixed to the wall of a warehouse or similar building.

A prefabricated structure consisting of sectional timber framed units that were bolted together. The structure was clad with weatherboarding and had a felted roof. They were used as temporary accommodation on airfields. Also see 'Type A'
A site where clay is both extracted and fired to produce bricks.
Vertical screens made of wood or steel framing mounted on concrete blocks were built to protect airships from cross winds when entering or leaving the airship sheds.
For the storage and recharging of battery-powered miners lamps.
A site where cementstone nodules are extracted under ground.

A type of large permanent military aircraft hangar with a curved steel frame and storage annexes on its side used in World War II. It was intended for storage purposes on Aircraft Storage Unit stations.
A deep pit used for the burial of plague victims.
A pillbox built to a design drawn up the chief engineer of Scottish Command
A refractory lined furnace in which an electric arc is struck between the electrode and the metal to be melted.
A place of worship for followers of the Pentecost (ie. emphasising the gifts of the Holy Spirit).
A workshop for the manufacturing of furniture.
A castle surrounded by two or more lines of walled fortifications.
A clamp in which alum shale was burnt in the initial stage of processing.
An area of hardstanding for parking aircraft, in a state of readiness, usually around the perimeter of an airfield.

A building used for the preparatory processes in which long and short staple flax fibres were separated by passing through combs. Flax dressing or 'heckling' shops may be located both on and off mill sites.
A small transportable hangar built by the Teesdie Bridge and Engineering Company. Mainly used on RNAS airfields for folding wing aircraft.
A well with an unusually high mineral content that combined with extensive periods of evaporation may give objects a stony exterior. Once believed to have been caused by magic or witchcraft.
A raised lawn in a garden or park.
Based on a typical 18ft span, 40ft long temporary brick hut but with two bay windows in the front elevation, one for the watch office and one for the chief instructor.
A structure used for the production of hydraulic power. A head of water was raised at the top of the tower by means of pumps. Used for powering machinery.
A short trench used to protect troops or to provide defensive fire from, often dug for practice purposes.
A factory or building where furniture is upholstered.
Fixed instrument to measure altitude of stars and planets.
A factory where gloves are manufactured.
A place where graphite is extracted.
A large shop supplying many kinds of goods from various departments.
An mill in which manganese was ground to a powder between two horizontal millstones.
A jettied house where the overhanging upper storey runs along the entire length of one side.
A mine yielding rock salt.
The hull of a dismantled ship used as a prison.
An area of a site or building providing a stable base for the firing of artillery pieces.
A room in which a judge sits to hear cases and undertake other official proceedings which are not of a sufficient importance to be brought into court.
Term used by the RAF to describe an open walled structure built of concrete, brick or sandbags which enclosed one or more machine-guns mounted on pintels for light anti-aircraft and ground defence.
An area within a building (usually the barn or stable) for storing husks from the grain crop (chaff) for animal feed after it has been threshed and winnowed in the barn.
A dome shaped structure, with an aperture open to the sky, used to house a telescope.
A small gateway cut through the curtain wall or its flanking towers. Used primarily as an outlet for counter-attacking forces.
Production of high quality steel by reheating cementation steel in a refractory crucible.
An establishment used for the manufacture of jacquards and dobbys, which are textile loom components that control the weaving of complicated or figured patterns.
A house or shelter for the storage and/or launching of boats.
A managed small wood or thicket of underwood grown to be periodically cut to encourage new growth providing smaller timber.
A site where concrete and concrete products are manufactured from a mixture of cement and aggregate.
A lock where the gates rise vertically. Rarely found on canals but common on navgable rivers in the Fens, particularly the river Nene.
An industrial complex concerned with the manufacture of gas for domestic use from coal and oil.

A type of military aircraft hangar of the Cold War, hardened and therefore protected against the effects of nuclear weapons. It comprises a semi-circular structure built of corrugated-steel supporting a reinforced-concrete skin. Three NATO designs.
An inhumation burial in which the body is covered by a shroud, placed in a coffin of stone, wood or lead and covered with gypsum, plaster or lime. Roman and early Medieval.
A pit or enclosed area used for cockfighting.

Blocks of solid concrete, in the shape of a round bottomed cone usually 2 feet 6 inches across x 2 feet 9 inches high. Buoys were mainly used in road blocks intended to impede enemy movement in the event of invasion.
An external structure used to sit on.
Building used for field studies and outdoor pursuits in the countryside and in an urban context.
A bell mounted on an anchored vessel, buoy, headland, rock etc and rung as a warning to mariners in foggy weather.
A workshop used for the small-scale production of leather goods.

Name given to a workhouse after 1929. The Local Government Act of 1929 abolished Poor Law Unions and Guardians, and control passed to public assistance authorities run by county boroughs and county councils. Lasted until 1948 when poor laws were repealed.
A linear open working along a lode vein, worked directy from the surface. Survives as a gully or ravine, normally with closed ends.
An establishment where tickets/reservations for events, journeys or entrance to a site can be purchased.
A separate residence for guests, a house on a private estate or a monastery building specifically for receiving visitors.

A high status building of the medieval period, consisting of a hall and attached room at first floor level with rooms below possibly for storage or living accommodation for a lower status family. The first floor was accessed by an external staircase.

A railway, usually by the sea, linking the beach with the cliff top. Various mechanisms were used the most common being that the cars were attached to a cable and winding drum and were balanced so that one travelled up, as the other came down.
To mark the end of a turnpike road.

Blocks of solid concrete, in the form of cylinders usually 2 feet across x 2 feet 6 inches or 3 feet high. Cylinders were mainly used in road blocks intended to impede enemy movement in the event of invasion.
An institution for the imprisonment and training of 16-21 year olds first established officially in 1908. Replaced by Youth Custody Centres in 1982.
A peat-based garden where various types of heather are grown.
A building where samples of corn were sold or auctioned during the early to mid 19th century. When not in use, between market days, the buildings were used as public halls.
A site where products containing sugar or honey, such as cakes, sweets, crystallized fruits or jam, were manufactured.
A lift powered by an hydraulic system.
A very long trough laid between the rails of a railway track to allow a suitably equiped steam engine to scoop up water whilst in motion.
A school for instruction in the art of horsemanship.
A windmill with a rotating cap containing the windshaft, and a stationary body in the form of a tower.
A building in which apparatus measuring the amount of water supplied/used is housed.

A long narrow rectangular earthwork enclosure of Neolithic date, usually defined by a bank and ditch and presumed to be of ceremonial function. Known examples range in length from less than 100m to c.10km.

A camp providing accommodation for members of the Canadian Forestry Corps along with facilities such as saw mills for the sawing and squaring of timber to create pit props, shoring, crates etc for the war effort.
A hillfort enclosure with defences composed of more than one bank and ditch.
Fairground attraction containing a number of ghoulish displays designed to scare visitors.
A dockside crane with a solid curving jib made out of rivetted iron plates.
A site where canvas, coarse, unbleached cloth, made from hemp or flax, was manufactured.
A coastal site producing salt by dissolving rocksalt or other impure salt in seawater, then boiling the concentrated brine in a PANHOUSE
Castles constructed between 1481 and 1561 for defence using heavy guns.
A rudimentary roofed building found in school playgrounds, open at the side. Used as a shelter from bad weather.
A factory for the manufacture of military tanks.
A crude, stone built structure, often roofless, used by tin miners to store equipment.
A landing circle marked out in white used as the airfield symbol.
A space used for the storage of chemicals.
Use only where evidence is specific, ie. copper/tin alloy. For working of copper based alloys of unknown composition use COPPER WORKING SITE.
A factory where glue is produced.

A building within a complex, such as a leisure centre, school, industrial site etc, often containing toilet and washing facilities, where individuals can change their clothes. For a changing room within a larger building, see Components.
A building used to pump sewage from the sewers to the filter beds of a sewage works.
A lock, often containing a fish ladder, which allows fish to swim upstream bypassing a weir or other obstacle.
A site where iron is smelted or iron goods made.
A building used as a headquarters and reporting centre for an Army, Navy or Air Force Group.
Engineering works specializing in the production and maintenance of non-passenger carrying railway rolling stock.
A building housing a beam engine.
A rustic building of picturesque design.
1st World War end-opening aeroplane hangar.
A building which provides the centralized market for trading in stocks and shares and for raising capital for industry.
A factory where preserved food is canned.
A stone set up on a road or path to mark the miles from or to a place.
A site used for the production of dyes from controlled chemical reactions. In use from the mid 19th century onwards.
A boarding or day school for children who had committed minor crimes or who lived in circumstances where they were likely to commit crime.
A pond with underwater arches where the poles for masts were stored to prevent them from drying and splitting.
A site where an army or body of troops is, temporarily or permanently, lodged, with or without entrenchments and fortifications.
A hard level roadway or other surface from which aircraft take off and land.

An educational institution, introduced in the 1960s. Distinguished from universities by traditionally training technicians in business, industry and commerce for an immediate local area, and offering more part-time classes, etc.
A steel framed transportable hangar similar in construction to Type T2 but about half the size. Designed in 1941 and 1942.
A factory used for the industrial manufacture of firelighters.
A tall wooden pole used to support telegraph wires.
Use for miniaturized monument type. Index with actual monument type where possible.
A factory where cheese is produced and processed.
A place of worship for Primitive Methodists, a group who were formed in Staffordshire and influenced by American evangelical ideas and who left the Methodists in 1811.
A factory where pianos are manufactured.
A bridge, often over a canal or road, allowing access between two parcels of land.
Reheating of iron from a finery, for rolling or slitting.
A site, often in a woodland clearing, used for the production of pure carbon by the controlled burning of wood and other organic materials.

Accommodation used as an alternative to the workhouse following several Poor Law Acts. Modelled on continental examples and first erected at the end of the 1860s, it is based on the idea of a "village" of small houses accommodating a small group.
A room with special ventilation used for the slow drying of foodstuffs.
A purpose built section of path linking two sections of a canal enabling a horse to be led over or around an obstacle such as a hill. Horse paths predate towpath tunnels.
A type of textile mill found in Lancashire in the 19th century. Small businesses paid the owner rent for space for their machines, and power from the mill engine or waterwheel.
A place of worship for followers of the Wesleyan Association. This group split from the Methodists in 1836 and were separate until joining the Methodist Reform Church in 1857.

A two-storey, structure with a brick ground floor and a reinforced concrete upper floor with balcony and large windows to the watch office and control room. This became the most common building design for air traffic control in the Second World War.
An area of land, heavily though not totally covered with trees, set aside for the royal hunt by Norman and Plantagenet kings.
The residence of a vicar, parson or rector.
A factory for the production of plastics by chemical processes.
Production of smokeless domestic fuel by roasting anthracite in a type of kiln.
An indoor alley for playing bowls or skittles.
A stable associated with a horse-drawn tramway system.
A chemical works engaged in the production of Ammonium Nitrate, used as a fertilizer or for use in the explosives industry.
A machine used to raise and move water and other liquids, compress gases etc. and powered by a steam engine.
Purpose-built housing for railway workers.
A mill with machinery used to cut slabs of metal into rods, or thin sections, for use in nail making or wire drawing.
A Very High Frequency device to allow aircraft to pinpoint their position as an aid to naviagation. Built as part of the Rotor programme.
A firm beach or foreshore used for landing and loading of ships and other vessels. In more recent times hards have been reinforced with concrete.
A factory where glue is produced.
A building used for meetings and other events by Scouts Associations.
Use broader site type where known
A quarry for the extraction of Serpentine, a major metamorphic mineral which is easily polished and easily carved. A major variety, lizardite, is found in Cornwall.
A detached subordinate building. Use specific type where known, eg. DAIRY.
A large, level structure, usually of stone or timber, built alongside water to allow warships to moor for the loading and unloading of guns.

Type of furnace used in the glass industry to pre-heat glass in crucibles, prior to the main melt. This may have been a separtate structure, or may have been part of the main furnace. All periods from the Roman onwards.
A laundry attached to a hospital.
Large covered spaces where the steel plate used for ship construction was cut and marked out, prior to being craned onto the hull, etc.
The residence of a lacemaker.
A library where books may be consulted but not taken away.
A site where the magnetic signature of ships was lowered thereby making them less susceptible to magnetic mines.
For chemical processes making nylon, rayon, etc.
A building used by labourers who clean and pump the docks, and in general, assist shipwrights.
An enclosure of stakes driven into the ground, sometimes for defensive purposes.
A specialist hospital for the medical treatment of patients suffering from epilepsy. Originally epilepsy was seen as a mental illness.
A prepared area of ground, featuring a 'mini' golf course with obstacles, used to undertake the leisure pursuit of miniature golf or 'crazy golf'. Often popular at seaside resorts.
A place in which turpentine is produced.
A passageway or lane between buildings.
A workshop used for the small-scale production of leather goods.
An area of a port, dock or harbour where cargo vessels can load and unload large storage containers. May include a rail terminal for containers which have been transported to the port by rail.
A licenced establishment where wine and other alcoholic drinks are sold for drinking on the premises.
A place in which the artillery is encamped or collected together.
A factory for the assembly of bicycles.
A building in which goods or items are stored. Use more specific type where known.
A monument consisting of parallel lines of spaced post- holes which appears to mark out an approach to another monument or monuments.
A building or buildings used for the manufacture of all types of wax.
A pit or tank containing chemicals for the preserving of animal hide.
A bookbinding workshop.
Pond, created specifically for providing power to water-powered forges, blast furnaces, helve or other hammers.
A chemical works engaged in the production or refining of toluene, a substance extracted from coal tar or specific types of crude oil, and used in the production of explosives during WW1.
A ventilating fan house with an expanding chimney.
A specialist hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of foot disorders and diseases.
A WWII structure designed to project sheets of flame across an area such as a beach, the sea or a road, to hinder attacking forces.
A site where barytes (barium sulphate) is mined. Barytes is also commonly worked from the waste tips of lead mines.
A jettied house where the overhanging upper storey runs along the entire length of one side.
A rectilinear ritual enclosure of Iron Age date
A mill for grinding ochre for the paint making process.
A plot of land longer than it is wide, can include any structures on it. Typical of medieval towns.
A dwelling-house with outbuildings and land assigned to its use.
A building, usually part of a complex, where medical treatment and hospital facilities are provided.
A type of pavilion sometimes found in public parks or country house estates.
An area or site used for the landing and take-off of aircraft, often including associated buildings, equipment and other installations.
A prepared area of cleared ground on which an aircraft could make an emergency landing.
A form of lock on a river, which increased the depth upstream and had a gated opening.
Small scale enterprise producing bricks but not at the same site as the extraction of clay.
A place in which turpentine is produced.
A factory manufacturing electrical cables.
A pen or enclosure used for containing sheep.

A human constructed underwater structure, usually built to promote marine life in areas with a generally featureless eas bed but have also been built to control erosion, block ship passage, or improve surfing.
A building housing material used to explain the significance of a site or landscape to the public e. g. an archaeological site or nature reserve.
A step or ramp in the bank of a canal to enable horses to climb out of the water.
A church, usually found in East Anglia, of early Medieval and/or Medieval date with attached or detached round tower.
Two or more adjacent locks where the upper gates of one lock serve as the lower gates of the next.
A long bed planted with mixed shrubs, usually found near the house.
A workshop used for the manufacture of clay tobacco pipes.
A factory or plant for the manufacture of ice using mechanized refrigeration techniques.
An area used for the training of personnel in civil defence procedures.
A centre for the teaching of crafts.
