A tower in which shot is made from molten lead poured through sieves at top and falling into water at bottom.
A cast iron post similar to a lamp post, with revolving top to carry either coloured plates, or an oil lamp with coloured glass at night. Associated with canal or river navigation locks.
A hostel for packhorse teamsters.
A residence of two or three monks of the Cluniac order dependent on an English mother house.
A court, usually with only 2 walls, used for playing pelota and its variants.
A telegraph pole, tree trunk or similar erected on the side of a road, or in an open space, to prevent the landing of hostile aircraft
A building situated next to a horse racing course with facilities for participants and spectators.
A building with first aid facilities to deal with accidents and other medical emergencies.
A place where stone is dressed or shaped for use in building, etc.
A building used in the Second World War to co-ordinate action against enemy air raids.
A place where boats are stored.
A stock exchange dealing in the prices for coal and shares in coal production.
A centre in which the public donate blood that will be used for the care of patients in hospitals.
A pit filled with rocks and metal, designed to be fired with an explosive charge.
A place of worship for followers of the Countess of Huntingdon's Connexion, a Calvinistic Methodist sect founded in the 1740s by Selina Hastings, Countess of Huntingdon.
A bridge which is fortified at one or both ends.
A stall where eels, either raw or cooked, are sold.
A supply of water used to keep canals that were vulnerable to water shortage topped up.
A coastal battery used for delivering fire at long distance thus forcing a warship threatening or bombarding shore installations to withdraw out of range.
A custodial institution for offenders below the legal age of responsibility.
A type of pottery kiln in which air rises up inside the oven to be forced back down and out through the base of the oven.
A factory where carpets are manufactured.
A kitchen set up, specifically during World War Two, to serve food to members of the public, especially families whose homes had succumbed to enemy bombing.
A place where dead animals are buried.
A slate situated at the end of a terrace for a coal company employee to wake the miners for their shift. The slate had the time of the shifts written on it.
Second World War defence work usually consisting of securinng points for a boom defence, associated gun, and searchlight, emplacements
A circular range of houses dating from the 18th century, eg. John Wood's Circus at Bath.
A non-vertical kiln where the shaft and burning zone is horizontal to the ground thereby allowing material to be fed in.

A prefabricated structure consisting of sectional timber framed units that were bolted together. The structure was clad with Canadian Cedar weatherboarding and had a roof of corrugated asbestos. They were used as temporary accommodation on airfields.
An abbey or priory of Cluniac nuns.
A vertical shaft, usually with an internal ladder, allowing access to a sewer or underground counduit for inspection and maintenance.
A factory or works used for the production of turpentine, wood alcohol and similar chemicals by the distillation of pulped wood.
A small building built over the end of a water conduit or spring.
An apparatus used for the process of condensing: the conversion of vapour into a liquid.
A specialist hospital where water treatment is given to patients suffering from muscular-skeletal complaints, etc.
A structure used to test the aerodynamics of aircraft or vehicles.
A mechanism through which crude coal gas is passed to remove any impurities eg Ammonia and Sulphur.
An early form of castle consisting of a flat-top steep-sided earthen mound, supporting a wooden tower, and a bailey.

Ditches interrupted by wide, regular causeways. Each section of ditch is about 30-40m long, and each causeway is 10-15m wide. In some cases, a network of fields has been created. Found mainly in the South East of England.
A room used primarily for storing food and drink.
A fighter satellite station watch office built to Air Ministry design drawing number 14383/40.
A building or set of rooms, primarily of the 18th century, in which social gatherings and balls were held.
The residence of a marsh keeper.
Factory making slippers.
An industrial site or building where the machinery is powered by a steam engine.
A two-storey watch office, built to Air Ministry drawing number 1959/34. It became the standard design for watch offices with a large, almost square, ground plan with a central observation tower.

Medieval Fenland ditched field system where the land is divided into strips for agricultural production. The strips are separated by hand-dug wide shallow drainage ditches with the spoil thrown up to create a dryer ridge.
A temporary brick and timber watch office based on the all-timber 2423/39. Built after 1941 on many Operational Training Unit airfields the design was superseded by 8936/40.
A place from which chalk is extracted.
A large scale works for cloth finishing processes.
A shed for storing fishing bait.
A small building housing a mechanism used for winding a cable.
Building housing apparatus for testing chain links.
An aisled timber or masonry hall, serving as the chief administrative public meeting centre and law courts for a Roman town. Usually located alongside the forum.
A calciner dating from the early 17th to early 20th centuries, usually made of brick and without moving parts, consisting of a reverberatory furnace, and used for the extraction of arsenic.
An office for the payment of wages, especially in industrial or commercial complexes.
A hall associated with a church, used for holding functions, meetings and for conducting parish business.
An underground structure for the storage of mineral oil.
A factory producing drabbet, a type of linen cloth.
A round hut, similar to a CHARCOAL BURNERS HUT, associated with forest industry. The bark was later used in the tanning process.
The residence of a dock worker.
Site used for the maintenance of aircraft.
Mill incorporating water-powered hammers for beating brass sheet, etc. into vessels, pots, etc.
A railway which runs beneath the surface of the ground, eg. the London Underground Railway.
A tower used as a watch tower by the coastguard. Often, though not always, built as part of a Coastguard Station.
A building or site where phosphorous-based fertilizers are produced by controlled chemical reactions.
A building used to coordinate movement of railway engines and rolling stock in the event of war.
An engine in which a vertical piston rod supplies energy via a crankshaft directly to the flywheel suspended above the cylinder. Extensively used as mine winding engines.
Railway constructed specifically for the movement of coal around the pithead of a coal mine.
A single storey mill used in the textile industry.
In Roman architecture either 1. A block of buildings enclosed by four streets or 2. A large tenement house or apartment block.
A building, administered by the Navy, Army and Air Force Institutes, providing retail and leisure services to members of the armed forces.
A charity school, usually housed in an almshouse.
A site where the process of combing, the preparatory process for long wools, takes place.
A man-made ridge to carry a railway across a declivity or area subject to flooding.
An iron, stone or concrete tower built up from the bed of a reservoir. From it the control valves of the pipes which draw off water at different levels are operated.

A large hilltop or hillslope enclosure in South West England, located close to rock outcrops, and surrounded by one or more circuits of stone built walls. All are prehistoric; some are definitely Neolithic.
A two storied open fronted structure comprising a cattle or cart shelter on the ground floor with a hayloft above. Most common in South West England.
A piece of prepared ground on which the game of polo is played.
An administrative building used by the official in charge of a dock or harbour.
A temporary fence of boards, often enclosing a building on which posters and bills are attached.
An excavation open to the sky, caused by the extraction of coal, stone or similar. Use with product type where known.
The residence of an employee with the duty of maintaining a section of a railway or road.

A large communal room often occupying the full height of the building, used for functions such as meetings, entertainments etc. Traditionally found in medieval buildings but also found in later buildings emulating medieval architecture.
A place where jockeys are accomodated.
A building containing machinery for operating sluices.
Where several minerals produced, use with other products and MINE, eg. ARSENIC MINE.
Engineering workshop intended either for final adjustments of new machinery or the fitting of replacement parts to machinery under repair.
A type of pavilion sometimes found in public parks or country house estates.
A hospital where people with learning difficulties receive medical treatment.
skos:Concept.skos:prefLabel: Hospital For People With Learning Difficulties

skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: A school serving or supported by a parish. Usually teaching religious as well as conventional education.

A square pillbox with walls up to 48in thick, designed to emplace a 2 pounder anti-tank gun. A large opening in the back allowed the gun to be wheeled into position at the large embrasure in the front wall. Designed by DFW branch 3.
An area or route marked out for the site of a race.
Office used by a Piermaster.
A place where soup and food is available to the homeless.
A small, industrially manufactured, air raid shelter, designed to be used inside buildings and to provide cover for nightwatchmen or firewatchers remaining on site during air raids.
Model village built as a holiday resort.
A grain grinding mill in which the meal is ground into flour between revolving metal rolls.
A holding on a smaller-scale than an ordinary farm.
An area of ground immediately surrounding a cathedral.
An establishment used to serve ice cream to the general public.
A building used for the crystallization process in alum making.

A small dispersal WWII military aircraft hangar featuring an "A" shaped steel frame clad with corrugated iron; end doors were supported by outriggers when open.Typically used on aircraft storage units or satellite landing grounds. Variations in size.
A building housing an economizer, a machine designed to preheat water for boilers.
A movable bridge lifted at one end by chains or ropes either to stop traffic passing over it or to let traffic pass under it.
Trading premises of a carter.
A pit where bears were housed for baiting and entertainment purposes. If not used for baiting use BEAR ENCLOSURE.
An ancilliary workshop used for repairs, etc.
A structure used to dry turf on. Turves were used as a fuel and as a roofing material.
A mill for producing abravive papers and cloths such as glass paper or emery cloth.
A place where students live, sometimes on a college campus.
A place where vehicles can be filled up with petrol, oil, water, etc.
Cubes of solid concrete, usually with sides of 3 feet 6 inches or 5 feet which when placed in rows were intended to form a substantial barrier to enemy armoured divisions in the event of invasion.
A place where perfume is sold, as well as manufactured.
A place where boats are built and stored.
A civil and administrative area incorporating a town of medieval origin.
A building in which wool or cotton were beaten to clean and separate the fibres.
A place where weapons are kept.
A box in which letters are deposited on delivery.
A monastic cattle ranch with associated buildings, paddocks and pastures.
An establishment for the preparation and selling of food to be consumed off the premises.
The space enclosed between the gates and side-walls of a lock.
A workshop used for completing the shape of a product or part by turning on a lathe or wheel.
A plant incorporating a range of ore processing operations such as buddles.
The masonry beneath a lock gate, sometimes projecting several feet from the gate.
A canal that can accommodate ocean-going ships, usually built across an isthmus or to give access to a river port e.g. Manchester ship canal
A centre where treatment and rehabilitation training is given to patients recovering from injuries or accidents.
A commemorative monument to victims of the plague.
A large house dating from the 16th century onwards, built as a symbol of the wealth and status of the owner but not intended to be defensible unlike the castles and manor houses it replaced.
A two-storey watch office, built to Air Ministry drawing number 1959/34 but with slight design modifications as detailed in drawing number 1960/34.
A mill manufacturing bobbins for the textile industry.
A building occupied by the corps responsible for police and disciplinary duties in the armed forces.

A building used by the Royal Observer Corps as a headquarters and reporting centre. It may also fulfil an observation and nuclear fallout monitoring role. Use term to describe headquarters for plotting and monitoring nuclear fallout.
A modern building in which the load is carried by a reinforced concrete framework. Use for reinforced concrete buildings.
An outlying farm or estate belonging to the Cluniac order.
A mine from which potash is obtained. Potash is a deposit of potassium carbonate: the only example of a potash mine in the country is at Boulby in Cleveland.
A building or site where boat sails are manufactured from processed cloth.
A building used for storing tree bark.
Grinding mill for producing dyes and pigments from natural materials.
A hillfort enclosure with defences composed of more than one bank and ditch.
A building, site or container used to store the bones of the dead after they have been removed from graves to allow new burials.
A site where tanks and armoured fighting vehicles can be stored.

A stone faced earth bank, usually with a concave batter, and with the base the same width as its height and the top half the width of the base. Vegetation usually grows out of the top. Found mainly in Cornwall, but also elsewhere in the Atlantic Arc.
Traditionally, the hall of a crafts, trade, or merchants' guild. Nowadays, often used to describe a TOWN HALL.

A type of temporary military hutting used throughout WWII constructed of brick in 'stretcher bond' 4.5 inches thick with a light steel truss roof usually covered with corrugated asbestos sheeting. Used for accommodation, as gyms, training huts etc.
A place where umber or oxide of iron and manganese, is extracted from an open cast mine.
An area of land, roughly shaped like a polygon and enclosed by a boundary ditch, bank, wall, palisade or similar barrier.
The highest judicial court where appeals can be heard and whose rulings are not subject to further review by another court.
A monument consisting of an area enclosed by a ditch, bank, wall, palisade or similar barrier, where the barrier follows an almost rectangular course.
A hospital for convalescents or consumptives.
An early form of lead furnace, set upon a hilltop or crest to utilize winds in smelting.

A type of large permanent military aircraft hangar with a curved steel frame and storage annexes on its side used in World War II. It was intended for storage purposes on Aircraft Storage Unit stations.
A building where tallow is produced, ie. solid animal fat that has been separated by heating, usually for making candles.
A road or street covered with small, rounded cobble stones.
A building used for the crystallization process in alum making.
Roman coastal forts fortified with large walls and a ditch, introduced to cope with raids from across the English Channel and North Sea.
An underground cell, usually hidden and accessed only through a trapdoor, in which a prisoner was confined and then allegedly forgotten about.
An underground cell, or group of cells, used for imprisonment.
An 18th century garden with a Chinese layout and ornaments.
A prepared piece of ground on which the game of Petanque is played.
A textile mill where thread undergoes the processes of twisting and doubling to provide material strong enough to be spun and woven.
A form of inhumation in which the skeleton is laid out in an approximately straight line, whether face up, face down, or on its side.
A factory used for the manufacture and assembly of lorries.
A steel framed seaplane hangar designed for Royal Navy Air Stations by the admiralty in 1917-1918.
A building adjoining a cricket pitch with facilities for players and spectators.
The gate of a sluice which can be opened or shut to let out or retain the water.
a wooden, metal or stone post used to tether a horse, or other animals.
A 20th century feature found in public parks and seaside resorts. The face of the clock is planted with low-growing flowers and plants, while the moving hands are covered with small foliage.
A structure for the storage of brine prior to processing, by evaporation, to extract salt.
A basin or harbour, which is open to the tides. Vessels can only enter and leave at high tide and are stranded at low tide.
A boiling vessel used in the direct boiling process, or the sleeching process, used for the manufacture of salt. For evaporating features associated with SOLAR and PARTIAL SOLAR sites use SALT POND.
A furnace used for melting metals for casting or for heating shot.
An establishment in which prostitution is practiced.
Ordnance, expended or otherwise, weapons, armour, personal effects, transport wreckage, or ship wreckage, left behind on the site of a terrestrial or naval battle.

A club often with a dance floor or small stage and featuring entertainment generally of an improvisational, satirical, or topical nature which can be watched by the clientele whilst they drink and dine.

A trench dug through topsoil in an arable field in order to extract underlying clay which was then spread on the field and ploughed in to improve soil fertility. Usually found in peaty soil areas such as the Lincolnshire and Cambridgeshire fenlands.
A site used for the extraction of metallic zinc by a variety of processes.
A building housing a board organized to protect the interests of commerce.
Area feature visible as an earthwork or cropmark with no known function.
A round hut, similar to a CHARCOAL BURNERS HUT, associated with forest industry. The bark was later used in the tanning process.
A stone-faced enclosure, with entrance closed by a floatable caisson or by gates, which can be pumped dry for inspection, maintenance, or repair of the hull or underwater fittings of a ship or ships.

A wall within a lead mine surrounding a dressing floor, where waste from mining and smelting is deposited, to protect livestock from entering and consuming contaminated material and becoming poisoned, or 'bellanded'.
A building or site for the industrial manufacture of locks.
A small structure providing cover and protected accommodation for a sentry.
A system of artificial or natural drains and ditches used to drain off surplus water.
A factory or group of buildings used for the production of plated goods. Plating is the process whereby one metal object is coated with a thin layer of another metal.
A cottage erected over a short period of time, by people who had no legal right to the land. Squatters were often tolerated by the landlord as they provided cheap labour.

Headquarters buildings on military airfields for administrative purposes housing offices, lecture rooms and in some cases a library and a meteorological office. On smaller airfields it is called Station Offices. Abbreviation SQH.
A room used for the ritual cleaning of the body prior to burial
A place where stained glass is manufactured, traditionally for church windows.
A factory producing drabbet, a type of linen cloth.
A component of another building, often a house, used for storing nets.
A building or buildings used for the production of paints, varnishes, colours and distemper.
The residence of a chauffeur or driver
An artificial paved bank or solid landing place built parallel to, or projecting out from, the shoreline to serve in the loading and unloading of vessels.
A lock or a dam in a river.
A large stone used by cattle to rub up against and so scratch themselves.

skos:Concept.skos:prefLabel: Coast Defence Chain Home Low Station
skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: A radar station with sets operating on a wavelenght of 1.5m established to provide radar plotting of both shipping and aircraft movements.
A large room or building at a school used for assembly and other activities.
Engine driving a continuous wire rope for the haulage of tubs in a mine and at the heapstead.
A mound in excess of 150 metres in diameter, of Late Neolithic date and presumed ritual function, eg. Silbury Hill.
A natural flow or current of water issuing from a source.
For chemical processes making nylon, rayon, etc.
A building used by the church to promote Christianity through lectures, study, etc.
A plant used for the manufacture of tubes and tubing, from wrought iron or steel.

A small prefabricated, reinforced concrete structure manufactured by Messrs Orlit Ltd for the Royal Observer Corps. The first were ordered in 1951, most were redundant by 1955, a few remained in use in eastern England until 1965.
A building used for the storage of fish.
A parterre consisting of square beds containing ornamental plants often laid out in intricate patterns mimicking embroidery.
The administrative office of a transport company who provide a service for the conveyance and transportation of either goods or people.
A tall, polygonal structure with ornamental roofs at each storey which is associated with Buddhist temples; the style was adapted for secular eyecatchers and pavilions in the 18th century in England.
A winch powered by a steam engine.
A plant where freshly mined coal was washed down and any dust removed before loading for transport away from the colliery.

A building complex, usually including kennels and cages and built close to a port or airport, in which animals can be securely held, for a designated period, to ensure that they are not carrying any infectious diseases which could be spread to others.
A type of pavilion sometimes found in public parks or country house estates.
A bridge which takes the towpath across the canal.
A small garden enclosure within a BOSQUET or surrounded by clipped hedges.
A factory complex consisting of PRINTING SHOPS, COLOUR HOUSES, DYE HOUSES, etc, in which patterns are printed onto calico.

Blocks of solid concrete, in the shape of a round bottomed cone usually 2 feet 6 inches across x 2 feet 9 inches high. Buoys were mainly used in road blocks intended to impede enemy movement in the event of invasion.
A CRUCK HOUSE where the cruck blades are truncated and joined by a collar beam, above which is a separate roof construction.
A place where an anti-corrosion coating of zinc is added to iron and steel products to prevent them from rusting.
An area within a hospital where patients with contagious diseases are isolated from the rest of the hospital.
A mine used for the extraction of the mineral Witherite. When secondary mineral, use with term for product, eg. LEAD MINE.
Wind or water-powered mill for land drainage in fens or marshlands.
Buildings and plant used for the extraction and purification of arsenic oxide into various forms of pure arsenic.
A WWII structure designed to project sheets of flame across an area such as a beach, the sea or a road, to hinder attacking forces.
A friary belonging to the Crutched Friars also known as Crosiers or Fratres.
A temporary kitchen set up in the field providing food for troops. Use with MILITARY CAMP if existence of this is known.
A place provided for leisure-time activities of young people.
A kiln principally used in brick making which gives a continuous operation.
A wall in a flower or kitchen garden, containing conduits or pipes for heating the wall.
An embankment of earth alongside a tramway.
Flats or houses first built by 19th century philanthropic societies as a model to encourage the development of approved working class housing.
Three storey house with a topshop; machinery powered by shafting through the upper floor.
An enclosure surrounded by a wooden stockade. A rare site type of Neolithic date.

A site which is known, or believed to be, where an aircraft crashed. It is an offence to interfere with the wreckage of crashed military aircraft without a licence (Protection of Military Remains Act 1986). Index with AIRCRAFT TYPE where known.
A building or site conducting research into communication techniques for use in the Royal Navy.
A mill for shredding cloth, for use in flock paper, etc.
A small house in which leeches were bred for medical purposes.
19th century school for the daughters of clergymen.
A burial monument, usually of Iron age date, comprising a small square ditched enclosure surrounding a central interment, which may also have been covered by a mound.
A storage rack for sections of steel plate used in the construction of ships.
A sign, situated near a road or bridge, indicating a toll.
A pavilion at the end of a PLEASURE PIER.
An aircraft hangar designed to Air Ministry specification (drawing number 6910/43). Similar in design to the ROBINS AIRCRAFT HANGAR but larger.
An electric fan used for the ventilation of mines.
Mud walled building found on the Solway Plain.
A crane suspended from running rails in the roof of an engineering workshop or similar establishment.
A mill where flax is processed to make linen, thread and yarn.
A Prehistoric monument type in South West England in which a natural boulder is surrounded by a man-made kerb of stones.
A building where advice, counselling and medical treatment is available.
A hospital block where pregnant women are accommodated and receive medical treatment before and after child birth.
A site where millstones have been cut to shape and/or fabricated from smaller pieces of stone.
A road used primarily, but not exclusively, for the rapid transport of military vehicles, equipment and personnel.
A factory manufacturing bearings, including ball bearings for use in precision equipment.
A meeting hall of the verderers, who were the officers appointed to maintain the King's forests.
Smoke generators (also known as smoke pots) were used to create a smoke screen to provide defensive cover for strategic targets
An enclosed area of land of varying size and shape which shows traces of defence.
A hydraulically-powered crane where the jib and windlass are mounted on a central pillar.
A lock at the end of one company's canal where it joins another company's canal.
A works, including an extractive site, producing a clay of high plasticity and firmness, used as a basic raw material for porcelain.
A mechanically operated lift used to transfer rolling stock from one level of track to another.
A factory or works housing machinery used to produce stockings and socks, using mechanized knitting processes.
When secondary product use with major product and MINE, eg. COPPER MINE.
Building housing apparatus for testing chain links.
A component building of an explosives works where cartridges were filled with explosives with the aid of cartridging machines.
A bridge constructed using rockwork to create a craggy, naturalistic appearance. A feature of 18th century rococo gardens and parks.
A complex of purpose-built or adapted buildings used for the maintenance, storage, assembly and control of sea mines and minefields.
An entrance chamber from tide water to basin, with gates at each end and means of pumping up or lowering the level of water to suit.
A garden incorporating features of Moorish-influenced Spanish gardens - water features, patios, benches, walls and compartments, evergreens, etc.
Engineering workshop used for the final assembly of vehicles or structures from parts produced elsewhere in an engineering works.
A building used to accommodate donkeys.

A kiln in which lime is made by calcining limestone. This type of kiln usually consists of a circular bowl surrounded by pennanular banks with a funnel exit on the lower side. They normally survive as an earthwork. Superseded by Flare Kilns.
A factory where biscuits are manufactured.
A type of 18th century public park, with refreshment houses, concert rooms, etc.
A vertical shaft, usually with an internal ladder, allowing access to a sewer or underground counduit for inspection and maintenance.
A place of worship for Sandemanians, a movement founded by John Glass after his expulsion from the Church of Scotland in 1728. It was spread to England by his son-in-law, Robert Sandeman.
A furnace for holding hot steel ingots to equalize their temperature before they are hot-rolled in a steel-making or rolling mill complex.

A prefabricated structure of standard lightweight timber wall sections bolted together. Externally the walls were clad with plasterboard covered with felt. Designed in 1940 for use as barrack accommodation.
The office of the body controlling a harbour and docks.

6 Type DFW 55373s placed in a 3X2 rectangular plan. Each projector was separated by 31-34m. Hardened personnel and ammunition shelters located midway between each projector, but ammunition stored outside the perimeter.
A building or site used for the storage and distribution of the essential logistical requirements of the Royal Navy.
A structure with semaphore arms and/or coloured lights used as a means of warning on railway systems.
Accommodation for the warrener(s) usually located within the boundary of the Rabbit Warren. They also provided a place to store nets, traps and other necessary equipment.
A dwelling built on marshy, boggy or waterlogged land using timber piles driven vertically into the ground to raise the floor above the ground to prevent flooding.

A commercially manufactured air raid shelter, using prefabricated parabolic concrete panels which could be combined to produce any length of shelter.Usually semi-sunken and covered with earth they were mainly used on RAF sites.
A school founded in or before the 16th century, for teaching Latin, later becoming a secondary school teaching languages, history, science, etc.
Small stone hearth set up in a shallow pit. Burns vegetation and coppiced twigs to produce potash.
An institution for the imprisonment of military personnel convicted under military law by a military court.
1st World War end-opening aeroplane hangar.
A soft, marshy garden, often peat-based where water- and peat-loving plants are grown.
A mine from which potash is obtained. Potash is a deposit of potassium carbonate: the only example of a potash mine in the country is at Boulby in Cleveland.
A school established by a charity.
A covered way or passage especially in a cathedral or monastic church, leading east from the cloisters between transept and chapter house.
A simple form of stone slab bridge, particularly associated with South West England.
A site with one or more defensive earthworks, often at a river crossing incorporating natural features which define parts of the curtilage.
Series of machines for mechanically slaking lime. 20th century.
A site where iron oxide and iron sulphates, used as brown pigments, are excavated.
A mine used for the extraction of any hard dark-coloured rock.
A pillbox with walls that have been thickened to protect against shells. Double index with specific type where known.
A pit for the extraction of fullers earth (a hydrous silicate of alumina), which was used for cleansing, and finishing, cloth and wool.
A factory used for the manufacture of screws.
A structure providing protection against the weather at bus stops.
Artificial water channel, usually leading to a mill.
A building or site incorporating equipment used for detecting the presence of enemy aircraft or ships. Radar Stations can also be used to aid aircraft navigation in dark or poor conditions.
A free-standing building with enough space to hang and dry nets.
A room or building used for the storage of fleeces.
A small works used for the production of agricultural tools such as hay rakes.
An area of common grassland in a village used for grazing cattle, recreational purposes, etc.
A pool of water and associated ancillary buildings designed to accommodate sea lions.
Used for the laying out and marking of the smaller parts of a ship prior to construction.
A bridge which is fortified at one or both ends.
A kiln in which stone is burnt as it falls through a heated and slightly inclined steel tube.
A commercial bakery or bread factory. If domestic use BAKEHOUSE.
A 16th century tower for observing tournaments, eg. at royal palaces.
A specially prepared track used for fast motorcycle racing.

Traditionally a building or site where stage coaches were built. Nowadays the term is applied to buildings used for the manufacturing of the body work and furnishings of motor vehicles and railway carriages.
Timber or metal structure consisting of upright and cross members designed to support climbing plants.
A stepped, roadside platform, usually of stone on which a sedan chair was placed to allow the porters to lift the chair without having to bend.
A medieval court for tin miners in Devon and Cornwall.
A pillbox constructed of prefabricated concrete panels. Double index with specific type where known.
An enclosure, usually within a zoo, designed to represent the natural environment for bears, including shelter. For bear baiting enclosures use BEAR PIT.
A radar station with sets operating on a wavelength of 10cm or less. They were highly accurate radars and gave better sea level coverage than the earlier Chain Home Low stations.
A long, narrow, rectangular plot of land used for the manufacture of rope. Usually walled, it may include small buildings and awnings at each end. Often attached to a warehouse.
A garden designed to provide living material for the study of botany and horticulture.
Machinery for raising and lowering men and equipment to and from the surface of a mine.
An entrance chamber from tide water to basin, with gates at each end and means of pumping up or lowering the level of water to suit.
A building used to house railway carriages.
A mill for grinding ochre for the paint making process.
A plastic covered tunnel designed to protect vulnerable plants from the weather and allow vegetables to be grown out of season
A building where motor cycles are assembled.
A hall or chamber in which justice is administered.
A series of arches, linked together, often made out of clipped hedges or trees with the trunks forming the uprights
A factory where tapestries were manufactured.
A bridge that incorporates a span that moves upwards vertically to provide a passageway for navigation.
A textile mill where crepe is manufactured.Crepe is a fine cloth particularly silk or mixture of silk and cotton.
A small artificial pond of water often found in parks and gardens, for decorative purposes.
A site where terracotta, made from weathered clay and grog, was manufactured.
A place where shoes and boots are mended.
A coastal battery constructed at short notice usually mounting a variety of artillery pieces.
A stone or platform on which lumps of ore are manually broken up.
A building, or group of buildings, deliberately designed for rhinos.
A tall wooden pole used to support telegraph wires.
A large wooden gate, positioned at either end of a canal or river lock, equipped with sluices to let water through.
A command post used to direct the guns of an anti aircraft battery.
An obstacle on a golf course constituting a hazard. Usually taking the form of a sand trap or dirt mound.

Regular courtyard farmsteads where the buildings are arranged as two linked ranges to create an L-shape. They can comprise a barn and an attached shelter shed to a cattle yard or an interlinked cattle housing and fodder range.
A complex of buildings and earthworks constructed for the storage of bombs and pyrotechnics.
A factory or works principally engaged in the production of a single base propellant, using nitrocellulose without the addition of nitroglycerine.
A garden maintained for the study and cultivation of plants for medicinal purposes.
A lodging house for apprentices learning a trade or profession. This accommodation was often provided in lieu of wages.
A hospital department for the medical treatment of ear, nose and throat disorders.
A hall, often associated with a synagogue, used for studying the Torah and other religious texts.

A perforated stone basin usually built into the wall of a church on the south side of the altar. Used for carrying away the ablutions (wine and water used to rinse the chalice, and wash the priests hands after communion).
An establishment or building where the breeding and training of birds of prey takes place.
A mechanism through which crude coal gas is passed to remove any impurities eg Ammonia and Sulphur.
A large structure, found at sports stadiums, from where television or radio broadcasts are made of the sporting events.

Area or zone of sea where a battle, skirmish or action was fought between naval ships or warships and privateers. Not to be used for enemy action upon mercantile ships or a sudden strike by mine/torpedo against an enemy warship.
A furnace used for melting metals for casting or for heating shot.
An embanked shute, often stone paved, allowing carts to tip their loads of coal from the road into a storage area.
A Neolithic burial monument comprising a stone-built chamber within a rectangular or trapezoidal earthen mound.
The premises of a coal merchant where coal and other kinds of solid fuel can be bought.
A site where Celestine or Celestite (a SrSO4), originally used in sugar beet refinement, is extracted from an open cast mine.

A late 17th - early 18th century house with a central chimney and fireplaces and a central door on the front; this door opened closely against the fireplaces, leaving a small lobby for access to the rooms.
A road whose upkeep and repair was financed by the exaction of a toll.
A factory for the assembly of bicycles.
A site where terracotta, made from weathered clay and grog, was manufactured.
A building used as a social venue by people interested in, and involved with, the sport of sailing. Often situated by a MARINA.
A building where lace was laid out to dry.
A mechanical structure, consisting of a roller or beam on supports, round which a rope or chain is wound, and used for various purposes, eg. raising a bucket from a well, etc.
A core part of a town or city that has or had a particular set of characteristics; for example an area of high status residences or an area where a particular industry/trade was centred.
A large, rectangular open space at the centre of a Roman town, incorporating public spaces and a market area.
A garden building usually in a secluded spot, resembling a hermit's dwelling and built as a resting place, retreat or viewing point.
A building housing the services of professionals with an expert knowledge of the law such as the offices of solicitors, barristers and lawyers.
A building housing a generator.
Civil building in Cornwall and Devon for assay and sale of tin ingots.
A lighted pillar or LIGHTHOUSE, eg. Dunston Pillar, Lincs., erected in 1751 to guide travellers over the heath.
A storehouse using mechanical means of controlling temperature rather than ice or insulation.
A mill used for the sizing and drying of warp threads before they were wound onto warp beams as part of the power-weaving process.
A house used to accommodate Llamas at a zoo or wildlife park.
A kiln in which the prolonged heating or roasting of materials to drive off water, volatiles and sulphur so that they may be reduced to a powder, was performed.
A building or group of buildings used for the storage and issuing of rations and equipment to an army unit.

6 Type DFW 55373s placed in a 3X2 rectangular plan. Each projector was separated by 31-34m. Hardened personnel and ammunition shelters located midway between each projector, but ammunition stored outside the perimeter.

A hut consisting of a frame of reinforced concrete posts into which panels of either pre cast concrete or corrugated asbestos could be slotted. Designed by the British Concrete Federation during WWII.
A shop where fish and chips are sold.
A building used to store fertilizers.
A three-storey RNAS control tower, incorporating meteorological office on the ground floor and an air watch office on the second floor.
A marker of some form used to delineate a route, especially ones associated with pilgrimages.
An attic workshop for textile manufacture, usually weaving.
A system of stones or wooden obstacles placed close together to impede the advance of enemy forces. Do not use for HILLFORT sites.
A factory used for the manufacture and assembly of lorries.
An early form of railway for the transportation of freight by sleds.
A distinctive, clerestory-roofed building of five 10ft bays, used for the drying, storage and packing of military parachutes and built to Air Ministry drawing number 11137/41.
Scaffolding intended to impede the advance of enemy armoured divisions. Often found in association with "one way" anti tank ditches.
A small, Iron Age/Romano-British enclosed settlement found in South West England.
A workshop or factory where brass articles are made by casting molten material into a mould.
A reinforced concrete structure, usually sited underground, intended to be used by the regional government as an air raid shelter in the event of a nuclear attack.
Fast arterial road with separate carriageways limited to motor vehicles
A furnace used for smelting or re-heating of iron, either for casting or for further working.
Trees planted in an ornamental circle. For earthwork surrounding trees use TREE ENCLOSURE RING.
The residence of a lock-keeper.
A place where manganese ore is extracted. Use with other ores extracted and MINE where relevant.
A large scale works for cloth finishing processes.
Large piston used to operate lifting bridges, lock gates, etc.
A factory where floorcloths are manufactured.
A military base used for training service personnel.
A small gate swinging in a U or V-shaped enclosure, which allows only one person to pass through at a time.
A textile mill where thread undergoes the processes of twisting and doubling to provide material strong enough to be spun and woven.
Machine, frequently horse powered, for mixing raw clay into brick earth.
An enclosure within a bailey which contained a keep and sometimes took the place of a motte.
A building or buildings used for the manufacture of metal boxes or cases.
An engineering workshop, often attached to an engine shed, for the running repairs of operational parts, etc.
A site where the process of combing, the preparatory process for long wools, takes place.

Component part of a mungo and shoddy mill, where non-wool fibres from shredded material are destroyed by either soaking rags in an acid solution or rotating them in drums in a hot acidic gas followed by heat. The result is an all-wool product.
A place where working men could educate themselves through lectures and the use of a reading room with newspapers, etc.

A place of worship for Wesleyan Methodists. This was the original Methodist church from which the other denominations seceded. In 1932 they joined the United Methodists and the Primitive Methodists to form the Methodist church.
A railway station or platform built specifically for the loading and unloading of goods.
A pit used to bury a large number of people who have died, or been killed, either as a result of warfare, epidemics or natural disasters.
An inhumation burial in which the corpse is laid on a wooden bed, often surrounded by a collection of grave-goods. Anglo-Saxon rite of 7th century AD.
A purpose-built factory for more than one occupier (eg. for several different workshops).
A bridge which takes the towpath across the canal.
A department devoted to the curing or correcting of physical deformities.
An engineering site where railway carriages are manufactured.
A structure providing protection against the weather at bus stops.
A military depot where horses were taken and trained for service in the army.
A complex of buildings used for the manufacture of radio valves or similar electronic components.
A school that is directly funded by central government (specifically, the Department for Education) and independent of direct control by local government in England.
A factory used for the manufacture of serge, a heavy woollen cloth.
A building in which engineered metal products are finished and polished.
A garden deliberately planted with white plants and shrubs.
The residence of a Royal Navy or Merchant Navy officer.
A playing area for the game of hockey. May be a grass or artificial surface.
A massive structure designed to transfer canal boats between different canal or river navigations, eg. Anderton boat lift.
An Anglo-Saxon fortified town or other defended site, not necessarily urban.
A mill used for the preparation of Barilla, an ash of burnt seaweed that was used for the production of soda.
A factory where cheese is produced and processed.
A residence used during short visits by an official and attendants of the Knights Templars for administrative purposes on their estates.
A factory where explosives and the components of munitions of all types are brought together for assembly.
Brewery which produces lager
Central two-storeyed tower surmounted by an octagonal glazed control room giving a 360 degree view. Flanked by single-storey wings.
A greenhouse used for growing palms and/or tropical plants.
A cemetery for baptist followers.
A factory used for the industrial manufacture of firelighters.
A shop where fish is sold.
The residence and office of an archdeacon.
A hearth used for the reheating of metal slag to extract further metal.
A shop which sells vegetables and fruit.
A mill used for the manufacture of twilled dress material of worsted with or without a mixture of cotton or silk.
An inn temporarily used for the performance of plays and other public entertainment.

A hospital ward block, completely open on the south side apart from a low railing and sun blind. It was thought beneficial for the recovery of wounded soldiers as well as those with diseases of the chest.
